=== reviewer_1 ===
He et al present a new language-model based protein design method and validate it by designing lysozymes and
chitinases. The paper claims that ORI enables de novo design, but there is no evidence of that in any section. Additionally,
the claims of designing better than natural enzymes have not been rigorously demonstrated. For these reasons, I consider
the paper to be misleading. There are other, perhaps less serious, problems with this paper, but I will focus only on these
two as they make this paper unpublishable.
De novo design:
De novo design means designing "from scratch", without natural templates. This is not done in this paper. The designs are
entirely within the natural sequence families. See Fig1. The median, represented by a dashed line, is at 96% sequence
identity. This is not de novo, but in addition, it's a very timid design. The authors conclude from this that their model is
excellent in designing validated proteins, but all it shows is that the model has memorised wild-type sequences. They then
cut the designs at a threshold of 90%, but this too is not de novo. All their designs are >35% sequence identity to a natural
template that carries out the same reaction. There are other design methods that enable robust design within sequence
families, but they don't and can't claim that they are de novo design methods. The repeated claims on "novelty" and "de
novo" in this paper are simply unfounded.
Designing proteins that are improved relative to natural ones:
The authors report that the lysozyme designs exhibit a 100-fold improvement over hen egg white lysozyme (HEWL). This
sounds impressive, but T4 lysozyme (T4L) is sold by Sigma and advertised as possessing 200-fold improved activity relative
to HEWL. T4L is within the training set and their design may be based on T4L, but the authors don't compare their designs'
activities to it, only relative to the less efficient HEWL. This is, again, simply misleading.
The highlight of the paper is the design of a multifunctional lysozyme/chitinase, which they claim is "entirely novel function
that have never existed before". This sounds impressive, but lysozyme and chitinase exhibit highly related catalytic
mechanisms and similar folds, and natural lysozymes and chitinases exhibit cross reactivities, albeit weaker than their
native activities. So this multifunctionality is entirely not novel and in fact exists in natural families.
To close, I reiterate that the paper suffers from other problems, but the three I briefly remarked on are sufficient to preclude
publication.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This is a very exciting and ambitious paper. The ORI system represents a creative integration of autoregressive language
models (PGM), pre-trained function predictors (USM), and a reinforcement learning loop with wet-lab feedback (RLWF), all
scaffolded around a structured ontology framework. The paper demonstrates the ability to generate proteins with useful
properties—enzyme activity, thermostability, and even multi-enzyme functionality—highlighted by experimental validation of
several sequences that outperform natural enzymes like lysozyme and chitinase. Overall, and the authors make a
compelling case for ORI as a full-stack generative biology system.
That said, to me, there are several areas where the manuscript falls short—particularly in mathematical clarity,
benchmarking, and contextualization with respect to recent generative modeling frameworks. I really think this paper could
benefit from significantly more rigorous comparisons to state-of-the-art models, as well as stronger justification for many of
the modeling decisions made. Below are five major concerns:
1. The mathematical formulation of the model is super vague and inconsistent throughout. The PGM model is described as a
decoder-only autoregressive Transformer (similar to LLaMA), but the training objective, tokenization schema, and prompt
structure are never clearly defined. On page 6 and Figure 1, we see prompts such as <Homo><Oxidoreductase>
<EC:1.1.1.181>..., but how these are tokenized, embedded, and used as prefix context is never precisely described. Is the
ontology token fed at the first position only? How long are the ontology sequences relative to the generated protein tokens?
Moreover, the RLWF formulation in Figure 3 and page 13 is highly condensed. The modified DPO loss used in training is
only given symbolically, and the preference dataset construction lacks clarity around sampling, control baselines, and
reward shaping. I’d strongly recommend the authors formally define the loss functions and generative process in each
phase, perhaps using equations in an appendix, as the current level of abstraction is insufficient for replication.
2. The comparisons to other generative protein models are incomplete and dated. There is no discussion of recent
generative models like DPLM, EvoDiff, DiMA, MeMDLM or AMP-Diffusion, all of which have shown strong performance in
different protein design tasks using diffusion models. Similarly, discrete flow matching models like Dirichlet Flow Matching,
Fisher Flow Matching, Gumbel Softmax Flow Matching are absent—yet these models enable guided, conditional generation
in a way directly comparable to ORI's ontology-conditioned decoding -- these should all be cited. The manuscript suggests
that reinforcement learning is the key innovation, but in reality, most modern generative biology frameworks rely on guided
discrete sampling rather than RL, due to the instability and sample inefficiency of reward-based learning in high-dimensional
sequence space. The authors should at minimum cite these models and explain what advantages, if any, RLWF provides
over guided discrete sampling. Otherwise, I cannot recommend acceptance if the authors don't acknowledge the state-of-
the-art in the field.
3. From my analysis, the experiments lack clear baselines against either modern PLMs or modality-specific generative
models. The only comparisons made are to ProteinMPNN, ESM2, and natural protein statistics? There is no head-to-head
against recent structure-free models like ProteinSGM, ProGen3, PepTune -- all of which can also be used to condition
generation on properties like stability, non-toxicity and other function. Further, for domain-specific baselines, tools like
UniPTM (for PTM prediction), PTM-Mamba, for PTM-aware embedding, and DPAC (for DNA-protein design) offer directly
comparable pipelines. The authors argue that ORI integrates sequence, structure, and function into a single prompt, but they
never show why this yields better results than methods that integrate these features more explicitly (via joint contrastive
training, or structure-conditioned diffusion). I suggest the authors benchmark ORI-generated sequences against outputs from
these domain-specific, particularly on shared tasks.
4. The experimental benchmarks are promising but not comprehensive. This is a big claim, and so the authors should
spend some time optimizing their work. Figures 2–5 show strong wet-lab validation on lysozyme and chitinase targets, but all
results are focused on enzymes with naturally high expression and well-behaved domains. Where are the harder targets?
All experiments are also single-round selections with no comparison to a baseline design tool (i.e., structure-based docking
or traditional motif grafting). Even for thermostability optimization (Figure 4), the authors never compare ORI-designed
proteins to sequences generated by ProteinMPNN or structure-based optimization with Rosetta. I’d recommend testing ORI
on harder problems, kike flexible loops, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), or viral glycoproteins—and benchmarking
against sequence-only models or structure-aware diffusion tools.
5. The literature review focuses almost entirely on highly cited or media-prominent papers (AlphaFold, ProteinMPNN,
ProGen) while omitting many state-of-the-art systems that define the actual technical frontier in generative biology. The
authors cite ProGen1 but not ProGen3 (which introduces functional conditioning), nor ESM-C (contact-aware language
modeling), nor FusOn-pLM (isoform-aware fusion modeling). The omission of Rinalmo and EvoFlow-RNA from the RNA
section is particularly surprising given their state-of-the-art performance. If the claim is that ORI is a general-purpose,
scalable generative system, the authors need to show that it outperforms or meaningfully differs from these prior systems:
and that it wasn’t just trained on more data with better engineering.
In summary, I believe ORI is an exciting and impactful system, but the authors need to be more rigorous in how they
describe, benchmark, and situate it. Without tighter math, stronger comparisons, and more comprehensive experiments, it’s
hard for me to evaluate what’s truly novel versus what’s just larger and better resourced.

=== reviewer_3 ===
The manuscript by Bing He et al. introduces ORI (Ontology Reinforcement Iteration), an AI platform for protein design. The
system takes as input feature requests from users that are interpreted by an agent generating candidates that are filtered and
validated with in-vitro assays. Results are then used to reinforce the generative process until it meets the user requirements.
The manuscript presents a series of three applications illustrating the functionalities and use cases of ORI.
Overall ORI is a valuable tool with promising performances. However, the current presentation has several shortcomings
that could prevent the readers to fully appreciate its potential.
1) The background and literature review in the introduction is incomplete. The idea of using reinforcement learning and
experimental assays as feedback for molecular design is not new (e.g., work of Baker’s group). A comprehensive review of
previous contributions is mandatory to contextualize this work.
2) My next concern follows the previous comment. It is not clear to me what is the main innovation of this work. It would be
important to clarify the contribution. Unless I misunderstood it, it feels more like a software contribution. The ORI platform is a
pipeline integrating multiple tools. Although, each individual component is not conceptually new, their integration in a unified
workflow has value. If such case, it would be eventually interesting to expand the discussion about the integration/use in
experimental labs.
3) Unless I missed it, the manuscript does not provide comparison or benchmark with other software and methods (it brings
us back to my first comment). As such, it is difficult to fully assess the technical advances of ORI. The examples provide in
the results section are interesting but do not replace a complete and rigorous validation of the platform. A large-scale (and
more quantitative) experiment (In contrast to a specific use cases) would also provide more confidence in the generalization
of ORI.
4) The analysis of the case studies presented in the paper could also be refined. Looking at the global sequence and
structure similarity is not sufficient. Further investigations of the designed proteins would help to validate the impact of the
output. For instance, it is not clear if the samples have highly similar active sites or if it could be found in the training data. It
would be important to show that similar result could not be obtained with a classical fragment assembly option, and could
also help to rule out any leak of information (I am assuming it is ok but the manuscript could expand the discussion).
5) In general, I would advise revising the style of writing. Currently, the text uses a lot of unnecessary superlatives that do not
bring anything to the scientific discussion. Some terms should also be more carefully chosen (e.g., in Figure 1, ORI does not
“understand” the needs, maybe “interpret” or another formulation would be preferable), and some statements be better
justified (e.g., on page 4, the authors say that “ORI can predict the optimal sequence and structure” but optimal is a strong
claim that should be proved).

**Reviewer Report**

**Reviewer:** [Redacted]
**Date:** October 26, 2023
**Manuscript Title:** Ontology Reinforcement Iteration (ORI): A Scalable Framework for Functional Protein Engineering

---

### 1. Significance and Novelty
The manuscript presents "Ontology Reinforcement Iteration" (ORI), a framework that integrates ontology-conditioned generative modeling with reinforcement learning from experimental feedback (RLWF). The integration of structured biological ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, EC numbers) as semantic prompts for protein generation is a compelling approach to address the "controllability" gap in current generative protein design. The reported experimental successes—specifically the 100-fold improvement in lysozyme activity and the engineering of a chitinase stable at 85 °C—are impressive and suggest that the framework effectively bridges the gap between computational latent space and wet-lab functional outcomes. The novelty lies in the systematic use of ontologies to constrain the generative process, which provides a more interpretable and modular alternative to standard latent-space conditioning.

### 2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design
The methodology is generally robust. The closed-loop workflow (generation → measurement → reward → update) is well-aligned with current best practices in active learning for protein engineering. 
*   **Strengths:** The use of cell-free expression systems for high-throughput validation is appropriate for the scale of the study. The inclusion of multiple enzyme families (lysozyme, chitinase) demonstrates the generalizability of the framework.
*   **Weaknesses:** The manuscript lacks detail on the "USM" (Universal Surrogate Model) architecture. Given that the RLWF process relies heavily on these models to provide reward signals, the potential for "reward hacking" or overfitting to the surrogate model is high. The authors must clarify how they mitigate the risk of the generative model exploiting artifacts in the USM rather than learning true biological principles.

### 3. Quality and Reproducibility
The experimental results are presented with clear comparative benchmarks (e.g., T4 lysozyme, Hevamine A). However, reproducibility is hindered by the lack of specific details regarding the RL training hyperparameters.
*   **Data Availability:** The manuscript mentions using UniRef90/50 and UniProtKB, but it is unclear if the specific "ontology-conditioned" training set and the trained model weights will be made publicly available. For a study of this nature, the release of the model checkpoints is essential for the community to verify the claims.
*   **Statistical Rigor:** While the authors report median improvements, the sample sizes for experimental validation (e.g., 20 proteins selected for lysozyme assays) are relatively small. The authors should provide error bars representing biological replicates (not just technical replicates) for all activity assays.

### 4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting
The manuscript is well-written and the logic flows clearly from the limitations of current diffusion/flow-matching models to the proposed ORI solution. 
*   **Missing Information:** The "Methods" section is truncated in the provided text, but the full version must explicitly define the "PDA" (Prompt-conditioned Decoding Algorithm) and the specific loss functions used during the RLWF phase. 
*   **Figures:** Figure 3 and 4 are informative, but the authors should include a "failure analysis." What percentage of generated sequences were insoluble or completely inactive? Understanding the "negative" space of the model is as important as the "positive" hits for assessing the true utility of the framework.

### 5. Specific Weaknesses to Address
1.  **Reward Hacking:** The authors claim the USM achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.818. This is a strong correlation, but in RL, models often find "shortcuts" to maximize reward. Please provide a t-SNE or UMAP visualization of the generated sequences versus the training set to demonstrate that the model is not simply collapsing into a narrow region of sequence space that the USM happens to over-predict.
2.  **Baseline Comparisons:** In the thermostability section, the authors compare ORI to ProteinSGM and ProGen3. It is unclear if these baselines were fine-tuned on the same experimental data as ORI. If ORI has access to experimental feedback that the baselines do not, the comparison is biased. Please clarify if the baselines were given the same "active learning" iterations.
3.  **Structural Validation:** While the authors show a TIM-barrel fold for the TX-ME design (Figure 5E), they do not provide experimental structural data (e.g., CD spectroscopy or X-ray/Cryo-EM). Given the claim of "multifunctionality," it is critical to demonstrate that the protein is well-folded and not a molten globule. At minimum, circular dichroism (CD) spectra should be provided for the top-performing variants.
4.  **Ontology Specificity:** The authors state that ontologies are used as prompts. Please provide an ablation study: how does the performance change if the ontology prompts are removed or randomized? This is necessary to prove that the ontology conditioning is actually driving the functional improvements.

### Final Recommendation
The paper is highly promising and fits the scope of *Nature Communications*. Provided the authors address the concerns regarding structural validation, potential reward hacking, and the transparency of the training data/model weights, this work will represent a significant contribution to the field.

=== reviewer_1 ===
Wang et al “DDX5 orchestras…”
Wang et al. explore the role of DDX5 in oocyte development by designing a mouse model specifically targeting DDX5. The
resulting mice are completely sterile. In a series of experiments, they describe the phenotypic alterations observed in DDX5-
deficient oocytes and conduct further investigations to uncover the mechanisms underlying this sterility. DDX5 is found to
interact directly with RNA polymerase II and with a substantial proportion of retrotransposons, and other RNAs, and to
influence nuclear mRNA export and MARDO assembly. The characterization of oocyte development, along with most
molecular analyses, is conducted with high quality, yielding intriguing results. The impact of DDX5 targeting on the
chromatin landscape, as well as the differences between oocytes and mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), is particularly
fascinating and relevant, especially in light of various epigenetic profiling studies also distinguishing the oocyte from any
other cells. However, there are some drawbacks to consider. As DDX5 is a known RNA helicase, the results do not clarify
whether the observed (molecular) phenotypes are associated with other activities of DDX5 or provide any mechanistic
insights.
Minor Comments:
The generation of targeted mice, verification of the knockout, and characterization of oocyte maturation are all carried out
extremely well and are quite interesting. Did the authors verify the normal expression of DDX5 in neighbouring ovarian
tissues or cells, such as follicular and cumulus cells?
The authors conclude that DDX5 interacts directly with RNA polymerase II. However, it is unclear whether the assays
conducted can distinguish between direct interaction with RNA polymerase II and mere co-localization due to DDX5’s
interaction with a broad range of RNAs (or other RNA binding proteins). The manuscript uses various terms for direct
interaction, including direct binding, physical interaction, direct association, and direct functional link. I assume these terms
are intended to convey the same meaning.
While most genes exhibit downregulation, there are also numerous upregulated genes. I assume the expression of
individual genes was normalized to the total amount of RNA?
DDX5 has been previously shown to be an RNA helicase and to interact with several other proteins, including various RNA
binding and RNA modifying enzymes. It may be beneficial for the authors to discuss these findings and their potential
relevance to the molecular phenotypes observed.
Overall, the phenotypic and molecular characterization of DDX5-targeted oocytes is impressive and presents notable data.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This manuscript presents a comprehensive investigation into the critical role of the RNA helicase DDX5 in mammalian
oocyte development. The authors employ a combination of in vivo models, high-throughput sequencing (ATAC-seq, RNA-
seq, RIP-seq), and detailed cellular and molecular assays to demonstrate that DDX5 is a master regulator essential for
female fertility in mice. The identification of DDX5 as a crucial factor in clearing retrotransposon-derived RNAs (LTR, LINE)
is especially interesting because this might be a vital quality control mechanism to maintain transcriptome integrity and
genomic stability during oogenesis. Other interesting findings include DDX5 loss disrupts nuclear mRNA export,
mitochondrial organization, and the assembly/function of the mitochondria-associated ribonucleoprotein domain (MARDO),
leading to premature translation and mRNA depletion. The work contain some novel findings and will be of significant
interest to the fields of reproductive biology, RNA biology, and developmental genetics. However, there are several
questions and points that the authors need to address before the manuscript is ready for publication:
1. How does DDX5 mediate retrotransposon RNA degradation? This is an interesting and important finding in this study but
has not been clearly determined. Although the authors showed some downregulated repeats in WT oocyte overlap with the
upregulated repeats in Ddx5 mutant, the effect of degradation could be indirectly. In Fig 6f, the author showed RIP-seq
results of DDX5 direct binding sites/transcripts. Are these DDX5-bound transcripts downregulated in the Ddx5 mutant? This
might tell us whether DDX5 is likely to be a direct participant of retrotransposon RNA degradation.

figures, the authors also showed week 6 data but the PreF follicle number seemed similar. Could the authors explain why
the PreF returned to the control level in the mutant?

**Reviewer:** [Redacted]
**Manuscript Title:** [Redacted]
**Journal:** Nature Communications

**General Assessment:**
This study investigates the role of the DEAD-box RNA helicase DDX5 in mammalian oogenesis using a conditional knockout (cKO) mouse model. The authors demonstrate that DDX5 is essential for female fertility, with its loss leading to meiotic arrest, aneuploidy, and fertilization failure. The manuscript proposes a tripartite mechanism for DDX5: (1) promoting Pol II-dependent transcription, (2) facilitating the clearance of retrotransposon RNAs, and (3) coordinating mRNA storage via nuclear export and MARDO assembly. The study is ambitious and addresses a significant gap in our understanding of RNA homeostasis during oocyte development. While the findings are compelling and the multi-omics approach is robust, there are specific methodological and conceptual concerns that must be addressed to strengthen the conclusions.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study provides a comprehensive characterization of DDX5 in oocytes, moving beyond its previously established roles in somatic cells. The identification of DDX5 as a "master regulator" that bridges transcriptional and post-transcriptional programs is highly significant for the field of reproductive biology. The novelty lies in the integration of these three distinct regulatory layers, which provides a holistic view of how RNA homeostasis is maintained during the transition from the NSN to the SN stage.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The use of *Gdf9-Cre* and *Zp3-Cre* lines to validate the phenotype is appropriate and standard for oocyte-specific studies. The integration of RNA-seq, RIP-seq, and high-resolution imaging is well-conceived. However, there is a potential confounding factor: the authors attribute the observed phenotypes (e.g., mitochondrial mislocalization, apoptosis) to the loss of DDX5. Given that DDX5 is a global regulator, it is difficult to discern whether these defects are primary consequences of DDX5 loss or secondary effects of the massive transcriptional dysregulation and cellular stress (e.g., ROS accumulation).

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The data appear high-quality, and the use of ERCC spike-ins for RNA-seq normalization is commendable, as it is essential for detecting global transcriptional changes in oocytes. The reproducibility is supported by the use of two independent Cre lines. However, the manuscript lacks sufficient detail on the "low-input RIP-seq" methodology. Given the low RNA content of oocytes, the authors must provide more information on the input material, the specificity of the DDX5 antibody used for immunoprecipitation, and the controls used to ensure the enrichment of retrotransposon RNAs is not an artifact of non-specific binding.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
The manuscript is generally well-written. However, the transition between the three proposed mechanisms (transcription, retrotransposon clearance, and mRNA storage) feels somewhat disjointed. The authors should explicitly discuss how these processes are "interconnected" rather than presenting them as parallel findings. For instance, does the failure in nuclear export (Mechanism 3) contribute to the observed accumulation of retrotransposons (Mechanism 2)?

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
The statistical analyses are generally appropriate. However, for the "Fuzzy clustering" analysis (Fig. 5d), the authors should provide the criteria for cluster assignment and the statistical significance of the differences between control and cKO trajectories. Furthermore, in Figure 7, the quantification of mitochondrial distribution and MARDO assembly requires more rigorous statistical testing (e.g., ANOVA with post-hoc tests) rather than simple t-tests, given the multiple comparisons involved.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Causality of Mitochondrial Defects:** The authors suggest that mitochondrial mislocalization is a direct consequence of DDX5 loss. However, mitochondrial distribution is highly sensitive to the metabolic state of the oocyte. The authors should perform a rescue experiment or provide evidence that the mitochondrial phenotype is not simply a secondary effect of the observed apoptosis or metabolic stress.
*   **Retrotransposon Specificity:** The claim that DDX5 promotes the degradation of retrotransposons is strong. The authors should perform a knockdown of the identified retrotransposons in the cKO background to see if this rescues any of the meiotic or developmental phenotypes. This would provide functional evidence for the mechanism.
*   **Pol II Interaction:** The interaction with RNA Pol II is mentioned in the abstract and introduction but is not sufficiently detailed in the results. The authors should provide co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) data or proximity ligation assays (PLA) to confirm this interaction specifically in the GV oocyte context.
*   **Premature Translation:** The authors claim "premature translation" of unprotected mRNAs. This is a significant claim that requires more direct evidence than just "increased translation activity." A polysome profiling or Ribo-seq experiment in control vs. cKO oocytes would be necessary to confirm that the specific mRNAs stored in MARDOs are indeed being translated prematurely.
*   **Data Availability:** The manuscript must include a clear statement regarding the deposition of raw sequencing data (RNA-seq, RIP-seq) in a public repository (e.g., GEO) with accession numbers provided.

**Conclusion:**
This is a strong study that significantly advances our understanding of oocyte biology. Addressing the mechanistic links between the observed phenotypes and providing more direct evidence for the "premature translation" claim will make this a definitive paper in the field.

=== reviewer_1 ===
- What are the noteworthy results?
In this paper, the authors claim to have developed a new approach that allows simultaneous cell type specific RNA and
proteomic profiling by adapting TurboID. Specific claims include:
1) TURBO ID allows enrichment-via-biotinlyation of both cytosolic RNA and protein.
2) This was validated in an in vitro system (BV2) cells
3) The method is sensitive enough to detect changes in response to a stimulus known to change proteome and
transcriptome (LPS on BV2 cells).
4) The method works in vivo as tested in comparing neurons to astrocytes (comparing to existing benchmark data)
5) They examine mRNA/protein concordance & discordance and report how this pattern differs by cell at the level of GO
terms.
They also generally argue this will be a useful method for biological discoveries in the future.
- Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields?
Being able to simultaneously measure RNA and protein in the same cell type, in vivo, is a potentially transformative
advance. As such, this is a very clever adaptation of existing tools, and a neat proof of concept study comparing two cell
types in the brain. I think it could open up new questions on gene and protein regulation in the brain and represents a nice
body of work potentially suitable for this journal. But, it is a bit fuzzy on what kind of new questions one could ask with it right
now. I have a couple of recommendations below of where they could address that. On the whole, I think it is a quite cool
idea, but it could benefit from a more concrete description of a couple clear use cases.
How does it compare to the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references.
It reminds me a bit of Alice Ting’s Apex-Seq, but since that requires Biotin-Phenol I am not sure it would work in vivo, but it
might be worth comparing this to that a bit in discussion or intro.
- Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed?
For the most part, the work does support the conclusions. But it is a bit unclear where the authors think this new approach
might make impact in the future. For example, this is a rather vague sentence to lead off the discussion: “Measuring
transcriptomic and proteomic levels is important to identify cellular and molecular mechanisms of biology.” The last para of
the discussion also has several similarly vague sentences about the contribution this new method could make. Can the
authors make these sections more concrete?
In general the discussion is a bit of a missed opportunity, as it spends a larger balance of the space restating the findings
and less time on describing that would be done next. Or discussing technical considerations on implementing this. For
example, is this time course of labeling required (something that might be addressed in experiments, see below)?
There is also probably one more set of experiments needed to understand the noise of the method in general (see ‘Is the
Methodology Sound’ section).
- Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? - Do these prohibit publication or require revision?
Overall, I view my comments as requiring revision rather than prohibiting publication.
Figure S7d: TurboID and RiboTag have substantial differences (thousands of DEGs in Figure S10) that are rather
underplayed here. I would recommend a couple of analyses digging into these differences more. Maybe something similar to
what they do in Figure S10?
The authors spend some time on page 8 speculating why the transcriptome and proteome are sometimes discordant. One
additional source of such discordance could simply be cellular compartment: it seems like even in vivo the TURBO-ID is
restricted to the cytoplasm? Yet the transcripts that code for all proteins in the cell (nuclear, mitochondria, etc), are largely
translated in the cytoplasm. So some of the discordance could simply reflect that the mature translated protein ends up
somewhere in the cell where it cannot be readily tagged. Likewise, any excreted proteins might be lost to TurboID labeling
(including potentially Lcn2, which they highlight in their discussion). When the come back discussing discordance on page
10, they do bring up this possibility that it is driven by cellular compartments in part. However, they may wish to revise these
sections, as the different cellular compartments is probably the simplest explanation and should be raised earlier.
The difficulty in interpreting RNA/Protein comparisons is the part of the paper I find the most challenging and that would
make me hesitant to bring the approach into my own lab. Is there anything that could be done informatically to address this?
For example, if they limit the analysis comparing RNA to Protein to the proteins that are in the cytoplasm (potentially by GO),
does the correlation improve between RNA and Protein? Does the ability to use things like protein half lives (or perhaps
codon usage) to predict Protein/RNA discordance improve? And can they start to look at cell differences in RNA/Protein
discordance in a more insightful way if limiting their analysis to proteins that have a better chance of being tagged (i.e., the
cytoplasmic ones)? On the whole, this comparisons seems to be one of the motivating aspects of the paper, so it would be
nice to have some recommendations on how to approach these questions with the current technique. (I appreciate that the
authors also discuss future method changes like removing the NES that might address this experimentally).
- Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
They need to better account for sex in their work (and in future studies, may want to balance for it, though there is clearly no
way to travel back in time to change samples now). For example, in Figure 2i. Did the neuron line samples have more
females than the astrocyte line samples? Otherwise can the authors explain why Xist (a female-only transcript) is a top
gene? Actually, this comes up across several other figures (e.g., Fig S7d, which also shows a lot of Y chromosome genes).
Ah, as I get to discussion, it does seem like the sexes were not well balanced in the experiment. Hmm.. the authors may
wish to flag sex-chromosome derived ‘DEG/DEPs’ as being potential false positives (driven by sex rather than cell type)
with a column in their supplemental tables and explicitly exclude them from volcano plots.
The method would benefit from a more quantitative characterization of the noise, as it is a new method. Did the author
sequence mouse brain samples that did not have the Turbo allele? I agree from the tapestations there is less RNA coming
down without it, but some is still there. Knowing what is in that RNA (and potentially filtering/subtracting it from the true
samples) is important to characterize noise, eliminate sources of false positives in some analyses (e.g., Riboseq vs. their
method) and potentially improve signal to noise in the future. Potentially similar experiments might be done with proteomics
too.
Can the authors address to what extent is it necessary to feed the animals biotin? I assume there is some biotin present in
the cells in vivo regardless. How does signal change with vs. without the added biotin in the diet?
Likewise, is there a relatively cheap and fast way to explore how features of the biotin pulse to the animal change the yield
(like just I.F. or quantifying tape station, streptavidin immunoblot or silver stain) that would give a sense of how much the
timing and magnitude of that pulse needs to be optimized by labs adopting this approach? Or if this is already done in prior
papers, perhaps allude to that in methods.
- Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced?
Yes. The methods were clearly written.
Typos/minor notes:
Should the A be underlined and bolded when defining the acronym for SPARO?
Figure 1l disagrees with the results text on the magnitude of a correlation (.68 vs .83).
Figure 1 legend about 1d: mRNA is usually not visible on a tapestation, just the rRNA.
“Hepacam, Glu, Aqp4, Plpp3, p ≤ 0.05, ≥ 1-fold change” should this be “> 1 log2 fold-change”?
Figure S10: If you calculate a logFC of RNA vs Protein, can you then compare the protein half lives to that? For ‘a’ does
seem to be a relationship between quadrant and protein half life coloration, though it seems to disappear by b and c. Being
able to more directly compare Protein/RNA to half life might have more explanatory power.
I am also confused by the next sentence “Less than 5% of gene products exhibit cell type-specific expression patterns (via >
4-fold enrichment), and as a result, bulk tissue -omics studies cannot completely resolve changes occurring at the level of
individual cell types55,59” I am trying to understand how the first clause of the sentence results in the second clause.
“which is in line with prior studies57–59” can the authors highlight more quantitatively the extent of correlation seen in prior
studies? Is it similar to their .24-27 (Figure S8) Are their bulk results (.47) more comparable in magnitude of correlation to
those prior studies?
This sentence does not make much sense “There are also limited resources to determine which allele of a gene yields a
particular protein isoform.” Aren’t all these mice inbred? And thus homozygous at most alleles?

NCOMMS-25-08576
Simultaneous profiling of native-state proteomes and transcriptomes of neural cell types using proximity labeling
The manuscript by Ramelow et al. outlines the development and application of a novel method for complementary profiling
of cell type-specific proteomes and transcriptomes called “SPARO” (simultaneous protein and RNA -omics). They validate
their approach using a microglial cell line in vitro and then in neurons and astrocytes in vivo using the same mouse lines for
cell type-specific, cytosolic expression of biotin ligase TurboID that they described previously in Rayaprolu et al., 2022,
Nature Communications. The main difference between the work in this manuscript and their previous work is that they
perform both proteomics and transcriptomics to investigate the correlation between mRNA and protein abundances, of which
is a useful analysis to glean insight on post-transcriptional regulatory processes. Owing to the cell type-specificity of their
approach, the authors compare the concordance between neuronal and astrocytic proteomes and transcriptomes. Although
SPARO, in theory, builds upon their previously published work, there are limitations that need to be addressed in order for
them to complete a meaningful assessment of mRNA/protein concordance. As is, the conclusions made from their
mRNA/protein concordance analysis are lackluster and lack experimental validation.
Major criticisms/suggestions:
1. Regarding Fig.1: The drastic difference in TurboID expression between LPS-treated and non-treated BV2 cells is
concerning. Why is the expression in the non-treated cells (as indicated by the V5 immunolabeling in Fig.1c) about half of
that in the LPS-treated cells? The streptavidin labeling is also dramatically different between the LPS-treated and untreated
cells (Fig.1c/Fig.S1a). To be able to compare the LPS-treated and nontreated transcriptomes/proteomes, the level of
cytosolic TurboID expression needs to be similar. Otherwise, differences in mRNA and protein abundances may reflect
differences in the extent of biotinylation/labeling, rather than bona fide differences in expression. In the methods, the authors
outline how they perform median centering of the log2 transformed intensity values to account for variability in TurboID
expression, biotinylated protein abundance, and streptavidin affinity purification efficiency. Given the magnitude of these
differences however, I am not confident that this normalization method is sufficient. For their transcriptomic data analysis, the
authors do not account for this variability. In Fig.1e, the LPS pulldown proteome has almost 20% more proteins than the non-
LPS pulldown proteome. In Fig.1f, the LPS pulldown transcriptome has 58% more mRNAs. Is this reflecting true changes in
protein/mRNA abundances or is it because of differences in the extent of biotinylation/labeling?
2. Regarding Fig.1: Does the 48 h LPS treatment lead to increased expression of TurboID? This needs to be investigated
and taken into consideration when interpreting results. The authors should include immunofluorescent images and
quantification of the V5 and streptavidin labeling of the BV2 control cells and BV2-TurboID cells before and after LPS (or
mock) treatment.
3. Throughout the manuscript, the authors mistakenly attribute what is likely Agilent TapeStation images as “RNA gel
electrophoresis”. The authors need to relabel this (perhaps as “RNA ScreenTape analysis” or something similar) because
the Agilent TapeStation does not use traditional gel electrophoresis, but rather microfluidics. The details are missing in the
methods. The authors state that “high levels of rRNA and mRNA were detected”, but there are no real bands except the 28S
RNA (~4000 nt) and 18S rRNA (~2000 nt) bands in Fig.1d. The authors should perform standard RNA polyacrylamide gel
electrophoresis instead.
4. Overall, validation of their findings is lacking (e.g., LPS treatment experiments in Fig.1 and Fig.S6). Validation (e.g.,
immunofluorescence imaging) is essential.
5. Regarding Fig.1e: The authors find only ~50% overlap between the biotinylated cytosolic proteome and the bulk
proteomes. They say that this is likely because the biotinylated cytosolic proteome doesn’t contain the proteomes of the
nuclear and mitochondrial compartments. The authors should look into this further to back up their claim. Why not subset
their bulk proteome data for cytosolic proteins and then do the comparison? Biotinylation by TurboID requires certain amino
acids to be present in a given protein and accessible. The authors could also determine the extent of the cytosolic proteome
(using annotated datasets) that is captured in the pulldown proteome and check to see which, if any, cytosolic proteins aren’t
being captured.
6. Regarding Fig.3: The authors compare the abundance/enrichment of ribosomal proteins in the cre-only control vs.
astrocyte-TurboID pulldowns and are able to capture 66 RPs and 67 RNA-binding proteins. A more important comparison
would be between the astrocyte-TurboID pulldown and the astrocyte-RiboTag HA IP eluate.
7. Regarding Fig.3: The authors state that “a notable difference between the SPARO and RiboTag transcriptomes is that in
SPARO, TurboID biotinylates 133 proteins that interact with RNA (e.g., ribosomal and RBPs), while the RiboTag approach
labels one ribosomal protein”. To back up their claim, the authors should report how many of these 133 proteins are detected
in the RiboTag IP HA eluates. I would assume that several RBPs will be detected, even without UV crosslinking.
8. Regarding Fig.4: Without whole-cell TurboID expression, mRNA/protein concordance analysis is problematic. A major
point of simultaneous proteomic/transcriptomic profiling is to be able to do this analysis in the first place. With cytosolic
TurboID, even with 2 weeks of labeling, caution and care needs to be taken in interpreting the mRNA/protein concordance
for luminal proteins localized within membrane-bound organelles as well as any protein localized within
double-membrane-bound organelles. The highly discordant genes (mRNA >> protein) related to mitochondria in both astrocytes
and neurons should be validated. Is the observed discordance because these mRNAs are co-translationally imported at the OMM,
and therefore escaping cytosolic biotinylation?
9. Validation of mRNA-protein discordant astrocytic/neuronal markers is lacking.
Minor criticisms/suggestions:
1. The gain should be increased in the silver stain image in Fig.S1c. The figure legend states that “several proteins were
enriched in the BV2-TurboID samples”, but it’s not obvious.
2. The authors mention how assessments of protein/mRNA concordance are confounded by differences in the sensitivity of
LFQ-MS and RNA-sequencing. Did they authors do data-independent acquisition (DIA), which is more sensitive than data-
dependent acquisition (DDA)?
3. In the discussion, the authors mention potential brain region-specific differences. Why do the authors not compare their
data (cortex) with the Soto et al., 2023 dataset (striatum)?

=== reviewer_3 ===
In this manuscript, Ramelow and co-authors present SPARO, a new method to simultaneously measure transcriptomes and
proteomes from living systems. They first benchmark this method against global transcriptomics and global proteomics using
an in vitro model, then go on to apply this method in an in vivo mouse model to simultaneously capture cell-type specific
proteomes and transcriptomes in the brain. From this data, they go on to interrogate protein-mRNA concordance and
discordance across cell types.
I enjoyed reading this manuscript, and I think that this method would be a valuable addition to the scientific community. The
in vivo cell-type specific profiling in particular was quite compelling, and certainly addresses a technological gap. I do,
however, have some questions and concerns that I would like to see addressed prior to recommending for publication. I
acknowledge that there are many points raised below, but I will preface that I am not asking for any additional experiments - I
would just like some clarification on the authors' methodologies and interpretation of the data, the inclusion of some
additional analyses, and more discussion in the main text on the points outlined below.
My major concerns are largely surrounding the in vitro method validation upon which the rest of the work is based, in
particular the technical robustness of both the transcriptomic and proteomic components of the TurboID enrichment method
for SPARO and the MS data acquisition and analysis. Due to these concerns, I also do not think this method would be
suitable for spatial transcriptomics as mentioned in the discussion. Further, due to the bias introduced by TurboID labeling,
I have concerns for SPARO being used to characterize RNA/protein concordance and discordance, although I do recognize
that it could still be very useful for comparing changes in these patterns between conditions and for proposing proteomic or
transcriptomic biomarkers. Below I have outlined these concerns and others, as well as some minor points to be addressed:
1. I appreciate the time the authors took in the introduction to discuss other technologies in this space to highlight current
gaps, however there were two additional methods that I recommend the authors include. The first is CITE-Seq from Illumina,
which allows simultaneous quantitation of transcriptomes and proteins from single cells - I think the differences (and
advantages) of SPARO are quite easy to highlight (limited panel of proteins that can be quantified in CITE-seq, custom
antibody reliance, cost). The other more relevant methods are APEX-seq and CAP-seq (see publications below), which are
other proximity labeling methods that can be used to capture cell-type specific proteomes and transcriptomes using very
similar workflows to SPARO. The main differences are that first, the proximity labeling enzymes used in these methods,
APEX2 and miniSOG, can biotinylate nucleic acids directly like they can biotinylate proteins, which could allow for fewer
false negatives compared to SPARO (although looking at the high correlation between your SPARO transcriptomes and
global transcriptomes, I don’t think this is actually an issue), but also allows harsh washing through the entire enrichment
protocol which could allow for fewer false positives (which I am concerned could be an issue for SPARO). The second major
difference is that these methods require either the addition of hydrogen peroxide (APEX2) or light (miniSOG) to initiate
labeling, therefore they would most likely need to be done ex-vivo (although there are a few in vivo studies for both).
SPARO has a clear advantage here, as the simple biotin labeling allows for non-invasive, live labeling in the intact animal.
a. Fazal, F. M. et al. (2019) Atlas of Subcellular RNA localization revealed by APEX-seq. Cell, 178, 473-490.
b. Padron, A. et al. (2019) Proximity RNA labeling by APEX-seq reveals the organization of translational initiation
complexes and repressive RNA granules. Molecular Cell, 75, 875-887.
c. Li, R. et al. (2022) Metabolic incorporation of electron-rich ribonucleosides enhances APEX-seq for profiling spatially
restricted nascent transcriptome. Cell Chemical Biology, 29, 1218-1231.
d. Wang, P. et al. (2019) Mapping spatial transcriptome with light-activated proximity-dependent RNA labeling.
Nature Chemical Biology, 15, 1110-1119.
2. Why did you choose to carry out the TurboID biotinylation for 24 hours? This is quite excessive to the 10 min labeling time
recommended for in vitro overexpression systems, particularly for the TurboID-NES construct. Yet, I was surprised to see
that the extent of biotinylation observed in the streptavidin blot of whole cell lysates was much lower than what I would have
expected for this long of a labeling period (Supplementary Figure 1a, comparing the biotinylation signal in the +TurboID
samples to the signal from the endogenously biotinylated proteins). Are your TurboID expression levels very low? Also,
does it appear that TurboID expression and thus biotinylation increases with LPS stimulation? If so, what are your thoughts
about this? It would be nice to have the V5 blot shown for the whole-cell lysate blots in addition to the pulldown blots.
3. I am a bit concerned about the efficiency of your pulldown, as there is robust biotinylation shown in the whole cell lysate
(Fig S1a) but very little in the eluate (Fig. 1c, S1c), in the silver it looks like it’s mostly endogenously biotinylated proteins
pulled down? Did you blot your flow through to show that you successfully depleted your whole cell lysate of biotinylated
material? Inefficient capture could explain the low now numbers you see in your MS data.
4. Does Figure 1d really show that you only enrich RNA with proteomic biotinylation? While you do have stronger
enrichment of the two darkest bands (rRNA?) with TurboID labeling, it appears to my eye that RNA of other sizes are
actually more strongly enriched in the non-Turbo samples - definitely not “negligible”, looks like many RNAs could be non-
specifically binding. Had you happened to run RNA sequencing on the TurboID negative samples? If so, how many
transcripts did you detect/quantify compared to TurboID positive samples and how do these compare to the bulk RNA seq
data?
5. I am quite concerned that you only quantify 1455 proteins in your global proteome. Honestly, this is very low and a red
flag, so please explain. For global proteomics, I would expect at least 7000 but up to 9000+ proteins. Only 1038 proteins is
also very low for a TurboID enriched proteome. For TurboID-NES, I would expect detection of at least 3000 but up to 5000+
proteins. I know that you state in your discussion that more sensitive MS approaches are likely to increase the depth of the
proteome, but the numbers you have here are far below what would be expected from a Lumos Tribrid MS instrument.
6. Is the fidelity of the TurboID vs global RNA-seq datasets suspicious given the large apparent bias in the proteomics
results that are claimed to be due to nuclear exclusion? Are there not several nuclear specific RNAs that you would expect
to miss for the same reason (not a leading question, genuinely asking as a non-expert)? Could this very high overlap
between the TurboID and global datasets further suggest that many of these RNAs being detected are ones that are being
non-specifically enriched and not due to the TurboID labeling?
7. Figure 1g is honestly a bit confusing for me. What is this dimensional scaling based off of, intensity as stated in the
legend, or log2FC as stated in the figure? If Log2FC, what is the Log2FC based off of since all four conditions are plotted
separately? How are you dealing with missing values? The default imputation option in MaxQuant is probably not the best
for this type of data. I’m not very familiar with MDS, but assuming I can read this like a PCA, this figure is saying that the
differences in proteins detected by global proteomics is lower than the differences detected by TurboID proteomics, but
opposite for the RNA data? Is there a technical or biological reason that would explain this? Could this also be due to batch
effects? DDA LFQ is very sensitive to technical variability, you discuss this caveat as well as tell readers of more reliable
quantitation methods like TMT or DIA in the discussion. As for this MDS plot, please explain more or remove entirely - as is,
this is not very meaningful. Honestly, showing the correlation between methods and the volcanoes within the methods
comparing the +/- LPS may be sufficient to show that you are successfully detecting the effect of LPS using the different
methods.
8. I saw in the methods that you are using a reference proteome from 5 years ago (and an old version of MaxQuant), which is
quite dated considering how often these reference proteomes get updated. Is this simply when the experiment was
conducted? If not, please justify why you are using this as the reference proteome. Also, does this reference proteome match
with the appropriate reference genome for the RNA-seq data? If there are discrepancies this could explain some of the
differences observed instead of being due to the biology.
9. For Fig. 1h, please explain where the 1455 shared proteins are coming from, because Fig. 1e indicates that only 1232
proteins are shared between the +LPS global and pulldown proteomes. Also, there should be more discussion on why there
is such low correlation in the protein abundances between the pulldown and global proteome datasets - likely, it is not
simply due to the nuclear exclusion of TurboID, but also how many solvent-exposed and sterically-accessible lysines a
protein has to be biotinylated by TurboID, how reactive these lysines are, how well a protein is able to be pulled down, etc. A
protein may be very abundant in the cytosol and highly detected by global proteomics, but if it isn’t capable of being labeled
by TurboID then it will not appear in the pulldown data.
10. For Fig. 1i, please explain where the 12742 shared transcripts are coming from, because Fig. 1f indicates that only
11947 transcripts are shared between the +LPS global and pulldown transcriptomes. Again here, I worry that the high
correlation between the global and pulldown datasets is suggestive that most of the RNA signal is not due to TurboID
enrichment. As discussed in the point above, due to the chemical nature of TurboID labeling, there is a bias in the proteins
enriched which I would expect to also bias the associated RNAs being pulled down.
11. Was the same cell lysis/sample preparation used for the global transcriptomics and the RNA enrichment for SPARO?
If so then it is encouraging that mitochondrial RNAs were only enriched in the global (Supplementary Fig. 2a), this would be
something that supports the TurboID enrichment is actually working for the RNA workflow of SPARO, but again it is
discouraging that you are not depleting nuclear RNAs as well. It is also interesting that you are so strongly enriching
ACACA, which encodes an endogenously biotinylated carboxylase - this is something that we would expect to see enriched
in the protein pulldown but why do you think you are enriching this RNA so strongly? Looking at your GO term enrichment,
are you surprised that the mitochondrial doesn’t come through more strongly, particularly in the non-LPS dataset? Your most
enriched gene sets appear to be cytoplasmic translation and ribosomal terms, not mitochondrial terms. I wonder if you would
have a clearer signal if you used fewer gene sets, and perhaps rolled up into more general subcellular components (e.g.
cytosol, nucleus, mitochondria, etc.)
12. For Supplementary Figure 3, looking at the GO term enrichment, it is not immediately obvious to me that you are more
biased to cytosolic proteins in the pulldown data and enriching more nuclear proteins in the global data. And given the
mitochondrial enrichment you saw in the global RNA data, why do you not see this same signature in the global proteomic
data? Again, I suggest trying to simplify these categories and your signature may become clearer, for example “Haus
complex” and “protein dimerization activity” are not useful terms for me as a reader to reach the same conclusion that you
have stated in the main text.
13. Not necessary but if you happen to have IF data of your TurboID-NES construct in the BV cell line it would be useful to
see so you can show that it is indeed nuclear excluded, and that you have a matching biotinylation pattern.
14. Looking at your methods, it appears that the TurboID transcriptome and proteome enrichments were done separately,
am I interpreting this correctly? I understand that these were both likely done from the same biological sample, but if the
pulldowns were done separately then this adds another source of possible technical variability. In the future, is there any
way that you could do the RNA pulldown first, elute the RNAs in a way that preserves the proteins on bead, apply the
stringent washes for the protein pulldown to the same beads, and on bead digest to elute the peptides?
15. I am by no means an expert in the BV cellular response to LPS, but I do not find the GO term enrichment shown in Fig.
1k, Supplementary Fig. 1g very useful for showing that you clearly enrich an LPS-treatment signature, again because you
used so many gene sets in your analysis. For the RNA data (Fig. 1n, Supplementary Fig. 1j), at least there are at least terms
with “LPS”, is there a reason you think that these are absent in the protein data? Is there perhaps a list of well
validated proteins that are known to be up-regulated/down-regulated in response to LPS treatment that you could highlight on
the volcano plot? I see that you later highlight a few proteins, but is there a more comprehensive list that you could show?
16. For Fig. 1l, the log2FC(+/-LPS) between global and pulldown shared proteins is basically the same as your protein
abundance correlation, which I thought would be higher because you are “controlling” for factors of labeling and pulldown
efficiency in the +/-LPS comparison. It is encouraging that your highest differentially enriched proteins correlate better
between the methods, but how do you explain why so many more proteins were found to be differentially
enriched with the TurboID vs global experiment? Is it possible that the TurboID experiment is detecting not just changes in
protein abundance, but also changes in protein localization? Also, again as a non-expert, would you really expect to enrich
anti-inflammatory markers in the -LPS dataset?
17. I know I am belaboring this point, but does the fact that your RNA Log2FC correlation data is so high compared to the
protein data again suggest that the pulldown is not working the same for the RNA and protein enrichment? For example, are
there not nuclear-specific RNAs that are differentially expressed in response to LPS that you would see biased towards the
global dataset (this is not a leading question, I genuinely don’t know the answer to this)? There really needs to be more
discussion on why the correlation between the methods is so different for RNA vs protein, I am concerned that this may be
due to the RNA data being largely based on non-specific binders and the proteomic data being due to poor enrichment
efficiency. Regarding the transcriptomic robustness, however, I am encouraged by your in vivo data that shows SPARO can
be used to capture cell-type specific transcriptomes, suggesting that there is minimal non-specific binding of RNAs from
other cells in the lysate.
18. For Fig. 2b, there are cells that are positive for biotinylation but negative for the astrocyte marker (S100beta) or neuron
marker (beta III tubulin), do you think these are still astrocytes/neurons (non-expert here) or are you concerned that this other
cell population will convolute the data? Also, again non-expert here, in Supplementary Fig. 4f, to my eye it appears that the
TurboID expression is affecting the gross morphology/distribution pattern shown by the cellular markers in the red channel.
For example, in the Cre-only control, it looks like the astrocyte maker is evenly distributed through the FOV but with TurboID
expression the cells have higher density at the top but are less dense going down the FOV. For the neuron marker, the FOV
for the TurboID expressing samples appear significantly denser than the Cre-only control. Are these differences due to
normal variation or was this differential pattern something that was seen consistently with TurboID expression? I know in the
main text you state that there were no adverse effects on the mice or cellular functions, but it would still be worth noting this
differential pattern post-TurboID labeling if it is consistent.
19. For Supplementary Fig. 5, the astrocyte data is quite compelling and clear, while the neuron data is a bit less clear. I
think this is interesting because what it suggests is that some cell types like astrocytes may be more difficult to purify in large
amounts thus resulting in a weaker signal, and SPARO provides a superior method to obtaining enough signal to clearly
profile this type of cell. The neurons on the other hand appear to be easier to purify and thus obtain enough material for high
neuronal signal (maybe because they’re more abundant/larger?), as SPARO and the cell enrichment give more similar
results of the top 50 genes overall, however SPARO has a clear advantage in having higher specificity as there is clear de-

**Reviewer:** [Redacted]
**Manuscript Title:** Simultaneous Protein and RNA -omics (SPARO)
**Journal:** Nature Communications

**General Assessment:**
The authors present SPARO, a proximity-labeling-based method utilizing TurboID to simultaneously capture cell type-specific transcriptomes and proteomes. The method is applied to both *in vitro* cell lines and *in vivo* mouse models (astrocytes and neurons). The study addresses a significant challenge in systems biology: the decoupling of mRNA and protein abundances in native cellular environments without the confounding effects of mechanical cell isolation. The manuscript is well-written, the experimental design is generally robust, and the data provide a valuable resource for understanding post-transcriptional regulation. However, there are critical concerns regarding the mechanism of RNA capture, the potential for non-specific labeling, and the interpretation of "concordance" that must be addressed.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study is highly significant. Current methods for joint profiling (e.g., RiboTag, TRAP) are limited to ribosome-associated species, while CITE-seq and SPARC are limited by antibody/probe panels. SPARO’s ability to capture a broader range of the transcriptome and proteome in a cell type-specific manner is a notable advancement. The novelty lies in the application of TurboID for dual-omics, which is conceptually sound given the known promiscuity of biotin ligases in capturing RNA-binding proteins (RBPs).

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The use of TurboID-NES and TurboID-noNES is a clever control to assess sub-cellular labeling bias. However, the mechanism of RNA capture remains somewhat opaque. The authors hypothesize that TurboID biotinylates RBPs, which in turn "pull down" associated RNA. While this is a plausible mechanism, the authors should provide evidence (e.g., via RNase treatment of the lysate prior to streptavidin pulldown) to confirm that the RNA recovery is indeed dependent on protein-RNA interactions rather than direct biotinylation of RNA or non-specific adsorption to the beads.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The data quality appears high, with good correlation between replicates. The inclusion of multiple cell types and the comparison with global datasets strengthen the reproducibility of the findings. The use of DIA-MS is appropriate for the depth of proteomic coverage required.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
The manuscript is clearly structured. However, the reporting of the "concordance/discordance" analysis requires more nuance. The authors use a percentile rank transformation to classify pairs. It is essential to clarify whether the observed discordance is a biological reality or an artifact of the different capture efficiencies of the two modalities (RNA-seq vs. MS-based proteomics).

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
The statistical approaches (MDS, GO enrichment, Pearson correlations) are standard and appropriate. However, the authors should address the potential for "batch effects" between the global and pulldown samples, particularly when comparing the two modalities. The use of n=17,998 genes and n=7,333 proteins for correlation analysis is robust, but the authors should explicitly state how they handled missing values in the MS data, as this can significantly bias correlation coefficients.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed:**

*   **Mechanism of RNA Capture:** As noted above, the authors must demonstrate that the RNA captured is truly protein-associated. Please perform a control experiment where the lysate is treated with RNase A/T1 prior to streptavidin enrichment. If the RNA signal persists, the method is not capturing "protein-associated RNA" as claimed, but rather direct biotinylation or non-specific binding.
*   **Normalization of Modalities:** The authors compare mRNA and protein abundances using Pearson correlations. Given that RNA-seq and MS have vastly different dynamic ranges and detection limits, how was the data normalized to make these comparisons valid? Please provide a detailed justification for the normalization strategy used before the percentile rank transformation.
*   **Interpretation of "Discordance":** The authors identify "discordant" genes (e.g., mitochondrial genes). It is well-established that mitochondrial proteins are imported from the cytosol, and their mRNA is often localized to the mitochondrial surface. The authors should discuss whether the observed discordance is a result of the spatial constraints of the TurboID-NES labeling (i.e., the enzyme is excluded from the mitochondrial matrix) rather than true post-transcriptional regulation.
*   **Data Availability:** While the authors mention Supplementary Data files, ensure that all raw mass spectrometry files (e.g., .raw or .mzML) and RNA-seq fastq files are deposited in public repositories (PRIDE/GEO) and that accession numbers are provided in the final version.
*   **Comparison with RiboTag:** The authors argue that RiboTag is limited. To strengthen the paper, a direct comparison (or at least a more detailed discussion) of SPARO vs. RiboTag data in the same cell type would be highly beneficial to demonstrate the "broader" coverage claimed in the introduction.

**Recommendation:**
The manuscript is of high interest and potential impact. Subject to the clarification of the RNA-capture mechanism and a more rigorous discussion of the limitations of cross-modality correlation, I recommend publication.

=== reviewer_1 ===
This study presents an intriguing hypothesis regarding the evolutionary origins of PYL genes, proposing to provide experimental evidence that suggests a bacterial PYL homolog that was transmitted to the plant lineage. However, the central claims of the paper, particularly as stated in the title, are not adequately supported by the presented data. Most of the experimental work essentially reproduces findings from previous studies rather than providing novel insights. Furthermore, the manuscript suffers from substantial clarity issues, with unsupported or misinterpreted claims in the introduction and a presentation of results that obfuscates key conclusions (see specific examples below).

Major Concerns
Query #1:
Functional Characterization of a Bacterial PYL Homolog
A central premise of this study is the identification of a bacterial PYL homolog with ABA-independent activity. However, the assays used fail to assess this function rigorously. The experimental systems either contain endogenous ABA (as in plant-based systems) or rely on overexpression, which can artificially drive protein-protein interactions independent of ligand binding. Notably, even well-characterized ABA-dependent receptors, such as PYL4, exhibit ABA-independent PP2C binding under similar conditions. A more appropriate in vitro approach, where protein concentrations are strictly controlled and ABA is entirely absent, is required to definitively assess ligand dependency.

Query #2:
Horizontal Gene Transfer Hypothesis Lacks Supporting Evidence
The claim of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is presented without substantive support. Establishing HGT in a system that diverged over 600 million years ago is inherently difficult. Yet, the authors fail to explore/roll out alternative evolutionary scenarios, such as convergent evolution, which remain equally plausible. A robust phylogenetic analysis should provide statistical confidence measures and exclude other evolutionary possibilities. If the phylogenetic tree showed plant sequences embedded within bacterial lineages, it could suggest recent gene transfer, but the current analysis lacks the necessary rigor. The arbitrary nature of the sequence relationships as presented does not substantiate the proposed HGT event. While the reviewer is not a bioinformatician, the absence of statistical validation and failure to test alternative hypotheses significantly weaken this claim.

Query #3:
Specific examples:
In the title “….in the seeds of land plants”
The relations described in the study extend beyond seed plants, as the PYL gene family is conserved across the entire lineage of land plants, not just in seed-bearing species. Also the title should explicitly state which functional aspect of PYL receptors has been retained throughout evolution—specifically, their ability to bind PP2C phosphatases.

Query #4:
Furthermore, the claim of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated/conclusion. As such, it should either be removed from the title or clearly framed as a hypothesis rather than a definitive statement. The current phrasing in the title risks misleading readers by presenting an unverified assumption as an established finding.

Query #5:
-Abstract: Has inaccuracies
Examples: Authors claim: “which requires constitutive activation of stress signaling, was mainly adopted by early land plants and persists in seeds.”
This statement is incorrect—ABA levels are crucial for seed dormancy and decrease to allow germination. During dormancy, ABA levels remain high to prevent premature germination. However, for germination to occur, ABA levels must decline (while gibberellins increase).

Query #6:
Authors claim: “Through evolution, the PYR/PYL/RCAR family (PYL) of ABA receptors gained several functions over the course of evolution, namely inhibition of protein phosphatases (PP2Cs), ABA-enhanced inhibition of PP2Cs, and ABA dependent inhibition of PP2Cs”
The only well-established physiological function of PYL receptors is their ability to inhibit PP2C phosphatases, which are central to ABA signaling. If the authors intended to suggest an additional function, they should clarify it and provide supporting evidence.

Query #7:
Authors claim: “However, it remains unclear how the ABA-irresponsive PYLs originated and whether they exist in land plant. “
This statement is incorrect—it has been shown that PYL receptors in land plants likely originated from algal ancestors, and homologous proteins are present across all land plant lineages.
