This manuscript presents a detailed experimental investigation of the temperature evolution of magnon damping in the van der Waals metallic ferromagnet Fe3-xGeTe2. Using inelastic neutron scattering, the authors observe a nonmonotonic temperature dependence of the magnon linewidth, characterized by a minimum at an intermediate temperature (~90 K), with increased damping both at low and high temperatures. This behavior is attributed to the interplay between thermal fluctuations and Kondo screening.
While the experimental data are of good quality, the results appear incremental in the context of extensive prior studies on this material. The key observation, nonmonotonic magnon damping, may be of interest, but it does not in itself constitute a conceptual advance sufficient for publication in a high-impact journal. Similar nonmonotonic behavior of the magnetic relaxation rate has been reported in heavy-fermion compounds as early as the 1980s. For example, Z. Phys. B 77, 95–104 (1989) and J. Magn. Magn. Mater. 74, 341–346 (1988) documented comparable temperature dependencies in Ce-based Kondo lattices. Theoretical interpretations of such behavior were also developed, including in J. Appl. Phys. 57, 3166–3168 (1985) and Phys. Rev. Lett. 54, 230–233 (1985). These precedents are not cited or discussed. If the intended contribution is to provide further evidence of Kondo physics in a 3d-electron system, this point has already been well established through multiple experimental techniques and in prior work by the same group. The manuscript does not make sufficiently clear what genuinely new insight is gained here.
The comparison with the FMKH model is, in my view, fundamentally flawed and overly simplistic. The model lacks direct relevance to the real material, which is a quasi-2D lattice system with multi-orbital degrees of freedom. The minimal 1D model presented here at best can serve as an illustration. It is unjustified to support a quantitative or qualitative comparison with experimental data. If the authors wish to pursue this model further, it would be more appropriate to present those results in a separate work, as has already been done in Ref. 56.

The authors present findings that reveal a role for GPR146 in the prevention of hepatic steatosis. They propose that it is GPR146's role in adipose tissue and lipid metabolism that prevents TG accumulation in the liver. GPCRs represent attractive drug targets and GPR146 has intriguing biology, however, several key questions remain.
If GPR146 KO affects adipogenesis, is that really desirable? The authors show similarities in pattern to the master adipose regulator Pparg and yet knocking out Pparg/disrupting adipogenesis is deleterious on metabolic health, including the liver. Especially since knocking down GPR146 affects hyperplasia (which is the healthier expansion compared to hypertrophy). If the adipose tissue isn’t expanding and the mice eat the same amount of HFD, as shown by the authors, then where is the extra fat going? Finally, if GPR146 affects adipogenesis, why don’t they observe lipodystrophy in the whole body or adipose specific KO?
Regarding the energy expenditure, several questions remain. Is the increase in catabolism that was observed in vivo also present in isolated adipocytes? What is the in vivo energy expenditure profile in the adipose specific KOs? Does the increased energy expenditure persist at thermoneutrality? How about on chow? The authors say the mechanism is not through canonical thermogenic cycles but Adrb3, which they show is up, is the major driver of both Ucp1 and non-Ucp1 dependent thermogenesis. And CL-316,243 does far more than just stimulate lipolysis.
Why do the author’s think that knocking Gpr146 down in cells has an effect when they haven’t added any ligand? Is it known if the ligand for GPR146 is endogenously produced?
All the in vivo findings involve prevention of steatosis because of constitutively expressed genetic models. Inducibly depleting Gpr146 after NAFLD has developed would significantly strengthen the manuscript.

=== reviewer_2 ===
In this manuscript, the authors investigated the regulatory role of the G protein-coupled receptor 146 (GPR146) in adipose tissue and liver lipid metabolism. In an in vivo model, GPR146 deficiency exhibited a protective effect against obesity induced by a high-fat diet, reducing liver steatosis and accompanying a decrease in circulating liver enzyme levels. Global depletion of GPR146 in mice affected energy homeostasis by increasing energy expenditure during high-fat diet feeding. The study revealed that specific depletion of GPR146 in adipocytes in mice could counteract diet-induced fatty liver by limiting the influx of free fatty acids. Additionally, the authors demonstrated that GPR146 deletion in vitro inhibits adipogenesis by blocking the activation of Gαq-PKC AKT signaling.
The subject matter of this study holds considerable significance in the realm of lipid metabolism. Nevertheless, the data outlined in the current version do not entirely substantiate the authors' conclusions. A notable deficiency lies in the absence of a mechanistic explanation detailing how GPR146 influences lipid turnover and adipogenesis. Here are specific comments aimed at potentially enhancing the manuscript.
1. The first question inquires whether the protein expression level of GPR146 is elevated in the adipose tissue of obese individuals compared to non-obese ones.
2. Does the expression level of GPR146 in wild-type mice also increase over time in various adipose tissues (eWAT, ingWAT, and BAT) during HFD feeding?
3. Global depletion of GPR146 in mice, as observed in Fig 2b by MRI measurements, led to an increase in the percentage of lean mass under HFD feeding. However, the data only indicate the percentage of lean mass. Is there an increase in the absolute amount of lean mass as well? Utilizing a whole-body composition analyzer might offer more precise in vivo measurements the mass of body lean, fat, and fluid.
4. Does the protective role of GPR146 deficiency against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity suggest a contrasting effect when GPR146 is up-regulated? The authors should provide or at least discuss the results induced by GPR146 over-expressions.
5. Moreover, the data from GPR146 deficiency do not entirely support the authors' conclusions regarding the promoting effects of GPR146 on adipogenesis. To strengthen this assertion, the author should include data from GPR146 overexpression experiments.
6. The author discussed ATP-consuming futile cycles in whole-body GPR146 deficiency. It raises the question whether similar findings could be observed in mice with adipocyte- or hepatocyte-specific GPR146 deficiency.
7. Since PKC is the endpoint of the proposed GPR146 signaling pathway, in the GPR146 depletion background, inhibition of PKC function by pharmacological reagent alone cannot support the authors' hypothesis that Gαq-PKC-pAkt is downstream of GPR146 signaling.
8. To address the roles of GPR146 in lipid turnover, the authors should provide more functional experiments, instead of just differential expressions analyses.
Minor points:
1. It would be helpful to provide a brief description of G protein-coupled receptors in mediating functional activities of adipose tissues.
2. The image should include a scale bar for reference.
3. Please include the sequences for the siRNA used.

=== reviewer_3 ===
The study by Shi et al. provides a large set of data investigating the effects of GPR146 on liver steatosis and particularly the role of adipocyte GPR146. The authors first describe findings extracted from public GWAS databases indicating association of GPR146 variants with increased plasma liver enzymes and CRP. In the following experiments they show that GPR146 knockout reduces liver steatosis and plasma ALT in mice. Liver metabolomics was used to characterize in more detail effects on lipids. GPR146 knockout also decreased weight gain and fat mass in response to HFD that appears to be related to elevated energy expenditure during resting periods. The authors used tissue specific knockout models to demonstrate that Adipoq-Cre but not Alb-Cre induced knockout alleviated the liver steatosis suggesting that adipocyte GPR146 mediates the steatotic effect. Adipocyte KO of GPR146 also reduced weight gain, fat mass and plasma FFA. In cell models GRP146 was found to promote adipogenesis potentially through Gαq-PCK-AKT pathway. The study is interesting and thorough. However, there are several points of concern:
1. The effect of Adipoq-Cre induced knockout on Grp146 expression in WAT requires further information. At least after 4 months of HFD the effect of the KO on Gpr146 expression appears either limited (ingWAT) or not existing (eWAT) (Extended Figure 7e). Please provide necessary evidence of the effect of Grp146 KO on GPR146 expression in different time points used in the study. The current data raises questions about the mechanisms of the observed effects in Adipoq-KO mice.
2. The authors state in several instances that GRP146 KO ameliorates hepatic inflammation. However, I don’t think any evidence is presented to support this notion. ALT cannot be considered and an inflammation marker. However, indeed it would be necessary to study the role of GPR146 in relation to liver inflammation and fibrosis. Simple HFD model may not be the best for this purpose, but it may require additional factors such as fructose feeding. The authors also reported elevated CRP associated with GPR146 variants in humans. What about in mice? Does the Gpr146 KO affect CRP?
3. The effect on glucose metabolism should be better explained. Do the increased liver hexose metabolites indicate upregulation of hepatic glucose uptake or what is the authors’ interpretation? It is not clear what the authors mean by statement that “GRP146 deficiency promotes glucose mobilization”, page 5 line 9-10. Indeed, glycogen storage was increased.
4. The authors claim that GRP146 KO ameliorates insulin resistance. However, this is not obvious. The KO improves glucose tolerance (fig. 2g) which could suggest better insulin tolerance. However, in ITT the effects can be seen only in late time points when the animals are recovering from the insulin effect. A true difference in insulin sensitivity should be seen in early time points when glucose is decreasing. This is especially obvious in female mice where the effect in ITT is observed only after 90 min (Ex. Fig. 3d) but also to some extent in male mice (Fig 2h). The results rather appear to suggest defects in counter-regulatory mechanisms correcting insulin-induced hypoglycemia. Also, there was no difference in plasma fasting insulin (Ex. Fig. 3e) again suggesting no clear effect on insulin sensitivity. HOMA-IR index, preferably calculated with the mouse modified formula (doi: 10.1177/0023677212473714) could be provided also.
5. The authors provide transcriptomics data suggesting decreased macrophage infiltration in the adipose deposits of the GRP146 KO mice. Is this supported by any other data such as histology?
6. The study includes several types of omics data; however, the full data has not been made available and no repository for data storage has been indicated?

The data are generally well-presented. However, the "AAV-mediated acute depletion" experiment (Fig. 8e) requires further validation. While the reported polarization is potentially significant for the field of ferroelectric oxides, the mechanism underlying this enhancement remains ambiguous. It is crucial to clarify how the multilayer HZO/HLO architecture influences the polarization, especially given that HZO single layers typically exhibit higher remnant polarization than HLO. Furthermore, if the films are composed of alternating HZO and HLO layers, the origin and nature of the in-plane strain should be clearly defined. The manuscript presents a interesting study on achieving near-theoretical polarization in HZO/HLO superlattices, supported by a combination of structural characterization, ferroelectric measurements, and DFT calculations. However, the clarity of the presentation and the robustness of certain experimental claims need significant improvement before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
1. The switching pathways are confusingly introduced. The authors first mention a “conventional T-pathway” and then refer to a “conventional N-pathway,” which is inconsistent with the literature. The definitions of T-path and N-path should be clearly and consistently explained early in the text, with references to prior work (e.g., Wu et al., PRL 2023).
2. The phrase “demonstrating well stabilized the ferroelectric phases” is grammatically incorrect and should be rephrased for clarity.
3. The use of the term “superlattice” is not fully supported by the experimental evidence. The EDX mapping shows a mixture of La, Hf, and Zr, and the authors acknowledge non-uniform La distribution due to resolution limits. This undermines the claim of a well-defined superlattice structure. Additional evidence (e.g., EELS line scans, XRD satellite peaks) is needed to substantiate the superlattice claim.
4. The statement “This work presents the first reported superlattice structure of its kind in HfO₂-based ferroelectric systems” is premature without clearer structural validation.
5. The description of “perfect epitaxial relationship” is an overstatement. Dislocations and imperfections are visible in the TEM images. The language should be tempered to reflect the actual microstructural quality.
6. The yellow lines in Figure 2d obscure structural details at the interface. Replacing them with arrows or dashed lines would improve clarity.
7. The xx and yy directions for strain analysis (Fig. 2e,f) should be clearly labeled in the figure or caption to aid interpretation, especially for non-specialist readers.
8. The GPA results are unusual. The LSMO reference region shows significant strain, which contradicts the assumption of a zero-strain reference. This raises concerns about the validity of the strain analysis. The authors should clarify the reference selection and compare their methodology with established practices in the literature.
9. The Methods section lacks sufficient detail to reproduce the work. Key parameters such as laser fluence, substrate preparation, and characterization details should be described more thoroughly.
10. Figures 3c and 3f present single data points without error bars or statistical validation. Multiple measurements or error estimates are necessary to support the reliability of the endurance and temperature-dependent polarization data.
11. The authors note that reducing layer thickness (increasing interface density) enhances ferroelectricity. It would be valuable to test even thinner layers (e.g., <0.9 nm) to explore the limit of this effect and strengthen the interface-stabilization argument.

**General Comments:**
This manuscript reports on the achievement of high remnant polarization ($P_r \approx 40$ μC/cm²) in epitaxially grown Hf$_{0.5}$Zr$_{0.5}$O$_2$/Hf$_{0.9}$La$_{0.1}$O$_2$ (HZO/HLO) multilayer films. The authors attribute this performance to the stabilization of the ferroelectric orthorhombic phase via in-plane compressive strain and the promotion of an unconventional "T-path" switching mechanism facilitated by La doping. The work addresses a significant challenge in the field of hafnia-based ferroelectrics—the discrepancy between theoretical polarization limits and experimental observations. The study is well-structured, and the combination of epitaxial growth, advanced structural characterization, and DFT-based mechanistic insight is compelling. However, several points regarding the experimental rigor and the interpretation of the "intrinsic" nature of the polarization require clarification before publication.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study is highly significant. By demonstrating a $P_r$ value that approaches the theoretical limit of 70 μC/cm² (along [001]), the authors provide a potential roadmap for overcoming the performance bottlenecks of current HfO$_2$-based devices. The proposal that La doping specifically lowers the energy barrier for the T-path switching mechanism is a novel mechanistic insight that adds value to the current understanding of dopant-induced ferroelectricity.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The experimental design is generally sound. The use of PLD for epitaxial growth on LSMO/STO substrates is appropriate for strain engineering. The comparison between different multilayer periodicities (Supplementary Fig. 6) provides a logical basis for the authors' claims regarding the role of interfaces and strain. However, the methodology for determining the "intrinsic" polarization needs more scrutiny.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility of the Results:**
The structural characterization (STEM, XRD) is of high quality. The use of Geometric Phase Analysis (GPA) to quantify strain is appropriate. However, the reproducibility of the $P_r$ values across multiple samples (beyond the three variations shown in Supplementary Fig. 6) is not explicitly discussed. Given the sensitivity of HZO to growth conditions, providing error bars or a statistical distribution of $P_r$ values from multiple devices/batches would strengthen the claims.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
The manuscript is clearly written. However, the transition from the experimental $P_r$ of 40 μC/cm² to the theoretical 69.3 μC/cm² along [001] relies on a geometric projection factor. The authors should explicitly state the assumed orientation relationship and the specific angle used for this conversion to ensure the reader can verify the calculation.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
The statistical rigor is limited. The endurance test (3×10⁹ cycles) is a single-point measurement. To be considered robust for *Nature Communications*, the authors should provide:
*   A statistical analysis of $P_r$ values across at least 10–20 devices to demonstrate uniformity.
*   A clear definition of the "intrinsic" nature of the polarization. While the temperature-dependent measurements (Fig. 3f) are a good start, they do not fully rule out contributions from trapped charges or defect dipoles, which can also exhibit temperature dependence.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed:**
*   **Defect Chemistry:** The authors mention oxygen vacancies in the DFT section (Fig. 4b) but do not provide experimental evidence (e.g., XPS or EELS quantification) of the oxygen vacancy concentration in their specific films. Given that oxygen vacancies are known to influence switching kinetics, this is a significant omission.
*   **Switching Kinetics:** The claim that the T-path is the dominant mechanism is supported by DFT, but experimental evidence of the switching pathway (e.g., through PUND measurements or switching current transient analysis) is missing. The authors should discuss whether the observed switching speed or coercive field behavior is consistent with the T-path mechanism.
*   **Strain vs. Doping:** The authors attribute the high $P_r$ to both strain and La doping. It is difficult to decouple these effects based on the current data. A control sample of pure HZO with similar strain (if possible) or a systematic variation of La concentration would help isolate the role of the dopant in lowering the T-path barrier.
*   **Clarity on "Rhombohedral-distorted orthorhombic phase":** The terminology is slightly ambiguous. Please clarify if this is a distinct phase or a strained orthorhombic phase. The XRD data should be presented with more detailed peak fitting to justify the phase assignment, particularly to distinguish it from the monoclinic phase.

**Recommendation:**
The manuscript is promising but requires additional experimental evidence to substantiate the mechanistic claims and to provide a more rigorous statistical basis for the reported polarization values. I recommend a major revision to address the points above.

In this manuscript, the authors run a small molecule screen using historical, immortilized glioblastoma cell lines to identify combinations of small molecule + OV to increase the effectiveness of the oncolytic-virotherapy oHSV-GFP. The manuscript identifies a small molecule inhibitor of the protein, LRRK2 which synergizes with the oHSV to specifically target cancer cells with enhance viral infection and oncolysis by attenuating the INF-mediated antiviral effects, specifically through the STAT1 pathway. These results were also demonstrated in mouse models.

Key Results:
LRRK2 inhibitors are well tolerated in human clinical trials to date, are blood-brain barrier penetrant, and reach good cerebrospinal fluid/unbound plasma concentration ratios. In combination with OV to target GBM, they are an attractive therapeutic combination. The MOA is interesting and appears to offer a unique mechanism for direct phosphorylation of the STAT1 which mediates the innate immune response. The results show convincing functional enhancement of OVs in GBM 2D models and in vivo mouse models.

Validity
Drug Screening/Screen Validation
The small molecule screen lacks considerable rigour as the screen reports no quality metrics that I can see, no raw data, and does not describe the normalization techniques. It also reports a “synergistic index” which is poorly defined and is more commonly called the “Combination Index” in cancer applications. LRRK2-IN-1 and other LRRK2 inhibitors s are poorly defined but all which are absolutely necessary to determine the quality of the compound/prob being used. Although the screen did validate in 6-cell lines, the statement “the results suggest that LRRK2-IN-1 is a broad sensitizer for oHSV in vitro” is premature. Patient derived GBM cells, including the treatment refractory glioma stem cells, are now readily available from repositories around the world at relatively low costs. These could/should also be tested to acquire nearer tumour results.

Viral Spread, oncolysis and apopotosis
Please describe Figure 3 E/F in more detail. Figure G is not quantified but does demonstrate a very large difference between the two cell types suggesting that there is broad range of virus production between cell lines. What is the virus spread and replication in the other cell lines previously test (i.e. – U-118, LN-18, etc)? The statement, “Collectively, LRRK2-IN-1 robustly enhances oHSV replication, spread…” is relatively poorly supported.

LRRK2i enhances the oncolytic activity of oHSV by suppressing antiviral responses
Although substantial supporting data is presented, it is probably more accurate to say STAT1-LRRK2 complexes are pathways are one potential mechanism for oncolytic activity.

Additionally, the mechanism of action is critically important in understanding oncolytic synergistic effects with LRRK2 inhibition. GBM has a strong immunosuppressive microenvironments established most likely from the innate immune cell component of the tumour, including >50% macrophages, microglia and astrocytes. Single cell interactions in the case of GBM, focussing on the cancer cell mechanism in this tumour microenvironment, would be very supportive of the proposed MOA. Here, scRNA transcriptomic of multi-culture organoids, either in vitro, PDX, or patient derived organoids, could support the results.

Immunocompetent GBM mouse model
The points of observation that the conbination treatment in enhanced viral replication and increase tumour cell apopotosis (Figure 7 H and I) are not supported empirically. Please quantify these results. These are links to in vivo results so are crucial to the conclusions for this section.

LRRK2 abundance in human GBM
Although it is encouraging that LRRK2 inhibition does not appear to target healthy astrocytes, macrophages and microgia, as well a neurons (all could be iPSC derived) and tested to interrogate all cell types found in primary and recurrent GBM.

Significance
The use of cell lines for screening are often an economically valid step as it considerably reduces experimental costs however, more complex and predictive models are now widely available using multicell organoids and patient derived organoid techniques. ### 1. Significance and Novelty
The study addresses a critical clinical limitation of current hyperkalemia therapies: the "counterion paradox," where the release of Na+ or other ions to facilitate K+ binding can exacerbate hypertension or metabolic comorbidities. The conceptual framework of using an antioxidant to trigger structural reconfiguration of a crystalline framework for ion sequestration is highly innovative and bridges materials science with clinical pharmacology. If reproducible, this represents a significant advancement in the field of gut-restricted therapeutic materials.

### 2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design
The experimental design is generally robust, utilizing both mechanistic characterization (DFT, XRD, XRF) and physiological validation in three distinct animal models (healthy, amiloride-induced, and 5/6 nephrectomy).
*   **Mechanism:** The use of DFT and spectroscopic analysis to support the "reduction-induced" hypothesis is compelling.
*   **Animal Models:** The selection of models is appropriate for testing the hypothesis that the material avoids the Na+-loading associated with SZC.
*   **Methodological Concern:** The preparation of "PB+VC" involves incubating PB with VC and then washing the pellet. The authors state that "VC component and its oxidation products dissolve in aqueous solution, yielding a final product consisting primarily of K+-adsorbed PB." This is a major point of ambiguity. If the VC is washed away, how does the *in vivo* reduction occur? Is the material "pre-reduced" or does the residual VC in the gut lumen drive the reaction? The manuscript must clarify the state of the material at the time of ingestion.

### 3. Quality and Reproducibility
The data presented are internally consistent. However, the reproducibility of the "in vivo reduction" mechanism is difficult to assess without more detailed kinetic data. The authors claim the strategy mimics electrochemical reduction; they should provide evidence of the redox state of the PB *after* transit through the GI tract to confirm that the reduction is indeed occurring *in vivo* as hypothesized.

### 4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting
*   **Terminology:** The term "metal counterion-free" is used throughout. While the material does not release Na+, it is technically an ion-adsorption process. The authors should be precise about whether any other ions (e.g., H+) are exchanged to maintain electroneutrality.
*   **Figures:** The figures are high quality, but Figure 1a (the schematic) is overly simplistic. A more detailed diagram showing the proposed lattice reconfiguration and the specific role of VC in the gut environment would improve clarity.

### 5. Statistical Rigor
The statistical analysis (ANOVA followed by post-hoc tests) is appropriate for the animal studies. However, the sample sizes for the animal models (n=3-6 per group) are on the lower end for a study claiming clinical paradigm-shifting potential. Power calculations or justification for these sample sizes should be included.

### 6. Specific Weaknesses to Address
*   **The "Wash" Paradox:** The Methods section states the PB+VC is washed three times before lyophilization. If the VC is washed away, the mechanism of *in vivo* reduction is unclear. Does the patient ingest the supernatant, or is the material simply "activated" PB? If the latter, the authors must demonstrate that the "activated" state is stable during storage and transit to the colon.
*   **Electroneutrality:** If K+ is adsorbed without a counterion release, the material must be gaining a negative charge or releasing a cation (e.g., H+). Therefore, it is unclear how the authors achieve SHG, Raman Stokes cascades, and cross-phase modulation (XPM) via the Kerr effect simultaneously within the same GRIN MMF. The manuscript should clearly explain the physical mechanisms and nonlinear processes involved, especially how SHG is realized in such a system. If SHG occurs through special means—such as surface-induced symmetry breaking, quasi-phase matching, or use of non-silica dopants—those conditions and techniques must be explicitly detailed and justified.
As the authors are aware, beam self-cleaning (BSC) in multimode fibers is a well-established nonlinear phenomenon that has been extensively studied in the literature. It is generally understood within the framework of four-wave mixing (FWM), nonlinear mode coupling, and optical thermalization processes. In light of this, the manuscript should clarify how the proposed XPM-induced BSC fits within or deviates from this established theoretical framework. Specifically, the authors should elaborate on whether the observed effects are a novel manifestation of existing BSC mechanisms or represent a fundamentally new regime. A more rigorous theoretical discussion, possibly comparing the dynamics and physical conditions of XPM-induced BSC with traditional FWM- and thermalization-driven models, would be necessary and valuable for positioning this work within the broader context of nonlinear multimode optics.

1. In high-power nonlinear regimes, energy transfer can critically affect the modal power balance of the SH beam, and this needs to be rigorously ruled out to support the core assumption of purely optically induced mode coupling (OIMC).
2. On the Nature of the Mode Power Distribution in Figure 2(c): The power distribution of the SH modes shown in Figure 2(c) appears unusually smooth, which raises the question of whether it represents a single-shot measurement or an averaged statistical result. === reviewer_1 ===
The discovery and characterization of bacterial defense systems are under extensive investigation. In this study, Zhou, Wei, and colleagues characterized the Upx nuclease, revealing a unique dual-nuclease architecture. As shown by biochemical and structural analysis, Upx contains two nuclease active sites: a classical C-terminal PD-(D/E)XK nuclease (CTD) and an atypical N-terminal PD-(D/E)XK nuclease (NTD). Functional analyses show that the CTD can cleave both ssDNA and ssRNA, whereas the NTD is specific for ssDNA. The authors further reported the cryo-EM structure of apo Upx, providing structural insights into the active site features of both NTD and CTD. Additionally, Upx harbors a middle domain (MD) that differentially regulates its nuclease activities—stimulating CTD while inhibiting NTD. While these findings are intriguing, additional experiments are required to fully elucidate the mechanism of Upx function
1. The authors demonstrate that Upx confers antiphage activity against ФV-1 infection but not against T6, Mu, P1, SP, T1, or vB phages. The authors should provide additional experimental evidence and analyses to clarify the mechanism underlying Upx-mediated phage resistance. Specifically, does ФV-1 possess a replication or transcription mode distinct from other phages that can be specifically targeted by the dual nucleases?
2. The authors claim that both CTD and NTD exhibit sequence-independent 3’-5’ exonuclease activity based on electrophoresis gel analyses. However, further experiments are needed to validate this conclusion:
(1) the degradation pattern of 5’-labeled ssDNA/ssRNA substrates suggests the presence of defined cleavage bands rather than a progressive degradation pattern typical of exonucleases.
(2) the observed degradation products appear longer than single nucleotides. To clarify exonuclease activity, the authors should analyze cleavage products using both 5’- and 3’-labeled DNA/RNA substrates. If Upx functions as a true 3’-5’ exonuclease, only single-nucleotide products should be detected with 3’-labeled substrates. In Supplementary Figure 5d, the substrate appears resistant to cleavage by Upx and its domains, suggesting additional substrate requirements.
(3) The authors should include DNA/RNA length markers in their gel analyses to accurately determine the length of cleavage products.
(4) The authors should further investigate CTD/NTD cleavage using substrates of varying lengths and sequence compositions to define nuclease sequence specificity and cleavage-site preferences.
(5) In Figure 4c, the labeled product should be "ssRNA fragments" rather than "ssRNA fragment."
3. In Supplementary Figure 2, class 1, 2, and 4 reconstructions contain additional densities adjacent to the NTD-MD-CTD region. The authors performed local refinement to obtain a high-resolution structure of Upx; however, these additional densities should not be disregarded. It is important to determine whether these densities correspond to Upx dimerization or oligomerization, co-purified substrates or potential interacting partners. A more detailed and careful structural analysis could provide valuable insights into Upx function.
4. The most intriguing finding of this study is that Upx contains two distinct nuclease active sites—one constitutively active CTD and one autoinhibited NTD. However, key mechanistic questions remain unresolved. Is NTD activity essential for antiphage defense? A loss-of-function assay targeting NTD activity would help clarify its role. Second, the mechanism of NTD activation remains elusive. Further analysis is needed to elucidate how NTD is activated. While the authors tested several substrates in Supplementary Figure 5, the precise physiological substrate of Upx remains unknown. Given its substrate preference for ssRNA/ssDNA, one possibility is that Upx targets transcriptional R-loops, which contain both ssRNA and ssDNA.

=== reviewer_2 ===
In their manuscript “Structural and Mechanistic Insights into the Dual-nuclease domain Defense 1 Protein as a Single-Molecule Anti-Phage System”, Zhou and colleagues report a cryo-EM structure of Upx. The structure shows that the protein has the previously identified PD-(D/E)XK domain at the C-terminus, a middle domain, and a PD-(D/E)XK like N-terminal domain, with a reduced number of beta sheets. The authors also report that the N-terminal domain has nuclease activity against single stranded DNA, and that the nuclease activity of the N- and C-terminal domains is controlled by the middle domain. The structures and their interpretation are satisfactory, but unfortunately, the structures provide little insight on how the anti-phage defense works, and how the specificity arises.
Criticisms:
• The authors report the experimental result that Upx28 provides defense against phage ФV-1 infection as a novel result. However, it was already known from prior work that the Upx28 defends against a relatively narrow spectrum of phages that includes ФV-1 (Gao et al., Science 2020).
• The identification of the N-terminal domain as a nuclease domain lacks controls. Since the authors have identified the active site, they should make inactive mutants to prove that the reported nuclease activity is not due to a protein contaminant.
• All evidence indicates that ФV-1 has a double stranded DNA genome. It therefore remains unclear what the ssDNA directed exonucleolytic activity of the N-terminal domain is directed against.
• The transition from the nuclease-inactive conformation with middle domain mediated autoinhibition to an active conformation is presumably triggered by proteins of the phage (this may also explain the narrow spectrum of targeted phages. For the manuscript to have the impact required for Nature Comm., the authors would have to identify the trigger that converts the inactive to an active nuclease, and would have to explain how this change occurs.
In summary, the manuscript contains a cryo-EM structure and some biochemical data that could be a starting point for a more complete story on how the anti-phage protein Upx actually works, but at this point, the story is too incomplete to permit biological insight into how the anti-phage defense system actually works.

=== reviewer_3 ===
In this manuscript, the authors provide a biochemical study of Upx, which they term DNDP. Using Cryo-EM and biochemical experiments, they define a second nuclease domain of Upx/DNDP, and provide preliminary evidence to suggest that the middle domain regulates the N-terminal and C-terminal nucleases. While exciting, the results feel incomplete. For Nature Communications, some additional data should be presented to validate the significance of the structural and biochemical work. The authors should not need to present a complete mechanism for Upx/DNDP for acceptance, but at current the manscript falls short of the standard of others published in this journal (a great example is https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58540-9 and https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-57397-2 where structural, biochemical, and in vivo microbiological experiments were integrated to give a fuller picture of antiviral function). For this reason, I suggest the manuscript should be rejected or subject to major revisions to address several critical issues:
1. The importance of biochemical results for phage defense is not examined. The authors identify several residues that are required for DNDP function and interactions between different domains which appear to regulate activity of different DNDP domains. None of these constructs are tested in the in vivo phage defense assay shown in Figure 1, which is critical to understanding whether different activities of DNDP are important for antiviral restriction. In particular, the importance of the NTD and interactions between MD and the NTD/CTD in defense against phage would be deeply interesting.
2. The authors assert that DNDP is a nonspecific 3ʹ exonuclease that targets ssDNA and perhaps ssRNA. Their data reveal several potentially important aspects of the protein – a second nuclease domain (NTD), and a regulatory middle domain. In their different biochemical analyses, the enzyme appears to degrade substrates to a variety of different extents, and is most active at full-length. Given that DNDP seems to inhibit only very specific phages, the authors should more carefully examine its mechanism and the relative importance and role of different aspects of the structure they have discovered. Using DNA-seq or RNA-seq to examine activity of Upx/DNDP or its mutants in vivo would help address the importance of their biochemical results. Alternatively, using additional DNA and RNA substrates in vitro and quantitatively assessing those which are most preferred by the enzyme would help define the most important substrates. DNA or RNA degradation timecourses may also be helpful for confirming a nonspecific exonuclease activity.
3. The importance/conservation of variant PD(D/E)XK nucleases like the NTD is touched on in the supplement. The authors should confirm they are descended from the PD(D/E)XK family using topology diagrams and/or structural trees (e.g. via foldseek). Further, they should consider showing that diverse homologs of these enzymes are functional by cloning/testing other potential phage defense systems containing these variant domains.
Minor points:
1. The authors state that the Upx gene was cloned from S. enterica NCTC6026. The original Upx system identified in Gao et al., 2020 was from E. coli NCTC8620. The authors should provide the exact Refseq accession or sequence of their cloned construct. It would appear that the gene cloned in this experiment matches at the protein level quite closely to the original Gao et al construct (judging by the sequence in the validation report). In the Gao et al., 2020 paper, Bacteriophage P1 was strongly restricted, but no P1 restriction is reported in this manuscript. It would be useful to clarify this point – is the construct the same?
2. The authors state their construct is cloned into pBAD, and is thus presumably arabinose inducible. Was induction used in the experiments?
3. Line 129-130: “These findings suggest the function of DNDP may be conserved across a large number of bacterial species.” How so? A single phage was restricted. Without more evidence (e.g. conservation of DNDP in different bacterial groups, etc), remove this statement.
4. Fig 4B: A single band is evident after NTD cleavage. What is this product? Could this indicate function as an endonuclease under certain circumstances?
5. Figure 3C: Error, “ssDNA fragment” should be ssRNA. Text states RNA oligo is 30 nt, but figure says 56 nt.
6. Figure 3D: Legend states the gel is representing dsDNA cleavage experiments, but the data figure appears to concern metal dependence of the CTD. Please fix legend. Text references 3D to provide dsDNA cleavage data. Include data in figures.
7. Figure 3D: Level of activity is low compared to data in 3B. Why?

The experimental workflow is logical, moving from bioinformatics to structural biology, biochemistry, and finally, in vivo validation. However, there are concerns regarding the "direct immunity" vs. "abortive infection" classification. The authors conclude Upx provides direct immunity based on growth at varying MOIs (Fig. 7c). While this is a standard proxy, it is not definitive. To strengthen this claim, the authors should perform a single-cell infection assay or a plaque-forming unit (PFU) efficiency of plating (EOP) assay to demonstrate that individual cells survive and produce progeny, rather than relying solely on bulk growth curves.

The manuscript is generally well-written. However, the description of the "noncanonical, basal exonuclease activity" of the NTD needs more precise definition. Is it truly noncanonical, or does it simply lack the canonical PD-(D/E)-XK motif? The authors should clarify the sequence alignment of the NTD catalytic core compared to known PD-(D/E)-XK members to justify the "noncanonical" label.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**

=== reviewer_1 ===
The manuscript “Defining expansions and perturbations to the RNA polymerase III transcriptome and epitranscriptome by modified direct RNA nanopore sequencing” by Verstraten et al. implements a new method, which the authors define as DRAP3R (Direct read and analysis of Polymerase III transcribed RNAs), which essentially depletes non-poly(U) RNAs and ligates poly(U)-targeting adapters, thereby targeting Pol III-derived ncRNAs, which possess 3’-oligo(U) sequences owing to the oligoT termination mechanism of Pol III transcription. The major strengths of the current study are (1) the direct sequencing of Pol III-derived RNA species, which provides some level of investigation regarding the chemical modifications of these oligo(U) RNAs - a major focus of the study - and (2) discovery of novel Pol III-derived RNAs. The authors also use the DRAP3R framework to query changes in tRNA levels and pseudouridine stoichiometry following infection. The implementation of this method and the expansion beyond currently annotated Pol III-transcribed genes are valuable contributions that are certain to be of interest across the Pol III field and beyond. However, there are notable concerns with the chemical modification (“epitranscriptome”) aspect of the current study that should be addressed, primarily with respect to the sparsity of in vitro transcribed, non-modified RNA species, which appear to be a critical requirement for interpreting all epitranscriptome results.
For example, Figure 2C is our first introduction to inferred pseudouridine stoichiometry of in vitro transcribed 7SK RNA – it was surprising to see such a high level of peudouridine stoichiometry for non-endogenous RNA, can the authors explain this? While the manuscript notes that filtering reduces false positive rates, it suggests that in vitro transcribed RNA is needed for each and every RNA species in order to interpret modification state. This is also the case for m6A methylation, shown for 7SK in Supplemental Figure S4a, and for the only other RNA species with IVT - EBER2 (Supplemental Figure S4c,d). In addition to this apparent technical challenge, there is a general lack of statistical analysis, such that it remains difficult to interpret. For example, we are told that filtering of IVT false positives facilitates identification of modification state, but what statistical framework was applied to achieve this result? Naturally, these are critically important for interpreting the broader analyses focused on RNA modification - for example, are in vitro transcribed tRNAs not necessary for interpreting the results of Figure 3b (and supplemental Figure S6)? There are then a number of stoichiometry count and density analyses layered on top of this that are difficult to interpret. For example, on the basis of evidence provided for in vitro transcribed 7SK and EBER1, it is possible that analyses and interpretations have more to do with uridine or adenosine densities rather than any true endogenous modification states.
In the event that the technical challenges noted above cannot be addressed, I would reiterate that direct capture and sequencing of oligo(U) ncRNAs and discovery of novel (potentially) Pol III products is significant, and the authors might consider reworking their study to emphasize these findings more prominently.
Major points:
There is a significant assumption that analyses are tied to nascent RNAs in the absence of any method to specifically isolate or enrich for nascent RNA. Though tRNAs undergo 3’ cleavage, other Pol III-derived RNA species are not processed in the same manner, and thus oligo(U) alone is not sufficient to describe an RNA molecule as nascent.
From the opposite perspective, the authors likely do not capture any mature or charged tRNA molecules, and thus all modification aspects related to the full dynamic pool of tRNAs is lost using this approach.
A statistical framework is necessary to interpret “highly confident modification sites”
There is no evidence provided in Figure 4 to support the claim that pre-tRNA levels are increasing while pseudouridine stoichiometries is decreasing upon HSV-1 infection. Projecting colors onto a correlation plot is not sufficient, instead a differential analysis is needed to draw “differential”-related conclusions. Though a volcano plot is provided in Supplemental Figure S7, we are not provided any details of what genes are up- and down-regulated.
Minor points:
Figure 1b:The average read length for PolyA+ RNA seems to be abnormally short in length, can the authors explain?
Figure 1c, the legend color of the virus RNA does not appear to match.
Supplemental S1e is missing a legend.
Figure S2c, pol II-specific inhibitor can be used to verify that the novel transcripts are Pol III transcribed; the authors might also consider using ML-60218 for Pol III-specific inhibition
Figure 3a, Why is RNY4 listed separately from other Y RNAs? It might help to group together and label each YRNA. In addition, specific RNA species are missing from this - perhaps most notable absent is 7SL (one of the most abundant Pol III transcripts). Can the authors comment on why 7SL was not captured (beyond the description in line 286)
Figure 3b,c,f are missing legends (we are to assume it’s the same as 3a).
Figure 4a. Given that samples are sequenced on individual minIons, how do the authors account for potential batch effects? This might be of particular concern if the libraries were sequenced at very different times, with potential for differences in minION batch and/or pore integrities. Overall, it is again difficult to “differential conclusions” drawn from single replicate comparisons, which the authors appear to be doing with respect to uninfected and infected samples.

=== reviewer_3 ===
Verstraten et al. present DRAP3R, a nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) methodology tailored for analyzing Pol III transcripts, leveraging their characteristic poly(U) tails. The approach involves depletion steps, a custom adapter, and specific analysis strategies to identify transcripts and modifications like Ψ and m6A. The authors validate the method, identify novel transcripts, and apply it to study changes during HSV-1 infection. The data hint at some interesting changes to pol III transcript (relative) abundances and modification profiles upon HSV infectoin, but this would require the analysis of further biological samples to firm up conclusions.
Major Comments
- Could the authors provide empirical evidence, perhaps via supplementary data, to demonstrate the specific advantages gained from the poly(A) and rRNA depletion steps, particularly given the use of a custom adapter designed for target enrichment? Quantifying the impact of these depletions on the yield and specificity of Pol III transcript capture would strengthen the methodological justification.
- The method's reliance on a 3' poly(U) tract means it may be biased against Pol III transcripts with non-canonical termini (e.g., resulting from imperfect termination). A discussion of this limitation, ideally supported by comparative data (e.g., using polyadenylation-based capture on the same polyA and rRNA depleted RNA), is warranted to assess the comprehensiveness of the captured transcriptome.
- Further justification is required for the chosen alignment parameters. Beyond increasing the percentage of aligned reads (Sup Fig 1c), how was the accuracy of these alignments confirmed, particularly considering the potential for spurious alignments suggested by the increase in secondary/supplementary hits?
- The rationale for selecting the 0.98 confidence threshold for modification calls (Ψ and m6A) needs clearer justification. An analysis demonstrating the sensitivity of key findings (like modification stoichiometry) to this specific cutoff value would strengthen the robustness of the conclusions.
- The presence of intermediate-confidence m6A peaks is an interesting finding that merits further discussion. Do these signals exhibit unique basecalling error profiles, map to positions of other known modifications, or show enrichment in specific transcript types/classes?
- Precision in terminology regarding modification timing and statements regarding sequencing of nascent transcripts. Is the evidence sufficient to distinguish installation 'during transcription and/or La binding' specifically. Is the protocol not capturing rather transcripts prior to 3' end processing?
- Statements regarding transcript expression changes upon HSV-1 infection require careful phrasing to reflect the relative nature of sequencing abundance data. Terms like 'reduces expression' or 'increases pre-tRNA levels' should be clarified as changes in 'relative abundance' within the sequenced library, acknowledging that absolute levels are not directly measured without appropriate normalization controls (which may be challenging here).
- Conclusions drawn about time-dependent effects or correlations with infection length in the HSV-1 experiments should be presented cautiously, acknowledging the number of replicates and time points analyzed (6 hpi and 12 hpi). Explicitly stating these limitations would provide better context for the claims.
- It may be worth explicitly noting in the limitations that, like standard DRS protocols, DRAP3R does not provide sequence information for the extreme 5' end of the RNA molecules.
- Clarity of the figure legends should be improved throughout. Explicit definitions for all visual elements, particularly color coding (e.g., Sup Fig 1d lines, gene classifications in Fig 1c/e), are needed for unambiguous interpretation.
Minor Comments
- Please reconcile the discrepancy between the adapter sequence described in the text (NNAAAA 3' overhang) and that depicted in Figure 1a (appears as AAAAAA).
- The read classification percentages presented in Figure 1c and discussed in the text (lines 162-189) could be presented more clearly to ensure all categories sum appropriately or unassigned portions are explicitly stated.
- In Sup Fig 1d, please clarify if the observed ~60-70nt difference between read length and alignment length corresponds primarily to the unaligned 3' adapter sequence, as expected.
Overall Conclusion
This manuscript introduces a potentially valuable tool (DRAP3R) for studying the Pol III transcriptome and epitranscriptome using nanopore sequencing. Addressing the points raised above, particularly concerning methodological justifications, potential biases, bioinformatics parameter choices, and careful interpretation of the data, would significantly strengthen the study and increase confidence in its findings.

=== reviewer_4 ===
Verstraten et al. present a novel direct RNA sequencing method for detection of Pol III-dependent transcripts. The authors’ approach is the first of its kind to assess this broad class of RNAs via direct RNA sequencing and uniquely facilitates identification of RNA modifications. The authors use their technique to assess three distinct human cell models in addition to IVT RNAs as a control to develop a tailored bioinformatics pipeline with high confidence dissection of these transcripts. This allows identification of putative new Pol III-dependent RNAs and direct calling of pseudouridine and m6A modifications. Their technique is corroborated by prior instances of RNA modification and provides clarity on discordant reports. Finally, they apply the technique to assess RNA shifts during viral infection and identify changes in RNA abundance and modification. The strength of this paper lies in development and benchmarking of the technique. The paper is well written and thorough in their representation of the data and how methodology was developed and verified.
Major comments:
1. I would ask the authors to be more intentional with how they refer to the RNAs distinguished by their technique. I feel a more appropriate term would be premature rather than nascent. This technique successfully identifies RNAs which contain a polyU-track. For most Pol III-dependent transcripts, the 3’ polyU tracks are removed during transcript maturation, however the exact rate at which they occur (as well as order relative to other maturation steps) is not clearly defined in humans. Or in some instances, such as U6, which the authors comment on in the discussion, polyU’s are still present in the mature transcript.
2. In line with my prior comments, I feel the biological significance of this manuscript would be bolstered by perturbation of at least one of the core steps of Pol III transcript maturation (e.g. La protein interaction, nucleolytic cleavage) and then assessment via DRAP3R. Alternatively, the authors could apply their technique to different subcellular RNA fractions, as the location for some of these RNA modifications is unknown. Such experiments would significantly broaden the scope of this paper and inform the RNA biology of Pol III transcripts.
3. The authors present their dataset in a number of interesting ways, I would ask that they expand on the following topics:
a. Short RNA reads (line 186-187): The authors remark on a proportion of reads which are quite short. I’m curious what these reads map to (type of transcript, location in transcript, etc) and if the stop location may indicate an RNA modification that their reverse transcriptase could not proceed through. Many other studies of Pol III dependent or other highly structured RNAs use a TGIRT-based RT step to aid with processivity. Please expand on these short products, including their parent gene loci, size, and whether they’re stop position correlates with previously published RNA modifications.
b. Pol II RNAs (line 183-185): Polyuridylation is a form of RNA processing by which U’s are added to the 3’ end of mRNA or ncRNA. This would be something I’d expect the authors could identify in their datasets for Pol II products by comparing the gene sequence to that of the potential 3’ overhang on their direct RNA read. This would be another very interesting benefit of their novel technique. Please include an analysis or discussion of whether their technique can detect this 3’ RNA processing event.
c. Viral RNAs (Fig 4b): It’s a bit hard to see with the color scheme of the column bar, but it appears the authors identified reads mapping to the virus in their dataset—at least there’s a legend box for virus. Please expand on these reads and whether they present as bonafide Pol III-dependent transcripts
Minor comments:
1. We would ask the authors to comment on how quantitative DRAP3R is. It does not appear that they introduced IVT spike-ins at early steps in the protocol, thus I am apprehensive of abundance comparisons in an experimental condition such as infection would robustly changes the RNA landscape. This does not change the major conclusions of this paper, but rather presents as a current study limitation that the authors should comment on.
2. To support the authors findings regarding novel Pol III transcripts (Fig. S2), I would ask that they integrate mapping of published ChIP-Seq datasets for the Pol III and II machinery at these gene loci. This would support conclusions regarding RNA polymerase dependency and suggest a classification (Type 1, 2, 3) for Pol III RNAs.
3. Fig. 1C and 4B. Please add a heatmap to expand the data presented in the column bar graphs regarding the RNAs represented in the Pol III-dependent categories.
4. Fig. 1C legend: Can the authors please define what they classify as “Pol III primary” or “Pol III pseudogene”, I’m assuming they refer to 5S rRNA, but the existing reference is ambiguous.
5. Please comment on the potential mechanism by which the virus alters Pol III-dependent RNA modification status. For example, what is known about the relative abundance or localization of the modifying enzymes.

**Reviewer Report**

**Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**General Comments:**
The manuscript describes DRAP3R, a methodology for the targeted sequencing of pre-mature RNA Polymerase III (Pol III) transcripts using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT). The authors demonstrate the utility of this approach in identifying novel Pol III transcripts, mapping epitranscriptomic modifications (Ψ and m6A) at single-nucleotide resolution, and characterizing the remodeling of the Pol III transcriptome during HSV-1 infection. The study addresses a significant gap in the field, as the pre-mature Pol III transcriptome has historically been difficult to isolate and analyze systematically. The methodology is innovative, and the application to viral infection provides compelling biological insights. However, there are significant concerns regarding the validation of the modification calling, the statistical rigor of the differential modification analysis, and the clarity of the experimental design that must be addressed before publication.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The development of DRAP3R is a timely and significant contribution. By focusing on the poly(U) tail characteristic of nascent Pol III transcripts, the authors provide a systematic way to study the "pre-mature" epitranscriptome. The ability to distinguish between co-transcriptional and post-transcriptional modifications by comparing DRAP3R data with mature tRNA-seq data is a conceptual strength of the paper.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Adapter Specificity:** The authors use a custom adapter with a 3’ NNAAAA 5’ sequence to capture poly(U) tails. It is unclear how this design avoids capturing poly(A) tails that might have been incompletely depleted or non-specific binding to other U-rich sequences. A more detailed analysis of the "off-target" capture rate is required.
*   **La Protein Silencing:** The authors perform La protein silencing but do not explicitly link this to the DRAP3R data in the provided text. If this experiment was intended to validate that DRAP3R captures La-bound transcripts, the results are missing from the excerpt.
*   **HSV-1 Infection:** The study uses an MOI of 10, which is high. The authors acknowledge the potential for capturing nascent Pol II transcripts at poly(T) tracts. Given that HSV-1 is a DNA virus with high transcriptional activity, the authors must provide a more robust computational strategy to distinguish between genuine Pol III-transcribed viral RNAs and Pol II-derived "read-through" or "stalled" transcripts.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
*   **Modification Calling:** The authors rely on basecalling error rates and probability scores (≥0.98) to identify modifications. While this is standard for ONT, the manuscript lacks a "ground truth" validation using an orthogonal method (e.g., bisulfite sequencing for Ψ or LC-MS/MS for global quantification) for the specific sites identified in the novel transcripts.
*   **Replication:** The HSV-1 infection experiments are limited to two biological replicates. Given the inherent variability in nanopore sequencing and viral infection kinetics, this is insufficient for robust statistical claims regarding the "decreasing Ψ stoichiometries."

**4. Statistical Rigor:**
*   **Differential Modification:** The authors claim a decrease in Ψ stoichiometry upon HSV-1 infection. It is unclear what statistical test was used to determine the significance of these changes. A simple correlation is insufficient; the authors should employ a generalized linear model (GLM) or a similar framework that accounts for read depth and variance between replicates.
*   **False Positives:** The authors note that unfiltered basecalls produce high false-positive rates. The threshold of 0.98 is arbitrary. A sensitivity/specificity analysis (ROC curve) using a synthetic control or a known modified RNA standard is necessary to justify this cutoff.

**5. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Section "DRAP3R":** The description of the adapter preparation is incomplete. Please provide the full sequence of the custom adapter and explain the rationale for the "NNAAAA" design.
*   **Section "Pseudouridine installation...":** The authors compare DRAP3R and nano-tRNA-Seq error rates to infer modification timing. This is a clever approach, but the authors must demonstrate that the basecalling models for both methods are comparable. Are the error profiles biased by the different library preparation chemistries?
*   **HSV-1 Analysis:** The authors observe "small numbers of HSV-1 poly(U) RNAs." They must perform a more rigorous analysis of these reads—specifically, do they terminate at predicted Pol III termination signals (poly(T) tracts)? If they do not, they are likely artifacts of Pol II transcription.
*   **Data Availability:** The manuscript mentions "Supplementary Data 2, 3" but these are not provided. Ensure all raw data and processed modification tables are deposited in a public repository (e.g., GEO/ENA) with clear metadata.
*   **Clarity:** The manuscript would benefit from a schematic diagram illustrating the distinction between the DRAP3R capture mechanism and standard ONT direct RNA sequencing.

**Summary:**
The paper is highly promising but requires more rigorous validation of the modification calling pipeline and a more conservative interpretation of the viral infection data. The authors should provide additional experimental validation for the novel Ψ sites and expand the statistical analysis of the differential modification stoichiometry.

This was a thorough analysis of a global collection of NTS genomes from different ecological and geographical regions and settings, culminating in an excellent attempt at understanding the diversity and transmission complexity and dynamics of invasive NTS disease. Authors leveraged on this unique resource to pursue three objectives: (1) to project the epidemiological landscape of iNTS, emphasising ST313; (2) to define population structure, intercontinental spread, and potential zoonotic transmission at single nucleotide resolution; and (3) to evaluate AMR and other influences on lineage replacement within ST313. The key novel findings and which have a huge implication for evolving NTS epidemiology and genomics were:
1. NTS L1 and L2 predominated in Africa and within L2, phylogenetic analysis revealed a novel sublineage beyond 2.0–2.3, designated 2.4. Notably, most isolates in sublineage 2.4 originated from Kenya (51/61, 83.6%).
2. Although ST313 has been considered a lineage restricted to human-to-human transmission, analysis of the 146 major clusters revealed potential cross-host transmission events in clusters 329 and 344, including human-canine transmission in cluster 329 in the UK
3. This analysis revealed additional previously unreported lineage-specific MGEs that drove evolution of systemic NTS disease
4.Although AMR correlated with L1 and L2 shifts, this was less evident in lineages L3-L5, which harbor few ARGs
The findings in these analyses clearly illustrate that NTS as a species is still evolving and the disease outcomes will largely depnd on what the bacterium picks or sheds along the evolutionary pathway. Clearly, our understanding of the forces that drive the evolution will be crucial in developing tools for mitigation against severe disease.
A couple of issues that require author response for clarification:
INTRODUCTION

=== reviewer_2 ===
The manuscript presents a large-scale genomic analysis of invasive Salmonella Typhimurium ST313, focusing on the emergence of sublineage 2.4, an emerging lineage 4, and their antimicrobial-resistance and evolutionary dynamics. This work is mostly descriptive. Clearer methodological justifications, more detailed phylogenetic analyses, and fuller discussion of limitations would improve the clarity, rigor, and interpretability of the study.
1. L100-103: Most of these identified gaps in ST313 evolution are barely addressed or untouched by the study.
2. L106-108: What do you mean by One Health framework? It appears the authors simply took a large collection of publicly available genomes, which are heavily biased toward human isolates. With only 0.5% animal isolates and 0.3% food isolates, how does this data set and study feature a One Health approach?
3. The manuscript reports a novel, highly antimicrobial-resistant sublineage 2.4 and an emerging lineage 4, but provides limited phylogenetic detail. To strengthen these important findings, the authors should include more detailed phylogenetic trees (e.g., high-resolution subtrees or supplementary figures) and present metrics quantifying genetic diversity within each sublineage/lineage—for example, distributions of pairwise SNP distances or other within-group diversity measures. Such analyses would not only better support the distinction and characterization of these newly described lineages but also help confirm that sublineage 2.4 is not merely a single clonal expansion. Demonstrating sufficient genetic diversity is essential to substantiate the reported association between sublineage 2.4 and its key antimicrobial-resistance genes.
4. The description of the dataset assembly raises some ambiguity regarding the precise definition of invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS). The authors state that genomes were “selected from human clinical sources (excluding fecal samples),” but do not specify the exact isolation sources included. Although the authors state that fecal samples were excluded, the term “human clinical sources” is broad and may encompass specimens such as urine, or even incompletely annotated fecal specimens. Given the variability in GenBank and EnteroBase metadata, please clarify how potential ambiguous sources (e.g., samples labeled only as “clinical” or “human”) were identified and excluded. Besides, please provide detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria for sample types, and clarify whether isolates were limited to blood and other sterile sites.
5. The methodological description of SNP analysis is a little ambiguous. It is not clear whether the core-genome SNP (cgSNP) analysis was restricted to Salmonella enterica ST313 isolates or applied to a broader iNTS dataset. In addition, the statement “a total of 9,238 cgSNPs were identified” does not specify whether this number refers to SNPs remaining after Gubbins recombination masking or to the unfiltered set produced by Snippy.
6. The description of the temporal signal test is ambiguous regarding the criteria used to declare a significant temporal signal. While the authors state that substitution rates from the original dataset were compared with those from randomized datasets, it is unclear what statistical threshold was applied (e.g., minimum R² from root-to-tip regression, p-value from permutation tests). Without explicit criteria, readers cannot assess the strength of the evidence. The authors should specify the exact decision rule and statistical measures used to conclude that a significant temporal signal was present.
7. The method used for transmission tracing infers putative transmission events solely from a fixed ≤3 cgSNP threshold. Without any epidemiological support/evidence, this is a questionable exercise that deviates from the established practices of genomic epidemiology. While SNP distance is an important metric, transmission inference based only on a hard cut-off is not best practice, given strain-specific evolutionary rate variation, sequencing artefacts, and potential reference-genome bias. Furthermore, The authors should provide a more detailed description of their simulations used to select this threshold, clarify how “optimal performance” was defined, and, ideally, incorporate additional epidemiological or phylogenetic evidence to corroborate genetic clustering and more reliably identify transmission event.
Although some details appear in the figure legend, the explanation remains incomplete. The authors did not clearly state their justification for using a 3-SNP threshold in the main text. While they explored thresholds from 1 to 50 and observed a plateau in inferred transmission events at 3 SNPs, they did not provide formal statistical criteria for identifying transmission events or independent epidemiological validation. The authors should explicitly present their rationale in the Methods or Results and supply additional statistical, phylogenetic, or epidemiological evidence.
8. The manuscript infers intercontinental transmission of ST313 based on genomic clustering but does not discuss the possibility that such patterns may reflect human travel or migration rather than direct bacterial transmission. This limitation should be acknowledged, and the authors should clarify that genome-based links alone cannot definitively distinguish person-to-person transmission from human-mediated dispersal across continents.
9. References are missing or incomplete in several places. Please ensure that all methods (e.g., line 510), software tools and their versions (e.g., lines 522 and 590–597), and key claims (e.g., lines 536–539) are consistently supported by appropriate citations throughout the manuscript.
10. Figure visualization could be improved to better highlight key findings. In particular, the annotation of important lineages and clusters is insufficient. For example, lineage 2.4 and the clusters emphasized in the text (e.g., Clusters 850, 695, 888, 579, 648) are not clearly or consistently labeled in Fig. 3.
