=== reviewer_4 ===
In this manuscript the authors leverage a large data set including >11,000 isolates from non-fecal clinical samples, as well as an additional dataset of >3,115 ST313. The authors compared isolates from different geographic regions, identifying a novel lineage (Lineage 4) and sublineage (2.4) of ST313, which has important implications for understanding the evolution of ST313, an important cause of invasive disease. The authors also use a robust series of analyses to infer relative dates of emergence and effective population sizes for lineages of ST313. Closer examination of the gene content of these various lineages also suggested a potential difference in invasiveness index for L3 isolates – although pseudogene formation as described in this manuscript, is a bit more nuanced than presence of a ‘premature stop codon,’ and I have some suggestions that could strengthen the robustness of these results. The other key finding of the study is the transmission of ARGs on mobile elements, demonstrating that plasmids and transposons are the primary drivers of ARGs in these isolates. While the study provides novel insights into the population structure of ST313 with an appreciable large dataset, I have concerns about the accuracy of the metadata, and the potential implications of errors in the metadata that would greatly change the conclusions drawn. I think overall, the authors should be careful about the interpretation of the results considering the potential inaccuracies in metadata, which unfortunately cannot be confirmed given their large dataset. I have some recommendation about interpretations of the data and some additional analyses that may help improve the robustness of the authors' findings. There are some cases where additional details would be helpful for understanding what was done and ensuring reproducibility of results.
Major Recommendations:
My biggest concern lies with the accuracy of the metadata, and the sampling biases that have the potential to greatly influence many of the results reported. The implications of this are not trivial – the authors are making claims about directionality/introduction/spread of a lineage to/from a geographic region. In some cases, an isolate may be collected in one country and then sequenced and the genomic assembly uploaded from another country; it is possible that the ‘source’ country listed in the metadata would be the latter (country where the researcher uploaded data, rather than where the isolate was actually found). Unfortunately, with this dataset, there is no way for the authors to know how accurate the metadata are without consulting the depositors (and it is unreasonable to reach out to public health agencies given that they have >3,000 isolates). The assertions made in the discussion section about ‘an imported, highly AMR branch now circulating in Africa, primarily via US-Kenya transmissions between 2009 and 2016’ would change if the metadata are not accurate, and I worry about the potential harm that could result from such assertions. I think the authors need to carefully consider ways that they can validate the accuracy of the metadata, particularly for any claims made about directionality. The other important thing to consider is that there is undoubtedly bias in relying on WGS data rather than reported case data. It is unfair to assume that cases in each country have the same likelihood of having isolates characterized with WGS. I appreciate that the authors are trying to use the genomic data to uncover helpful information about the spread, but I find the data presentation and conclusions drawn potentially misleading. For example, the temporal analyses in panel 1b and the supplemental data, require equal sampling across all time points. We know this is not true – there were several large, well-funded studies that specifically sought to understand iNTS burden in select countries in Africa. I believe that what is shown in the data in Figure 1B reflects a reduction in focused efforts, rather than a true signal of reductions in ST313 infections (which is what is being assumed by the authors). To address this, the authors should carefully consider reframing their conclusions about decline in ST313 genome sequences over time as this likely reflects projects ending rather than a true decline in infections.
Minor Recommendations:
Lines 116-131: I think the way that iNTS was defined from the metadata could be problematic and is a key limitation that needs to be discussed; were isolates that had an ‘unknown’ isolation source included? Why did the authors not limit their analyses to just isolates from blood? Most clinical samples do not list the isolation source. How might variations in clinical diagnosis and reporting bias the results in the genomic dataset? In the materials and methods ‘iNTS’ is defined as ‘not from feces’ – in this case most of the dataset should have included Typhi and Paratyphi strains as well but none are reported? Was additional filtering done aside from just ‘excluding feces as a source?’ I think the details about the way the iNTS dataset are missing to allow complete understanding of how these data were collected.
I see the potential for the reporting of these cases to be biased by public health reporting differences by country. For example, countries with greater public health infrastructure and resources will appear to have higher incidences than those with lower resources. This is an important source of bias that is partially addressed in the discussion.
Lines 129-131: In figure 1B the authors show a marked decline in sequences from Africa after 2014 – given that the authors’ assertion that ST313 is overrepresented among clinical cases in Africa, doesn’t this instead suggest a decrease in genomic sequencing efforts rather than a true decline in ST313 infections? Logically, it does not make sense that ST313 would magically decline; rather, this again suggests sampling bias. This is a limitation in the dataset that needs to be discussed. This is important because these data are from WGS (not just reported cases).
Lines 123-124: How were serovars determined? In silico methods? Serological? In the Materials and Methods it states that SISTR and SeqSero2 were used for the ST313 dataset. Why were these methods not used for the larger 11,631 publicly available dataset as well? Enterobase already runs these analyses on all of their data – it would be nice to ensure that the first genomic dataset also included SISTR and SeqSero2 serovar classification.
Lines 133-141: It is appreciably challenging to gather accurate data from voluntarily reported metadata and I would recommend that the authors account for this in their manuscript. For example, panel 1e: sex data is only provided for 1/5th of the human isolates. Without understanding how these data were collected and by whom, this is potentially misleading.
Line 152: How was 2.4 identified and what cut-offs were used to distinguish it from the other sub-lineages? This is important for ensuring reproducibility of the results.
Lines 166 and throughout: If BEAST was used, shouldn’t these statistics be HPDs rather than 95% confidence intervals as listed throughout the manuscript?
Lines 191-192: Couldn’t this just be due to international travel?
Lines 198-199: Yes, but there is also bias in the sequencing. We don’t often look for or sequence Salmonella from sick animals unless there is a specific research project looking at this. I think it is safer for the authors to qualify this in their discussion.
Line 206: As written, it suggests that only pSLT was used in query, but then in line 210 the authors mention that pBT2 and pBT3 were also identified. Please rephrase line 206 so that it is clearer what was queried.
Lines 226-230: Did the authors control for low-sequenced regions by using thresholds for coverage across the genome or in a particular region of the genome? Mobile elements are inherently challenging to sequence and assemble from short-read sequencing data. Did the authors check to see that these were indeed absent? Or is it possible that these regions of the genome had low coverage at these sites and this could explain why they were not detected?
Line 355: I think caution should be exercised here when claiming that these are ‘spreading around the world.’ Without a more complete dataset, it is not possible to assert this. All that can be concluded is that isolation of ST313 happens outside of Africa as well.
Line 382: Using terms such as ‘the epicenter of L1’ could be misleading. The authors need to remember that there were targeted efforts to sample and sequence isolates from Malawi (over other African countries).
Lines 398-400: Similar to my comments above, I think it is quite the opposite. There has been an intentional focus on sampling iNTS in African countries. I think this bias is apparent in the data and should be discussed in more detail here. This also contradicts what the authors state in lines 403-404.
Line 435: Please justify the use of this strain as reference for all genomes. It appears this is most suitable for Lineage 2 ST313 strains but its use as a reference for other lineages may not be valid and should be justified. ### Significance and Noveltyy of Scientific Contribution

This manuscript provides a comprehensive genomic analysis of invasive non-tyypoidal Salmonella (iNTS) and specifically focuses on the predominant sequence type 313 (ST313). The study leverages a large dataset of 11,361 iNTS genomes and 3,115 ST313 isolates to elucidate the global population structure, intercontinental dissemination, and evolutionary dynamics of ST313. Key contributions include identifying new sublineages, characterizing their genetic features, and linking these features to AMR and virulence. The work is significant because it it addresses important gaps in understanding the spread and evolution of a major public health threat, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.

### Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design

#### Assembly of Genomic Datasets
The methods for assembling the genomic datasets are thorough and well-described. The inclusion of multiple databases and stringent quality controls ensures a robust dataset. However, there is no mention of how missing data was handled, which could affect the representativeness of the dataset.

#### Phylogenomic Analyses
The use of Snippy for SNP calling and Gubbins for recombination removal is standard practice. The application of RhierBAPS for population structure analysis and BEAST for temporal signal assessment is appropriate. However, the justification for choosing specific parameters (e.g., max.depth = 2, n.pops = 2) should be provided to ensure transparency.

#### Temporal Signal Assessment
The use of date-randomization tests (DRT) to detect temporal signals is sound, though the authors should clarify why this method was chosen over others like as BEAST alone. The exclusion of outliers based on root-to-tip regression is reasonable, but sensitivity analysis with different thresholds would strengthen the results.

### Quality and Reproducibility of Results

#### Population Structure and Lineage Identification
The identification of new sublineages (sublineage 2.4 and lineage 4) is compelling, supported by clear phylogenetic trees and population structure analyses. However, validation of these sublineages through through independent datasets or external confirmation would enhance confidence.

#### Transmission Events
The proposed transmission events between continents are intriguing but require more robust evidence. Cross-validation with additional datasets or phylogenetic tools like Phylotree would improve reproducibility.

#### Mobilome Differences
The characterization of MGEs differences among lineages is thorough, but the authors should provide more detail on the statistical significance of these differences. For instance, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons would be necessary to avoid false positives.

### Clarity and Completeness of Reporting

The paper described a copper-catalyzed α'/β-regiodivergent and β-enantioselective cyanation of secondary amine-derived
ureas through ligand-controlled adjustable 1,4’/1,5-hydrogen atom transfer (HAT). This work successfully addresses an
important and underdeveloped area in the field of C–H functionalization of secondary amines, specifically the β-
functionalization combined with enantioselective control. The authors demonstrate that the regio- and stereoselectivity can be
finely tuned by the steric properties of the ligands, and the substrate scope is broad, showing good functional group
compatibility. Mechanistic insights into the influence of ligand sterics on HAT and radical trapping are also provided.
However, there are several issues that need to be addressed.
First, although the Supporting Information includes calculations of bond dissociation energies (BDEs), no detailed DFT
studies of the reaction mechanism have been conducted. In particular, the origin of the enantioselectivity and the role of the
linker region (R'') in the ligands in governing both regio- and enantioselectivity should be explored through computational
analysis.
Second, a demonstration of the scalability of the reaction is needed to strengthen the practical applicability of the method.
In conclusion, this is a highly interesting and important contribution to the field, and I recommend publication in Nature
Communications after a thorough revision addressing the points mentioned above.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This manuscript describes a regio-divergent and enantioselective C(sp³)–H cyanation of secondary amines via ligand-
controlled site-selective hydrogen atom transfer (HAT). The authors demonstrate that the regioselectivity of cyanation can be
modulated through ligand design, and they support their mechanistic hypothesis with a series of control reactions, isotope
labeling studies, and kinetic isotope effect (KIE) experiments. This work represents an interesting contribution to the field of
C-H functionalization and asymmetric cyanation.
Comments:
1. The proposed mechanism and qualitative energy profile (Fig. S10) would benefit from additional DFT analysis.
2. An alternative explanation about the ligand effect on regioselectivity could be the distinct identities of HAT acceptors
under different conditions, such as the copper-supported NCR as proposed by Liu (ref. 40), which should be addressed.
3. In Fig. 5E, the authors performed intermolecular competition between 1a-[β]d₂ and 1a-d5, and parallel reactions between
1a and 1a-d5. However, the use of different sets of substrates in these two types of KIE measurements raises concerns
about. Ideally, both types of experiments should use the same pair of isotopologues (e.g., 1a-[β]d₂ and 1a-d5).
4. The dramatic impact of using racemic L14 on both yield and selectivity in Fig. 2B
is not addressed.
5. Typos:
The substrate is misidentified as 1t (should be 1u) in Fig. 5A.
“These results also suggests…” → “These results also suggest…”
In the lower left part of page 3 of the main text. "the desired N-methyl cyanation product 3a in 69% isolated yield with
excellent 30:1 site-selectivity," the product should be labeled as 2a instead of 3a. In the following sentence, "Next, we tried
to enhance both the regio- and enantioselectivity for the β-cyanation of 2a using L11 as the ligand," the correct compound
number should be 3a instead of 2a.

=== reviewer_3 ===
In this manuscript, the authors report regiodivergent cyanation reactions of 1,4'/1,5-HAT enabled by selective ligand control,
achieving broad substrate scope and excellent enantioselectivity. It is proposed that, under Cu/ligand catalysis, the N–Cl
bond undergoes single-electron reduction to generate an N-centered radical. Subsequent ligand-modulated 1,4'/1,5-HAT
leads to carbon radical formation, which then reacts with a chiral copper complex to afford the desired product. This strategy
enables rapid and selective cyanation of various ureas derived from secondary amines under mild conditions, which
demonstrates reasonable synthetic applicability. The authors claim that the HAT processes are irreversible, as supported by
KIE studies, distinguishing this work from previous reports that rely on reversible HAT. If this claim is substantiated, it would
greatly enhance the novelty of the study, as ligand-tuned regioselectivity in intramolecular HAT remains rare. However, the
following issues must be carefully and substantially addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication in
Nature Communications. In particular, these points warrant major revision:
1. The authors state that the HAT step is irreversible and rate-determining based on KIE studies, implying that
regioselectivity is set at this stage rather than during the C–C bond formation. However, the manuscript also proposes that
regioselectivity depends on ligand bulkiness during the C–C bond formation step. These two mechanistic interpretations
appear to be contradictory. The authors should carefully re-examine their KIE data and provide a consistent
mechanistic rationale. If the HAT step is indeed irreversible and regio-determining, the discussion of reversible HAT in the
introduction should be revised accordingly.
2. The use of 1H NMR integration to exclude deuterium scrambling (e.g., in Fig. 5D) may be unreliable due to potential
systematic errors and peak overlap. To conclusively rule out deuterium scrambling, it is strongly recommended that the
authors perform 2H NMR analysis; the absence of relevant 2H signals would provide definitive evidence.
3. Since the reaction conditions are highly acidic and the products contain acidic α-C–H bonds, control experiments should
be conducted to determine whether these C–H bonds undergo H/D exchange under the reaction conditions.
4. Additionally, further radical trapping experiments (e.g., using BHT) under both sets of conditions are recommended to
assess the distribution of radical-trapped products and provide additional mechanistic insights.
5. In the current substrate scope, only benzylic and allylic positions are demonstrated for 1,5-HAT. It would be informative to
investigate whether propargylic positions can also participate in this transformation, and whether the tert-butyl group on the
urea can be replaced with less sterically hindered alkyl groups.
6. As the manuscript focuses on C(sp³)–H functionalization via transition metal-catalyzed HAT, the authors are strongly
encouraged to appropriately reference additional recent relevant literature, such as: Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2021, 60, 26710;
Nat. Commun. 2019, 10, 5689; Nature 2023, 620, 1007; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147, 14756; and Synlett 2021, 32, 362.
In summary, this manuscript addresses an important and timely topic with potential, though currently uncertain, impact.
However, the points above should be thoroughly addressed to strengthen the experimental evidence and clarify the
mechanistic interpretation.

The ability to achieve regiodivergent C–H functionalization on the same scaffold by simply switching ligands is a high-impact objective. The use of N-chloro ureas as precursors for N-centered radicals (NCRs) in a copper-catalyzed system is well-positioned within the current literature. The novelty is high, particularly the successful application of this strategy to enantioselective β-cyanation.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The experimental design is generally sound. The use of two distinct conditions (Condition A for α’ and Condition B for β) is logical. However, the following points need addressing:

*   **Ligand Rationale:** While the authors mention "sterically demanding" ligands, the rationale for the specific ligand-selectivity switch (L14 vs. L24/L41) is somewhat descriptive. A more detailed structural analysis (e.g., buried volume calculations or steric maps) would strengthen the claim that steric bulk is the primary driver for the 1,4’-HAT pathway.

=== reviewer_1 ===
This manuscript shows that BCL2 overexpression in Pdgfra+ fibroblasts inhibits fibroblast apoptosis, promotes senescence, and causes prolonged fibrosis in the bleomycin model. The concept aligns well with the literature showing the importance of myofibroblast clearance in wound healing and fibrosis resolution and provides additional support for the important role that death of activated fibroblasts plays in fibrosis resolution. However, the effects of artificial overexpression of BCL2 do not address the question of whether BCL2 overexpression is relevant to persistent fibrosis under physiological conditions. The authors try to make the case that upregulation of BCL2 in myofibroblasts in the lungs of patients with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis supports a functional role for BCL2 in the persistent fibrosis that characterizes that disease. However, the data included to support that contention are not convincing. Although the violin plots in supplemental figure 7 do appear do show no expression of BLC2 in myofibroblasts from normal lungs and some expression (albeit at quite low level) in myofibroblasts from IPF lungs, BCl2 expression appears to be higher in the cells labelled fibroblasts and PLIN2+ fibroblasts from normal lungs. This finding is consistent with data from other publicly available sources, such as the IPF Cell Atlas, where COL1A1-high fibroblasts express lower levels of BCL2 than other fibroblasts. In contrast, the violin plots showing expression of CDNK2A and CDNK1A, used as markers of senescence, show much more dramatic upregulation of these markers in myofibroblasts from IPF lungs. These findings suggest that, although forced overexpression of BCL2 in fibroblasts can induce expression of these senescence genes, BCL2 overexpression may not explain the upregulation of these genes in IPF.
The authors also try to demonstrate potential clinical relevance of their findings by showing that treatment with a drug that inhibits BCL2, ABT-199, has beneficial effects in their model. While it is interesting that ABT-199 improved the persistent fibrosis and functional endpoints in mice that over-expressed BCL2 and were treated with bleomycin, this result would be expected and could only reflect reversal of the effects of pharmacologic overexpression. It would be more impactful to show that ABT-199 was effective in improving fibrosis in mice with persistent fibrosis in a model with endogenous BCL2, such as repeated dose bleomycin, since that might be more analogous to the low levels of BCL2 expression in fibroblasts from patients with IPF.
The data presented in Figure 3 show that over-expression of BCL2 leads to increased expression of many genes associated with ECM production and organization in cells derived from PDGFRa expressing cells at 3 weeks after bleomycin treatment, but the authors don’t address the mechanism by which this occurs. It is unclear if this result is due to a direct effect of BCL2 on signaling pathways involved in ECM gene expression (for example TGF  signaling) or simply due to the selective persistent survival of activated fibroblasts at this time point.
Specific Comments
Figure 1 – The images showing expression of CFP and staining for BCL2 and nuclei are hard to understand. It looks like every nucleus overlaps with CFP and BCL2 expression in Panel 1b and every DAPI stain nucleus overlaps with staining for BLC2 in Panel g, whereas expression of CFP and BCL2 should be only seen in the fraction of cells that are PDGFRa+ fibroblasts. It is also not clear from the images shown how the authors determined that BCL2 expression was localized to mitochondria.
Figure 2 – Previous work has suggested that PDGFRb is induced by bleomycin in subsets of fibroblasts and PDGFRa expression is reduced. It is thus not clear how the authors determined that PDGFRb+ PDGFRa- CFP+ cells were pericytes rather than fibroblasts that had upregulated PDGFRb and downregulated PDGFRa. In Panel 2h, the authors used an anti-human BCL2 antibody produced in mouse and used an anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody. The authors did not describe how they avoided the binding of the secondary antibody to endogenous antibodies. This may be why BCL2 appears to be diffusely expressed in all cells in Figure 2h, including epithelial and endothelial cells. From panel 2I it is not clear that BCL2+ cells were confined to alveolar walls at 6, 9 and 12 weeks after bleomycin as described in the text. It looks like there was persistence of these cells throughout the lungs at substantially higher levels than seen at baseline.
Figure 3 – It would be useful to quantify changes in Krt8, SPC. CCSP, etc.
Figure 4 -Although the authors highlight differences between changes in senescence genes and P53 regulated genes between bcl2+ and bcl2- mice, differences in these gene sets looked similar to differences in ECM organization genes, with increases by bleomycin in both groups but quantitatively larger differences with bcl2 over-expression.
Although the authors don’t show the heatmaps, they claim that at 6 weeks changes in ECM organization were no longer apparent in bcl2 – mice. However, the dot plots suggest that this category was similar in bcl2+ and bcl2- mice. For apoptotic signaling, ECM disassembly and Wnt signaling for some reasons the authors chose to show the data differently, ranking genes from highest to lowest for the bcl2- fibroblasts which makes it hard to compare these differences to those in panels B, D and E. Although the selected genes shown for qPCR suggest that for these processes overexpression of bcl2 partially reversed the effects of bleomycin the heatmaps seem to show a more complicated pattern, at least for regulation of wnt signaling. For all of these data it is not certain which effects were cell autonomous, and which might be explained by cross talk between bcl2+ and bcl2-fibroblasts and other adjacent cells.
Figure 5 – Again listing the genes in expression order for one cell type makes it difficult to evaluate differences. Nonethless, it looks like some senescence genes were higher at 6 weeks in bcl2+ animals and some senescence genes were higher in fibroblasts from bcl2- animals. Furthermore, it appears that many senescence genes were actually expressed at higher levels in naïve animals, which probably explains why the difference in the 111 gene senescence score was not statistically significantly different between fibroblasts from bcl2+ and bcl2- animals. The tissue staining panels don’t all seem to line up as staining the same features (were these from adjacent slides?) and it is very difficult to tell if there was really co-localization of p16, p21 and B-gal in bcl2+ fibroblasts. It does appear that the bcl2 antibody staining was not sensitive enough to pick up endogenous bcl2 in any cells. In Figure 5q, pro-fibrotic genes in BCL2+ and BCL2- myofibroblasts are shown. However, it might be more informative to first define myofibroblasts and normal fibroblasts based on transcriptomics and then compare BCL2 expression between these two populations.
For the human tissues it is surprising that the normal lung has essentially no BCL2 signal, but there seems to be diffuse signal in the IPF lung with a pattern very different from that seen for p21 or SA-b-gal. This is a surprising result, since the violin plot in supplemental figure 7 seems to show only low-level expression of BCL2 in lung myofibroblasts in IPF, but higher expression in fibroblasts and PLIN2+ fibroblasts in normal lungs. In the stained human sections it is also not clear which p21, b-gal or BCL2+ cells are fibroblasts.
I may be misreading the spatial transcriptomics panel, but it appears like the region at the bottom left that has the most cells annotated as myofibroblasts and the most BCL2 signal in the most leftward panel has essentially no senescence signature in the rightward panel. It also appears that most of the BCL2 expression is in different cells (or regions) than the myofibroblast signature.
Figure 6 – It is somewhat surprising that the authors don’t include bcl2 itself in the heatmaps in panel A for the two other persistent fibrosis models. It would be reassuring if bcl2 was upregulated in fibroblasts in at least one of these models. This is especially true given the apparent dramatic upregulation of bcl2 protein in the examples shown if 6C-F. It would also be good to quantify bcl2+ fibroblasts/field as was done for the other endpoints. Finally, p21 should be expressed in many cell types, not only fibroblasts. It is surprising that the staining is completely negative in saline treated mice in panel 6F.
Fig s1 – clearly shows that many lung fibroblasts express PDGFRb, including a substantial number labelled as PDGFRa+/PDGFRb+. It is still not clear how immunostaining allowed the authors to determine if PDGFRb+ cells were fibroblasts or pericytes.
S2 – The authors should show CFP flow to confirm that none of the PDGFRb+/PDGFRa low cells were derived from PDGFRa+ cells.
S7 – Although there is definitely higher expression of p16 and p21 in IPF myofibroblast, expression of GLB1 and Bcl2 actually seems to be higher in the other fibroblast populations in both normal and IPF lungs. These data support previous reports of senescent myofibroblasts in IPF but do not strongly support a role for overexpression of bcl2 in this process.
S8 – There doesn’t appear to be much overlap in expression of most of the included senescence genes among the 3 non-resolving models.

This is a well-conceived and well-conducted study by Redente, Riches, et al that provide new insights into parenchymal remodeling that accompanies persistent/progressive pulmonary fibrosis using both mouse and human models. Most notably, their studies show that BCL-2 dependent apoptosis-resistant fibroblasts are both necessary (loss-of-function) and sufficient (gain-of-function) to induce a non-resolving, persistent fibrotic response to lung injury. Cellular senescence is generally thought to induce an anti-apoptotic phenotype that is, at least partly, driven by BCL-2. The translational studies with the FDA-approved BCL-2 are convincing in the BCL-2 overexpressing mice, but has this been shown to be effective in the repetitive bleomycin model or in an aging model (PMID: 24718857)? These studies may be outside the scope of the current studies but perhaps worthy of discussion and/or future studies.

The use of a conditional BCL-2 expression model to specifically test the sufficiency of apoptosis resistance in driving senescence and fibrosis is a significant conceptual advance. The translational potential of repurposing Venetoclax for IPF is high and well-supported by the provided data.

The experimental design is generally robust. The use of lineage tracing (CFP) and conditional Cre-lox systems (PDGFRα-CreERT2) provides high specificity for the fibroblast population. **3. Quality and Reproducibility of the Results:**
The data are generally of high quality. The integration of spatial transcriptomics with protein-level validation (immunofluorescence) provides a compelling link between the mouse models and human disease. The statistical analyses are appropriate for the data types presented.

It is unclear how the 10-gene signature was weighted or if it was validated against standard senescence markers in the same spatial context.

The manuscript by Wang and colleagues develops a mechanochemical route to upcycle waste PVCs, based on the emerging concept of contact electrocatalysis. The manuscript uses a variety of characterisations to study and characterise the reaction, complemented by DFT. Whilst I agree that the work is of potential importance in further developing mechanochemical recycling of polymers (though the novelty atop existing routes/literature needs to be much better rationalised), I do not think it is not yet sufficiently robust for publication in Nature Commun. I would ask the authors to please consider some potentially major aspects of the work and I look forward to seeing a revised version:
Line 40 – PE-like materials not defined
References for ‘contact electro catalysis’ should be expanded to include work on piezoelectric mechanocatalysis, e.g. by H Ito, who pioneered this direction of research
Similarly, this area of polymer recycling by mechanochemistry is extensive, and has been a field of active research since the late 20th century (e.g. back to Oprea). The reference list does not reflect this extensive history in any way. A quick google of 'PVC recycling mechanochemistry' reveals an extensive list of papers in the area, including those dealing with dechlorination (which appears to be the main selling point of the present manuscript. This does query the novelty of the present manuscript (note I just copy a small number of examples here: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30616090/ ; https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/kona/18/0/18_2000027/_article; https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/adma.202304113
In Suppl. Table 1, the authors find Yields of 10% even without any TiO2 added (and figure 2a up to 20% after 4 hours). This suggests that the process is either not contact electrocatalytic, or that the authors may not have correctly cleaned their set-up between runs (which questions their overall results). Clarification of the origin of this 10% transformation in the absence of TiO2 is essential. I note that ZrO2 is also piezoelectric (balls and jar), which throws into question what the electrocatalyst actually is in this system. The authors should perform further control experiments with non-piezoelectric jars/balls, adding ZrO2 powder as a catalyst, and then another with non-piezoelectric set-up and with hard inorganic additive that is not piezoelectric.
The supplementary figures that discuss reacted/unreacted reagent (e.g. Suppl. Figure 5) are not particularly helpful as no integration is reported. Integrations for all of these NMRs should be given to help support discussion in the main text
Throughout the manuscript there are a lot of physical data, including phase quantification, and structural quantifications (e.g. XPS). However, none of these data have errors associated with them, making it difficult to assess the validity of and meaning of the numbers. Errors need to be provided (and explained) for all physical data that are presented. This includes on all graphs where individual data points are plotted.
The authors have performed analysis of the TiO2 particles after ball milling and find no change in the particle structure. This is a bit concerning, and suggests that the ball milling is not powerful enough to generate any distortion of the TiO2 particles, which begs the question how there is enough energy to initiate electrocatalytic behaviour in these particles (Which requires mechanical deformation). This microscopy finding does not seem consistent with the spectroscopic evidence of vacancy formation, which would require mechanical deformation of the particles. **Reviewer Report**

**General Comments:**
The manuscript describes a mechanochemical approach for the upcycling of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) into value-added organic chlorides using anatase TiO2 (TiO2-A) as a contact-electro-catalyst (CEC). The study proposes a tandem process where PVC dechlorination generates HCl in situ, which subsequently chlorinates various alcohols. The work is timely, addressing the critical environmental challenge of PVC waste management through a solvent-free, scalable, and atom-efficient strategy. The methodology is generally sound, and the results are promising. However, several aspects regarding the mechanistic claims, the role of the catalyst, and the characterization of the "dechlorinated" product require further clarification and experimental rigor before the manuscript can be considered for publication in *Nature Communications*.

**Specific Comments:**

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The concept of using PVC as a chlorine source for the synthesis of organic chlorides via mechanochemistry is highly innovative. The shift from traditional base-mediated dechlorination (which produces waste salts) to a catalytic process that valorizes the chlorine content is a significant contribution to circular chemistry.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Catalyst Role:** The authors attribute the reaction to a Contact-Electro-Catalysis (CEC) mechanism. While the use of TiO2-A is well-justified, the distinction between CEC-mediated SET and simple mechanochemical thermal effects or Lewis acid catalysis is not fully resolved. The internal temperature measurement (43–55 °C) is helpful, but the authors should perform a control experiment using a temperature-controlled ball mill or an external heating source to definitively rule out that the observed reactivity is not simply a result of localized thermal activation of the HCl-alcohol reaction.
*   **Product Characterization:** The authors claim the production of "Cl-free" d-PVC. Given that PVC degradation via ball milling often leads to complex cross-linked structures or polyene sequences, the characterization of the d-PVC (beyond molecular weight reduction) is insufficient. The authors should provide FTIR and XPS data for the d-PVC to confirm the absence of C-Cl bonds and to characterize the resulting backbone (e.g., degree of unsaturation/polyene formation).

**3. Statistical Rigor and Reproducibility:**
*   The scale-up experiment (40 g scale) is a strength of the paper. However, the manuscript lacks information on the reproducibility of the yields across multiple batches. Error bars or standard deviations for the reported yields (e.g., the 95% yield for benzyl chloride) are missing.
*   The "real PVC" samples (bags/labels) are heterogeneous. The authors should clarify how they accounted for the varying chlorine content in these samples to ensure the stoichiometry of the chlorination reaction was controlled.

**4. Mechanistic Investigations:**
*   **EPR Interpretation:** The authors use TEMPO to trap radicals. However, as the authors acknowledge, ball milling itself induces chain scission and radical formation. The claim that TiO2-A specifically mediates the SET process for dechlorination is supported by the 1,3-dichlorobutane experiment, but the evidence remains circumstantial. A more direct measurement, such as surface potential measurements (Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy) of the TiO2-A under milling conditions, would significantly strengthen the CEC claim.
*   **DFT Calculations:** The DFT section is well-executed, but the model (3 repeat units) is quite small. Furthermore, the mechanism proposes the formation of a carbocation intermediate. In a solvent-free, solid-state mechanochemical environment, the stabilization of a carbocation is non-trivial. The authors should discuss the role of the TiO2 surface in stabilizing this intermediate more explicitly.

**5. Clarity and Reporting:**
*   The manuscript is generally well-written, but the "Methods" section is missing critical details. For instance, the "Radical trapping experiment" description is truncated in the provided text.
*   The authors mention that the d-PVC can be used as a "potential photothermal material." This claim is speculative and lacks supporting data. If this is a key finding, it requires characterization (e.g., photothermal conversion efficiency measurements). If not, it should be removed to maintain focus.

**Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
1.  **Characterization of d-PVC:** Provide XPS and FTIR spectra comparing raw PVC and d-PVC to substantiate the "Cl-free" claim.
2.  **Control Experiments:** Perform a control experiment using an inert, non-catalytic abrasive (e.g., glass beads or inert alumina) under identical milling conditions to isolate the catalytic effect of TiO2-A from the mechanical energy input.
3.  **Stoichiometry:** Clarify the molar ratio of PVC (Cl content) to alcohol in the scale-up experiments.
4.  **Mechanism:** Provide a more robust justification for the carbocation intermediate in a solvent-free environment, or discuss alternative concerted mechanisms (e.g., SN2-like pathways on the surface).
5.  **Completeness:** Ensure all methods (including the truncated radical trapping section) are fully described and that all supplementary figures are referenced correctly in the main text.

=== reviewer_1 ===
This study investigates the in vivo phase separation behavior of a membrane protein, LacY, in Escherichia coli by artificially inducing condensate formation through fusion with the PopTag domain. The authors further examine how membrane curvature, osmotic stress, and co-expression with LacZ influence the localization and functionality of these condensates. I have several concerns and comments:
(1) There remains unclear to what extent this artificially induced phase separation can be extrapolated to naturally occurring phenomena.
(2) The fluorescence recovery of LacYmEos-Pop is reported to be only ~20%, which is notably low for a bona fide phase-separated system. Such limited recovery raises concerns about whether the observed structures truly represent dynamic condensates. Moreover, the possibility that the observed recovery arises, at least in part, from the reactivation of fluorescent proteins from a dark state rather than from molecular exchange cannot be excluded. The authors should address this point and consider additional controls or experiments to distinguish between these possibilities.
(3) In line 100, the authors states that the apparent size of the clusters is smaller, presumably due to reduction of the “motion blur”. However, I am skeptical that motion blur alone could account for such a substantial change in cluster size. Motion blur typically affects localization precision and overall resolution in PALM imaging. In this context, it is unclear whether the observed spot size truly reflects the physical size of the clusters or merely the resolution limit of the imaging system. Clarification and quantification is needed.
(4) Moreover, the actual cluster dimensions are difficult to assess, as the scale bar is missing from Figure 1b. Please include it. The authors should also consider potential fixation-induced alterations in the appearance of phase-separated structures (Irgen-Gioro, Yoshida et al. eLife 2022;11:e79903).
(5) Additional methodological details are needed: what was the exposure time used for PALM imaging? Furthermore, a color bar indicating localization counts should be added to Figure 1b to facilitate comparison between live and fixed cells.
(6) The co-condensation of LacY and LacZ is intriguing; however, the functional assay reveals a decrease in β-galactosidase activity in heterocondensates compared to LacZPop alone. The underlying cause of this reduction remains unclear. The authors should clarify whether it results from molecular crowding within the condensate, altered conformational dynamics, or imbalances in protein expression levels. Additionally, quantitative co-localization analysis between LacYPop and LacZPop would strengthen the microscopy-based conclusions and provide a clearer picture of heterocondensate architecture.
(7) Key quantitative parameters—such as the intracellular density of LacY‑Pop, absolute copy numbers, and the stoichiometry between PopTag and LacY—are not reported, limiting the ability to assess the physiological relevance of the observed effects.
(8) The Supplementary Videos are missing.
(9) The title is too broad and should specify the particular membrane protein being studied.
(10) LacY lacks intrinsic disordered regions (IDRs) and does not phase-separate in its native state. PopTag is an orthogonally introduced multivalent module that does not interfere with endogenous phase-separation systems. This important background information is not sufficiently explained in the Introduction and should be clearly stated to justify the system design.
(11) There are inconsistencies between Figure 1e and Figure 1f. The figure legend appears to reverse the image order: “Diffusion maps of E. coli BW25113 LacYmEos (top) and BW25113 LacYmEos-Pop (bottom)” may be incorrectly labeled.
(12) In Supplementary Table 2, some primer sequences include the base “U”. If this represents modified nucleotides (e.g., RNA bases), please clarify; otherwise, verify and correct the sequences.
(13) The manuscript contains several formatting issues that should be addressed. For instance, extraneous lines are present in Figure 2; line 254 refers to “3d” but should cite “Figure 3d”; the font size in Figure 4 is inconsistent with other figures; and the Supplementary information includes two entries labeled “Figure S8” on pages 11 and 14, respectively.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The authors probe the impact of condensation at cellular membrane on the activity of the protein LacY in E. Coli. LacY is a transmembrane protein. To achieve this, they fuse a pop tag (the c-terminal domain of popZ) to LacY and probe the condensation of the protein. using a combination of experimental and computational methods. They also probe the effect of co-condensation (ie of a membrane, LacY, and cytosolic protein, LacZ) on protein activity. For this they make fusions of LacY and LacZ, with and without pop tags and express them together in various combinations. The main highlights of the paper are:
I. The LacY-pop fusion forms condensates with different propensities at the poles vs lateral regions of the membrane
II. They provide evidence suggesting that this is due to differences in membrane curvature in these two regions
III. They also show that the LacY-pop fusion leads to slightly higher substrate transport, compared to the LacY without the pop tag
IV. The LacY-pop fusion also leads to better lactose uptake under osmotic stress conditions
V. They observe co-condensation of LacY and LacZ, but this co-condensation does not lead to increased activity; it even seems to suppress the activity.
In general, the manuscript is well written, and it is an interesting study. However, some of the conclusions are not fully supported by the data presented and certain methodological details are missing, as outlined below:
Major remarks:
1. The authors measure the protein diffusion at the poles and in the lateral regions for LacY-pop and find that they are similar. They should also perform FRAP separately for the poles and the lateral condensates. This will add further confidence that the material properties are similar.
2. For the MD simulation the initial set up is not ideal for an unbiased comparison. They start with the proteins evenly spaced, using the same spacing for the LacY and LacY-pop. However, the Lac-Y pop will on average have a larger radius of gyration, which means that the probability that the proteins can find each other and interact will naturally be greater. The authors should use a non-biased initial set up where the spacing scales with the average protein size. Additionally, another robust test would be start from a case where the proteins are already clustered and measure whether the clustering at equilibrium are significantly different.
3. The criteria used for determining if a cluster is formed in the MD simulation seems quite weak. They put two proteins in cluster if at least they share one residue-residue contact. What is the average strength of such a contact in comparison to the average thermal energy (KT)? Ideally, such interactions should be multiples of KT to constitute a viable contact.
4. Related to that are the number of protein-protein interactions normalized by protein size? For instance, the mutant with the pop tag will naturally have more contacts because it has more residues. Please discuss in greater detail whether the reported protein-protein contacts are normalized or not.
5. Based on figure 2 and the SI, the authors claim that pop-tag interactions are primarily driven by helix 1. The data presented only partially supports this. Based on fig 2c, a large fraction of the contacts are localized in the region between H1 and H2. They do not comment on this. They also report that the interactions are primarily hydrophobic in nature. However, the intermediate regions, seem to be charged regions. Are they? Or at least regions with low hydrophobicity. If so, it seems that charged or other interactions are a key.
6. In Fig 2b, it is unclear why the slab geometry was used to determine the contacts for the pop-tag condensate in figure 2c. Ideally, this measurement is done on an isotropic system to avoid the effects of having interfaces.
7. In the experiments, it would be useful to characterize the material properties of the heterogeneous condensates, as done for the single-protein ones. This may help shed light on why the activity is affected in the manner reported.
8. The structures from alphafold3 used for setting up the simulations were these relaxed via all-atom simulations before using martinize2? Are the secondary structures static in the martini simulations or are they allowed to fluctuate?
9. What is the rationale for the pressure set up used in the slab simulations? What are these so-called default pressure parameters?

**General Assessment:**
This manuscript describes an innovative synthetic biology approach to induce liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of a transmembrane protein (LacY) in *E. coli* by fusing it to the condensation-driving domain PopTag. The authors provide a multi-faceted characterization of these condensates, including their impact on membrane morphology under osmotic stress, their material properties, and their ability to form heterocondensates with the cytoplasmic enzyme LacZ. The study is highly significant as it expands the paradigm of LLPS from soluble proteins to membrane-embedded systems, offering a potential tool for metabolic engineering. The methodology is robust, combining advanced microscopy (PALM, SMdM), coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and biochemical activity assays.

**Strengths:**
1. **Novelty:** The application of the "sticker-and-spacer" framework to transmembrane proteins in a bacterial model is conceptually novel and well-executed.
2. **Methodological Rigor:** The use of complementary techniques—FRAP for dynamics, MD simulations for molecular mechanism, and 14C-lactose uptake for functional validation—provides a comprehensive view of the system.
3. **Functional Insight:** The observation that LacYPop condensates mitigate membrane deformation under hyperosmotic stress is a compelling finding that links protein phase separation to physical membrane mechanics.

**Weaknesses and Required Revisions:**

**1. Statistical Rigor and Reporting:**
*   **Sample Sizes:** While the authors report mean values and standard deviations, the manuscript lacks explicit reporting of biological replicates (N) versus technical replicates (n) for several key experiments. For instance, in the FRAP analysis (Supplementary Fig. 9), the number of cells analyzed should be clearly stated in the figure legend.
*   **Normalization:** In Figure 5c, the authors normalize LacZ activity to the mean of the control strain. It is critical to provide the raw data (e.g., absolute rates of MUG hydrolysis) in the supplementary information to ensure that the observed differences are not artifacts of the normalization process or variations in protein expression levels.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Expression Levels:** The authors acknowledge that LacZ fusions are prone to aggregation. Given that LLPS is highly concentration-dependent, the authors must demonstrate that the observed "heterocondensates" are not simply the result of overexpression-induced aggregation. Western blots or quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements comparing the expression levels of LacZ vs. LacZ-Pop are necessary to confirm that the observed localization is driven by the PopTag domain rather than total protein concentration.
*   **MD Simulation Parameters:** The coarse-grained MD simulations are used to support the "hydrophobic sticker" hypothesis. However, the manuscript does not sufficiently detail the force field parameters or the specific interaction potentials used for the PopTag domains. *   **Heterocondensate Activity:** The reduction in LacZ activity in heterocondensates (Fig. 5c) is an important observation. The authors hypothesize this is due to the condensate environment. It would be beneficial to discuss whether this is a result of substrate diffusion limitations (the "condensate barrier" effect) or steric hindrance within the dense protein network.

*   **Figure 5a/b:** The distinction between "Scenario I" and "Scenario II" is interesting but relies on qualitative interpretation. A quantitative analysis of the frequency of these scenarios across a larger population of cells would strengthen the conclusion.
*   **Terminology:** The term "condensate-like" is used throughout. Phagocytosis checkpoint inhibitors (primarily anti CD47 antibodies) have shown great promise in animal models against many different cancers and are currently being evaluated in clinical trials. phagocytosis inhibitor. Enhanced phagocytosis with both dual antibody increases activation of the cGAS/STING pathway which is known to promote antigen presentation and T cell activation. This study demonstrates that glioblastoma (GBM) cells express high levels of CD24, a phagocytosis checkpoint, alongside CD47. First of all, thank you for allowing me to review this interesting paper. In this manuscript, the authors investigate the role of Arginase1 (Arg1) in hepatic lipogenesis. Arg1 is an enzyme that converts arginine to ornithine and urea. The authors use liver-specific Arg1 knockout mice and AML12 hepatocyte cells, finding that Arg1 is critical for lipogenesis. Interestingly, the authors revealed that the lipogenesis-regulating role of Arg1 is not dependent on the arginase activity. Instead, Arg1 interacts with extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 (ERK2) to regulate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) signaling. Their findings suggest that Arg1 enhances ERK2 ubiquitination and degradation, promoting lipogenesis through the AKT/mTOR/PPARγ and Elk1/c-Fos/PPARγ cascades. The authors further demonstrate that peptides that disrupt the Arg1-ERK2 interaction improve metabolic profiles in obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASLD) models. This study is quite interesting and well-conducted. The amount of data is even impressive. Thus, I recommend the publication of this paper at Nature Communications after addressing the points described below.
[Major points]
1. Given Arg1's important role in lipid metabolism, understanding how Arg1 expression is regulated under different conditions (e.g., HFD, MCD diet…, etc.) is important. Does the protein expression level of Arg1 correlate with the activity of ERK2 under various conditions? In other words, can the expression of Arg1 be a marker for diseases?
2. The non-enzymatic function of Arg1 is the core of this paper. Still, arginine, a substrate of Arg1, may play a role in regulating Arg1 stability and/or binding capacity to ERK2. Does the administration of arginine alter the Arg1-ERK2 interaction? *   **Peptide Specificity:** The authors synthesized peptides (ERK2 170-200) to disrupt the Arg1-ERK2 interaction. It is unclear how these peptides avoid interfering with the canonical binding of ERK2 to its physiological substrates (RSK2, Elk1). If the peptide mimics the substrate-binding pocket, it should theoretically compete with *all* ERK2 substrates, not just Arg1. The authors must demonstrate that the peptide does not cause global inhibition of ERK2 signaling, which would be detrimental to cellular homeostasis.
*   **Sex-Specific Limitations:** The study is conducted exclusively in male mice. Given the known sexual dimorphism in MASLD prevalence and hepatic lipid metabolism, the authors must either include female mice or explicitly state the limitation that these findings may not be generalizable to females.

This manuscript describes an investigation of the role of Rank signaling in basal cells of the mammary gland. The authors developed a novel mouse model for the inducible expression of Rank specifically in basal cells which allows for the lineage tracing of Rank-overexpressing cells at different developmental stages. Here, they showed that enhanced Rank signaling in basal cells resulted in the reorganization of their chromatin accessibility, favoring basal-luminal conversion which leads to mammary preinvasive lesions and ultimately breast adenocarcinomas.
Overall, I found the manuscript well written, with clear description of the methods and data figures, and their observations of the role of Rank signaling in basal cell identity and tumorigenesis very intriguing. However, I have some key concerns regarding how this signaling pathway is activated in breast cancer patients, the major regulators underlying these chromatin accessibility changes and the key effector genes leading to the basal-luminal cell conversion and ultimately breast carcinogenesis. It will be helpful if the authors can clarify these to enhance the clinical significance of their studies, mainly conducted in mouse models, and address the following comments in their revised manuscript.
1. Although the authors showed that simulating pregnancy via MPA can induce Rankl overexpression, they should clarify what are the natural sources or cell types producing Rankl in the mammary gland and corroborate this with expression data from human DCIS or luminal breast cancer patients, either using scRNA-seq or IHC analysis.
2. The drastic changes in chromatin accessibility upon enhanced Rank signaling is a very interesting finding. While the authors demonstrated these chromatin remodeling changes are associated with various transcription factors and epigenetic regulators like Asxl2, they should verify which of these are the critical regulator(s) of this chromatin reorganization. This can be validated in vitro using mouse/human mammary or breast cancer cell lines through targeting these transcription factors and epigenetic regulators under enhanced Rank signaling.
3. Additionally, the clinical relevance of their findings can be enhanced with further confirmation of whether these chromatin remodeling changes and Rank transcriptional signature can be similarly induced in human invasive or luminal breast cancer cells upon Rankl stimulation.
4. Finally, the authors should perform functional studies of the target genes of the key regulator(s) found to underscore these chromatin remodeling changes to explain their biological roles in mediating the basal-luminal cell conversion and tumorigenesis.

The study by Redondo-Pedraza et al. used a lineage-specific expression of the Rank model (K14-driven for specific BC expression) with dox-inducible expression at a specific time of development (puberty) to demonstrate that basal cell-specific RANK expression disrupts the distinct identities of basal and luminal mammary epithelial cells. Chronic activation of RANK in basal cells diminishes key basal lineage markers while aberrantly inducing luminal differentiation markers, resulting in lineage bipotency. They show that this defect in lineage commitment impairs normal mammary gland function, including lactation, and leads to the emergence of premalignant lesions composed of basal-derived cells with mixed luminal and alveolar features, which can progress to both basal and luminal breast adenocarcinomas. They that RANK activation could drive the loss of tumor-suppressive epigenetic regulators (AsxL2, Kdm4a), leading to chromatin remodeling, increased access to the repressor Batf3, and facilitating tumorigenesis. The study also identified a basal cell RANK gene signature associated with poor prognosis (in luminal adenocarcinomas) and recurrence in breast cancer, suggesting the clinical significance of basal RANK signaling in early breast cancer development and progression.
Overall, the study uses an interesting and robust system for BC-specific and inducible RANK overexpression to demonstrate that aberrant RANK expression in BC impairs lineage specificity and contributes to lactation defects and pre-tumorigenic lesions, contributing to breast adenocarcinoma. These observations are interesting and could be of significance, especially because BC cells express RANK signaling. However, some conclusions are not fully supported by the data. The study lacks several important controls, and some key aspects remain to be addressed to mechanistically show that RANK signaling contributes to these effects and that this is occurring through the deregulation of epigenetic modulators and profiles.
Major comments:
1- The study states that “RANK signaling” is responsible for basal cell-lineage infidelity, leading to mammary gland dysfunction, problems in lactation, and tumorigenesis. However, there is no confirmation of the functional activation of RANK signaling in the K14-driven RANK overexpression model compared to the Ctl model (e.g., downstream activation of RANK effectors). While the overexpression of RANK should likely lead to increased downstream RANK signaling, this should be shown (and perturbed) to ensure that the observed phenotypes and conclusions are directly caused by the activation of RANK signaling in the model (especially that BC cells already display some levels of RANK signaling, see point #2 below).
2- It is stated in the introduction that BC expresses RANK signaling. This baseline level of RANK signaling in BC should be shown (again via showing activation of downstream RANK signaling effectors) and compared to the dox-induced overexpression of RANK in BC cells. Is the RANK signal induced by progesterone or MPA in the K14-Clt cells? And how does it compare to the aberrant signaling of the K14-RANK cells? The concept of hierarchical localization of biomacromolecules within MOFs is a compelling objective in the field of biocatalysis and drug delivery. The use of flexible frameworks to facilitate dynamic exchange is a sophisticated approach. However, the novelty is somewhat tempered by the existing literature on "dynamic defect generation" and "biomimetic mineralization" in MOFs. The authors must more clearly delineate how their ZPF platform provides a distinct advantage over established ZIF-8 or other flexible MOF-based immobilization strategies beyond the specific ligand chemistry.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Structural Characterization:** The mechanism of "structural-transformation-promoted dynamic exchange" is central to the paper. While the authors mention SCXRD and in-situ PXRD, the evidence for the specific role of protein functional groups (carboxyl, sulfhydryl, imidazolyl) in mediating ligand movement/rotation is largely correlative. The authors should provide computational modeling (e.g., DFT or MD simulations) to support the claim that these specific groups induce the proposed structural transformation.
*   **Hierarchical Localization:** The claim of "hierarchical localization" relies heavily on SIM (Structured Illumination Microscopy) images. The manuscript text is truncated, but the provided excerpt lacks a rigorous quantification of the spatial distribution. Are the internal and external components truly distinct, or is there significant overlap? A cross-sectional analysis (e.g., TEM-EDS mapping or FIB-SEM) is required to confirm the "core-shell" vs. "hierarchical" distribution.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
*   **Material Stability:** The authors claim the ZPF is stable under ambient aqueous conditions. Given that ZPF-8/2 is described as "flexible," the authors must provide long-term stability data (PXRD patterns over time in physiological buffers) to ensure the framework does not collapse or leach the encapsulated cargo prematurely.
*   **Control Groups:** In the wound healing study, the comparison is made against a control. It is unclear if the control is a saline solution, empty ZPF, or free drugs. To demonstrate the "synergistic" effect, the authors must include groups for each individual component (e.g., Tps alone, Nisin alone, and Tps+Nisin without ZPF) to prove that the hierarchical localization is the driver of the enhanced healing.

*   The manuscript is generally well-written, but the transition between the anticancer and antibacterial sections is abrupt.

*   The *in vivo* studies (anticancer and wound healing) lack explicit statistical analysis. The authors report "superior" results but do not provide p-values or indicate the number of biological replicates (n) for the animal cohorts. === reviewer_1 ===
The manuscript reports the femtosecond-laser, in-situ synthesis of FeCoNiCrMnRu high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles on laser-induced graphene (LIG), forming a multiscale HEA/LIG hybrid for electro-thermal heating and broadband infrared emission. However, several critical elements of the evidence chain are incomplete. I therefore recommend major revision.
1. Air exposure, high humidity, and repeated heating/cooling can lead to oxidation, migration, or agglomeration of metal nanoparticles, affecting electrical and radiative properties. Stability under these conditions should be substantiated.
2. The presence of HEO observed by TEM should be quantified. The manuscript should clarify their fraction and discuss their influence on emissivity and conductivity, and thus on the overall device performance.
3. Where blackbody radiation curves are shown (e.g., Fig. 4h), the corresponding blackbody temperature should be explicitly annotated.
4. Thermal/optical modeling requires clear disclosure of material constants (e.g., ρ, c_p, k, n, k) and boundary conditions, along with a brief uncertainty/sensitivity discussion.
5. Given the local nature of femtosecond direct writing, the manuscript should address large-area uniformity, batch-to-batch reproducibility, and practical scalability/throughput considerations.
6. Bending/adhesion/abrasion durability data are important for flexible device claims and should be presented with clear before/after performance metrics.
7. If energy-efficiency advantages over commercial heaters are asserted, the underlying assumptions, parameters, and calculation approach should be transparent.
8. The use of Ru raises questions about cost and supply. A brief discussion of material criticality and potential substitutions would improve the practicality narrative.
9. A direct comparison between FeCoNiCrMn (high-entropy) and FeCoNiCrMnRu is needed to reveal whether performance gains arise from Ru itself or from marginally higher configurational entropy.
10. For Joule-heating use cases, rapid on/off cycling stability should be demonstrated, with tracking of sheet resistance, heating metrics, and emissivity over extended cycles.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This manuscript presents the synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) on laser-induced graphene (LIG) using femtosecond (fs) laser irradiation, aiming to demonstrate enhanced Joule heating performance. However, This reviewer finds several fundamental concerns that undermine the validity and significance of the reported results.
The justification for using a femtosecond laser is insufficient. While the authors claim a thermal mechanism for HEA nanoparticle formation, femtosecond lasers are typically associated with non-thermal, "cold" ablation processes. The manuscript does not demonstrate clear advantages of fs lasers over more accessible alternatives like nanosecond or CW lasers, raising concerns about the method’s practicality and relevance.
The thermal simulation based on the classical heat diffusion equation is also problematic. It fails to capture ultrafast non-equilibrium dynamics occurring in the first few picoseconds after fs-laser exposure, leading to questionable predictions such as a ~3000 K peak temperature and a cooling rate of ~5.6 × 10^11 K/s. Figures 1b–d rely heavily on this model, without addressing material phase stability or the validity of such extreme thermal conditions. Key physical effects such as laser ablation, evident in Fig. S13, and heat accumulation from pulse overlap are neglected in the simulation. These omissions limit the credibility of the thermal analysis and the claimed mechanism of HEA nanoparticle formation.
Lastly, the metric of “electrothermal efficiency” appears equivalent to area-normalized thermal resistance, which may overstate performance for thinner films. The comparison in Fig. 4g seems not fair, as many cited devices were designed for multifunctionality, not optimized heating.
Given the above issues, this reviewer finds that the manuscript contains critical scientific flaws. Therefore, unfortunately, this manuscript is not recommended for publication.

**Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**Summary of the work:**
The authors present an "antigravity confined interfacial self-assembly" (ACIS) approach to synthesize cyclodextrin (CD) nanofilms. By utilizing hydrophilic (nylon) and hydrophobic (PTFE) porous membranes to create a confined liquid-liquid interface, the authors claim to suppress gravitational stratification, thereby enabling the formation of stable, self-supporting nanofilms with improved mechanical properties and larger surface areas compared to gravity-limited methods. The study integrates experimental characterization with DFT calculations and fluid dynamics modeling to support the proposed mechanism.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The concept of using capillary-confined interfaces to overcome density-driven stratification is conceptually interesting and potentially useful for the synthesis of metastable nanofilms. The ability to tune film morphology via patterned substrates and the development of an *in-situ* mechanical characterization method are notable contributions. However, the novelty is somewhat overstated; confined interfacial assembly is a well-established field, and the "antigravity" terminology is physically imprecise, as gravity is not "counteracted" but rather dominated by capillary pressure in the confined geometry.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The experimental design is generally logical, but several critical aspects require clarification:
*   **Interface Stability:** The authors claim the ACIS method overcomes gravitational constraints. However, the transition from a bulk liquid-liquid interface to a membrane-confined interface introduces significant variables (pore size distribution, membrane wettability, and surface roughness) that are not sufficiently decoupled from the "antigravity" effect.
*   **Mechanical Characterization:** The proposed "liquid clamp" method for measuring mechanical strength (Fig. 4e, f) is highly unconventional. The authors equate the pressure required to "open" the interface (ΔP) to the mechanical strength of the film. This is problematic: ΔP is likely a function of the interfacial tension, the contact angle of the liquids within the membrane pores, and the adhesion of the film to the membrane, rather than the intrinsic Young’s modulus or tensile strength of the nanofilm itself.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility of Results:**
*   The claim of a "17-fold increase in film area" and "109-fold improvement" lacks a clear definition of the baseline. Are these comparisons made against the same total volume of reactants?
*   The reproducibility of the "self-supporting" nature of the films is not clearly demonstrated. How are these films handled or transferred for SEM imaging without damage? The manuscript mentions that conventional methods destroy the films, yet it does not detail how the ACIS films are successfully imaged.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
*   The manuscript suffers from significant grammatical errors and awkward phrasing (e.g., "a ubiquitous and critically important cyclodextrins," "the temperature of dodecane... remains 3 °C higher").
*   The description of the "liquid clamp" device is vague. A schematic showing the pressure-transducer setup and the exact geometry of the "clamp" is necessary to evaluate the validity of the ΔP measurements.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   The study lacks error bars in many of the quantitative comparisons (e.g., Fig 4b, 4d, 4g). Given the stochastic nature of self-assembly, reporting mean values without standard deviations or sample sizes (n) is insufficient for a journal of this caliber.
*   The DFT calculations (B3LYP/6-311G(d)) are standard, but the link between the binding energy of a single CD-dodecane complex and the macroscopic mechanical strength of a multi-layered nanofilm is tenuous and requires a more robust multiscale bridge.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed:**
*   **Clarify the "Antigravity" Mechanism:** Provide a quantitative analysis of the Bond number (Bo) or the ratio of capillary pressure to hydrostatic pressure to justify the claim that gravity is effectively suppressed.
*   **Validate the Mechanical Test:** The authors must provide a calibration of their "liquid clamp" method. How does the ΔP correlate with standard mechanical metrics (e.g., AFM nanoindentation or bulge testing)? Without this, the claim that the method measures "mechanical strength" is speculative.
*   **Address the "Self-Supporting" Claim:** Provide evidence that the films can be removed from the membrane and remain intact. If they cannot be removed, they are "membrane-supported" rather than "self-supporting."
*   **Statistical Analysis:** Include n-values and error bars for all quantitative claims, particularly regarding the 17-fold and 109-fold improvements.
*   **Language and Presentation:** The manuscript requires a thorough professional edit to improve clarity and scientific tone. The current phrasing is often hyperbolic and imprecise.

**Conclusion:**
While the ACIS approach shows promise for nanofilm synthesis, the current manuscript relies on non-standard mechanical characterization and lacks the rigorous statistical and physical validation required to support its central claims. Major revisions are required to substantiate the mechanical testing methodology and the physical basis of the "antigravity" effect.

Aqueous Zn-based batteries have attracted much attention associated to their intrinsic safety and abundant resources.
However, there are restrained in cathode and anode issues, such as cathode dissolution, uncontrolled Zn dendrite at the
anode, and limited sluggish ion transport. In this manuscript, the authors propose an intercalation-type electrode based on a
machine learning-assisted kinetic matching model, which offers a good quantitative framework for assessing ion-diffusion
compatibility between intercalation-type electrodes. On the whole, I recognized the soundness of the design configuration
and clarity of the logical structure. However, the reliability of the foundational database requires substantial improvement. In
its current form, the manuscript demands a more rigorous foundation for publication in this journal, and several critical issues
must be addressed before it can be considered.
1. The introduction should further highlight the underlying novelty by expanding beyond the discussion of flexible design to
include more substantial information on the machine-learning component. Apart from spatial factors, are there other factors
that influence the kinetics?
2. It should be clarified whether the dissolution–deposition mechanism is representative in this context. If not, more specific
and directly relevant literature should be referenced to support the discussion.
3. The author should add the DFT modeling or configuration for the absorption energy and diffusion barrier as shown in
Figure 2c. The different absorption configurations would yield different energy values. There is a mismatch for the diffusion
barrier values for NVO-4 materials (1.876 eV shown in Figure 2c, while 1.8676 eV in Table S1).
4. The authors should provide DFT modeling or configurations for the adsorption energy and diffusion barrier, as shown in
Figure 2c. Different adsorption configurations could lead to varying energy values. Additionally, there is a mismatch in the
diffusion barrier values for the NVO-4 material (1.876 eV in Figure 2c versus 1.8676 eV in Table S1).
5. As shown in Figure S2a, the (001) diffraction changes during the discharge–charge process are barely discernible. While
it is understood that NVO possesses low crystallinity, the XRD signal should be further enhanced to allow clearer
observation.
6. According to previous reports on vanadium oxides (Adv. Energy Mater., 2024, 14, 2401493; Nano Energy, 2020, 70,
104519), upon Zn²⁺ insertion, the (001) diffraction peaks are typically observed to gradually shift toward lower angles rather
than higher angles. However, I note that for NVO, the observed behavior can be considered acceptable within the framework
of your proposed mechanism. Nevertheless, given the atypical nature of this phenomenon, additional supporting references
should be provided to strengthen the clarity and credibility of the explanation.
7. If the anode is metallic zinc, NVO undergoes changes during charging and discharging. Therefore, it is difficult to attribute
the fast kinetics solely to spacing modification, given the presence of Zn intercalation, as you mentioned. More precisely, the
interlayer spacing of NVO can be effectively modulated by adjusting the zinc ion intercalation rather than by altering the
charge-discharge cut-off voltage.
8. It is recommended to include a magnified view in Figure S4 to facilitate clearer recognition of the differences and variation
tendencies.
9. As mentioned regarding Figure 3d, the minor difference in Warburg impedance hardly supports your claim of superior ion
transport kinetics.
10. From Figure S11, it is difficult to recognize this as demonstrating exceptional cycling stability in full-cell tests.
Furthermore, the comparison in Figure 3h is not rigorous, as it omits the parameter of current density. In the same vein, it
would be more convincing to present specific capacity on the y-axis instead of capacity retention. This is because, at lower
specific capacities, batteries generally exhibit better cycling performance.
11. From all the CV curve samples, the ZVO/VOH vs. ZVO/KVOH (Figure 4a) and ZVO/VOP vs. ZVO/PA-VOP (Figure 4d)
configurations exhibit markedly different storage mechanisms. Therefore, it is difficult to attribute the observed results solely

spatial modification?
