Review of manuscript “New paleomagnetic evidence constrained tectonic drift to trigger the Early
Permian aridification of North China” by Ren et al. for publication in Nature Communications.
This manuscript presents new paleomagnetic and U-Pb geochronology results from 2 Permian
section in North China. The authors then use the obtained age and paleolatitude constraints to
establish a paleolatitude sequence and argue for tectonic explanations for the observed climatic
shifts in North China compared to Pangea. Furthermore, using a Monte Carlo simulation the
authors argue for rapid northward motion that caused the aridification in the area.
While I do generally agree with the authors that the data is of high quality and the conclusions are
certainly based on the data, I do find some problems in the presentation and argumentation, which
should be addressed before the paper can be published.
I will focus on the paleomagnetic data and implications, because this is what I know best. I am not
a particular expert for the Permian climatic evolution, especially the differences between North
China and Pangea. After reading this manuscript, I do agree that the topic is important and of great
interest. However, it sounds more like the authors strengthen a former hypothesis with new high-
quality data. This does not address the complexity in climatic evolution between an island and a
neighbouring supercontinent including a more or less confined ocean basin. So I am not sure if the
presented story is rightly placed at Nature Communications. Having said that, I do believe that
robust data is always good especially for controversial topics like this.
Regarding the general presentation, I would suggest the authors get some native English speaker
with knowledge of geology to correct the English language. The text sounds often very strange to
me, which makes it at times hard to understand (e.g. l.63: “It provides important a unique…”).
Secondly, I am very sceptical that the fold test of the Qingfengshan Fm is correct. Fig. 2c shows the
fold test for the Dahongshan Fm, which has some high scatter before untilting and far less scatter
after untilting. There the picture in Fig.2c is very likely. However, the directions of Qingfengshan are
very similar, which should not result in such a graph, but a much flatter one. Doing a fold test
myself, I got a vey different result with an almost flat line (the maximum is still around 100%).
Maybe I missed something, but the authors should definitely check this. I am not arguing against
primary origin, which is also shown by the reversal test, but the presentation should be consistent.
Finally, and most importantly, I do have some problems with the arguments for the high plate
velocity. Generally, the arguments by the authors makes sense, and it is very justified to argue for
climatic changes related to latitudinal changes. However, I have some points of criticism in the
authors argumentation: (1) why do the authors not use data from the same section with maybe the
same lithology? In Siziwangqi for example, there is an age of 277 not far above the sampling with
similar volcanic rocks, which would be a good target as well? Seeing the latitudinal changes in one
section would be more convincing, since both areas are also represented by different lithologies.
This leads to my second point (2) the inclination shallowing correction is very well carried out, while
112 samples are sufficient but on the lower end (Tauxe and Kent are proposing to use more than
100), but the uncertainty of this analysis is quite large. This is related to the lack of elongation
and to the method itself. In my experience, this technique is very susceptible to outliers, so it is not
very stable with this low amount of samples. In any case, the uncertainties of this analysis should be
taking into account, which the authors don’t do. In the study, if I understand it correctly, the authors
use the resulting inclination with the corresponding alpha95 value, which is very small. Only
using this values the authors get a high shift in latitudes. Taking the uncertainties into account would
only require a very low latitudinal shift between the two results when taking the low end of the EI
uncertainty interval. Again, I do believe the data is of very high quality and this is a good story, but I
think some more discussion should be presented to take the data seriously.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This is a clear and interesting study arguing for the primary trigger of the late Paleozoic to early
Mesozoic aridification of North China by paleomagnetism, which yields two seemingly robust Early
Permian paleomagnetic poles from the northern margin of the North China Block (NCB), indicating
a fast-northward drift from the tropical humid to subtropical arid zones during the period between
~290 and ~281 Ma. Although the topic, rapid-northward drift of the NCB triggered the aridification of
North China, could be traced back at least more than two or three decades ago (e.g., Wu, HN et al.,
Chinese J Geophys. 1990; Cope et al., Inter. Geol. Rew. 2005), and the comprehensive review of the
published late Paleozoic to early Mesozoic paleomagnetic poles shows the rapid latitudinal
movement of the NCB (from ~10°N to >20°N) was occurred around the Permian-Triassic boundary
(i.e., ~260-240 Ma, Figure 3 of Huang et al., Earth Sci. Rev. 2018), the new Early Permian robust
paleomagnetic results from this study provide more robust evidence to constrain the northward
drift history of the NCB, which might be the primary trigger for the aridification of North China
during the late Paleozoic to early Triassic times.
Firstly, the first Early Permian paleomagnetic pole (~290 Ma) is isolated from a suit of lava flow with
robust field tests supporting its high quality for paleogeographic reconstruction. Whilst another
Early Permian pole was identified from a clastic sequence, of course, with some tuff interbeds
providing absolute geochronological dating age around ~281 Ma. Both dual polarities and positive
fold test result indicate the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) was very likely the
primary romance acquired during the formation of the member I of the Qingfengshan Formation
(~1000-m thick). Although either the ~290 Ma pole from the volcanic rocks or the ~281 Ma pole from
the siltstones yield a comparable paleolatitude of around ~13°N-16°N at reference site (42.5°N,
119.5°E) for the NCB during the period of ~290-281 Ma, the authors prefer to use the E/I method to
perform an inclination shallowing correction for the clastic rocks and then yields a much higher
paleolatitude (~22°N) for the member I of the Qingfengshan Formation. Considering the late
Paleozoic volcanic and clastic rocks from the North China, South China and North Qiangtang
blocks (Zhao et al., 1990; Huang et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2013; Supplementary Table 3) yielded
compatible paleomagnetic results, which indicating none or no significant inclination shallowing
was observed from these clastic rocks in these blocks, I wonder if the ~281 Ma clastic rocks are
really suffered from significant inclination shallowing? If so, the main finding of this study (very fast
northward drift of the NCB during the Early Permian) should be a missense. For this issue, I suggest
the authors to do further studies such as the anisotropy of high-field IRM (hf-AIR, Billardello &
Kodama, 2009) to confirm if the suspicion is correct. In addition, noting that Meert et al. (2020)
state that “… any poles based on flattening corrections will not meet the R5 criterion unless the
inclinations are corroborated by paleomagnetic data from either intercalated volcanic rocks that
have a similar R-value or other sedimentary rocks within the same sequence that do not require
flattening corrections (Section 3.5, page 10)”, I do not think the ~281 Ma clastic flattening-corrected
pole (this study) is a robust evidence for the very fast northward drift history of the NCB during the
late Paleozoic to early Mesozoic.
Secondary, noting that paleomagnetic calculation of plate drift rate is strongly depend on the age of
paleomagnetic pole, the estimated age uncertainty of the selected paleomagnetic poles
(Supplementary Table 4) should be a key point for the discussions. I note that the authors give a age
error of 1.6 Ma for the ~281 Ma clastic pole; however, this age error is a geochronological dating
error for the tuff layer in the middle of the sampling section (Figure 1d) rather than the duration of
the sampled siltstone sequence (i.e., the member I of the Qingfengshan Formation), which was
conformably covered by the member II and member III of the Qingfengshan Formation with two
geochronological ages of ~257 to 254 Ma in the top of the member III and of ~273 Ma in the bottom
of the member II (Figure 1d). Considering the three members of the Qingfengshan Formation have
comparable thickness of ~1000 m, the member I of the Qingfengshan Formation may have a
duration around 10 million years, and if taking this age uncertainty into account, estimation of the
northward drift rate of the NCB during the Permian should be quite different. Anyway, for this issue,
the authors need to provide details about the age-error in the calculation.
Thirdly, the authors use the distribution of coal seams and red bed deposits to be the climate
indicators for the tropical humid and subtropical arid zones of the NCB, respectively, and conclude
that the NCB’s transition from the tropical humid to subtropical arid zone is diachronous ranging
from the Early Permian in the western and northern parts to the Late Permian in the southern
margin of the NCB (Figures 3-4 and Supplementary Figure 11). This view might be valid; however,
whether a suit of red rocks indicates an arid sedimentary environment also depends on its lithology
and sedimentary facies. For example, it was well known that Permian rocks in North China
basically began to turn red from the Lower Shihhotse Formation (Cisuralian), while the
sandstone actually turned red from the Shiqianfeng/Sunjiagou Formation (Lopingian). The Lower
Shihhotse and Upper Shihhotse (Cisuralian, Wu Q et al., Geology 2021) formations of North China
basically developed in delta plain environment, where sediments were deposited above the sea
level, in distributary channel or flood plain facies. In this sedimentary environment, the Lower
Shihhotse and Upper Shihhotse sandstones, developed in distributary channel facies, actually does
not show red color, while the flood plain facies mudstone, exposed in the air and experienced
long-term oxidation after sedimentation, generally displays red color. In other words, the red
mudstone in the flood plain facies probably does not represent a totally arid
environment. Instead, the assemblage of red mudstones and yellowish sandstones in
delta plain environment might reflect a transitional subhumid to subarid environment.
Generally, colors of terrestrial sandstones developed in fluvial facies or distributed
channel facies, having not been long-termly exposed to the air after sedimentation,
could be more reliable indicator of an arid environment. In North China, it was not until
the latest Permian (the upper part of the Lopingian Shiqianfeng/Sunjiagou Formation) that the
strata sequence was actually transformed into a fluvial facies red bed. In addition, Wu Q et al.
(Geology 2021) proposed a tectonism-related sedimentary unconformity of ~20 million years from
the late Cisuralian to Guadalupian (~280–260 Ma) between the Upper Shihhotse and Sunjiagou
formations, based on high resolution CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb dating. Regardless of whether the
unconformity is of general significance in North China, they clearly pointed out that the Upper and
Lower Shihhotse formations in central North China belong to the humid to subhumid zone, and only
evolved into an arid climate during the formation of the Lopingian Sunjiagou Formation. Thus, the
transition from tropical humid to subtropical arid environments was more likely a step-by-step
process.
Finally, even if the timing of the rapid northward migration of the NCB (from tropical humid to
subtropical arid zone) constrained by paleomagnetic data coincides well with the timing of the
aridification of the most of North China, whether the rapid migration of North China from tropical
humid to subtropical arid zone is the triggering mechanism or the primary factor of aridification in
North China still needs further studies. As concluded by Wu Q et al. (2021), “similarities in the floral
and climate shift histories between Euramerica and North China suggest that aside from the
regional tectonic controls and continental movement, extensive volcanism during the Cisuralian
may have played a major role in the global warming and aridification in the aftermath of the late
Paleozoic ice age (LPIA)”. In other words, current study may provide robust evidence for the rapid
northward migration of the NCB from the tropical humid to subtropical arid zones during the late
Paleozoic; but its significance and originality to the aridification of North China as well as the global
climate change after the LPIA is open to debate.

The manuscript presents new U-Pb ages and clumped isotope analyses from calcite veins formed in the eastern Betics. The
data reveal a single or multiple fluid event(s) from 8.5 to 5 Ma, which the authors link to extension and retreating
delamination. In addition, single-grain alpha-ejection corrected AHe ages of apatite give ages ranging from 15.2 to 3.1 Ma.
The data set is interesting and the U-Pb ages of calcite veins appear to be of high quality.
The main goal of the paper is to test if “delamination… triggered uplift at the origin of the Messinian Salinity Crises”. The
authors argue that there is “insufficient temporal resolution … to allow a clear distinction between delamination, detachment
and shortening as the main drivers of the uplift and exhumation that led to the MSC.” This may well be true, but it is not clear
how the authors’ data (U-Pb calcite ages of 8.5-5 Ma; AHe ages of 15.2-3.1 Ma) provide greater temporal resolution
concerning processes related to the origin of the Messinian salinity crises. In addition, the study only considers southern
Spain (Betic Cordillera) and not northern Morocco, where the most ages from volcanic rocks are available and where the
deepest marine gateway between the Atlantic and Mediterranean was located.
Lines 249-253: “Alternatively, elevation can also be well reproduced by the upwelling of hot asthenosphere, likely with a
fraction of melt as indicated by low S-wave velocity domain of 4.2 km.s-1 around 100 km (Figure 5a). Based on
parametrization of shear wave velocity-temperature 51 we determine anomalously high sub-lithospheric temperatures of
1550°C. Such a low viscous channel could easily explain the observed mean topography of 500 m around Tabernas Basin.”
In order to derive sufficient dynamic uplift to achieve the 500 m elevation of the Tabernas Basin, they need an
asthenospheric temperature 1550°C. This temperature is much higher than the standard asthenospheric temperature of
~1350°C and would require the presence of a mantle plume, for which there is no evidence. Using more realistic
temperatures for the asthenosphere, it is difficult to explain uplift of more than 300m. Therefore, the results of the modelling in
the manuscript seem unrealistic.
Lines 369-374: “It has been suggested that the transition from oceanic subduction to continental delamination was
responsible for the change between the pre-MSC high-K calc-alkaline, shoshonitic and ultrapotassic volcanism and the
emplacement of the most primitive magmatic rocks, comprising the isolated emission of post-MSC Na-alkaline basalts
(hawaiite) (2.9-2.3 Ma) 71. In contrast, we argue that the 3 Myrs gap between pre-MSC and post-MSC magmatism observed
in eastern Betics (Figure 6) is the consequence of shortening.” Certainly, shortening (compression) could be an explanation
for the 3 Myrs gap between silica-saturated calc-alkaline and K-rich volcanism and the silica-undersaturated Na-rich
volcanism, in comparison to Morocco where there is no such significant gap in the transition. Nevertheless, the manuscript
does not explain the sequence of volcanism. For example, in the model (figure 7) both the calc-alkaline and K-rich silica-
saturated volcanism appear to come from the metasomatized SCLM and result from lithospheric delamination, so why aren’t
both types of volcanism produced simultaneously? In other words, why does calc-alkaline volcanism preceed the K-rich
volcanism? It is also not clear why the external basins subside instead of being uplifted in conjunction with lithospheric
delamination. Uplift should result from removal of the dense lithospheric root, such that the overall density of the overlying
lithosphere is lower, but also to a lesser extent due to upwelling hotter asthenospheric mantle. The Na-rich volcanism
appears to be derived from the asthenosphere in their model. Considering that delaminating lithospheric mantle will cause
asthenosphere to upwell in its place, why isn’t there any silica-undersaturated Na-rich volcanism during the Miocene phase
of extension? Why does the silica-undersaturated sodic volcanism first appear with breakoff of the delaminated lithospheric
mantle in the author’s model?
Lines 374-378: “The MSC occurs during the latest stages of continental delamination retreat and extension initiated as early
as the EAB magmatic arc formed around 11 ± 1 Ma (Figure 7). We link the MSC to the topographic uplift caused by the
combination of mantle lithosphere thinning, magmatism, and mantle upwelling producing dynamic topography.” How is this
different from previous models, e.g. Duggen et al. (2003)? How have the author’s constrained the timing of these events
better with their data?
In figure 5, there is no scale relating color to seismic velocity.

The manuscript by Wei Feng and co-authors presents laboratory-derived evidence of fault weakening that appears to be controlled by the phase of water present at the frictional interface. With the help of a new hydrothermal rotary shear apparatus, the authors have probed a previously unexplored combination of controlled parameters:
1. sliding velocities spanning 5 decades, ranging from nucleation up to intermediate sub-seismic values,
2. large slip distances, and
3. water in liquid, vapor, or supercritical form.
The authors argue that previously documented mechanisms, i.e., dynamic weakening and strain localization in shear bands composed of aligned phyllosilicate minerals, are insufficient to explain the results of their experiments. Instead, based on the mechanical data from the experiments as well as extensive post-mortem analyses of the gabbro specimens, the authors propose two possible weakening mechanisms:
1. a chemistry-driven mechanism, whereby water in liquid or supercritical state weakens the gabbro interfaces to produce gouge consisting of weakly-bonded phyllosilicate minerals, and
2. a mechanical/physical mechanism, whereby the mixing of gouge particles with water produces a lubricant of appropriate viscosity to cause macroscopic weakening of the frictional interface.
A couple of limitations of the study, that, in my opinion, do not weaken its key conclusions, are:
1. The comparatively small total displacement in some of the experiments with the lowest sliding velocities, which may have prevented the system from reaching its steady-state. However, it is understandable that at such slow sliding velocities, reaching large displacements would require a significant amount of time.
2. For the modelling of temperature jumps, the assumption that all the mechanical energy is converted into heat is problematic, as there is evidence of gouge production in the experiments. This manuscript presents results of experimental measurements of frictional properties of gabbro at high-temperature hydrothermal conditions. The authors used a confined rotary shear apparatus to investigate how friction evolves as a function of slip and slip rate, specifically focusing on the state of aqueous pore fluid. The authors conducted experiments spanning 3 possible states of interstitial water: liquid, steam, and supercritical fluid. This is important because transitions between the states may significantly affect the fluid properties, solid-fluid interactions, and frictional strength. Such transitions can occur both as a function of depth, and as a function of slip rate when coseismic heating may substantially modify the local temperature on a slip interface. The authors find that the fluid state indeed controls the frictional properties of gabbro: for liquid water, friction is both slip and velocity weakening, while for steam (vapor) and supercritical state, friction is nearly velocity-neutral (but still slip-weakening). The authors attribute such different behaviors in part to formation of clay minerals, which they verified using a post-experiment microscopy analysis. The presented results are new and warrant publication in Nature Communications. Overall, the manuscript is well written and logically organized. The experimental procedures are well documented, and the methods are state of the art. The results should be of interest to a broad readership, including, but not limited to, experimentalists, seismologists, modelers, and field geologists. I recommend that this manuscript is published, pending a moderate review to address several comments, as described below.
1) While the experimental part of the study is robust, I am less convinced by the interpretation that appeals to the elasto-hydro-dynamic lubrication (EHDL) mechanism. For this mechanism to work, the fluid has to be essentially incompressible. The latter condition applies to water in a common liquid state, but not to water vapor or supercritical fluid, both of which are highly compressible, and therefore would not be very efficient at "flattening" the slip interface by elastic deformation. Between the three fluid stated, the EHDL would be most efficient in case of liquid water; however, the experiments show that in this case the residual dynamic strength is nearly independent of the slip rate (Fig. 1a,b). Based on these arguments, the EHDL is an unlikely mechanism responsible for the observed variations in dynamic friction.
2) The authors do not mention thermal pressurization as a possible mechanism. Is this because the slip rates are too low to cause a large enough temperature increase? Please elaborate. (The argument about fluid compressibility raised above would also apply in case of thermal pressurization.)
3) All of the presented experiments exhibit evolution of friction from "peak" to "steady state" over a characteristic distance of the order of 1 m (Fig.1 a,c,e). A similar evolution (although of smaller magnitude) was reported in rotary shear experiments on dry gabbro (e.g., www.nature.com/articles/nature11370). Could there be a common mechanism, possibly enhanced by the presence of fluid? Please discuss.
4) line 35. Instead of "at seismic deformation conditions", consider "at seismic slip rates", or "at seismogenic conditions".
5) line 78. "to a much extent" -> "to a much greater extent".
6) line 90. "After the experiments, the slip surfaces were ultra-polished and lineated" - it would help to include a figure illustrating this, perhaps in Supplementary Materials.

The authors note that these pathways are also found in mesophilic *Nitrospira*, which undermines the claim that these are specific "cold-adaptation" strategies. The authors should tone down the deterministic language regarding these genes unless they can provide comparative genomic evidence showing enrichment of these pathways in Antarctic vs. non-polar *Nitrospira*.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   The statistical analysis of the geochemical data is sufficient.
*   However, the link between the abundance of comammox and the rate of nitrification needs stronger statistical support. Did the authors perform correlation analyses (e.g., Spearman/Pearson) between the relative abundance of *amoA* genes and nitrate concentrations across the different sites? This would strengthen the claim that these organisms are the primary drivers.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Chlorate Specificity:** The authors must explicitly address the limitations of chlorate inhibition in the Discussion. They cannot claim it confirms comammox activity without acknowledging the potential for off-target effects on other nitrifiers.
*   **Genomic Speculation:** In the section "Adaptation to oligotrophic conditions," the authors admit that the *mtnE* gene is missing in their MAGs. They should clarify if this pathway is truly functional or if it is a pseudogene/incomplete pathway.
*   **Data Availability:** The manuscript must include a Data Availability statement confirming that the 1968 MAGs have been deposited in a public database (e.g., NCBI/ENA) with accession numbers provided.
*   **N2O Production:** The authors state that comammox *Nitrospira* have low N2O production potential. Please provide the specific genomic evidence (e.g., absence of *nor* genes) to support this, rather than relying solely on the incubation results.
*   **Clade B vs. A:** The authors emphasize the dominance of Clade B. A brief phylogenetic tree (or reference to one) showing the placement of La1-X1 and La3-X1 within the broader *Nitrospira* phylogeny would be helpful for readers unfamiliar with the specific clade B/A distinctions.

**Final Assessment:**
This is a strong paper that will be of interest to the microbial ecology community. Addressing the limitations of the inhibition assays and tempering the claims regarding "cold-adaptation" genes will significantly improve the manuscript's impact and scientific accuracy.

=== reviewer_4 ===
SUMMARY:
Kizovski et al 2024 present evidence gathered by the Perseverance rover for Fe-phosphate minerals on the surface of Mars.
This evidence includes textural, chemical, spectral, and diffraction analyses of grains discovered in a conglomerate outcrop
named “Onahu”. The evidence for the presence of Fe-phosphates in general is compelling, representing the most definitive
evidence for their presence on Mars presented thus far. The study also interrogates the specific minerals that occur in this
location and begins to build a paragenetic model of their occurrence. Data is assessed to be most consistent with the
minerals beraunite, metavivianite, and ferrolaueite. The fact that these minerals occur within a conglomerate made up
largely of ~basalt is unusual, but the key to their occurrence appears to be that this is a highly alternated conglomerate that
contains carbonate-rich matrix material. Indeed, the Fe-phosphates are apparently restricted to the matrix. Both authigenic
and a detrital models of origin for the minerals are discussed, followed by a brief discussion of the implications of the
findings for habitability. Overall, the paper makes a compelling contribution to the literature. I have some questions and
comments about the proposed paragenetic models and the discussion about habitability. On this basis, I recommend minor
revisions for the paper.
COMMENTS:
Is the origin of the minerals authigenic or detrital?
I did not fully understand the arguments presented regarding an authigenic or detrital origin of the Fe-phosphate minerals.
The authors seem to provide really quite compelling evidence against a detrital origin. In particular, the minerals are:
1) Only found in the carbonate-rich alteration matrix.
2) Soft minerals that have never been observed to survive the conditions of transport required to form a conglomerate.
3) Form on Earth either in surficial weathering zones or in oxidised hydrothermal systems in granitic pegmatites.
As far as I can tell, these points would seem to render a detrital origin extremely unlikely.
1) The alteration matrix formed in place after the conglomerate had already lithified, as indicated in the authors’ Fig. 4. A
detrital origin would presumably require a different texture i.e., where the minerals are no longer present in what looks pretty
clearly to be a post-deposition texture.
2) Minerals that are both very soft and low abundance are hard to preserve as detrital phases. Physical
feasibility of detrital secondary late paragenetic Fe-phosphates seems tricky.
3) Perseverance is sampling only surficial weathering zones. This lines up nicely with these minerals being weathering
products rather than detrital having formed in some earlier alteration phase of the material that was then transported to form
the conglomerate.
All of this is simply to say that, whilst the paper does not give a definitive answer either way and presents a detrital origin as
basically equally plausible to an authigenic one, I do not think the evidence seems to support that level of ambiguity. It would
probably be better if the discussion came down more clearly on the side of authigenesis, as per Fig. 4, having listed the
issues with a competing detrital hypothesis.
When did the minerals form?
Something else that was unclear to me is when in the life of Mars the authors imagine the minerals may have formed? I
know we cannot give any exact dates but could the authors contextualise the sequence of events in the history of Mars?
Mars is strongly oxidised today and ceased to have widespread aqueous activity a while ago. Is Onahu telling us something
about the changing surficial conditions, i.e., from reducing to oxidising to dry?
I think this would be useful to comment on. The authors hint at it with “evolving paleoenvironmental conditions” but do not go
on to say if this fits with emerging evidence for the environmental evolutionary timeline of Mars and the crater in general.
I am also wondering about the timing because the Onahu conglomerate is apparently >3.2 billion years old. I am a tad
sceptical that these secondary late paragenesis Fe-phosphates could be 3.2 billion years old, given how recent and
ephemeral the same minerals are when found in weathering zones on Earth. Then again, Mars is far less active than Earth
so perhaps the same rules do not apply. Could the authors add a rough timeline of events to their figure 4 along with a
corresponding broader environmental history of the crater and of Mars as a whole?
- Prebiotic chemistry and habitability
The implications of identifying Fe-phosphates for habitability and prebiotic chemistry on Mars are definitely substantial.
However, I think the paper could go a little further in specifying what these implications are. Mention is mainly made of the
fact that the conditions were probably habitable. However, this seems quite unsurprising. What is more exciting from my
perspective is that vivianite is an important mineral in the early P cycling literature. Therefore, we should be able to put some
numbers on P availability to early life and to prebiotic chemistry. Could the authors double check the literature and report
likely phosphate concentrations in the altering fluids that are consistent with vivianite precipitation? And again, echoing the
comments above, the timing of all this is important. Can we learn from these minerals about P availability 3+ billion years
ago, or only somewhat more recently?

This manuscript presents very interesting observations and proposes a compelling explanation for the observations.
Overall, I think that the manuscript is well written and well organized.
I do feel, however, that the title is a bit over-the-top. The fact that the observations indicate energy-dependent drifts is not a property of intrinsic magnetospheres (though that is where they have been observed so far); it is a property of magnetic field configurations larger than the gyroradius of the particles. Such behavior has been hypothesized to occur in smaller-than-global magnetic field configurations elsewhere including the Moon and Mars. I think these observations are very interesting, and a first for Mars, but not necessarily surprising.
Additionally, I do have some relatively minor comments below.
Figure 4: I am having some trouble understanding Figure 4b. I guess in general I understand that it illustrates the magnitude of the magnetic field along the magnetic equatorial plane, but I don’t understand the axes – particularly the vertical axis. What is the radial distance measured with respect to, and how does it go negative?
Figure 5 caption: I don’t think that “polygon” is the best descriptor for the shaded shapes in Figure 5. Perhaps it is more of a crescent shape (polygon implies straight rather than curved edges).
Line 433: On this line SWIA should be SWEA since it has to do with electron measurements.
To what altitude are the magnetic field lines traced? High order spherical harmonic magnetic field models become unphysical at too low an altitude. The manuscript states that the magnetic field model represents the crustal fields well at altitudes above 120 km. Are the field lines traced lower than that altitude?
Additionally, although it is not explicitly stated, I assume that the gradient in the magnetic field is calculated using the magnetic field model plus the constant offset rather than just the model (this is mentioned for the field line tracing but not for the other magnetic field calculations).
Supplementary Figure 5 (and line 220): It is mentioned and shown that no proton cyclotron waves are present locally. However, Supplementary Figure 5c does appear to show some wave power at a slightly lower frequency on the order of 0.1 Hz. Are these waves significant and can they be identified?
Supplementary Table 1: I am curious as to why the solar wind dynamic pressure is included in this table. I don’t recall dynamic pressure mentioned elsewhere in the manuscript. Additional, it brings up questions as to how the dynamic pressure was calculated given that MAVEN is not in the solar wind during the time of observation. Personally, I would be interested in the possibility of variations in the upstream dynamic pressure during the observations; could dynamic pressure variations drive upstream waves (as mentioned on line 207)? But I wouldn’t think that this information would be available given the spacecraft orbit.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The paper presents interesting MAVEN plasma and magnetic field observations around closest approach, when the spacecraft traverse through a region of crustal magnetic fields. The authors report, for the first-time, observations of wedgelike dispersion signatures of protons, exhibiting butterfly-shaped distributions within the Martian crustal fields, a feature observed in intrinsic magnetospheres. The authors argue that the observed structures can be understood in terms of drifts motions, despite the relatively weak and large inhomogeneity of crustal magnetic fields, compared to planetary global intrinsic magnetic fields. The authors also report the identification of 16 additional wedge-like dispersion events within the crustal magnetic field of Mars, observed by MAVEN.
In my opinion, this manuscript presents new, original observations suggesting wedge-like dispersion signatures of protons at Mars. This is worthy of further investigation and opens the possibility for complementary studies involving magnetic reconnection and planetary ion escape, in connection with crustal magnetic fields. The main concern I have with this paper is that the authors do not sufficiently explain the observed signatures in terms of particle drifts within crustal magnetic fields. I think the manuscript would benefit from additional estimations of relevant parameters, based on the properties observed by MAVEN and current crustal magnetic field models available in the literature.

=== reviewer_3 ===
Comments on “Discovery of Intrinsic Magnetospheric Ion Behaviour at Mars” by Zhang et al.
The manuscript describes observations of protons in Martian crustal magnetic fields that have dispersed energy signatures and oblique (or “butterfly”) pitch angle distributions that are asymmetric and correlated with the radial component of the crustal magnetic field. The manuscript discusses how the protons are injected into the crustal fields (reconnection), what causes their periodic occurrence in the crustal fields (periodic injections, heating, or variations in the source population), how the pitch angle distributions came to be asymmetric (scattering/drift of field-aligned/90-degree pitch angles), and how the energy dispersion signatures formed (higher energy ions drift deeper into the crustal fields).
Overall the phenomenon reported in the manuscript is novel for ions in the Martian magnetosphere (and any small-scale magnetosphere). I therefore believe that the community should be made aware of this work through publication, perhaps after some relatively minor comments below are considered. The main question in my mind is whether the work should be published in a high impact journal such as Nature Communications. Here, I am less certain, for three related reasons:
1. The signatures reported here for ions are similar in many ways (energy-time dispersion, bursty and periodic) to a previous report of observations of electrons in Mars crustal fields in 2016 by one of the manuscript’s co-authors, with similar interpretation about mechanisms. These similarities are not mentioned in the present manuscript at all, even though the paper (Harada et al.) is referenced. Though it is very interesting to see the same signatures in ions, what is learned overall from this manuscript about plasma behaviour in Mars crustal fields is therefore not particularly new.
2. The manuscript makes many references to “intrinsic magnetospheric behaviour” that the ion observations provide evidence for - saying in the opening paragraph that “…we report the discovery of intrinsic ion magnetospheric behavior at Mars…”. I am not fully convinced that this is a discovery, since there have been many previous reports of intrinsic magnetospheric behavior at Mars (e.g. aurora, magnetic reconnection). It may be that the emphasis in this phrase is on “ion” as opposed to "intrinsic magnetosphere", but I find this less compelling since the community is already aware that the crustal fields behave as intrinsic magnetospheres in other regards, and there are published studies of ion observations near crustal fields from both Mars Express and MAVEN.
3. The manuscript mentions that only 17 examples of these observations have been found in 5 years of observations. This suggests that the evidence of intrinsic magnetospheric behaviour is the exception, and not the rule.
I note that the figures are informative and useful, and the paper is generally well-written.
My detailed comments follow:
L26-28: The wording of this sentence was awkward for me. I think I understand the intent: “The Martian magnetosphere is unusual and different from intrinsic magnetospheres”. But I might have worded it a little differently: “Mars lacks a global dynamo magnetic field, and instead possess small-scale crustal magnetic fields, making its magnetic environment fundamentally different from intrinsic magnetospheres like those of Earth or Saturn.”
L31: Clarify “butterfly-shaped pitch angle distributions”
L36-37: This last sentence of the paragraph is vague, and ultimately not revisited in the manuscript in any detail.
L43: suggest change to “…play a key role in the planet’s atmospheric…”
L48: suggest change to “…how do the crustal fields control…”
L49: re: “provide new insights” - this statement would be stronger if the kinds of new insights that are possible are described.
L52: suggest change to “mini-magnetospheres”
L53: The Harada et al. paper is referenced here, in a general statement about scaled-down intrinsic magnetospheres. But the electron signatures are so similar to the ion signatures that they should really be called out. Otherwise it feels like they are being deliberately minimized in the present work. (I’m not surmising this is the authors’ intent. I’m just pointing out the impression it may give!)
L76-77: “can be regarded as key plasma evidence of intrinsic magnetosphere behaviour”. This statement is setting up the argument for the present manuscript that dispersed ion structures are evidence of an intrinsic magnetosphere. It reads to me like a bit of an overstatement - that dispersed ion structures are the -only- evidence of intrinsic magnetosphere behaviour. However, there are many signatures of intrinsic magnetospheres, and several have been previously reported for Mars. And dispersed energy-time ion signatures have been previously reported in the Martian magnetosphere - just not near crustal fields.
L83: suggest changing “could” to “does”
L105-106: suggest change to “…traversed the nightside terminator…”
L133: add “the” before “energy”
L134: suggest changing “were” to “was”
L144: please provide a reference here in the text to the crustal field model, since there are many in the community.
L164: remove “meticulous”
L195-197: What is the evidence that magnetic reconnection causes the injections of ions? Are there other possibilities? This section has two sentences - one basically gives the question and the next gives the answer with no substantive justification. I suggest adding more discussion here.
L202-203: “the pitch angle…Br”. I may have misunderstood this phrase, but think it could be reworded to be more clear. The specific pitch angle (e.g. 140 degrees) is not determined by Br. Instead, the asymmetry between parallel and antiparallel pitch angles is determined by Br.
L210: How could these three options be distinguished from each other?
L231: anisotropy —> anisotropic
L269: coordinates —> coordinate
L280-281: It seems like a lot of effort went into proving this statement that interior crustal field lines have higher field strength at the magnetic equator. This seems self-evident to me, without any demonstration required. Am I missing something? Second comment: The “MFL” and “MEP” acronyms are not standard in the literature, as far as I am aware. I understand why they were used - to avoid repetition in the discussion. But I ended up getting repeatedly lost while reading this paragraph and the several preceding paragraphs.
L303: suggest change to “According to the above results, the complete scenario of observed…”
L390-391: Are there peculiarities in the external conditions for the 17 identified events that could explain why they are only rarely observed?
L415-416: “crustal fields can locally provide a plasma environment similar to the planetary-scale intrinsic magnetospheres”. I agree with this statement, but don’t think this manuscript was the first to demonstrate this. Perhaps give other examples from the literature?

**Reviewer:** [Redacted]
**Date:** October 26, 2023
**Manuscript Title:** [Redacted]
**Journal:** Nature Communications

### 1. Significance and Novelty
The manuscript reports the observation of wedge-like ion energy dispersion structures within Martian crustal magnetic fields using MAVEN data. This is a compelling finding, as such structures are traditionally considered hallmarks of large-scale, planetary intrinsic magnetospheres (e.g., Earth, Saturn) where adiabatic drift motion dominates. The authors argue that these observations demonstrate that Martian crustal fields can act as "mini-magnetospheres" capable of supporting magnetized ion dynamics, effectively bridging the gap between unmagnetized and magnetized plasma regimes. This study provides a significant contribution to our understanding of solar wind-Mars interactions and the role of crustal fields in ion transport.

### 2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design
The methodology is generally sound, utilizing high-resolution data from MAVEN’s suite of instruments (SWIA, STATIC, SWEA, MAG). The use of Minimum Variance Analysis (MVA) to define the local coordinate system and the classification of magnetic topology are appropriate for identifying the closed-field line environment. The distinction between temporal and spatial effects—supported by the observation of both rising and falling tones—is a standard and robust approach in magnetospheric physics.

### 3. Quality and Reproducibility of Results
The results are presented clearly, and the identification of the dispersion structures is convincing. The correlation between the observed magnetic field and the crustal field model (with the addition of a steady background field) provides a plausible physical context for the observations. However, the reproducibility of the "butterfly" pitch angle distribution analysis is somewhat limited by the lack of detailed error propagation regarding the SWIA field-of-view (FOV) limitations. While the authors mention that 8% of the FOV is blocked, they do not explicitly quantify how this affects the pitch angle distribution symmetry in the specific energy bins (30–50 eV, 50–100 eV, 100–200 eV).

### 4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting
The manuscript is well-written and logically structured. The figures are informative, particularly the energy-time spectrograms. However, there is a significant gap in the reporting of the "induced field" component. The authors state that the observed field is a superposition of the crustal model and a constant vector [14.8, −0.93, −4.15] nT. The physical origin of this constant vector is not sufficiently explained. Is this a manifestation of the Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF) draped over the crustal field? If so, the authors must clarify how this influences the drift velocity calculations.

### 5. Statistical Rigor
The statistical rigor is generally acceptable for a case study. However, the authors assume that the dispersed ions are entirely H+. Given that the energy range (25–200 eV) overlaps with potential solar wind alpha particles (He2+) and that the mass-per-charge (m/q) resolution of STATIC can be ambiguous at low energies, the authors should provide a more quantitative assessment of the potential contribution of non-H+ species to the dispersion patterns. A simple assumption is insufficient for a high-impact journal.

### 6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed
Before the manuscript can be considered for publication, the following points must be addressed:

*   **Physical Origin of the "Induced Field":** The authors introduce a constant magnetic field vector to reconcile the model with observations. This needs a more rigorous physical justification. Does this vector represent the local IMF? If so, how does it interact with the crustal field to create the specific drift paths observed?
*   **Pitch Angle Distribution (PAD) Asymmetry:** The authors note an asymmetry in the butterfly distribution linked to the polarity of $B_r$. They must demonstrate that this asymmetry is not an artifact of the spacecraft’s orientation relative to the magnetic field vector or the SWIA FOV. A plot showing the coverage of the pitch angle space for the specific time intervals would be beneficial.
*   **Adiabaticity Check:** The authors claim the structures are "adiabatic." To support this, they should calculate the ratio of the ion gyroradius to the scale length of the magnetic field gradient ($\rho/L$). If the motion is truly adiabatic, this ratio must be significantly less than 1. Providing this calculation would greatly strengthen the claim that these are "mini-magnetospheres."
*   **Mass Composition:** The assumption that the dispersed ions are 100% H+ should be tested or at least qualified. Please provide a more detailed analysis of the STATIC mass-per-charge data to justify the exclusion of He2+ or other light ions.
*   **Clarity on "Wedge-like" definition:** The authors compare these to Earth’s magnetosphere. Please clarify if the drift velocity calculated from the dispersion slope is consistent with the expected $\nabla B$ and curvature drift velocities in the estimated crustal field geometry.

**Recommendation:** Minor Revision.

=== reviewer_1 ===
I very much enjoyed reading this manuscript, and find myself in the rather unusual position of having very few comments. My only substantive concern, detailed below, is that lack of information provided about spatial autocorrelation. Such information should absolutely be included in a revised manuscript, and ideally included in your mixed models.
L41-67. Although I am personally a little sceptical of the mechanistic explanations proposed to explain observed size reductions, it is nonetheless quite clear that such declines are occurring. And so I very much enjoyed reading this introduction, which nicely links the side-dependence of size declines with the use of predator-prey mass ratios as indicators of trophic interactions, and then to ecosystem function. Nice work.
Figure 1. My first impression when viewing this figure is that there is likely to be significant spatial autocorrelation in the data, which has the potential to significantly undermine your conclusions. I was therefore very pleased to see that you considered spatial autocorrelation in the data (L322). However, I was then disappointed that I cannot find any information about these analyses in the main text or supplementary information to reassure the reader. I apologise if I have missed this somehow, but I think that it will be important to present this information in a revised manuscript (and ideally you would account for the presence of spatial autocorrelation in your mixed models).

=== reviewer_2 ===
The study is carefully designed and the manuscript well written. I like how authors have combined predator and prey observations with the sampling of potential prey in the field. The subject is timely and impactful and helps to better understand the effects of temperature on community structure and biotic interactions. The outcomes demonstrate the effects of temperature after environmental and biotic filters have shaped the community. This, in my view, makes the work very informative for projecting the long-term effects of warming.
My primary concern is the emphasis on temperature effects on physiology and body size that authors have used to contextualize the paper. However, this paper examines the body size effects of temperature on the myctophid community. Hence, declines in body size can both be driven by changes in body sizes due to a physiological temperature effect on species, as well as community assembly processes that select differently sized species along the temperature gradient.
In my view, all observed outcomes can also be interpreted through the lens of community assembly, without necessarily considering potential physiological temperature effects on body size. For instance, there is a noticeable absence of zooplankton between -2 and 0 log10 gram in the warmer waters (Fig 3B). This absence forces large fish to feed on relatively small prey (Fig 3A and indicated in lines 201-202). Consequently, the larger fish are outcompeted by smaller ones in warmer waters, which can be expected when both small and large fish target the same small size prey (as shown in the right part of Fig 3A). As a result, assembly processes favor small fish in warm waters and shift the size distribution of the myctophid community towards smaller body sizes (Fig 2B).
Importantly, this alternative narrative is not intended as a criticism of the current line of thinking but aims to encourage the authors to consider a different, non-physiological, explanation for the observed patterns. The above line of reasoning also introduces some uncertainties to two results of the manuscript:
• the decline in size preference in large fish (Fig 3A) could be driven by the absence of large prey in the environment, instead of, as stated in the manuscript, large predators preferring smaller prey in warm waters (lines 172-173),
• the temperature-size response of fish can solely be explained through a zooplankton community shift with temperature that, through assembly processes, selects for smaller sized myctophids. This contradicts the statement that there is a stronger temperature-size response among the myctophid predators than their smaller prey (line 118 and 155-156).
I would recommend that the authors leverage the community perspective and emphasize the distinction between individual/species and community-level processes in their interpretation of the results. This may only need some re-writing of the manuscript. Possibly, authors may be able to uncover the relative importance of the two processes (selection of different species by community assembly along the temperature gradient versus body size shifts with temperature in species). Authors should have information on the species composition in warm and cold waters. In addition, authors may be able to use the information from two co-authors (Saunders and Tarling, Bergmann’s rule paper) to estimate the expected decline in body size with temperature within each species. However, this analysis is not essential for the paper.
--- minor comments ---
1) Initially, I was worried that there was too strong a focus on temperature without testing any other potential factors that may affect predator and prey size. It might be good to mention in the result section that the effects of CHL-A were insignificant (it is now only stated at the end of the paper). It might also be good to mention that fishing intensity is low (is it?) as fishing could have a much stronger effect on body size than temperature.
2) My suggestion would be to avoid stating that there is a stronger temperature-size response among the myctophid predators than their smaller prey and mainly discuss that this is a likely explanation of the observed patterns.
Authors make this statement already in line 118 and 155-156, while the available evidence for such a statement is limited at that stage. The observations of prey only consist of the selected prey that are in the stomach, and these do not reflect the size distribution of the “prey” populations in the field. The prey populations could still have a strong temperature-size response.
Only after seeing the dashed lines in Fig 3B (lines 168-176), there is some evidence that the temperature-size response is small on the prey (i.e. average size of prey is unchanged with temperature). Nonetheless, there still seems to be a clear decline in the 5 to 10% largest zooplankton with temperature in Fig 3B.
3) Lines 261-268: were all stations sampled in all three surveys (and seasons/years)? I expect this is the case but please make it explicit. If all warm water communities were sampled in a specific season/year, this could generate a bias that might not be accounted for with the random effect.
4) The mean prey size in the stomach is in some sampling stations >0.1 gram (Fig 2C), whereas the body mass distributions of zooplankton in the environment tend to be smaller (Fig 3B). Did authors obtain samples where the prey size in the stomach was not observed in the environment? How did authors estimate size preference in that case?

Review of “Imaging volcanoes during unrest: Ambient Noise Tomography of a transient plumbing system, Vulcano, Italy.” by Stumpp et al., submitted to Nature: Communications.

Overview and Impact:
This work provides a novel isotropic S-wave velocity model of the volcanic structure under Volcano Island using surface wave dispersion curves obtained from Ambient Noise. Dispersion curves were obtained from data recorded at a novel high-N (≈ 200 ) nodal seismic array deployed at the volcano using advanced deep neural network strategies. The final Bayesian MCMC inversion leads to a preferred velocity model that is interpreted with available geophysical and geological/volcanological data in terms of the volcano's deep structures, leading to unrest.

It is daunting to describe so many recording sites and the corresponding data processing. The authors use a rigorous and very robust approach for dispersion curve quality selection, exploiting recent advancements in deep neural networks. The overall preliminary work on the data is at an excellent standard. The figures are of exceptional quality, especially Figs. 1 and 3, which provides the necessary framework to interpret the results. Fig. 4 represents a clear, high-impact view of the structures and processes interpreted by the authors under Volcano. The interpretation is based on the most recent research regarding Volcano’s unrest, which is skillfully used by the study and explains nicely trade-offs between deformation and previous seismic models. Nature: Communications is an appropriate outlet for such a work, considering the many high-impact works published on this topic by the journal through the last decade.

We present several critical comments, which are divided into Technique and Interpretation (which includes representation). Additional comments can be followed at the discretion of the authors in case they can improve the flow of the paper and correct Typos. If published, the paper would be highly impactful, providing much-needed data on the deep volcanic structure and processes. We can only provide sufficient expertise to review the seismology used by the study, evaluate the reliability of the volcanological interpretation, and assess the general quality/impact of the study. However, the results might become a standard for the understanding/interpretation of volcanic processes at Volcano. For this reason, we highly recommend a revision from a volcanologist expert in the processes acting under the volcano.

In Summary, we answer the primary questions proposed to reviewers by this journal as follows:
- What are the noteworthy results? Any work using seismological data from massive arrays like this is remarkable and valuable. The selection process in a volcanic environment is extremely challenging and addressed very well by the study. The interpretation of the results is grounded on very extended literature and a relevant amount of volcanological data and experience. The retrieved connection between the volcanic systems of Lipari and Volcano, with its deep source under the second, represents an important result for our understanding of the two volcanic systems.
- Will the work be of significance to the field and related fields? How does it compare to the established literature? If the work is not original, please provide relevant references. The work is original and represents an important improvement relative to the current geophysical understanding of the volcano.
- Does the work support the conclusions and claims, or is additional evidence needed? Further evidence is required in order to support all the work’s claims.
- Are there any flaws in the data analysis, interpretation and conclusions? - Do these prohibit publication or require revision? None of the flaws in data analysis, interpretation and conclusions we found forbid publication, but they require revision.
- Is the methodology sound? Does the work meet the expected standards in your field?
The methodology of the current study requires further work and clarifications to meet the standard in our field.
- Is there enough detail provided in the methods for the work to be reproduced? The details provided are currently insufficient.

Critical Comments:
1) Technique
a) 2-D group-velocity maps:
While the processing and quality assessment of dispersion curves are excellent, the technical description of how they obtain 2-D group velocity maps lacks clarity and details:
1. The only paper mentioned is [54], but the reader cannot rely only on that. The authors should say more about the experimental assumptions they make. For example, do they take into account finite frequencies, or do they use ray theory to describe wave propagation? They mention a "Nonlinear inversion", but it is not clear what they are referring to. If they use ray theory, does it mean that they take ray bending into account? Assuming ray theory, what algorithm do they use for forward modelling? Do they solve the Eikonal with the Fast Marching/Sweeping Method, or do they use a Shortest Path Network? Despite the sharpness required by the journal, it is their job to clarify these points.
2. The authors talk about refinements of the parameterisation (i.e., discretisation?), but they do not say anything about the type of basis functions they use. Do they use pixels? Do they use splines or sines/cosines? What does this refinement of the parameterisation consist of? Is it done a priori based on the coverage? Showing a figure to clarify is necessary.
3. The 1. authors do not discuss the inversion method. We guess they use an iterative approach with linearisation at each step, like the Gauss-Newton or Levemberg–Marquardt method. If this is the case, do they use some regularisation (Norm vs roughness damping.)? If it is roughness damping, do they use the first or second derivative of the model? How did they select the damping?
4. More generally, while the paper [54], developed by Cabrera-Peréz, is a starting point, it remains a theoretical paper that starts from concepts applied to the nonlinear inversion of seismic refraction profiles. To understand its full reliability, the authors must accurately develop and describe the model and approximations within this study, especially in the Supplementary Materials. For example, the authors use a test for „scales“ without clearly defining what this scale is: as it is, it appears redundant with Fig S3. Only by reading previous literature can one guess that in the case of Fig S4, scale is (maybe!) node parametrisation. The reader is supposed to get all the information necessary here without having to guess the steps that have led to the results.
5. The scale is selected based on 0.02º x 0.02º anomalies (Fig. S4), but the entire workflow and all results are interpreted at a resolution of 0.01º x 0.01º. This is inappropriate, and assessing with 0.01º x 0.01º is central to understanding eventual trade-offs in the increasing parametrisation strategy used by the inversion.
6. We need to understand why a single checkerboard test is shown for the group velocities (Fig. S3). The authors use five periods between 0.5 s and 2.5 s: the period is not declared for Fig. S3, and no resolution assessment is made for the other periods. Does the previous selection criteria require the same source station pairs to be available at all periods? This could be the explanation, but it would reduce the number of available data without reason.

b) Vs model (MCMC inversion):
We also have critical comments about the final Vs inversion:
1. The authors use a Bayesian inversion, but they do not show the resulting uncertainty anywhere.
2. We do not understand what their favourite model is. Is it the ensemble mean or the median? How far apart are the mean and median? Typically (certainly in our experience), when the mean and median are quite far apart, it indicates that some Markov chains are stuck in some region of the parameter space associated with a relatively high (low) likelihood (misfit) that is not associated with a sensible earth model. For example, high velocities at shallow depths and low velocities at depths can produce low misfits in the inversion of surface-wave dispersion curves. Still, such a 1D model needs to make sense geophysically, even within complex volcanic structures.
3. Regarding the Bayesian sampling, we need to understand how many models the authors save (among the accepted ones) in the iterations after the burn-in. This information is important because keeping all the accepted models in a perturbative approach (where each proposed model is proposed by randomly perturbing the last accepted model) means having a final ensemble that is highly autocorrelated, which goes against the Bayesian paradigm, whereby the various models that compose the ensemble are independent of each other.
4. To mitigate this autocorrelation problem, most Bayesian sampling software saves one model for every N accepted models. BayHunter does it differently: it saves them all, and at the end of the inversion, it selects a random subset of the ensemble. This generally works fine; however, the authors only run ~17,300 iterations after burn-in, which means that the randomly selected subset could still be affected by autocorrelations. Given this, we suggest increasing the number of iterations after burn-in to at least 100k total iterations.

2) Interpretation
a) Assessment and Figures
The paper's figures are of high quality and very well crafted; however, they do not consider the results of the checkerboard testing accurately, and novel synthetic tests appear necessary when interpreting features. This adds to our concerns about testing different group velocity maps for various periods.
1. The checkerboard tests are shown for horizontal sections and different periods, but parts of the areas cannot be recovered adequately. These parts are still present in the S-wave velocity maps (Fig. 2) and are sometimes interpreted. Fig. 2 should report only areas where the velocity model can be reconstructed at a level allowing interpretation (thus at a minimum of 0.01º x 0.01º), Fig. S3F. The shading on unresolved areas should consider the results of testing scales for 0.01º x 0.01º checkerboard anomalies.
2. Fig. 4 will be indubitably the one the majority of readers will remember, sparking interpretations about the volcanoes from different disciplines. This figure must better acknowledge resolution issues. Volumes below 2.5 km are defined as those where resolution is maximum and then starts to decrease: we strongly disagree. If looking at Fig. S7, only periods of 2.5 s (primarily) and 2 s (partially) have any sensitivity at this depth. Resolutions on the volumes below this depth might not even be at a scale of 0.02º x 0.02º. The authors effectively have no way to assess if the contrast observed in Figure S5 at 2 s is real with the current materials. The contrast is strongly dampened at 2.5 s. It is necessary to shade any volume below this depth for all figures, certainly avoiding drawing any interpreted feature in Figure 4 below this depth.
3. Anomalies H1 and H4 are both in the northern part of the study area, where resolution testing is negative. The two H1 anomalies have quite an important role in the interpretation [Lines 121-139]. Still, at present, its recovery cannot be considered reliable, even less its description as a spherical anomaly and, consequently, its interpretation. A spike test of the corresponding dimension could better prove its reliability. The authors only note H4 as it corresponds to the high velocities of [42], so its lack of recovery is not as problematic, but the lack of resolution should be acknowledged in the text. A second spike test would better clarify the resolution.
4. While L1 can be recovered in the resolved depth span, we recommend a wider synthetic test of L1 at all periods considered. This would provide stronger evidence that L2, and especially the low-velocity pathway connecting to Lipary through Vulcanello, are no ghosts.

b) Interpreted features
Here, we discuss interpreted features, highlighting where we find inconsistencies.
1. Throughout the paper, the authors make no mention of high-velocity anomalies that might correspond to crater rims. Velocity tomography (Di Stefano et al., 2002; Vanorio et al., 2005; Battaglia et al., 2008), including ANT results (De Siena et al, 2018) show that high-velocity shallow anomalies (< 1.5 km) like those recovered around L1 are the buried trace of such rims at 1 km (Figs. 2 and 3): the correlation with the crater rims shown in Fig, 1 of H2 and H3 supports this interpretation. This interpretation would greatly simplify the discussion and fit with the conclusions and discussions better than what is currently proposed.
2. The break in the high-velocity continuity around L1 in the NNW can be due to the collapsed caldera collapse, as discussed by the authors. In this case, we need to understand the role of H1. Are the authors claiming these anomalies are a signature of supercritical fluids? Are they a remnant of past intrusions? Suppose the anomalies can be resolved separately (see previous point). In that case, do we see them as forming a caprock for low-velocity fluids feeding Baia di Levante (see, e.g., Vanorio & Kanitpanyacharoen, 2015), as suggested by the „Sealing cap“ in Fig. 4 (but never mentioned in the text? Lines 121-139 should better clarify the geochemistry of the fluids involved, making the interpretation of the S-wave velocity anomaly unclear. From our experience, such an interpretation is challenging without measurements of Vp/Vs (Vanorio et al., 2005; Vanorio & Kanitpanyacharoen, 2015).

Review of “Large biomass carbon losses from droughts in the northern temperate ecosystems during 2016-2022 ” by Li et al. This manuscript analyzes time series of changes in above-ground biomass during the period 2010-2022 over ecosystems north of 30N, with the goal to derive trends in carbon storage. The dataset has annual resolution which allows temporal trends, and extreme years to be analyzed. This leads to the most important result reported here: an apparent reversal of a positive trend in biomass storage into a negative trend, which signifies loss of carbon from forests in the NH since 2016. Reduced carbon uptake in these regions was seen before in this dataset, at a time when it only reached to 2019, while 3-years of additional data now allow significant trends over large subsets of the pixels of the NH. Moreover, earlier speculations of this reversal being in progress, and driven by large-scale disturbances from fires and droughts, can be confirmed by the inclusion of post-2019 large climate extremes in Siberia, Europe, and North America. Since these events were separately studied and reported (some also from the perspective of ΔAGB) in previous publications, the novelty of this manuscript is in the analysis of the longer time series, and the focus on the decline in forest biomass since 2016. In the Methodology, the authors properly benchmark the new dataset against other biomass products, and make a credible case for its agreement with bottom-up derived changes in forest carbon storage at country level. This leaves little doubt that the observed trend is a real signal, and not an artefact of the data used, nor of its known sensitivity to water that partially absorbs the microwave signals from SMOS. Statistical analyses are mostly straightforward and properly tested for significance. Error estimates and propagation of errors are present in the numerical results in the text and tables, but should be added in some of the Figures. The extended analyses of the dataset focus on the possible drivers of the biomass decline, and this part does not fully satisfy me. Quite some words and figures are spent on a machine-learning effort on the spatial patterns of ΔAGB, which ends up with a large number of contributing proxy variables, with unknown and likely non-linear relations to the data trained on. The purpose of this effort seems to have been to explain the variations in the dataset with certain proxies, rather than to find a predictive model for untrained data (or events yet to come). If indeed the purpose is to understand the role of various drivers, then a regular multilinear regression, or a principal component analysis seems more logical to me. These allow you to optimize and quantify the variance explained by each proxy, instead of letting a ML-method combine them in a way that is afterwards untraceable, and interpretable only from their rank in the prediction. Any reply to this concern would at the minimum warrant a justification and explanation of the added value of the use of the ML-model in this manuscript. About the outcomes of the ML-approach: I see that highly informative variables end up to be partly related to forest structure (tree cover, soil nitrogen load, age), and partly to changes in hydrological conditions (Δsoil moisture, ΔVPD, Δradiation, ΔT). The latter are all likely to be strongly covarying as they are different representations of drought conditions, or known consequences (Δfire). The outcomes show some interesting relations (e.g. a sharp gradient in the relation with ΔVPD) which feel like they need to be further discussed or analyzed. It also seems to me that the machine-learning predominantly confirms -qualitatively- the conditions that were described in previously published analyses of these events, rather than new insights. This paper uses a spatially expansive selection of sediment cores distributed across eastern Siberia and Alaska to assess potential vegetation extirpations or extinctions using sediment aDNA. By pooling multiple DNA datasets, the authors had improved taxon assignments, and identified ~60 potential sequences that had no modern match. Their aim was to understand the potential role of megafaunal extinctions and abrupt climate change on vegetation turnover and/or taxon extirpations or extinctions during a period of widespread global change.
While I find the study's premise exciting and the broader topic is of high relevance, this paper is undermined by several flaws in the framing and the approach. These could perhaps be ameliorated, but there will still be some limits that need better qualification and transparency. The paper could be better organized, and it often feels as though the megafauna story is tacked on as an afterthought. There are also a number of key references missing (even understanding the brevity necessary for a paper of this type). As a result, the overall scholarship fails to position the paper within broader dialogues about drivers of plant diversity, extinction, and megaherbivore ecology. This in turn undermines the arguments, as some statements (noted throughout below) are either incorrect or are more nuanced or complex than is being represented here (for example, our understanding of the underpinnings of extinction risk is much more nuanced and dynamic than is represented here).
As an example, the authors state that “we identified potential plant taxa loss events that happened in parallel to both the Plesistocene mammoth-steppe loss (vegetation turnover) and the megafauna extinction showing the importance of of past trophic interactions and potential co-extinction events in parallel to the loss of past biota," but this argument is not well-scaffolded throughout-- the setup and supporting literature are missing, and the discussion focuses more on the approach, at the expense of the ecological questions this paper is attempted to grapple with. This is a fixable problem, but it's going to take a lot of engagement with the literature and some reframing of the text.
Perhaps more critically, though, I have two major concerns about the experimental design. While I'm enthusiastic about these questions and the promise of the methods in addressing them, it just may not be possible to do what you're trying to do, and at a minimum, this text needs a lot of qualifying statements. My first concern is that the taphonomy of sedaDNA does not allow for us to say anything about extinction or even extirpation at this coarse spatial resolution. We can certainly say that some sequences were locally extirpated, but this requires a more up-front framing of what "local" means in a sedaDNA record (i.e., within the catchment area of the lake, within the proxy's representation, etc., which is not large for sedaDNA). In terms of spatial grain, eight lakes spanning a broad geographic range is not sufficient to capture biodiversity loss, especially when the source area of sedaDNA is so small compared with, e.g., pollen (which has too coarse a taxonomic resolution).
Secondly, I am not convinced that an incomplete ASV match means that the taxon has been lost, and while the authors do identify some caveats, many are missing. There could be some within-species variation in sequences due to local adaptation, and we know that many reference datasets have taxonomic errors (i.e., the assignments are not accurate because the species was incorrectly identified). But more importantly, there are gaps in our reference datasets, particularly within the region of this analysis. While it may be the case that the 60 taxa identified as "missing" have actually disappeared (though see my previous point about spatial grain), it's just as likely that you have an incomplete library problem. I may have missed it, but this appears not to have been discussed at all, even in the caveats section.

Promoting mangrove restoration is a crucial strategy in the fight against climate change. It leverages the ecosystem's capacity to sequester carbon efficiently while providing a range of other ecological and socio-economic benefits. This study aims to investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of mangrove blue carbon stocks and conduct an investment-benefit analysis of potential mangrove restoration—important questions indeed. The idea of tracking global mangrove SOC stock dynamics is innovative. However, there are some concerns regarding the quality of data and methodology, detailed below.
SOC stock data: The authors updated the database by searching several databases with keywords, but it is unclear whether this constitutes a systematic review. Data from peer-reviewed literature may be subject to publication bias. How was the quality of the SOC stock data ensured? What are the data resolutions? SOC stock change during mangrove loss and gains: A paper published in 2020 titled “Quantifying net loss of global mangrove carbon stocks from 20 years of land cover change” appears similar to this study. SOC Stock in new mangroves: Insufficient detail has been provided about the SOC stock in newly gained mangroves. Were these stocks considered equivalent to natural mangroves?
