teabags decay experiment, I am missing a functional characterization of the soil communities that
would aid in the interpretation and significance of the work.

based on the evidence at hand. The title needs to be rewritten to encapsulate the main findings of
the study, which are limited in their capacity to predict future microbiome activity and function in
forest landscapes

=== reviewer_2 ===
Netherway and colleagues examined how mycorrhizal associations affect surrounding soil
microbiomes and ecosystem function across a latitudinal gradient in Europe. They found strong
effects of EM and DSE fungi but smaller effects of AM fungi on the relative abundance of soil
saprotrophs, pathogens and decomposition. In general, effect sizes were larger in temperate
compared to boreal forests. This work is a nice overview of fungal effects belowground across
climatic gradients and one of the first to included DSEs as well as AM and EM mycorrhizal fungi.
However, I have several comments on the novelty, hypotheses, analysis, and conclusions of this
work. Detailed comments are below.
Novelty: Several studies have targeted similar questions. Here it would be helpful to distinguish
how the current work is different from previous studies on microbiomes associated with different
mycorrhizal types (e.g., Bahram et al. 2018) or those focused on biogeochemical differences
among mycorrhizal types.
Hypotheses: Overall the hypotheses are difficult to follow in the results and discussion sections. It
would be helpful to include language in both sections about testing certain hypotheses and if they
were rejected.
In addition, the hypotheses could be clearer by pointing out the contrasting conditions you’ve
studied. For example, why would temperate forests have the highest impact? Compared to what
other ecosystem(s)?
Is colonization reflective of the strength of symbiosis? What if the colonizing fungi are more
parasitic than mutualistic?
Statistics. It is unclear how the linear models accounted for the hierarchical design of the plots and
sites. Each model should have plot within site as a random effect. Do the spearman rank
correlations include this information?
Colonization v. molecular relative abundance: It’s unclear why both methods were performed. In
addition, how was the relative abundance of the different fungal groups calculated in the soil? Are
the databases good enough to define DSEs accurately? How many taxa were assigned to each
group? If most of the sequences were assigned to a fungal functional group, then relationships in
each focal group could be caused by the change in another group, not necessarily the focal group.
References
Bahram et al. 2018. Structure and fuction of the global topsoil microbiome. Nature 560:233-237.

Seismic liquefaction of sand is a quite complex phenomenon. Its generation, development and
dissipation are mainly restricted by the physical properties, stress state and boundary conditions of
soil. There are many influencing factors, such as soil density, soil structure, clay content,
saturation, gradation, water permeability, initial stress state and dynamic load characteristics.
Generally speaking, the mechanism of earthquake liquefaction can be expressed as follows：
The shear wave propagates upward from the underlying rock and soil layer during the earthquake,
and causes alternating stress in the soil, resulting in vibration pore water pressure, which is the
main reason for the liquefaction of saturated sand. Under the action of alternating stress, new
stress will be generated at the contact point of soil particles. When this stress reaches a certain
value, the original connection and structural state between soil particles will be destroyed, and the
sand particles will be separated from each other. At this time, the stress originally transmitted by
sand particles through the contact point will be transmitted to the water in the pores to bear,
resulting in the increase of pore water pressure. With the increase of the number of stress cycles,
the pore water pressure increases due to the gradual accumulation. On the one hand, pore water
tries to discharge upward under a certain vibration pore water pressure; On the other hand, soil
particles try to sink down under the action of self weight, so that at the moment of structural
damage or within a certain period of time, the downward sinking of soil particles is hindered by the
upward discharge of pore water, so that the soil particles are partially or completely suspended,
and the shear strength disappears locally or completely, which means that the soil has varying
degrees of deformation or complete liquefaction.
In other words, the seismic liquefaction of sand is related to the ground motion excitation and the
properties of soil. The ground motion excitation here mainly refers to the peak acceleration and
the duration of earthquake. For the earthquake liquefaction phenomenon in the region far away
from the epicenter mentioned by the authors, being far away from the epicenter does not mean
that liquefaction will not occur, and the peak acceleration in the region far away from the epicenter
may not be low. Studies have found that liquefaction occurs when the earthquake intensity is as
small as moment magnitude 4.5 (Green and Bommer, 2020). The existing mechanism of seismic
liquefaction mentioned by the authors is based on undrained conditions. In fact, drainage and
undrained conditions are not unnecessary conditions for seismic liquefaction of sand. Undrained
conditions are only to explain that pore water pressure offsets gravity. Even under drainage
conditions, pore water pressure may dissipate slowly, but sand liquefaction is slow. Soil structure
is also an important factor to control the liquefaction of sand. After the structure is damaged by
earthquake vibration, the vibration pore water pressure gradually increases with the increase of the
number of stress cycles, and its size is finally enough to make the saturated sand lose its
shear capacity locally or completely. That is, the seismic liquefaction of sand is affected by the
compactness of soil. Even if there is a new mechanism of sand seismic liquefaction, it should be
based on particle mechanics, such as the so-called shear jamming mechanism. The innovation of
this study is limited.
In general, according to the current status of this study, the reviewer regrets that, it is not
recommended to be published in this professional journal.

how can the initial, downwards propagation of a front separating liquefied from non-liquefied soil
be explained (e.g. [33])? Is this an aspect of response that can be captured with your analytical
approach? This downwards propagation of a “liquefaction” front precedes the reconsolidation

partially drained events.

events. One would expect liquefaction to happen (for loose sands) in the first few cycles of
earthquake shaking. Fluidisation can happen and continue into the post seismic period.
4. The concept of ‘liquefaction front’ moving from soil surface towards the bedrock as the shaking
starts and the ‘densification front’ moving from the bedrock towards the soil surface have been
previously identified by many researchers (e.g. ref 33). There is a large body of dynamic
centrifuge test data to show these fronts experimentally occurring in layers of ~ 10m deep. The
authors may want to include some of these references into the manuscript.

amplitude threshold i.e. earthquakes that cause shear strains above this threshold cause excess
pore pressure generation while those below won’t. I feel this is more physical as shear strains are

2. Multiphysics analysis of metasurfaces is important.
3. The proposed framework can be used for inverse design.

1. No execution time comparisons or rigorous accuracy metrics have been provided for the frequency transfer. it is unclear how to choose the bounds and the width of the extrapolated frequency band. Also, it seems that the authors' approach is data driven, although frequency transfer has recently been demonstrated for neural operators in a compelling way.
2. The few comparisons of S_E and S_M show that there is little difference between the two. In fact, Fig. 6 shows a very low S21. Some difference between the two is observed at 6.7 GHz, but it is not explained. Is it real, or is it a numerical artifact ?
3. Various ANNs, GANs etc have been already shown to drive inverse design of metasurfaces. Therefore, the results presented here do not demonstrate any breakthrough.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The authors proposed a multi-physics deep learning framework that combines several techniques. This work is interesting and seems beneficial. However, the framework is complex, and each subnetwork is not novel. The manuscript does not clearly explain or compare the necessity and advantages of the different components. Moreover, the problem statement is not very clear at the beginning. To improve the paper, the reviewer suggests the authors to revise the paper by addressing the following concerns:

=== reviewer_3 ===
In this manuscript, the authors present a data-analytic, hybrid framework that could offer zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization with respect to operating frequency, dubbed “frequency transfer” by them. At the core of the framework is the multifidelity DeepOnet approach, which aims to incorporate both a data-driven machine learning (ML) model and a physics-based analytic model. The proposed framework is validated for both forward modeling and inverse design of electromagnetic-thermal metasurface subject to multiphysics coupling. Experimental validation shows good agreement with the computational result.
This manuscript addresses zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization with respect to operating conditions, a topic that has been largely under-explored in the literature but could have far-reaching impact in wave-based systems beyond electromagnetic metasurfaces. In this regard, this manuscript could be a timely, important addition to the literature. The authors’ approach, which attempts to take advantage of both data-driven modeling and physics through the multifidelity modeling, is a good demonstration of scientific machine learning (SciML). While this point is commendable, the manuscript in the present form has major deficiencies in several different regards. It will require major revisions to meet the quality that readership of Nature Communications would anticipate.
Major Comments
Comment 1 (OOD generalization)
To raise the impact of the work, Introduction could be significantly expanded to include major approaches on OOD generalization existing in the literature. In recent years, OOD generalization has been one of the most intensely studied topics by diverse communities. Within the scope of Scientific Machine Learning (SciML), there are two mainstream approaches to extrapolation of data-driven models:
1. Multifidelity modeling with a sparse amount of data given in the extrapolation
2. Fine-tuning for new data
The two approaches in common is that they require data in the extrapolation region or re-training of models. The following reference has a good introduction of both approaches, with a good amount of empirical results and analyses included:
- Zhu, Min, et al. "Reliable extrapolation of deep neural operators informed by physics or sparse observations." Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 412 (2023): 116064.
In addition to the extrapolation approaches reported from the SciML communities, there are physics-based approaches to extrapolation, e.g., spectral generalization by wavelength normalization reported in the following reference:
- Tanriover, Ibrahim, et al. "Deep generative modeling and inverse design of manufacturable free-form dielectric metasurfaces." ACS Photonics 10.4 (2022): 875-883.
The authors are also recommended to go beyond the scope of frequency transfer into areas such as polarization transfer and dispersion transfer in literature review, which can help readers better understand the context of this manuscript and the relationships of these topic areas.
Comment 2 (DeepOnet)
The authors should consider to significantly to expand the introduction of existing methods in SciML. Most importantly, it is difficult for the reviewer to find a convincing answer to “Why DeepOnet?”. Including convincing justifications, at least qualitatively, is essential, in particular since in this manuscript no empirical validation is provided against competing techniques, e.g., physics-informed neural nets (PINN), neural operator, etc. The authors may refer to the following references which articulated in what aspects operator learning could be powerful, e.g., sample/parameter efficiency, discretization invariance, capability to capture non-local interactions:
- Augenstein, Yannick, Taavi Repan, and Carsten Rockstuhl. "Neural operator-based surrogate solver for free-form electromagnetic inverse design." ACS Photonics 10.5 (2023): 1547-1557.
- Lee, Doksoo, et al. "Deep Neural Operator Enabled Concurrent Multitask Design for Multifunctional Metamaterials Under Heterogeneous Fields." Advanced Optical Materials (2024): 2303087.
The authors should clearly state the exclusive advantages of including DeepOnet in the proposed framework to achieve frequency transfer.
In addition, considering the readership in Nature Communications, it is highly recommended to provide (1) a brief introduction to operator learning, (2) a canonical, simplified formulation on DeepOnet (as one form of supervised learning), and (3) an exposition on how it distinguishes again “conventional” machine learning surrogates, e.g., multilayer perceptron or convolutional neural nets. Such introduction centered on SciML (e.g., PINN; neural operator) seems more necessary than the reviews on VAE and GAN in Introduction.
Comment 3 (data-analytic multifidelity modeling)
As mentioned above, the use of multifidelity modeling as a means to incorporate machine learning and physics is commendable. Nevertheless, the descriptions and justifications on multifidelity modeling in the manuscript have a large room for improvements. The radar plot at the bottom right of Fig. 1 is better suited as a conceptual illustration of the motivation; but it currently lacks supporting arguments of the effectiveness of the approach. As a relevant point, the authors are claiming:
“In our scheme, the pressure of multi-physics data collection is relieved by a priori knowledge, and the properties at frequency out of training range are predicted with a latent space, benefiting vast applications involving multi-frequency and multi-physics domain.”
The reviewer found the claim to be very weak, in particular, no quantitative investigation in any aspect of multifidelity modeling has been reported in this paper. Possible numerical experiments may include (1) performance gain against single-fidelity modeling, (2) the influence of the sampling interval ratio between Net1 and Net2, (3) the trade-off between computational cost and accuracy. The authors are encouraged to search more relevant papers built on multifidelity machine learning and include similar types of validation experiments in their manuscript. A non-exhaustive list is provided as follows:
- Pilania, Ghanshyam, James E. Gubernatis, and Turab Lookman. "Multi-fidelity machine learning models for accurate bandgap predictions of solids." Computational Materials Science 129 (2017): 156-163.
- Howard, Amanda A., et al. "Multifidelity deep operator networks for data-driven and physics-informed problems." Journal of Computational Physics 493 (2023): 112462.
- Tran, Anh, et al. "Multi-fidelity machine-learning with uncertainty quantification and Bayesian optimization for materials design: Application to ternary random alloys." The Journal of Chemical Physics 153.7 (2020).
- Buterez, David, et al. "Transfer learning with graph neural networks for improved molecular property prediction in the multi-fidelity setting." Nature Communications 15.1 (2024): 1517.
- Li, Shibo, et al. "Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization via deep neural networks." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 8521-8531.
- Lyu, Yanfang, et al. "Multi-fidelity prediction of fluid flow based on transfer learning using Fourier neural operator." Physics of Fluids 35.7 (2023).
Comment 4. (On the architectural design)
It is questionable whether the presented architectural design, illustrated in Fig. 2, consists of essential components. For example, the reviewer wonders why the same geometric input (G) should go over the progressive feature extraction twice, once in Net1 and once again in Net 2. More detailed description of the presented architecture is recommended. In doing so, naming each major net, simply indexed as Net1, Net2, … for now, in relation to their role(s) would be a good starting point.
Comment 5. (the scope of OOD generalization)
As opposed to in-distribution generalization that most readers would be familiar with, OOD generalization performance could involve a different scope, thus it is important to clearly specify the scope of the generalization. Throughout the manuscript, only the generalization result for the band 10-14 GHz has been reported. What would be the performance at the lower frequency regime (i.e., for a band < 2 GHz) could be included. Also important to observe is sharing whether the frequency transfer works well even beyond 14 GHz. If not, what would the deviation pattern look like? Intuitively, the error trend would presumably show a strong positive correlation w.r.t. the amount of frequency deviation (i.e., the larger the frequency deviation the larger the error would be). This could better present the strength/weakness of the presented frequency transfer.
Comment 6. (Training description)
Regarding the architectural design and their implementation in this work, it is recommended to report the details of the architectures (e.g., the number of trainable parameters), as well as an example result of the network training (e.g., hyperparameters; deep learning platforms used for the training; optimizer) in Supporting Information. The description on the training procedure under “Numerical simulation and training details” is insufficient to reproduce what’s presented in the manuscript. While enabling reproducibility seems optional, details of the implementations could be practically informative/insightful for readers who are interested in either implementing the presented framework or developing their own upon the demonstration showcased by this work.
Comment 7. (The meta-atom Library)
One of the primary motivations of deep learning assisted photonics has been to embrace high-dimensional, (quasi-)freeform meta-atoms. Although the authors seem to have achieved the frequency transfer within the specified scope, the coverage of meta-atom geometry seems very narrow. Based on the reviewer’s understanding the pre-defined meta-atom representation only spans the space formed by a predefined topology, fully specified by a handful number of parameters without representation learning. Spanning and exploring only this narrow scope are questionable for the reviewer since operator learning, including DeepOnet, is known to be powerful in dealing with high-dimensional input/output fields. The authors might want to include any discussions on this point in their manuscript.
Comment 8. (Editorial proof)
English could be improved. The manuscript has a lot of typos that are not difficult to spot. To name a few:
- Experimental experiment
- “Take metasurface as an example” (in page 2)
- “However, the multi-physic field coupling problems 25-27 widen the gaps between the practical engineering applications and numerical simulation.” (in page 2)
- “Experimental experiment is also conducted to verify the accuracy of the framework with a comparison experiment to show a significant EM-thermal effects.” (in page 3)
More thorough proofreading is highly recommended.
Minor Comments
Comment 9. (Descriptions on GAN)
Regarding the comment:
“Generative adversarial network (GAN) 39,40 , as one of the most popular frames in inverse design these years, constructs both forward and inverse models at the same time by adversarial strategy, partly alleviating the problem of non-uniqueness.”
The inverse model is constructed only for conditional GAN, not the vanilla GAN (Ref. 40). Vanilla GAN involves unsupervised learning (i.e., being agnostic to the property / output), thus what it does at most is “pre-processing method to compress the data space”, borrowing the authors’ expression. This is not to say that a quantitative analysis of the documents should not be done, but the framing of such an analysis should take into account this limitation arising from the data source of strategy documents that may not fully reflect a country's policy priorities.
b. The paper should provide additional interpretation and policy contextualisation, particularly regarding the high numbers from individual countries, such as Russia. This will help to interpret the high headline number reported at the beginning of the paper.
2.Methodology:
a. The methodology used to extract data from the documents should be clarified. **Reviewer Report**

**Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**General Comments:**
This manuscript addresses a critical gap in climate policy research: the translation of abstract, tonne-based carbon dioxide removal (CDR) targets in Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and Long-Term Low Emissions Development Strategies (LT-LEDS) into tangible land-use requirements. The study provides a timely and significant contribution to the literature on the feasibility and governance of net-zero pathways. The finding that national pledges imply a land-use change of approximately 1 billion hectares—a rate of change that is historically unprecedented—is a compelling and policy-relevant result. However, the methodology relies on a series of assumptions that require greater transparency and sensitivity analysis before the conclusions can be considered robust.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study is highly significant. While previous reports (e.g., the Land Gap Report) have touched upon these themes, this manuscript provides a systematic, global-scale synthesis of UNFCCC submissions. It successfully highlights the "transparency gap" in climate governance, where the reliance on land-based CDR is often decoupled from the spatial and social realities of land management.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The methodology for converting emissions-based pledges into land-area requirements is the most sensitive part of the study.
*   **Conversion Factors:** The authors state they use IPCC removal factors, but the manuscript lacks a detailed appendix or supplementary table explicitly linking specific country pledges to the chosen sequestration rates (tCO2/ha/yr). Given the vast differences in sequestration potential between biomes (e.g., boreal vs. tropical forests), applying generalized factors could lead to significant over- or under-estimations.
*   **Double Counting:** There is a risk of double counting between "restoration" and "afforestation" categories. The authors must clarify how they disentangled these in countries where definitions of "forest" are broad or overlapping.
*   **The "100% Land Area" Issue:** The authors note that some countries (e.g., Dominica) pledged >100% of their land area. While this is addressed in the text, it suggests a fundamental flaw in the reporting of the pledges themselves. The authors should perform a sensitivity analysis excluding these outliers to demonstrate that the global aggregate of 1 billion ha is not driven by data artifacts.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The study is generally well-structured, but reproducibility is hampered by the lack of a comprehensive dataset in the supplementary materials. To meet *Nature Communications* standards, the authors must provide:
*   A machine-readable file (e.g., CSV/Excel) containing the raw data extracted from each of the 194 pledges, the conversion factors applied, and the resulting land area calculations.
*   A clear definition of the "search terms" used for each of the seven land-use categories to ensure that the categorization process is replicable.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
The manuscript is well-written and the narrative flow is logical. However, the distinction between "direct land-area pledges" and "emissions-based conversions" should be more clearly demarcated in the results section. It would be beneficial to present a table comparing the aggregate land area derived from direct pledges versus those derived from emissions-based conversions to show the level of uncertainty inherent in the latter.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
The use of ranges (0.9–1.1 billion ha) is appropriate, but the authors should explicitly state how these ranges were derived. Are they based on the uncertainty of the sequestration factors, or the uncertainty in the interpretation of the pledges? A more formal uncertainty propagation analysis would strengthen the findings.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Spatial Explicitly:** The authors acknowledge the lack of spatial data. They should discuss the implications of this limitation more critically. For instance, how does the lack of spatial planning in these pledges affect the feasibility of the 13 million ha/year conversion rate?
*   **BECCS vs. Afforestation:** The manuscript conflates different types of land-use change. BECCS requires land for bioenergy crops, which is fundamentally different from forest restoration in terms of biodiversity and food security impacts. The authors should separate these in their aggregate figures to provide a more nuanced picture of the "land rush."
*   **Policy Context:** The discussion on the "spiral of delay" is insightful, but the authors should be careful not to over-interpret the pledges as "intentions" when they may simply be placeholders for future technological CDR that the countries have not yet fully costed or planned.
*   **Methods Section:** The truncated text in the provided excerpt (e.g., the definition of "Old secondary forests") must be completed and expanded to include the full logic for the seven categories.

**Conclusion:**
This is a strong paper that addresses a vital topic. With a more rigorous treatment of the conversion factors, a transparent release of the underlying data, and a more nuanced discussion of the differences between various CDR methods, this work will be a valuable addition to the climate policy literature.

Summary
This article presents a comprehensive assessment of the land requirements for carbon dioxide removal (CDR)
pursuant to national climate mitigation plans. The authors analyze the land area committed to CDR in the Nationally
Determined Contributions (NDCs) and Long-Term Strategies (LT-LEDS) submitted to the United Nations Framework
Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) up to December 2023. They categorize the pledges into three types—direct
land-area, indirect land-area, and emissions-based—and convert the latter two into land area using IPCC removal factors,
yield values, and conversion efficiencies. The study reveals that the land area required for CDR is substantial, with 1.0
billion hectares (100 million ha) allocated globally. Approximately 40% of this area is intended for reforestation,
plantation, or energy crops, while the remainder focuses on restoring degraded forests, agricultural lands, or coastal
ecosystems. The authors also examine the geographical and temporal distribution of these pledges, highlighting that
Russia, Saudi Arabia, the USA, and Canada account for nearly 70% of the total land commitment. The analysis concludes
that the rate of land use change for CDR is unprecedented and comparable to historical land transformation rates, raising-
ing concerns regarding the feasibility and equity of these pledges.
Strengths
• Comprehensive scope: The study covers a wide range of countries and pledges, providing-ing a robust global perspective.
• Methodological rigor. The authors employ a systematic approach to categorize and convert pledges into land area,
ensuring-ing methodological consistency and transparency.
• Policy relevance. The findings offer valuable insights for policymakers, stakeholders, and researchers interested in
national-level CDR strategies and land-use planning.
Weaknesses
• Limited spatial resolution. The study lacks spatial disaggregation, making it difficult to assess regional disparities and
potential conflicts with local land-use priorities.
• Uncertainty quantification. While the authors acknowledge limitations related to data source and conversion methods,
they do not provide quantitative uncertainty bounds, which limits the confidence in the results.
• Temporal aggregation. The analysis aggregates pledges over multiple years, which may obscure short-term dynamics and
policy evolution.
Suggestions for Improvement
• Spatial disaggregation. Consider incorporating spatial data to better understand regional variations in land use and
conflicts with local priorities.
• Quantitative uncertainty. Provide quantitative uncertainty bounds for the land area estimates to improve confidence in the
results.
• Temporal disaggregation. Analyze pledges on a yearly basis to capture short-term dynamics and policy evolution.
Conclusion
This study offers a valuable contribution to the understanding-ing of national-level CDR strategies and their land-use implications.
However, improvements in spatial resolution, uncertainty quantification, and temporal disaggregation would strengthen the
analysis and enhance its applicability to real-world decision-making processes.
Overall Assessment
The study is well-executed and provides significant insights into the land requirements for CDR pursuant to national climate
mitigation plans. However, improvements in spatial resolution, uncertainty quantification, and temporal disaggregation
would strengthen the analysis and enhance its applicability to real-world decision-making processes.
Recommendation
I recommend acceptance pending minor revisions to address the suggestions outlined above.

**Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**Summary of the Study:**
The manuscript argues that polar regions (Arctic, Antarctic, and the Third Pole) are currently marginalized in the UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) framework. The authors posit that these regions act as the “shortest stave” in Liebig’s barrel—a limiting factor for global sustainability due to their role in climate tipping elements. The study combines bibliometric analysis, an expert survey, and a review of IPCC reports to propose a new SDG target (13.4) and five specific indicators to better integrate polar regions into global governance.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study addresses a timely and important gap in global environmental governance. The conceptualization of polar regions as a “limiting factor” for global SDGs via teleconnection effects is compelling and aligns with current discourse on planetary boundaries. However, the novelty is somewhat tempered by the descriptive nature of the proposed indicators. While the call for “localization” of SDGs is well-supported, the manuscript would benefit from a more rigorous justification of why existing indicators (e.g., those under SDG 13 or 15) cannot be adapted through policy interpretation rather than requiring the creation of new, potentially redundant, indicators.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Expert Survey:** The methodology for the expert survey is insufficiently described. The manuscript mentions an “online expert survey” but fails to provide critical details: the number of participants, their disciplinary backgrounds, the selection criteria, the response rate, and the survey instrument itself. Without this information, the “consensus” claimed (e.g., the TESmean scores) cannot be validated.
*   **Bibliometric Analysis:** The bibliometric approach is standard, but the link between the frequency of mentions in IPCC reports and the “criticality” of an SDG for polar regions is a leap in logic. Frequency of mention does not necessarily equate to policy priority or ecological impact.
*   **Data Integration:** The use of ERA5 and TPMFD datasets is appropriate for characterizing climate trends, but the manuscript lacks a clear analytical bridge between these physical climate data and the proposed social/governance indicators.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The manuscript relies on secondary data (ERA5, IMBIE, OGGM). While these are reputable sources, the reproducibility of the *survey* results is currently impossible due to the lack of raw data or detailed methodology. The authors must provide the survey questionnaire as supplementary material and clarify the demographic composition of the expert panel to rule out selection bias.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
The manuscript is generally well-written, but the transition between the physical science (climate tipping points) and the social science (SDG indicators) is abrupt. The “Liebig’s barrel” analogy is used effectively as a framing device, but it is not mathematically or empirically tested in the paper. **5. Statistical Rigor:**

This manuscript presents a series of carefully conducted set of experiments that show the intriguing interactions between the
CRY1c blue light receptor and GL2, a protein in maize that is hypothesized to function in very long chain fatty acid
elongation in the ER, thereby impacting the types of cuticular wax products that are made. The mechanism by which GL2 in
maize or CER2 in Arabidopsis is still not well understood. This manuscript provides interesting new insights into how GL2
itself may be regulated by blue light. A series of different techniques (yeast-2-hybrid, IP-MS, BiFC) demonstrate that GL2 and
CRY1c can interact, and that this may specifically enhance cuticular aldehyde synthesis. This manuscript greatly adds to our
understanding of the regulation of cuticular wax biosynthesis and provides more context relative to the role of GL2, and is an
impactful addition to the field. The manuscript could benefit from additional consideration in a few key areas provided below.
Specific comments are also listed by line number.
Major themes/suggestions:
1. Readability: The manuscript needs to be carefully edited for grammar and correct tense/form of different words. There are
many instances in which the incorrect form of a word is used (for example, in line 54, “reversal” should be “reverse”). The
intended meaning of some sentences may be obscured, so careful editing is required.
2. Introduction: The introduction could be improved with some reorganization. The first paragraph presents interesting
background information about CRY1 and CRY2. However, it is not organized by protein or by theme and instead bounces
between CRY1 and CRY2. Also, from this paragraph it is unclear whether CRY1 and CRY2 actually have photolyase
activity, as it is stated toward the end of this section that these proteins do not have DNA repair activity. The introduction also
does not include information about the hypothesized functions of GL2 (and GL2-Like) in maize and CER2 (and CER2-Like)
in Arabidopsis in very long chain fatty acid elongation. See specific comments/suggestions below.

The study combines advanced experimental techniques with theoretical modeling to provide new insights into the deformation behavior and anisotropy of hcp-Fe-2Si-0.4C alloy. The findings are novel because they explore the combined effect of multiple light elements on the anisotropic properties of iron alloys, which has not been extensively studied previously. Additionally, the work offers a quantitative basis for linking chemical stratification to the observed anisotropy in the Earth's inner core, providing a plausible explanation for the depth-dependent anisotropy pattern.

#### Sample Preparation
The sample preparation protocol is thorough and follows established procedures. The use of a piston-cylinder apparatus for synthesis ensures good control over the conditions, and the electron probe microanalysis confirms homogeneity of the alloy. However, the lack of a direct measurement of the exact composition of the starting powders could introduce variability.

#### High-Pressure Experiments
The use of resistively heated diamond anvil cells (DACs) is appropriate for studying high-pressure, high-temperature conditions. The inclusion of gold markers for pressure calibration adds reliability to the experimental setup. However, the absence of a hydrostatic environment might introduce non-hydrostatic stresses, which could affect the results.

#### Data Analysis
The Rietveld refinement technique for extracting lattice strain parameters and textures is well-established. The use of Fityk for precise determination of peak positions when MAUD analysis was insufficient is reasonable. **1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study addresses a fundamental problem in deep-Earth mineral physics: the origin of the IC’s heterogeneous seismic anisotropy. By moving beyond pure iron and binary alloys to a ternary Fe-Si-C system, the authors provide a more realistic model for the IC. The hypothesis that chemical stratification drives the observed radial anisotropy gradient is compelling and provides a testable framework for future geodynamic models.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Temperature Limitations:** The experiments are conducted up to 1100 K. While this is a significant technical achievement for radial DAC experiments, it remains far below the estimated temperatures of the IC (~5000–6000 K). The authors rely heavily on EVPSC modeling to bridge this gap. The manuscript must explicitly discuss the potential for a change in the dominant slip system (e.g., from basal to prismatic or pyramidal) at temperatures significantly higher than 1100 K, which could fundamentally alter the resulting LPO and anisotropy.
*   **Pressure-Transmitting Medium:** The authors state that no pressure-transmitting medium was used to "maximize non-hydrostatic stresses." While this is standard for radial diffraction, the lack of a medium can lead to significant stress gradients across the sample. The authors should clarify how these gradients were accounted for in the calculation of the yield strength and whether they might bias the texture development.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
*   The synthesis of the Fe-2Si-0.4C alloy is well-documented, and the microprobe characterization confirms the desired composition.
*   The use of gold as a pressure standard is appropriate. However, the manuscript lacks a detailed discussion of the potential for chemical reaction between the sample and the gold or the gasket material at high temperatures, which could affect the sample composition or the diffraction patterns.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
*   The manuscript is generally well-written. However, the transition from the experimental results (1100 K) to the IC conditions (5000+ K) in the "Anisotropy in the Earth’s inner core" section is abrupt. The authors should provide a more detailed justification for why the basal slip mechanism remains dominant at IC temperatures.
*   The comparison with Brennan et al. (2021) is useful, but the authors should provide a more nuanced discussion of why their EVPSC approach is superior to the linear extrapolation used in previous studies, specifically regarding the physical basis for the "saturation" of hardening.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   The error bars on the yield strength and viscosity calculations are mentioned, but the propagation of uncertainties from the diffraction data through the EVPSC model is not fully transparent. *   **Seismic Interpretation:** The authors claim their results are consistent with the "outer regions of the IC." This is a well-documented paper which casts doubt on the credibility of records purporting to show the
8.2 ka event in cores from the Nordic Seas. The data are of high quality, well set out in figures and
tables, and entirely credible. Is clear that for evidence of the 8.2 ka event cores from other locations
must be employed. The Storegga slide caused a well-documented tsunami for which bottom velocities
are calculated here and demonstrated to be adequate to resuspend shallow sediments which then flow
down slope in the form of turbidity currents contaminating any climatic records of that time. This is a
significant and important result as negative data is not always accorded the significance that is due to
it.
I do not think the words ‘Confusion and’ are needed in the title as ‘contamination’ is quite sufficient.
One can reasonably conclude that one will lead to the other.
In places I find the authors to be rather too tentative, for example on line 44 ‘most likely’ could be
removed, also ‘could’ on line 167, and ‘likely’ rather than ‘possible’ on lines 203 and 240.
There are two aspects that need revision by the authors.
1. They are using three terms for the water surface perturbation due to the Storegga slide; ‘surface
elevation’, ‘wave amplitude’, and ‘wave height’. In figure 2 the caption is ‘wave height’ but the
reference to it on line 115 is ‘wave amplitude’. Normally in wave theory wave height is twice the wave
amplitude. The authors need to sort out the terminology here. Is ‘surface elevation’ wave height ?
2. The authors should not be using the archaic Hjulstrom curve for critical erosion conditions. This was
improved by his student Sundborg (1956), but the most commonly used curve based on analysis of
large amounts of data is that due to Miller et al (1977). These authors give an equation for the flow
velocity measured at 1 m above the bed for the coarse end of the grainsize spectrum (D >2 mm) as U
= 160D^0.45 giving a speed range of 0.6 to 1.2 m/s for 1 to 5 mm coarse sand-fine gravel. This, as
with the condition based on Yalin (1977) which they cite, is also based on Shields curve. The period of
the tsunami wave is sufficiently long (>20s) that the flow may be considered unidirectional and thus
the wave velocity of Komar & Miller (1973, 1975) is not needed.
References.
Komar, P.D & M.C. Miller, 1973. The threshold of sediment movement under oscillatory water waves.
Journal of Sedimentary Petrology, 43, 1101-1110.

316.

*   **Experimental Limitations:** The pilot study was conducted exclusively in Beijing, China. The climate in Beijing is not representative of the tropical or arid regions where the technology is most needed. **General Assessment:**
This study presents a high-resolution 27-kyr paleo-oxygenation record from the eastern Tropical North Atlantic (ETNA) using the Enhanced Benthic Foraminifera Oxygen Index (EBFOI). The authors argue that AMOC slowdowns during Heinrich Stadial 1 (HS1) and the Younger Dryas (YD) led to intensified subsurface subtropical cell (STC) circulation, resulting in increased oxygenation at the ETNA OMZ margin. The topic is timely, given current concerns regarding AMOC stability and OMZ expansion. While the dataset is valuable, there are significant concerns regarding the interpretation of the proxy data, the mechanistic link to AMOC, and the statistical rigor of the uncertainty quantification.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study addresses a critical gap in understanding the coupling between global overturning circulation and regional OMZ ventilation. The use of a high-resolution benthic foraminiferal record is a robust approach to reconstructing past oxygenation. However, the novelty is somewhat tempered by the reliance on the EBFOI, which is known to be sensitive to organic matter flux (food supply) in addition to oxygen. The authors must better disentangle these two variables to claim that the observed shifts are primarily driven by ventilation changes rather than productivity-driven oxygen consumption.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Proxy Confounding:** The authors acknowledge that benthic foraminifera distribution depends on both food and oxygen. While they compare their results to "stress species" (Fig. 5c), this is a circular argument if those same species are used to calculate the EBFOI. The authors need to provide independent evidence (e.g., TOC, C/N ratios, or benthic/planktic foraminifera accumulation rates) to demonstrate that the observed oxygenation changes are not simply a reflection of fluctuating surface productivity.
*   **Core Location:** The site is at 793 m, which is at the lower boundary of the OMZ. The authors interpret this as a proxy for the OMZ core, but the dynamics at the boundary are often dominated by vertical mixing and lateral advection of different water masses (NACW vs. ESACW). The T-S diagram (Fig. 6) is a good start, but the authors should discuss how the relative contribution of these water masses might have shifted independently of AMOC strength.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The methodology for the EBFOI calculation is well-documented in the supplementary material. However, the "reproducibility" test (using 6 samples from the last 2.6 ka) is insufficient. A standard deviation of 7 µmol/kg based on only 6 samples is statistically weak and likely underestimates the true analytical and environmental noise inherent in the proxy.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
The manuscript is generally well-written, but the reporting of the "95% confidence interval" is misleading. The authors state they combined the standard deviation of the modern calibration with the age model uncertainty. This is not a true 95% CI of the oxygen reconstruction; it is a propagation of error that ignores the inherent uncertainty in the EBFOI transfer function itself. The authors should clarify this in the text to avoid overstating the precision of their reconstruction.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   **Age Model:** The use of BACON is appropriate. However, the authors should provide a more detailed discussion on the potential for reservoir age changes in the ETNA during the deglaciation, which could significantly shift the timing of the HS1 and YD peaks relative to global records.
*   **Correlation:** The link between the oxygen record and AMOC (via 231Pa/230Th) is largely qualitative. A formal statistical correlation (e.g., cross-correlation analysis or wavelet analysis) between the oxygen record and a regional AMOC proxy stack would strengthen the conclusion.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Mechanism:** The authors claim that AMOC slowdown intensifies the STC. This is a non-trivial claim that contradicts some modeling studies suggesting that AMOC slowdown leads to a weakening of the Atlantic gyres. The authors must provide a more robust physical oceanographic justification for why an AMOC slowdown would increase oxygen supply at this specific site.
*   **Dissolution:** The authors mention that tests are "well preserved," but they should provide quantitative data (e.g., fragmentation indices or weight-per-specimen) to rule out dissolution, which can bias benthic assemblages and, consequently, the EBFOI.
*   **Data Presentation:** Figure 4e is the core of the paper. The "95% CI" shading is very wide in some sections. The authors should discuss whether the observed peaks are statistically distinct from the background noise, particularly during the B-A period.
*   **Supplementary Data:** The link between the EBFOI and the specific species list (Supplementary Data 2–4) is essential. Please ensure that the oxygen preferences assigned to species are not biased by the same core site data used for the reconstruction.

=== reviewer_2 ===
Summary of review: The manuscript presents the application of a regolith depth evolution model to the Chang’E 5 landing site. While the model application has merit pending validation, the key conclusion concerning the impact rate relies on an unsupported correlation between regolith thickness and surface age. Because of this, I do not believe that it satisfies the goal of Nature Communications “to publish rigorous and comprehensive papers that represent advances of significance to specialists within each field.”

Review:
1) The state of scientific knowledge does not support the fundamental assumption made in this manuscript that regolith depth is clearly and directly linked to the impact flux. The manuscript claims a “strong correlation between regolith thickness and age across different geological units 18,23” (Lines 64-65); however, this statement is not supported by the literature and is not supported by the provided citations.
Recent studies examining the abundance of excavated bedrock on mare surfaces indicate a poor relationship between mare regolith depth and time (Chertok et al., 2023; Elder et al., 2023). For example, the abundance of rocky craters suggests that Mare Humorum has the shallowest regolith despite being the oldest mare in the study by Chertok et al. (2023). In general, the depth of the rock-free regolith shows significant variability, which is not correlated to the age of the surface (e.g., Elder et al. 2019; Venkatraman et al. 2023). Rather than developing due to fluctuations in the impact rate over time, regolith depth in the maria may be dominantly controlled by the material properties of the bedrock, as was proposed by Chertok et al. (2023), Elder et al. (2023) and also suggested by Zhang et al. (2022) who stated, “Target properties greatly influence the crater size and hence the volume of regolith produced by impact cratering. For subhectometer impact craters, the strength of bedrock plays a prominent role.”
Remote sensing radar also illuminates the poor correlation between observed regolith depth and surface age. For example, Shkuratov & Bondarenko (2000) reported that Sinus Rorus and Mare Nectarus have similar regolith depths despite having drastically different surface ages (Sinus Rorus is < 2 Ga, while Nectarus is ~ 4 Ga; Hiesinger et al. (2011)). Further, regolith depths derived from crater morphology (Bart et al. 2011) from various maria suggest no clear trend in mare regolith depth with time. The regolith depths reported in this manuscript (Lines 158-160) fit within the existing picture of a poor correlation between surface age (and, by analogy, impact flux) and regolith depth.
The 3-D regolith evolution model utilized in this manuscript is not validated against observations of regolith depth as a function of time through the lens of morphology (e.g., Bart et al. 2011), radar (e.g., Shkuratov & Bondarenko 2000) or rock abundance (e.g., Elder et al. 2023; Chertok et al. 2023; Elder et al. 2019; Venkatraman et al. 2023); the evident validation was a reference to the model by Hirabayashi et al. (2018) shown in Zhang et al. (2022); however, although Hirabayashi et al. (2018) validated their model against the Apollo 15 landing site, Hirabayashi et al. did not validate the relationship of regolith growth with time. Comparison to another theoretical model is not validation.
In conclusion, because there is no unambiguous statistically significant link between regolith depth and surface age in the lunar maria — the literature suggests surface age and mare regolith depths are, in fact, completely un-correlated — the extrapolation of flux from regolith depth and surface age is fundamentally flawed and requires validation not yet present in the literature nor provided in the manuscript.
2) It is unclear whether the results presented in this manuscript are statistically significant. In Figure 4b, all points lie within error, and only a 2σ error is shown, rather than the errors inherited from uncertainty in flux, crater morphology, and material properties. The treatment of secondary impacts may have led to the finding of a high cratering rate relative to the NPF. The manuscript utilized an absolute secondary cratering rate significantly lower than that used by Costello et al. (2021), who showed secondary impacts dominate regolith mixing at sub-hectometer scales and validated their model against the Apollo cores (Morris 1978) and the observed flux of ‘splotches’ (Speyerer et al. 2016). Secondary impacts are more abundant than primaries at hectometer scales. An underestimate in their contribution would lead to an overestimation of the relative contribution of primaries and the false conclusion that there are more primaries (an uptick in the flux). Including secondaries in a crater count is a known cause of offset from the NPF. The manuscript did not sufficiently rule out the likely possibility that secondary craters are the culprit in driving offsets from the NPF.

=== reviewer_3 ===
The study, titled “Increased Small Impactor Flux on the Moon as Inferred from Regolith Thickness at the Chang’E-5 Region” by Mingwei Zhang et al., is very well-written and brought a novel approach to understand the Moon’s impact flux. The research goal is clear; it aims to determine the main driver of unusual regolith thickness constrained from the observed morphology of small craters from Chang’E 5 landing site. The research method volumetrically calculates the contribution of regolith during cratering under different target properties, allowing the authors to separate out the influences of small primary craters, invisible primary craters, secondary craters, and topographic diffusion. By using a conventional chronology functon(Neukum) where a constant impact flux is assumed as constant in the past 2 billion years, the modeled regolith thickness on average with parameter tuning (secondary population and diffusivity) cannot match the regolith thickness constrained by observation data, therefore impact flux in <2 Ga is required to increase for thickening regolith and unusual growth. However, the observed drilling core and seismic data shows a more complicated layer structure of regolith, instead of the underlying assumption that uses two layers model to classify the crater morphology. How the Zhang et al. model tackles this complexity (regolith dynamics and interaction with cratering) is unclear in the current manuscript. In addition, the crater population in Chang’E 5 site is fitted with Neukum function and seems relatively consistent with isotopically dated ages of mare basalt (2 Ga). In the current manuscript, it is not clear that how the crater population with increased impact flux in the model differs from the observed crater population. Some concerns in terms of model capability and stochastic nature of cratering have to be addressed for the finding: the increased impact flux is recorded in the regolith thickness data at the Chang’E 5 landing site. Please see the annotated document for more details and suggestions to improve the clarity of the manuscript.
Warm regards,
Ya Huei Huang

Li-rich layered oxides have high capacity because of high-voltage oxygen redox activity. Li-rich cathodes with a high nickel content exhibit improved voltage stability but suffer from poor discharge capacity. This work tailors the LiNiMn5 superstructure content by modification of Ni and Li contents. The study finds that an excess of LiNiMn5 impedes the extraction/insertion of lithium ions during charging/discharging, resulting in incomplete oxygen redox activity (retention of molecular O2) at low potential (~3.3 V, versus Li+/Li). While the general concept of tailoring local order in Li-rich materials is known, the specific identification of LiNiMn5 units as a hindrance to Li-ion kinetics and oxygen redox reversibility in high-nickel systems is a valuable contribution. The proposed strategy of adjusting the Li/TM ratio to tune these units is practical and industrially relevant.

**Methodology and Experimental Design:**

This paper, "Functional variants at 1p36.23 confer risk of schizophrenia through modulating RERE," investigates how specific genetic variations contribute to schizophrenia (SCZ) risk by affecting the RERE gene. The study characterizes previously identified functional variants, rs159961 and rs301792, located in the intronic regions of the RERE gene at the 1p36.23 risk locus. These variants exhibit allele-specific enhancer activity. The risk alleles of both variants lead to higher enhancer activity, which is associated with increased RERE expression in human brain tissues. The risk allele of rs159961 reduces the binding of the transcription factor REST. The risk allele of rs301792 increases the binding of POLR2A. Both mechanisms result in stronger enhancer activity that subsequently regulates RERE expression. The study concludes that the functional variants rs159961 and rs301792 contribute to schizophrenia risk by upregulating RERE. This upregulation, in turn, affects neurogenesis, dendritic spine density, and synaptic transmission, thereby increasing SCZ risk. These findings provide a framework for translating GWAS findings into an understanding of disease biology and offer insights into SCZ pathogenesis. While the paper is comprehensive, it is fairly difficult to follow- especially how new versus reanalyzed data are presented is not made clear in the results or figure legend text. === reviewer_1 ===
The generation of specific high-affinity GPCR antibodies for use in research, in vitro diagnostics, in vivo imaging and therapy undoubtedly remains to be a challenge. GPCRs contain seven transmembrane domains, which results in a large portion of the protein hidden in the lipid bilayer and also leading to a high flexibility of the conformation. With predominantly extracellular and intracellular loops and the terminal sequences available as antibody binding sites, many approaches to obtain suitable antibodies have failed or have resulted in non-specific antibody preparations. Many of them are sold commercially and they continue to appear in the scientific literature even though their specificity was not validated or disproven.
This manuscript thus addresses an important scientific issue. The authors chose to generate macrocyclic peptides derived from the neurotensin receptor 1 extracellular loop 2 sequence and immunize chicken to obtain four different antibodies. The manuscript describes the process of production and characterization of these antibodies using a wide variety of pharmacological and immunological methods. While the concept of using constrained, e.g. cyclic peptides for immunization is not new, the path chosen here is an interesting one, which resulted in unique polyclonal antiboy responses and warrants further investigation.
However, several issues need to be addressed.
i. My biggest concern is about the principal approach taken here. While using macrocyclic peptides for mimicking ECL conformation is a great idea, and using chicken as a host for immunization is also favorable, the result of the process are polyclonal antibodies, i.e. cocktails of different antibodies resulting from the immunization of an animal. Consequently, all assays done with such a mixture of antibodies will result in data that represent the sum or rather a mean value of data for the many different molecules within a polyclonal antibody. The conclusions drawn from such a dataset will necessarily refer to a collective set of properties with no knowledge about individual molecular structures and their properties. Some of the features identified with the four antibody preparations may stem from different subpopulations of immunoglobulins. Without molecularly defined, i.e. monoclonal antibodies, the approach is severely limited in its use.
ii. The manuscript reports on an antibody mixture from just one animal per peptide, effectively resulting in an N=1 sample size for each condition or each macrocyclic structure. Individual animal differences in the antibody response pattern are not considered. Still, the authors draw conclusions about the association between (linker) structure of the peptides and the resulting polyclonal antibodies.
iii. While immunopurifying serum immunoglobulins will lead to an enrichment of antibodies directed against the immunogen used, this process may also lead to the depletion of the most high-affinity antibodies, which may not be eluted from the peptide agarose. Thus, an important fraction of the immune response may not have been evaluated here. This is another strong argument for cloning individual antibodies using any of the nowadays available strategies.
iv. While GPCR antibodies are not easily obtained, there is a large body of scientific publications describing very efficient approaches, even with chicken as the host species (see e.g. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5384726/).

In this manuscript, Nepveu-Traversy and colleagues propose a new approach for producing specific antibodies against a GPCR extracellular loop. Their strategy consists of an initial rational design of a macrocycle mimicking the GPCR region of interest, which is injected into chickens as immunogenic agents.
Given my expertise, I will mainly focus on the in silico methods used for the macrocycle rational design.
The approach described here is interesting and could potentially be applied to other proteins with exposed regions.
However, I have several concerns regarding the reproducibility and clarity of the proposed approach:
1) In the “Conformational Search” section, the authors describe an initial sampling of the peptides' conformational space using LowModeMD, implemented in the MOE software. It is not clear why they used R-field as solvation model instead of Generalized Born, which seems to be recommended for LowModeMD
(https://video.chemcomp.com/watch/RamuDvR9u5C9BxiEyYyAvq; https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ci900508k).
2) Then, the lowest-energy conformation was used as starting configuration for molecular dynamics simulations. However, the authors should clarify why they used a time step of 3 fs. Usually, the hydrogen bond length is constrained, and a time step of 2 fs is used.
3) The authors should improve the description of the methods used in the “Analysis of the molecular dynamics simulation” section.
They analyzed the molecular dynamics simulations using the time-lagged independent component analysis (tICA). Still, it is not clear which software was used and whether they used the whole trajectory or just the 20000 extracted structures.
Moreover, they should clearly describe which feature was used for this analysis (e.g., RMSD, internal distances, cartesian coordinates, etc.) and which lag-time was chosen.
Furthermore, it is not clear how many components were used.
4) The authors should clearly describe and show (if possible) how “The optimal combination of tICA components was chosen by comparing the corresponding GHMM timescales, and the optimal number of GHMM states was chosen via the Bayes information criterion”, to convince the reader that the chosen combination was actually optimal.
5) Finally, the authors should show a validation of the identified Markov states showing the convergence of the relaxation timescale vs lag-time plot and a statistical test for the Markovianity like the Chapman-Kolmogorov test (http://www.emma-project.org/latest/tutorials/notebooks/07-hidden-markov-state-models.html; https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4828816).
In my opinion, the current description of the computational methods is not enough to understand it, judge its robustness, and reproduce it. In this regard, I have to point out that no simulation data or scripts of the described analyses have been shared.
To improve both the reliability and reproducibility of the present study, I would suggest following the “Reliability and reproducibility checklist for molecular dynamics simulations” https://www.nature.com/articles/s42003-023-04653-0 included in the Nature Communication Computational tools reporting guidelines https://www.nature.com/ncomms/submit/resources.

The device described in this study is a wearable system that adheres to the skin and operates in a bent state; therefore, verification of repeatability and long-term stability is essential, and additional data demonstrating stability across at least 5000 bending & stretching cycles with moderate bending radius are required.

Although in principle a strain gauge should ideally be independent of stretching speed, crack-based strain gauges are expected to show frequency-dependent behavior, with GF decreasing or saturating at higher frequencies. 5. 3. Methodological dependence on a single pipeline. The entire study relies on one RAMPAGE-based detection pipeline. Given the diversity of available TE-derived TSS detection methods (e.g. ChimeraTE, LIONS, TEProf), the conclusions would be more robust if cross-validated with at least one complementary approach. This would help address potential biases or artifacts unique to the chosen pipeline.
4. Overcrowded pipeline figures: Figures 1 and Sup. Fig. 1 attempt to show too many methodological details at once. Simplifying the pipeline schematic and moving QC checks to supplementary material would improve readability.

10. Young vs. old TE promoters: The contrast between precise “young” and dispersed “old” promoters may be overstated. TE “age” criteria should be clarified, and the pattern reframed as a continuum rather than a strict dichotomy.

The methodology is generally robust. The use of RAMPAGE—which provides base-pair resolution of TSSs—is superior to standard RNA-seq for this purpose. The filtering criteria (e.g., entropy filtering, read-pair linking to exons) are stringent and appropriate for minimizing false positives. This manuscript reports the results of a longitudinal study on recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) and the risk of dementia among participants in the Kaiser Permanente Southern California database. Strengths of the investigation include the large sample size, the validation of outcome, the use of a vaccinated control group, and the extensive sensitivity analyses. Although the apparent protective effect may appear robust, there is a major source of potential bias that apparently has not been considered:
A very large proportion of unvaccinated individuals are censored because they received RZV during the period of follow-up. Although this proportion is not directly reported, it can be inferred from the data provided in Extended figure 1 -- for example, between years 2 and 3 after the index date, the number at risk declines by 20% in the vaccinated and by 57% in the unvaccinated, a difference almost certainly entirely due to incident RZV vaccination. This is problematic, because it is plausible that individuals remaining at risk are more likely to have cognitive decline and be at higher risk of dementia.
I cannot think of an easy fix of the potential bias above, but at the very least it should be acknowledged and the Authors should report the results of sensitivity analyses in which unvaccinated individuals continue to contribute to follow-up to the unvaccinated group until 31 December 2023, or until they are censored for other reasons. This would be a very conservative analyses, i.e. biased toward the null, because RZV vaccination could reduce risk of dementia in the unvaccinated group, but any remaining inverse association between RZV and dementia would be far more convincing.

=== reviewer_2 ===
Thank you for the opportunity to review this study investigating the relationship between two doses of the recombinant Zoster Vaccine (RZV) and subsequent dementia incidence in a large sample of adults in Southern California. The study is well designed and methodologically rigorous. It will make an important contribution to the evidence base for assessing the potentially protective effects of Herpes Zoster (Shingles) vaccines against dementia - an area of substantial public health interest.
The study uses a retrospective matched cohort study design with inverse probability of treatment weighting to improve balance between groups. Of particular note is the extra effort to compare the RZV vaccinated group with a non-shingles vaccinated group (Tdap) and a negative control. These extra analyses help provide reassurance that the findings are unlikely to be explained purely by health vaccinee effects which have been limitations of prior studies.
I have only minor comments for the authors to consider:
1. It seems that one key difference between the RZV group and their matched controls was that the RZV groups must have interacted with a health service provider in the period 1 April 2018 and 31 Dec 2020, whereas the unvaccinated controls may not have had any interaction? 2. It was not clear why there was a six-month delay included between index date and follow-up commencement – this could be explained more clearly.

The results report: “There were 2,118 Tdap-vaccinated individuals (3.2%) who contributed person-time to both cohorts as they were vaccinated with RZV during follow-up” . **Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**General Comments:**
This study investigates the association between the recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) and the risk of incident dementia in a large, well-characterized cohort of older adults within the Kaiser Permanente Southern California (KPSC) system. The authors report a significant reduction in dementia risk (aHR 0.49) associated with RZV vaccination, which persists—albeit attenuated—when compared to a Tdap-vaccinated control group (aHR 0.73). The study is timely, addresses a significant public health question, and utilizes a robust dataset. However, several methodological concerns regarding the potential for residual confounding, the definition of the index date, and the interpretation of the Tdap comparator require clarification before the findings can be considered conclusive.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study provides important real-world evidence regarding the potential neuroprotective effects of RZV. Given the discontinuation of the live-attenuated vaccine (ZVL) and the widespread adoption of RZV, this research is highly relevant. The novelty lies in the use of a large, integrated healthcare system to evaluate RZV specifically, rather than the older ZVL, and the attempt to mitigate "healthy vaccinee bias" through a Tdap-comparator cohort.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Index Date Definition:** The authors define the index date as the date of the second RZV dose. This introduces a potential "immortal time bias" or "selection bias." Individuals must survive and remain dementia-free for the 4–6 months required to complete the two-dose series to be included in the RZV group. While the authors attempt to mitigate this by assigning the same index date to the unvaccinated matches, the unvaccinated group does not have a corresponding "waiting period" requirement for a second dose. This may lead to an imbalance in the health status of the two groups at the start of follow-up.
*   **Healthy Vaccinee Bias:** The use of Tdap as a comparator is a strength, but it is not a perfect control. Tdap is often administered to health-conscious individuals who may have different health-seeking behaviors than those who do not receive any adult vaccines. The authors should discuss whether the Tdap cohort was restricted to those who received the vaccine *during the same study period* to ensure temporal alignment of health-seeking behavior.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The study is well-documented, and the use of IPTW to balance covariates is appropriate. The inclusion of E-values provides a helpful metric for assessing the robustness of the results against unmeasured confounding. The data sources (EHR) are reliable for a study of this nature.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
The manuscript is generally well-written. However, the "Methods" section is truncated in the provided text. The authors must ensure that the criteria for "dementia diagnosis" (ICD-10 codes) are clearly justified, particularly regarding how they distinguish between incident cases and pre-existing cognitive decline that may not have been formally coded.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   **Proportional Hazards Assumption:** The authors note a violation of the proportional hazards assumption in the MCI analysis and correctly stratified the analysis. They should explicitly state whether the proportional hazards assumption was formally tested (e.g., Schoenfeld residuals) for the primary dementia outcome.
*   **Sensitivity Analyses:** The sensitivity analysis starting follow-up at 1 year is excellent, as it helps address potential reverse causality (i.e., individuals with prodromal dementia being less likely to seek vaccination). The persistence of the effect (aHR 0.60 vs. unvaccinated) is compelling.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Confounding by Indication/Health-Seeking Behavior:** The authors should provide a more granular comparison of the RZV and Tdap cohorts. Specifically, compare the number of primary care visits, preventive screenings (e.g., colonoscopies, mammograms), and flu vaccination rates between the two groups prior to the index date to further validate the "healthy vaccinee" adjustment.
*   **Competing Risks:** Given the age of the cohort (≥65), mortality is a significant competing risk for dementia. The authors should clarify if they performed a competing risk analysis (e.g., Fine-Gray model) to ensure that the observed reduction in dementia is not simply a reflection of differential mortality between the vaccinated and unvaccinated groups.
*   **Missing Data:** The manuscript does not explicitly detail the handling of missing data for covariates used in the IPTW. Please clarify if multiple imputation was used or if missingness was handled via indicator variables.
*   **Generalizability:** The KPSC population is insured and integrated. The authors should include a brief discussion on how these findings might translate to populations with less consistent access to primary care or different socioeconomic profiles.

**Conclusion:**
This is a high-quality observational study. If the authors can address the potential for immortal time bias in the index date definition and provide a competing risk analysis, the findings will be significantly strengthened and suitable for publication in *Nature Communications*.

We commend Jaratlerdsiri et al. on an interesting manuscript, which describes unprecedented diversity in Namibian genomes, and clarifies questions of population structure among Khoe-San-descent populations and neighboring groups. The addition of Damara, Khwe and Hai//om genomes from the Khoe-language family are especially exciting. We have several minor comments regarding nomenclature and clarification (there is some awkward phrasing throughout). We recommend de-emphasizing the estimates of population divergence as derived from MSMC analysis, as these estimates have been shown to be biased by gene flow, sequence coverage, cryptic structure and, as also highlighted here, phasing. Despite the appealing simplicity of MSMC analysis, fully parameterized demographic models are more interpretable (and the authors are missing key genomes from eastern Africa which represents a migration into southern populations). There is also a bit of confusion about using the term " ǂNu ̄ khoen Forager" as applied to populations other than the Damara and the ancestry component that is clearly shared among the Himba/Herero/Hai\om/Nama/Tjimba etc.
Minor comments:
— We recommend hyphenating “Khoe-San” throughout the paper and figures when referring to the southern African Khoe-San populations collectively and where southern African ancestry is not referred to as “southern African Foragers”. In the past, members of the South African San Council requested to remain distinct from their Khoe-speaking neighbors, and to be referred to by their specific ethnic identities or generally as the San (Schlebusch, C. (2010). Issues raised by use of ethnic-group names in genome study. Nature, 464(7288), 487–487. https://doi.org/10.1038/464487a). Previously, we have acknowledged their difference in identity through hyphenating and capitalizing ‘Khoe’ and ‘San’ while referring to the collective ancestral component. See also Schlebusch 2020, MBE.
— Our second recommendation regards the nomenclature around language. We’ve found it easier to refer to the population / ancestry as “Khoe-San”, given the above, and use “Khoisan” to reference the language phylum, consistent with how linguists have previously referred to the larger category.
-- Line 60. There are 25 Khoe-San genomes in Schlebusch et al (2020, MBE); 84 Nama in Ragsdale et al (2023, Nature); 30 !Xoo and Juu in Fan et al. (2022, Cell); 6 in HGDP. This is a rough total of 145 genomes. --> "To date, in-depth WGS has included only about 150 Khoe-San individuals representing eight linguistic groups from four countries. We double the number of available genomes, including previously unrepresented linguistic groups."
