=== reviewer_3 ===
Jaratlerdsiri and colleagues report about 150 new high-coverage Southern African genomes from Namibia. The coverage of several different groups makes this a highly valuable dataset. Unfortunately, the analysis presented in the paper does not do justice to this unique dataset. I have outlined my major concerns about the data and the analyses below.
1. Ethics, consent, and sharing: The manuscript does not provide sufficient details on the data collection. Given that these genomes are from highly marginalized populations that have previously been aggrieved by genomics research, it is pivotal that the ethical aspects of the study are evaluated critically.
i. Firstly, did the Namibian San council approve the study? Proof of approval needs to be provided.
ii. A full section on the recruitment of the participants and the ethics are provided. This should answer questions such as:
a. When were the Kho-San participants recruited? Who performed the recruitment?
b. What did the participant information sheet/Case report form say?
c. How were the concepts of whole genome sequencing, and secondary data sharing explained?
d. Which languages the informed consents were translated into? Could the participants sign? If not, how it was captured?
e. Did the informed consent have a provision for individual-level data sharing?
f. How will the access to the data be regulated? Who will oversee that?
iii. Could the authors clarify how the "extensive and continued engagement" as mentioned in the manuscript was performed?
a. How many times the participants/communities were visited before the study and how many times they have been contacted after the sample collection?
b. What was the mechanism and frequency of community feedback
a. The author list includes only two authors from Namibia and none of them seem to have expertise in genetics or history – so how was it ensured that the participants/communities understood the key messages and nuances?
2. Population structure: The authors had the unique opportunity to investigate the population structure and correlation between genetics and ethnolinguistic identities of individual San populations. Surprisingly the authors did not compare these genomes to any of the public genomics datasets (Schlebusch et al. 2017, Choudhury et al. 2020, Sengupta et al. 2022, Ragsdale et al. 2023, Tallman et al. 2023, Fortes lima et al. 2023) from Southern Africa that could have a provided a framework to interpret the variations and the structure reported in these novel genomes.
Even in terms of presentation - the 3-dimensional PCA plots with only a few populations are difficult to interpret. Phylogenetic trees with only a subset of genomes were not very informative either. The authors should present their genomes in the backdrop of at least some of the previous datasets and if possible, employ some of the more recent approaches such as UMAP and GCAE to visualize the population structure in a more informative way.
3. Population divergence and demographic history: A 13,000-year split between ǂNūkhoen and Bantu speakers is one of the highlights of the results. However, this does not align with the current understanding and models of African population migration and history. Moreover, this claim is based only on a single method and concerns have been raised about the accuracy of PSMC/MSMC-based population divergence estimates. Therefore, the authors need to employ other approaches such as SMC++ and RELATE that can analyze a larger number of sequences per group to support their claim. Also, it would be useful to check whether the same results are obtained if other proxy Bantu-speaker populations are considered.
As a lot of work needs to be done to support this claim, in case the authors find that it might take a substantial time to do this, they can take this section out.
4. The comparison of European ancestry Australians to Khoe-San to identify lifestyle-associated selection is perhaps the weakest section of the manuscript.
There are several layers of differences – including strikingly different demographic histories (out-of-Africa related and probably tens of strong bottleneck events thereafter in one group), genetic drift, non-random/assortative mating, introgression from groups such as Neanderthal and Denisovans, the geographically stratified impact of pathogens, the impact of different climatic conditions that could have caused these populations to harbor different alleles at different frequencies.
The attempt to relate the differences in the populations with such old divergences and extremely different histories to be just due to “forager" and "Western" lifestyle is not meaningful. Had the comparison been performed to related African populations with different lifestyles it might have still made sense.
Although the dN/dS ratio-based selection scan has been in use for a long time it is rarely employed these days for identifying signatures of selection in humans. In case, the authors believe that this is superior to other well-established (allele frequency-based. LD-based, SFS-based) methods then they need to demonstrate it using specific cases and in-depth comparisons with results from other methods. I am not sure if that is within the scope of the current manuscript. Given that the premise they are applying the selection scan to is in itself problematic. I believe this section should be taken out completely.
Minor comments
1. The scheme of nomenclature is not uniform – the abstract starts with Khoe-San and the introduction say this is a Khoe-San genomic resource, but then the rest of the manuscript goes on to describe the populations as “Southern African forgers”.
2. Several statements that are not well-founded and need to be removed or reframed. For example, the paper states that - "Our forager populations also maintained 21 ancient and inactive AluJo mobile elements (thought to integrate into primate genomes ∼65 million years ago41), again supporting their prehistoric lifestyles."
How do the authors know that the other populations did not lose these elements due to strong bottleneck or genetic drift but that the Khoe-San retained these due to prehistoric lifestyle? Did they check whether these elements are fully absent in all other humans, especially African populations? Is there a reason that the prehistoric lifestyle is benefited by this?
In summary, I would recommend the authors demonstrate that the data was collected, and stored with proper ethics, permissions (especially the San council), and community engagement. They also need to show that they have the necessary permissions from communities/authorities for cross-border sharing of individual-level data.
They need to expand their population structure section and bring in other relevant public datasets. I would recommend the authors take out sections on selection. Also, they need to either provide additional data for supporting the PSMC/MSMC-based claims or take out the section too.

In this manuscript entitled “Hemostatic Tough Adhesives Rapidly Seal Tissue and Control Hemorrhage”, the authors present a biocompatible hydrogel system (HTA) composed of alginate-polyacrylamide and a chitosan-based adhesive, designed to rapidly achieve hemostasis on solid organs even under active bleeding conditions. The authors perform a series of ex vivo and in vivo evaluations, demonstrating superior burst resistance, interfacial toughness, and sealing capacity compared to commercial hemostatic agents in porcine models. The HTA’s performance under coagulopathic conditions and its biocompatibility are particularly noteworthy. While this work holds clear translational potential, several key issues should be addressed before the manuscript is suitable for publication.
1. In the Materials and Methods section, the authors describe mechanical testing (e.g., pure shear tests using Instron), but no corresponding data are presented in the Results section or figures. The absence of these data weakens the claim that HTA offers superior mechanical robustness under physiological or supraphysiologic conditions. More importantly, the authors do not match HTA mechanical parameters (e.g., modulus, fracture energy, elasticity) with those of the target tissues (e.g., liver, spleen).
2. The manuscript claims that HTA provides effective sealing under active bleeding and in coagulopathic states (e.g., after heparinization), but offers minimal mechanistic explanation. The role of chitosan is briefly mentioned, but given its generally hydrophilic and mucoadhesive nature, it remains unclear how waterproofing or hemorepellence is achieved.
3. None of the physical test images or histological figures (e.g., Figures 2–4, S9) include scale bars, making it difficult to assess dimensions or tissue-material interactions.
4. The authors state that the HTA adheres in <3 minutes, but whether this qualifies as “rapid” compared to standard clinical practices is unclear. Moreover, there is no discussion of whether continuous active bleeding affects the adhesion process. The manuscript states that HTA can be “easily trimmed to fit wound geometry,” but this feature is neither visually demonstrated nor quantified.
5. Several recent bioadhesive strategies (e.g., barnacle-inspired pastes, nanoparticle-crosslinked gels, topological adhesives) have reported similar or related functionalities, including sealing wet surfaces and coagulation-independent hemostasis.

Feng et al. conducted an analysis using proteomics data from the UK Biobank, investigating the association between proteomics and incident Crohn's Disease (CD). Their study is notable, with data from 52,896 adults using the Olink Explore panel, among whom 139 developed CD over a median follow-up of 13.6 years. This is an interesting body of work that might provide new insights to the preclinical phase of CD. While the study is interesting, several concerns arise regarding the analyses and interpretation of the results:
-The average age at baseline for this cohort was 56.8 years (SD 8.2). However, it is unclear what the duration of follow-up is for the 139 individuals who developed CD. Summary statistics (minimum, maximum, IQR, median, mean) for the follow-up duration (from baseline to diagnosis) among the 139 cases should be provided. Additionally, the age at diagnosis for the 139 subjects should also be shown.
-Presumably, the age at diagnosis is close to or above 60 years, indicating that the CD cases in this cohort are predominantly elderly onset. This represents a relatively small subgroup of incident CD cases in the general population, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to the broader incident CD population. This limitation should be clearly acknowledged.
-The diagnosis date was determined by the earliest recorded appearance of ICD-10 codes. However, a likely discrepancy exists between the actual diagnosis date and the date of ICD-10 code appearance. Some cases diagnosed near the time of code appearance may have had earlier diagnoses that were not captured by the ICD-10 codes. Were any efforts made to reduce this potential bias? This is distinct from the issue of diagnosis delay. Did the authors set a minimum follow-up duration prior to a CD diagnosis? At a minimum, a sensitivity analysis excluding cases that developed CD within 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 years before diagnosis should be conducted.
-In the baseline characteristics table, the authors compared those who developed CD over time to those who remained healthy as of October 2022, which should be explicitly stated.
-The authors employed a machine learning algorithm to combine the 10 significant proteins from either model 1 or model 2. It appears that they developed a model to classify a binary outcome and subsequently applied this model to cumulative cases over time, up to 16 years. Have the authors considered using a machine learning algorithm with a time-to-event extension? Additionally, can they provide calibration data for the model in the testing set?
-There is significant class imbalance in the dataset. The authors mention the use of balanced class weighting in the figure legend, but further details on how this was implemented should be provided.
-The authors seem to have used an optimal cut-off based on the Youden index and then reapplied the same cut-off to the same cohort from which it was derived. This raises concerns about potential overfitting. It is unclear whether the cut-off was derived from a training set and then applied to a testing set.
Minor Points:
-The authors used the optimal proteins from the PREDICTS study and applied them to the UK Biobank cohort. However, it should be emphasized that the SOMAscan assay and the Olink Explore panel are two different assays with limited overlapping proteins.
-The authors stated that the time before diagnosis in the GEM cohort was relatively short compared to the UK Biobank cohort. It should be noted that these two cohorts differ in how the CD diagnosis date was defined (physician-confirmed in GEM vs. ICD code appearance in UK Biobank) and represent different populations (at-risk first-degree relatives in GEM vs. an elderly general population in the UK Biobank).

The core objective of this study is to develop a panel of serum protein biomarkers to predict Crohn's disease prior to disease onset. The study analyzes data from the UK Biobank (n > 52K), where baseline plasma proteomics measurements were taken, and patients were followed for up to 16 years. Additional variables, including clinical data, serum assays, polygenic risk scores, and demographic information, were also incorporated to compare the model based on the protein signature alone and in combination with these variables.
The methodology is standard, starting with feature selection based on univariate statistical analyses (Cox proportional hazards model) and proceeding to feature importance ranking with SHAP analysis (resulting in a selection of 10 proteins). These selected proteins were then used as inputs in the LightGBM algorithm (for protein-only, combined indicators, and other combinations). Validation was conducted using a random data split or 5-fold cross-validation (internal validation).
Overall, while the study may have some clinical merit, more robust validation is needed to clarify its potential utility. Here are some specific comments:
1) It is unclear whether feature selection was performed on the training data alone or on the entire dataset. Based on the description, it appears that feature selection may have been conducted on the entire dataset, with data splitting only performed for model training and validation. If true, this would introduce information leakage, compromising the model’s generalizability.
2)The initial feature selection approach is univariate (Cox model), followed by SHAP analysis to filter out less contributive features based on correlation analysis. While this is a reasonable approach, it is fairly basic. There have been several advances in machine learning feature selection methods that could be leveraged to enhance model performance.
3) Only one machine learning model, LightGBM, was employed. Although LightGBM is a valid choice, the approach could be broadened by exploring multiple models or ensemble methods, such as meta-learning or superlearners, to integrate predictions from various algorithms and potentially improve performance.
4) Multi-modal integration: The study uses only a simple concatenation of features (early fusion) for multi-modal integration. This approach is valid but basic.
5) Internal validation: The study uses a single run of 5-fold cross-validation. To increase rigour and reduce selection bias, multiple runs of 5-fold cross-validation could be implemented, accounting for potential bias introduced by initial random ordering.
6) Lack of external validation: The absence of external validation significantly impacts the generalisability and clinical relevance of the findings. The authors could consider testing their signature panel in an external dataset, such as the PREDICT study (Torres, 2020). Notably, the PREDICT study reported an AUROC of 0.76, comparable to the findings here. However, upon validation within the UK Biobank samples, the AUROC in this study was observed to decrease, highlighting the importance of independent validation to confirm model robustness and applicability.

The authors present a proteomic-based machine learning model for the prediction of incident Crohn’s disease (CD) using data from the UK Biobank (UKB), with external validation in the EPIC-Norfolk cohort and a small cross-sectional cohort from Southern China. By analyzing 2,736 plasma proteins, the authors identify a 9-protein signature (including CD274, CHI3L1, and IL6) that demonstrates predictive utility for CD onset up to 16 years prior to diagnosis. The study concludes that this proteomic panel outperforms clinical risk models and provides a robust tool for early risk stratification.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study addresses a critical gap in gastroenterology: the lack of reliable, non-invasive biomarkers for the preclinical phase of CD. The use of the UKB-PPP dataset is a significant strength, allowing for a longitudinal analysis that exceeds the temporal scope of previous studies (e.g., the PREDICTS study). The identification of a 9-protein signature that maintains predictive value across geographically distinct cohorts is a notable contribution to the field of precision medicine in IBD.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The methodology is generally robust, utilizing a large-scale prospective design. However, there are significant concerns regarding the cross-sectional validation cohort:
*   **Cohort Mismatch:** The Southern China cohort (n=74) is cross-sectional, comparing established CD patients to non-IBD controls. This is fundamentally different from the prospective, longitudinal design of the UKB and EPIC-Norfolk cohorts. Using a cross-sectional cohort to "validate" a predictive model for *incident* disease is methodologically flawed, as the protein levels in established disease may reflect the inflammatory state of active CD rather than the preclinical biomarkers of future onset.
*   **Protein Measurement Discrepancy:** The UKB and EPIC-Norfolk cohorts utilized Olink PEA technology, whereas the Southern China cohort utilized ELISA. While the authors state this was for "reproducibility," the lack of cross-platform calibration data makes it difficult to determine if the observed AUCs are comparable.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility of Results:**
The internal consistency within the UKB and the external validation in EPIC-Norfolk are commendable. However, the "reproducibility" in the Southern China cohort is overstated given the differences in disease status (preclinical vs. established) and assay technology. The authors must clarify whether the ELISA results were normalized to the Olink NPX scale or if they are reporting raw concentration values.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
The manuscript is well-written and the figures are informative. However, the reporting of the "16 years pre-diagnosis" claim requires more granular detail. It is unclear if the predictive performance (AUC) remains stable across the 16-year window or if it decays significantly as the time-to-diagnosis increases. 1.  **Time-to-Event Analysis:** Provide a time-dependent AUC analysis to demonstrate how the model’s predictive power changes as the time-to-diagnosis approaches the 16-year mark.
2.  **Validation Cohort Clarification:** Explicitly acknowledge the limitations of using a cross-sectional, established-disease cohort for validating a predictive model. Biomarkers of Response to Neoadjuvant Palbociclib Plus Anastrozole in Endocrine-Resistant Breast Cancer
The manuscript investigates potential biomarkers of response to a combination treatment of palbociclib and anastrozole
(ANA/PAL) in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+)/HER2-negative breast cancer that is resistant to standard endocrine therapy.
In this study, the authors analyze tumor biopsies from 34 patients to identify molecular features associated with treatment
resistance or sensitivity. The primary endpoint was the rate of complete cell cycle arrest (CCCA), defined by a significant
decrease in the proliferation marker Ki67.
Key findings include:
-A 57.6% CCCA rate was observed among patients receiving ANA/PAL, indicating that this treatment combination may
suppress proliferation in a subset of endocrine-resistant tumors.
-Resistance to ANA/PAL was associated with certain intrinsic subtypes (e.g., LumB and HER2-E) and the activation of
signaling pathways related to cell cycle progression (e.g., MYC and mTOR), immune response (e.g., interferon), and
immune tolerance markers such as IDO1.
-The authors propose that certain molecular markers, particularly gene signatures related to cell cycle control
and immune modulation, could serve as predictive biomarkers of response to ANA/PAL.
Major Issues
While this study provides a detailed descriptive analysis of biomarkers in a small cohort of endocrine-resistant breast cancer
patients, the following key issues limit its suitability for publication in a high-impact journal like Nature Communications:
1.Small Sample Size (34 Patients) The small sample size significantly limits the generalizability and statistical power of the
study’s findings. With only 34 patients, there is a higher risk of variability and limited ability to draw reliable conclusions
about potential biomarkers of resistance or sensitivity to ANA/PAL. For studies of predictive biomarkers in cancer, larger
cohorts are typically needed to achieve statistical robustness and validate associations between molecular characteristics
and treatment outcomes.
2.Descriptive Nature Without Experimental Validation The study is largely descriptive, identifying potential biomarkers
without functional experiments to validate their roles in modulating response to ANA/PAL. It is just a number of -omic studies
conducted in a sampleset with a clinical outcome, but not real hypothesis-driven scientific work. For a biomarker study
intended for a journal like Nature Comms experimental validation is essential. This could involve in vitro or in vivo assays to
confirm whether the identified markers directly influence treatment efficacy. Without such experiments, the study does not
establish causative relationships, making it less impactful for the field.
3.Lack of an Independent Validation Cohort An independent validation set is absent in this study, which limits the
reproducibility and reliability of the findings (kind of in line with point 1 – but equally essential). High-impact studies in
biomarker research typically require validation in a separate cohort to confirm that observed associations are not specific to
the initial sample. The absence of a validation cohort reduces confidence that these biomarkers will be effective in broader
patient populations.
4.Redundancy of Certain Findings Some findings, such as the association of intrinsic subtype with response to CDK4/6
inhibitors, are already well-documented in the literature. The association between high-risk subtypes like LumB and reduced
responsiveness to CDK4/6 inhibitors has been previously established (e.g., Aleix Prat et al, Journal of Clinical Oncology,
2021; 39(13): 1458-67), which diminishes the novelty of this manuscript. While the study provides additional detail on
molecular signatures, the insights presented do not substantially advance current knowledge.
Conclusion
In summary, while the manuscript offers an informative descriptive analysis of potential biomarkers in endocrine-resistant
breast cancer, these limitations in sample size, experimental work, lack of independent validation, and the redundancy of
some findings preclude its publication in a high-impact journal like Nature Communications. Strengthening the study with a
larger cohort, experimental validation of biomarkers, and a validation set would significantly enhance its impact and
suitability for such a journal.

=== reviewer_1 ===
Unal et al. report a fully human closed-loop gene circuit (ARCH) for autonomous blood pressure regulation. The authors
rewire AT1R into a biosensor that detects angiotensin II (AT-II) and couple it to the expression of a secretion-engineered
soluble ACE2 (stACE2). They demonstrate restoration and maintenance of normal blood pressure following implantation of
microencapsulated ARCH-transgenic human cells, providing convincing proof-of-concept evidence. Overall, this study
represents a significant advance in the application of synthetic biology to chronic disease therapy and offers a promising
approach that warrants further investigation. Before publication, I have some minor concerns as follows:
1. Lines 244-249, the AT-II sensor was functional across multiple mammalian cell types, with the strongest response
observed in HEK-293T cells. Could the authors speculate on which factors might underlie these differences, such as
receptor expression levels or cell-type-specific signaling efficiency?
2. Lines 314-321, the stable monoclonal HEKARCH cell line showed ~300-fold higher AT-II sensitivity compared to
transiently transfected cells. Could the authors explain the potential factors underlying this enhanced sensitivity? For
example, is this improvement due to increased copy number, higher expression stability, or other cell-intrinsic mechanisms?
Clarifying these factors could provide valuable guidance for improving the sensitivity of similar systems in future studies.
3. Lines 294-304: sACE2 is described as a licensed ad hoc drug for the treatment of Covid-19. Given that hypertension is a
chronic condition requiring long-term treatment, could the authors discuss the potential risks associated with prolonged
ACE2 protein secretion? Although ACE2 expression and secretion are controlled by the AT-II sensor, it would be important
for the authors to comment on what levels or duration of AT-II sensor-responsive ACE2 expression could be considered
safe.
4. Could the authors provide information on the response kinetics of the system? Specifically, how rapidly can the AT-II
sensor–controlled ACE2 expression respond to changes in AT-II levels, and how quickly does this translate into measurable
blood pressure reduction?
5. If possible, could the authors verify whether the system is capable of responding to blood samples from hypertensive
patients? Demonstrating responsiveness in clinically relevant samples would further support the translational potential and
therapeutic relevance of the system.
6. This study demonstrates synthetic gene circuits with potential for treating chronic diseases. To contextualize these
findings and highlight their potential applications, the authors may refer to representative previous works, including synthetic
gene circuits for treating chronic diseases via inhalation (PMID: 38321056) and for diabetes therapy in large animals (PMID:
31645456, 34608325).
7. The black bars obscure the distribution of individual data points; please consider using a different color to improve
visibility. Regarding Fig.1a, the current schematic is overly simplified. It would be helpful to provide a more detailed
illustration of the signaling pathway and the operational process of the system.

=== reviewer_2 ===
In this study, Unal et al. designed a cell-based therapy for hypertension called ARCH (autonomous regulator of chronic
hypertension), which utilized human cells co-transfected with type-1 angiotensin receptor (AT1R) and a chimeric promoter
(PCSN, CRE-SRE-NFAT-Pmin) driven soluble therapeutic ACE2 (stACE2). Increased blood Angiotensin-II (Ang-II) levels
under hypertensive conditions would activate AT1R, which then induce the expression of stACE2 through the chimeric
promoter. The authors first tested this system in cultured cells and then tested its therapeutic potential in the Ang-II infusion
model of hypertension in mice. The same research group has designed similar closed-loop systems for the treatment of
experimental arthritis, obesity, and diabetes, but its application in hypertension is new. However, there is a major concern of
utilizing Ang-II levels as the activation switch, as blood Ang-II levels in patients with hypertension vary. Although Ang-II
levels are usually elevated in patients with severe essential hypertension, renal hypertension, and malignant hypertension,
its levels are usually normal in benign and uncomplicated essential hypertension. Moreover, blood Ang-II levels can be
altered by drugs including many anti-hypertensive medications. Thus, the utility of such a system in hypertensive patients is
questionable.
In addition, the following concerns are noted about the proposed cell-based therapy:
1. Plasma Ang-1-7 levels should be measured in the in vivo validation experiment.
2. The Ang-II infusion model is an acute, not chronic, model of experimental hypertension.
3. The anti-hypertensive drugs used in Figure 4a affect Ang-II levels in vivo, thus this cell-based (HEK 293) assay cannot
rule out the interactions of ARCH with canonical hypertension medications.
4. The tai cuff method is less reliable than radiotelemetry, especially for diastolic blood pressure measurement.
5. What behavioral monitoring was conducted in these mice (line 347)?
6. The authors stated that “the cell-containing capsules were harvested at two weeks post-implantation together with the
surrounding peritoneal lavage (line 352-253),” but this is not consistent with how the cells were implanted, line 214-215
“Therapeutic cell capsules were injected subcutaneously (1 mL, ~5 million cells per mouse) on day 4 in the caudal region.”
7. Leukocyte activation markers should be included in the leukocyte profiling (Supplementary Figure 5).
8. A two-tailed t-test is more appropriate than the one-tailed t-test used in this study. What statistical methods were used
when more than two groups were compared?
9. Please list the number of mice used in each group in the in vivo experiment.

=== reviewer_3 ===
Unal et al showed a proof-of-concept therapy based on a synthetic biology approach to treat hypertension. The technology
involved the development of a fully human, closed-loop gene circuit named ARCH (Autonomous Regulator of Chronic
Hypertension), that leverages the angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) and a stabilized, secretion-engineered angiotensin-
converting enzyme 2 (stACE2), to autonomously sense and regulate blood pressure. This is a highly innovative approach,
and experiments clearly showed possible application.
1. It is not clear why the authors included an NFAT response element in the synthetic promoter, because, as depicted in
Figure 1C, PNFAT did not respond to Ang II.
2. In supplementary figure 2, the authors showed a basic (panel a), and a booster (panel b) sensor design. It is not clear
whether the experiments performed in the manuscript were done using the basic or the booster design.
3. In figure 2b, angiotensin A, angiotensin-(1-9,) and angiotensin-(1-5) should also be tested.
4. In figure 2f, the drugs were added in the presence of Ang II? Because in the figure appears as - AT-II + Drug
5. Only protein levels of stACE2 were measured. Because the enzymatic activity of ACE2 is important for its biological effect,
stACE2 activity should also be measured.
6. How stable is the HEKARCH (Stable, monoclonal) cell line? Because synthetic gene circuits may undergo genetic drift or
silencing over time.
7. The in vivo experiments were performed using an Ang II-infused mouse model. Because hypertension is multifactorial and
not solely Ang II dependent, a different hypertension model should be tested, for instance, on spontaneously hypertensive
rats.
8. In the in vivo experiment, a control verifying that the decrease in blood pressure is due to stACE2should be included, i.e.,
by using an inhibitor of stACE2.
9. In the animals, are the levels of Ang II decreased and the levels of Ang-(1-7) increased?
10. Produces this approach also a reduction of cardiac remodeling, vascular remodeling?

=== reviewer_4 ===
The study approach is unique and novel model to use ARCH-transgenic human cells and elevate stACE2 to treat AT-II
hypertension. In this approach, it is expected that stACE2 will break down (reduce) hypertensive AT-II and increase anti-
hypertensive Ang1-7 peptide hormones. However, to validate these mechanisms, some measurements, as follows, are
important.
1. Plasma as well as tissue, particularly kidney levels of AT-II and Ang (1-7) will tell whether the levels of these peptide
hormones really changed and contributed to lowering the BP. Please measure the levels of these peptides.
2. ACE2 activity, not just the expression, is critical to correlate with the changes in AT-II and Ang(1-7).
3. Blocking/reducing AT1R is known to increase the renin activity, which has independently profibrotic activity via pro-
renin receptors. So please measure renin activity in the plasma and the kidney.
4. AT-II model of hypertension is good in animal models to understand the mechanism. For translational purposes, a salt-
sensitive model of hypertension could be more helpful.

**Reviewer Report**

**Reviewer:** [Redacted]
**Date:** October 26, 2023
**Manuscript Title:** Autonomous regulator of chronic hypertension (ARCH)

**1. Significance and Novelty**
The manuscript describes the development of "ARCH," a synthetic biology-inspired gene circuit designed to provide closed-loop, autonomous control of angiotensin II (Ang-II) levels in the context of hypertension. The integration of a native receptor (AT1R) with a synthetic promoter to drive the secretion of a therapeutic protein (stACE2) is a sophisticated application of mammalian synthetic biology. The novelty lies in the transition from traditional pharmacological intervention to a cell-based, homeostatic feedback system. Given the global burden of hypertension and the limitations of patient adherence to daily medication, this work addresses a significant clinical need. The study is highly relevant to the field of precision medicine and synthetic gene circuits.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design**
The experimental design is generally robust. The authors move logically from circuit design and optimization in HEK-293T cells to *in vivo* validation in both an Ang-II infusion model and a high-fat diet (obesity-associated) model. The use of stable monoclonal cell lines (HEKARCH) to improve sensitivity and reduce variability is a critical methodological strength. The inclusion of human serum validation (Fig. 7) provides a necessary bridge toward translational relevance.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility of the Results**
The data presented are of high quality. The dose-response profiles (Fig. 3) clearly demonstrate the benefit of stable integration over transient transfection. The *in vivo* data (Fig. 5) show a compelling restoration of normotension. However, the reproducibility of the "closed-loop" nature of the system relies heavily on the long-term viability of the microencapsulated cells. While the authors show data at two weeks post-implantation, the long-term stability (e.g., 3–6 months) of the alginate-encapsulated cells in an immunocompetent host remains a concern for chronic disease management.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting**
The manuscript is well-written and the logic is easy to follow. The methods section is detailed, and the supplementary information provides necessary context. However, the reporting of the "human serum" experiment (Fig. 7) lacks sufficient detail regarding the patient cohort. It is unclear how many patients were included, the demographic diversity, or the specific criteria used to exclude other confounding factors that might influence Ang-II levels in human serum.

**5. Statistical Rigor**
The statistical analyses are generally appropriate for the sample sizes used. However, in Figure 5, the comparison between ARCH and "other hypertension medications" (valsartan, etc.) requires more rigorous statistical justification. It is unclear if the "other medications" were administered at doses equivalent to the therapeutic output of the ARCH device, or if they were administered at standard clinical doses. This comparison could be perceived as biased if the dosing regimens were not normalized for potency.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed**

*   **Long-term Biocompatibility and Efficacy:** The study only reports data up to two weeks post-implantation. Given that hypertension is a chronic, lifelong condition, the authors must address the potential for fibrosis of the alginate capsules, which is a known failure mode for encapsulated cell therapies. Does the system maintain efficacy at 8 or 12 weeks?
*   **Safety and "Off-Target" Sensing:** While the authors demonstrate that valsartan blocks the circuit, they do not adequately address the risk of "hypotensive excursions" in the event of a sudden drop in endogenous Ang-II due to external factors (e.g., dehydration, acute illness). The authors claim no hypotensive excursions were seen, but the data provided (Fig. 5d) are limited. A more rigorous stress test (e.g., challenging the mice with an ACE inhibitor while the ARCH device is active) is required to prove the system does not drive blood pressure to dangerous, sub-physiological levels.
*   **Human Serum Validation:** The data in Figure 7 are promising but preliminary. The authors should provide a more detailed breakdown of the patient cohort. Furthermore, the correlation between Ang-II levels and stACE2 expression in human serum should be analyzed with a larger sample size to account for the high inter-individual variability in human RAS activity.
*   **Cell Line Origin:** The use of HEK-293T cells is standard for proof-of-concept, but these are not clinically suitable for human implantation due to their tumorigenic potential. The authors should discuss the feasibility of porting this circuit into a more clinically acceptable cell line (e.g., mesenchymal stem cells or patient-derived fibroblasts) and whether the sensitivity (EC50) would be maintained in such a context.

=== reviewer_1 ===
This study by Polina Beskrovnaya and colleagues investigates the molecular mechanisms involved in the biogenesis of the
outer membrane (OM) during spore germination in Acetonema longum, a diderm spore-forming bacterium from the
Firmicutes phylum. A. longum is notable for its ability to form spores with two membranes: an inner spore membrane (IsM)
and an outer spore membrane (OsM). The research focuses on how the OsM transitions into a true OM during germination.
The authors utilize structural biology, biochemistry, and genomics to explore the role of the β-barrel assembly machinery
(BAM) complex, particularly BamA, in this transformation. In mature spores, key outer membrane proteins (OMPs), including
BamA, are absent, suggesting that the true OM only forms once germination begins. In vitro experiments demonstrate that
BamA can spontaneously insert into lipid bilayers under physiological conditions, indicating its potential role in de novo OM
biogenesis during germination. Additionally, proteomic and phylogenomic analyses identify two conserved proteins—SonA,
a β-barrel OMP, and SonB, a putative OM lipoprotein—that are likely auxiliary factors supporting BamA in the membrane
remodeling process. The study proposes a model in which BamA, along with SonA and SonB, facilitates the formation of the
true OM during spore germination. This remodeling also includes the insertion of other OMPs, such as LptD, which is crucial
for maintaining the proper lipid composition of the OM. These findings emphasize the dynamic nature of bacterial membrane
remodeling and the central role of the BamA complex in this process. The study offers new insights into the evolutionary and
functional aspects of OM biogenesis in diderm spore-forming bacteria, with a robust methodology supporting its conclusions.
Specific points:
1, The article primarily focuses on the functional characteristics of BamA and its critical role in membrane remodeling and de
novo outer membrane biogenesis. However, the authors also delve into the biosynthesis and transport of
lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and phospholipids in the results section. How does this discussion relate to the broader context
of the study? Specifically, how do these lipid transport processes intersect with BamA’s function in outer membrane
assembly?
2, While the study suggests that SonA and SonB assist BamA in its function, this remains a speculative assertion. To
strengthen the study's conclusions, the authors could incorporate experimental approaches such as co-immunoprecipitation
to validate the interactions between BamA, SonA, and SonB during the membrane remodeling process.
3, The proteomic analysis identifies several outer membrane proteins (OMPs), but the detection of only about 50% of the
predicted proteins indicates that some low-abundance proteins might have been overlooked. To further support the authors’
conclusions, could more advanced mass spectrometry techniques be applied, or could membrane-associated proteins be
selectively enriched to capture a wider range of proteins involved in membrane biogenesis?
4, In the experiments demonstrating the insertion of BamA and SonA into liposomes (Figure 6), the authors used trypsin for
BamA and both trypsin and proteinase K for SonA. What was the rationale behind using two different proteases for SonA?
Additionally, why did the inserted form of SonA disappear entirely following treatment with proteinase K?
5, Since both BamA and SonA are β-barrel proteins, it would be beneficial to include a control group where samples are
either heated or left unheated before undergoing SDS-PAGE. This would ensure that the proteins adopt the correct spatial
configuration, providing further confidence in the folding and insertion data obtained from the experiments.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The assembly of the diderm cell envelope has, so far, been studied primarily in a few model “Gram-negative” species from
the Proteobacteria. In contrast, very little is known about outer membrane biogenesis in diderm Firmicutes, an ancient group
of bacterial species. This study focuses on diderm spore-formers such as Acetonema longum and investigates how the
organism reconstructs a “normal” vegetative outer membrane following spore germination.
The authors demonstrate that the spores possess two membranes; however, the outer spore membrane (OsM) differs
significantly from the vegetative outer membrane because it is derived from the cytoplasmic membrane of the mother cell.
Although the system is not genetically tractable, the authors perform gene expression and proteomic profiling, suggesting
that the OsM lacks typical outer membrane proteins. These include essential components for outer membrane biogenesis,
such as BamA (required for β-barrel protein assembly) and LptD (required for LPS transport).
The authors propose that during spore germination, BamA in Acetonema longum may be capable of self-inserting into the
phospholipid bilayer of the OsM due to its unique structural properties, thereby initiating the conversion of the OsM into a
typical outer membrane. Additionally, they suggest that BamA may interact with two unique partner proteins, based on gene
synteny analysis.
Overall, this is an interesting and thought-provoking study that provides a valuable starting point for investigating outer
membrane biogenesis in non-model organisms such as diderm Firmicutes. However, I have several important concerns, as
some of the data appear to be overinterpreted.
Major Comments:
1. Misleading Use of “De Novo Outer Membrane Biogenesis”:
The phrase “De Novo Outer Membrane Biogenesis” is misleading. For most readers, this implies de novo synthesis of the
outer membrane from scratch, not remodeling of a pre-existing membrane (OsM). While I understand that the OsM is
fundamentally different from the vegetative outer membrane , being derived from the mother cell's cytoplasmic membrane
and likely consisting of a phospholipid bilayer with distinct protein content, the process described in the manuscript is better
characterized as remodeling rather than de novo synthesis. Furthermore, there are several known bacterial species in which
LPS is non-essential under certain conditions, demonstrating that the outer membrane can transition to or from a
phospholipid bilayer. Therefore, the transformation of the OsM into a functional outer membrane does not constitute true de
novo synthesis.
2. Insufficient Evidence for the Absence of LPS in OsM:
The authors infer that the OsM lacks LPS based on the apparent absence of LptD and periplasmic Lpt components (lines
284-286). However, this alone is not sufficient evidence. Interestingly, the authors also show that LPS biosynthesis genes are
upregulated during sporulation. Since LPS biosynthesis occurs on the cytoplasmic leaflet of the mother cell's inner
membrane — which becomes the outer leaflet of the OsM — this raises the possibility that at least some LPS may be
present in the OsM. Direct assays are needed to confirm the presence or absence of LPS and support the conclusion.
3. Protein Abundance and Detection Limitations:
The proteomic data show a significant reduction in outer membrane proteins (OMPs), including
BamA. However, it is unclear whether these proteins are completely absent. In E. coli, essential OMPs such as BamA and BamD can be reduced by over
100-fold and remain undetectable by mass spectrometry, yet cells remain viable under slow-growing conditions. What is the
detection limit in the current mass spectrometry experiments? Can low levels of these proteins truly be ruled out? The
immunofluorescence experiments are also inconclusive, as residual spore coat layers may obscure detection of proteins on
the OsM. Positive controls are needed to validate these results.
Additionally, based on the stages of endospore formation (Fig. 1), what prevents the transport and self-insertion of BamA,
and therefore later OMPs and LPS, from the prespore into the mother cell-derived membrane during engulfment? From the
prespore side, the mother cell membrane looks the same as the inner leaflet of the outer membrane.
4. In Vitro Folding and Interpretation of BamA Assays:
The comparison between A. longum BamA and E. coli BamA relies on previously published data. A side-by-side in vitro
folding comparison would strengthen this point. The protease digestion assay used here is not a standard approach for
studying BamA folding. If protease sensitivity were only detecting membrane insertion, one would expect digestion of
exposed domains (e.g., POTRA domains), with only the membrane-embedded β-barrel remaining intact. However, multiple
undigested bands were observed (with no identification provided), suggesting unexpected protease resistance of
subdomains and complicating interpretation. Additionally, since these assays were conducted using E. coli phospholipids
rather than native lipids, the physiological relevance is uncertain. It is also worth noting that E. coli can be viable with BamA
alone in a strain lacking all Bam lipoproteins (with a specific bamA mutation), presumably because it self-assembles in vivo,
raising questions about the uniqueness of A. longum BamA's behavior.
5. SonA and SonB as Putative BamA Partners:
The identification of SonA and SonB as potential BamA partners is based on synteny. Since the authors generated anti-
BamA antibodies, they could perform co-immunoprecipitation or pull-down experiments to test for physical interactions.
In Proteobacteria, synteny between bamA, LPS biosynthesis demonstrated functional linkage, rather than physical protein
partnerships.
Other Comments:
1. The Introduction is overly long and reads more like a review article on outer membrane biogenesis. I suggest removing
details that are not essential for understanding the manuscript’s focus.
2. Lines 93–94: There is strong evidence suggesting non-overlapping functions.
3. Line 122: This statement is misleading. HxcQ does not self-transport; it contains a lipoprotein signal sequence and is
transported via the Lol pathway.

bacteria. Here Breskronaya et al cleverly use a sporulating Gram negative (A. longum) to study how the OsM transitions to a
bona fide OM. They convincingly show that expression of OM biogenesis machinery is timed to germination and
subcellularly locate the appearance of BamA and SonA OMPs to the emerging OM during germination. With a few additional
controls and experiments (Major points outlined below, related to concerns on the in vitro refolding assay) I would support
publication of the manuscript.

1) In vitro folding assay (Fig 6):
a): 6A: Where are the undigested controls?
b) A proportion of the unfolded BamA and SonA is resistant to proteolysis. How do the authors know that retained bands are
resistant to the protease due to folding and membrane insertion or instead merely due to aggregation forming precipitates
that are resistant to proteolysis? The experiments should be repeated by running heated and unheated samples. Folded
barrels are resistant the SDS denaturation and exhibit different electrophoretic migration than the unfolded form when the gel
is run at 4C. Since the authors already have this assay established, repeating the this assay with the above conditions
should be achievable in a short time frame.
2) The puncta of BamA is similar to the “assembly precincts” observed by the Lithgow group by super resolution microscopy.

This paper introduces a portable hip exoskeleton robot aimed at improving the quality of life for stroke patients by reducing their walking metabolism, which is highly significant in the current field of exoskeleton robotics. However, due to the complex and distinct walking kinematics, dynamics, and lower-limb musculoskeletal characteristics of stroke patients compared to healthy individuals, focusing solely on metabolic improvement is not comprehensive enough. For exoskeleton robots designed for stroke patients, it is desirable to enhance their mobility and metabolism without imposing additional burdens on other lower-limb joints and muscles. Overall, this paper holds substantial research value, but requires more comprehensive analysis of lower-limb joints and muscles in assisted stroke patients to confirm that hip exoskeleton assistance can effectively improve their quality of life.
1. The statement in the third paragraph, “This hyperextension increases loading on the knee, which can increase pain and the risk of secondary conditions, such as osteoarthritis,” indicates that elevated joint force may heighten the risk of joint pathologies (e.g., osteoarthritis). If assistance is applied at the hip joint, how would the joint force at the hip, knee, and ankle change? Would this impose greater force on the joints, potentially causing further harm to patients?
2. Gait asymmetry is a defining characteristic of stroke patients, as elaborated in the fourth paragraph: “Moreover, the unaffected side must compensate for the weakness and lack of coordination of the affected side, making hemiparetic gait highly asymmetric.” However, this critical feature was not analyzed in the study’s results. Could a comparative analysis be conducted on gait symmetry before and after hip exoskeleton assistance, alongside existing assistive strategies for stroke patients?
3. Although no prior studies have specifically targeted metabolic reduction in stroke patients, hip exoskeletons have been extensively investigated for reducing walking metabolic rate in healthy populations. Does the methodology of this study fundamentally differ from those previous works? What adaptations were made specifically for stroke patients? Does its application in stroke patients demonstrate superior efficacy compared to existing research?
4. This study shares similarities in research methodology with "Powered hip exoskeleton improves walking economy in individuals with above-knee amputation." Could you elaborate in detail on the methodological improvements in this study, as well as the advancements in the exoskeleton hardware?

Manuscript Number: NatComm – 617508
Portable Hip Exoskeleton Improves Walking Economy for Stroke Survivors
SUMMARY OF WORK:
This manuscript examines whether a bilateral, powered, autonomous hip exoskeleton (Fig 1a.) can reduce the metabolic cost of fixed-speed treadmill walking in people with stroke (Table 1). The authors designed and conducted a rigorous and comprehensive within-participant experimental design comparing metabolic and lower-limb joint mechanical effort without (No exo) and with (With exo) the hip exo providing clinician supervised ‘self-tuned’ timing and magnitude (ED Fig. 1) on each leg (paretic and non-paretic) (Fig. 1b, Fig 4.) The results indicate that hip exo assistance can reduce metabolic effort (W/kg) by 18% (Fig. 1c) and this is accompanied by significant reductions in users’ hip joint (29%) and total combined-lower-limb (14%) mechanical work. In addition, the authors detail how the exoskeleton contributes to hip work for each leg and phase of the gait cycle (Fig. 3) and show that the exo increases paretic limb toe clearance (ED Fig. 2).
Overall, the manuscript is excellent and presents the first evidence that hip exoskeleton can reduce metabolic effort post-stroke. The writing and presentation are logical and concise – with clearly stated objectives, aims and hypotheses. The analysis is already comprehensive and mechanistic as it stands, however, there are some key limitations in its ability to support the data with full rigor. The reader is left with some key questions that when resolved will increase the confidence in what will be a surefire landmark finding in the field. I offer my suggestions below in an effort to help strengthen the findings and ultimately the impact of the work.
COMMENTS/SUGGESTIONS:
There are two major issues that need to be addressed.
1. The authors mention that a number of the participants used handrails. This is fine as long as the handrail support is not measurably different in the No exo vs. With exo conditions (i.e. handrail support is not more/less on average in No exo vs. With exo condition). The authors address in their results stating:
‘For safety, all participants were instructed to rest their unaffected hand on a side-mounted handrail during all treadmill walking tests, using the smallest amount of handrail support needed. There was no statistical difference between the force applied while walking without the exoskeleton compared to with the exoskeleton. The handrail force was also low, ranging from 1 - 4% of each participant’s body weight.”
This is super. But, please add detail on the level of the forces measured over the gait cycle (e.g., participant average hand rail force time series graphs and a table showing avg. values per participant in ED.)
2. Based on documented efficiency of muscular positive mechanical work - user metabolic savings should not exceed ~ 4x user mechanical savings due to exoskeleton mechanical input. For this study the net metabolic power savings was ~0.5 W/kg which would suggest savings in positive stride cycle average mechanical power across the combined lower-limb of ~0.125 W/kg. However, the authors report metabolic results in W/kg and mechanical results in J/kg making this ‘back of the envelope’ gut check difficult without knowledge of the stride frequency. To add rigor and physiological grounding to the metabolic result please formally relate user metabolic savings (change in user input) to the user mechanical savings (change in user output and/or the exoskeleton mechanical input (device input) in consistent units and report for each individual. The preferred approach would be to plot these data in a scatter graph – and fit a line to the data – analyzing the value of the slope of the fit. Versions of this have been documented in the literature and termed ‘apparent efficiency’/ ‘performance index’ (Sawicki-Ferris), or ‘augmentation factor’ (Mooney-Rouse-Herr, Siviy-Walsh).
Some minor critiques.
3. Given that the participants vary widely in their walking speed – and metabolic rate is function of walking speed it would be a nice addition to present the data in speed normalized form as a function of speed (i.e. cost of transport (net met power/speed = J/m/kg vs. speed graph) for No exo vs. With Exo and use it to discuss what would happen if these participants were free to increase/decrease walking speed With Exo.
4. Given that the participants vary widely in their ‘tuned’ exoskeleton torque assistance profile, it would be a nice addition to add some discussion (if not analysis) on what features of the exo torque primarily drove the mechanical and metabolic changes.
5. It would be nice to indicate on the key results Fig. 1c what the ‘added mass penalty’ of the device is (i.e. Exo No Power). In other words- how much of the exoskeleton work went to offset it’s own mass? This would help more clearly define the performance ceiling of a more streamlined design.
6. Has this device been tested on able bodied controls? If so, what are the results and how do they compare to the stroke cohort. This would be especially interesting to note with respect to the ‘apparent efficiency’ (see comment 2). Discussion point?

In this work, authors presented a hip exoskeleton that provides active mechanical assistance bilaterally and bidirectionally to the hip joint during treadmill walking in seven individuals with hemiparesis. The use of their exoskeleton was able to reduce the metabolic cost of walking by 18%, likely by reducing positive biological hip work. This work has great potential to offer a portable solution for individuals with mild-to-moderate hemiparesis that enables them to walk for longer duration, leading to improved recovery and integration into the real world. Presentation of the work can be substantially improved by reorganizing the introduction and discussion, providing more detail in results (particularly in comparisons of non-metabolics related outcomes) and methods (particularly in training and tuning), and a more comprehensive discussion synthesizing results of different outcomes evaluated.
Introduction
The intro should be restructured to improve its cohesiveness. In this submission, authors jump back and forth between the discussion of post-stroke impairment and exoskeleton. Instead, consider centering the introduction around impairment-specific challenges related to metabolic cost, followed by discussion of demonstrated benefits and limitations of currently explored exoskeleton solutions to target these challenges, and why the authors’ solution - bilateral and bidirectional hip exoskeleton - is a promising alternative solution.
Please use people-first language when appropriate. “Individuals with above-knee amputation” is people-first, while “above-knee amputees” is not.
Results
Consider moving information from Extended Data Fig 1 into the main text when discussing tuning for both legs. From evaluating the figure it appears most individuals were tuned to receive similar level of assistance between the two legs, except for one participant. Results would be more comprehensive to include this quantification.
There seems to be a mix of statistical model-driven results and qualitative results. If this is the case, the authors should clarify which comparisons were statistically compared and which were not by distinguishing their language between these sets of comparisons. If all comparisons were statistically driven, then these comparisons should also include relevant statistical output (method, p value).
On a similar note as the previous comment, it is unclear whether the authors compared any hip work during stance, foot clearance, and kinematic variables with and without exo assistance using statistical methods.
Reporting percentage of change alongside actual numbers is helpful in sensing whether the change in outcome due to assistance is a big or a small change. The authors should include this information throughout - currently not included in hip work during stance, foot clearance, and kinematics.
In “exoskeleton assistance,” please provide quantifiable results that lead to authors’ claim that “peak power generated on the unaffected side was greater than that generated on the affected side” for both hip motion.
Discussion
In the discussion of symmetry restoration through exo, consider linking this back to metabolic cost reduction (i.e. relationship between asymmetry and increased metabolic cost)
However, the solution is unique since this device provides bilateral assistance. Authors should consider reframing this statement to highlight the advantages and rationale for choosing a bilateral solution with active assistance bidirectionally compared to other approaches.
Discussion paragraph acknowledging the smaller sample size and lack of difference between different groupings could be better polished by synthesizing these results more. While further studies with increased sample are certainly warranted, consider the possibility that these results suggest this exo could be a viable solution for people with wide range of impairment, size or sex, and use of other assistive devices.
Broadly speaking, the organization of the discussion could be improved, similar to the reviewer comment with the introduction. Some suggestions include: 1) Inclusion of a limitation paragraph towards the end of the discussion so they appear together (small sample size, weight, tuning method), 2) more transitions between paragraphs, and 3) grouping ideas together.
The discussion of manual tuning and potential direction for optimization seems incomplete. First of all, these two sections can be combined (but there is currently an unrelated paragraph in between - see notes on organization above). Second, the discussion would be more comprehensive with authors’ comments on how they think the decision to manual tune impacted their results, and why they decided to do it this way. After that, the authors could acknowledge automatic optimization pipeline as a potential future direction.
Methods
Please provide more detail on the training sessions individuals received - what was the average number of sessions and average duration over which time period? For individuals who received more than one training, did the authors tune the parameters fresh? Or start at the converged parameter from the previous training? How did the authors accommodate if user preference and comfort has changed between training?
Please provide more detail on how the authors used “feedback from participants and the experimenter’s judgment” to tune the assistance parameters.
In the last paragraph of methods (discussion of stats), please include additional information regarding how the authors determined the assumptions of a two-tailed paired t-test were evaluated and met for the data.

Review for ‘The Curious Mind: Eye Movements to Maximize Scene Understanding’
Summary and strengths
This paper addresses a fundamental question about human gaze behaviour: What are people doing when they are ‚free
viewing‘, that is, looking at a scene without a specific task or instruction? This question is of particular importance as many (if
not most) key publications and databases on human gaze rely on free-viewing data. Previous models assume that people
primarily fixate on locally salient or meaningful regions or on objects which share semantic similarity with many other objects
in the scene (‘concept maps’). The authors propose that instead, people try to understand the scene. This proposal is similar
to Loschky’s SPECT theory about event comprehension but applies it to the free viewing of static images. Specifically, the
authors propose that people fixate those parts of a scene most which matter most for its global understanding.
The paper tests this hypothesis with a clever experimental design, which disentangles local salience and meaning from
importance for contextual, global understanding. Stimuli come in pairs of images, in which a given object is once crucial and
once irrelevant for scene understanding, because of its relevance for a depicted or inferred action (see Fig 1b of the paper as
an example). As predicted under the authors’ hypothesis, an object is far more potent in attracting human gaze when the
context renders it crucial for the global understanding of the scene. Crucially, this effect is not adequately predicted by any of
the previous models but can be captured with ‘scene understanding maps’. These maps are produced by iteratively
removing objects from a scene and quantifying the changes this removal causes in scene descriptions (either via human
ratings or LLM embeddings). The authors further show that this effect cannot be reduced to the objects being perceived to be
gazed at or grasped by actors in the images. Finally, the authors run a separate forced fixation experiment with brief
presentation times, showing that there is a causal connection between scene understanding and fixating the crucial object.
Fixating on the irrelevant object instead leads to erroneous descriptions of the scene.
In our view, there is much to like about this paper. It presents a simple but powerful hypothesis for an unsolved crucial
question and presents convincing evidence across a range of predictions and experiments, enabled by a clever design.
Given the broad relevance of free viewing data for studies on gaze behavior in psychology, neuroscience, computer vision
and clinical fields we think it is a highly important contribution for the broad readership of Nature Communications.
Nevertheless, we think a few improvements are possible, which we suggest below.
Suggestions
- How important is scene understanding for typical free-viewing behaviour? The paper convincingly shows that scene
understanding is a strong driver for the type of images used in this study. The authors discuss that this may not generalise
well to ‘empty’ scenes not implying any past, present or future actions, which we appreciate. However, it also seems unclear
how strong the effect is for other images depicting people and events, which are not designed to imply a crucial role for a
single object. Scene understanding maps may capture fixation behaviour which previous models fail to do, for other images
of scenes and events as well, but we don’t yet know this. This seems a relevant and exciting question, esp. because scene
understanding maps are potentially image computable with the help of multimodal transformers. We think this warrants
further discussion. To be clear, we do not consider this a problem for the main conclusion of the paper. It’s a virtue of the
study that the authors deliberately designed their stimuli to be maximally sensitive to the hypothesized effect and
disentangle it from other forms of saliency. However, it’s a relevant question for future research how important this effect is
relative to other baseline models for everyday scenes, not specifically chosen for this purpose.
- A related and important point is the nature of images and differences between image pairs. We applaud the authors for
making the stimuli available but encourage them to show more examples in the paper and describe them in more depth. The
current description of ‘small’ changes between images seems a bit misleading. Changes go beyond an object’s position
_or_ actor’s posture. Typically, there is a whole array of changes to imply a different narrative, including changes which will
affect the low-level salience and local meaning of the object (e.g. the laundry being placed more centrally or the projector
being switched on in the example given). This of course is controlled for by the baseline models but seems worth pointing
out. Also, some of the scenes seem hard to understand. The analysis focussing on misunderstood scenes used an image-
wise deviation from the gold standard description of 1 SD as cut-off. We suspect this may mean very different levels of
(mis)understanding for different images. It would be good to provide a feeling for this by showing some example descriptions
and discuss the nature of the scenes in this light.
- The discussion points out that models like DeepGaze could in theory pick up on contextual clues but may fail to do so
because of the images they are trained on. Another important reason seems that these models are trained to predict fixation
density maps, rather than peaks in those maps. The main analysis of the paper uses metrics that these models simply
weren’t optimised for, and Fig S2 shows that they perform at the same level as scene understanding maps when considering
AUCs for the whole map. This doesn’t take away from the clear evidence for the importance of scene understanding for free-
viewing over and above what these previous models can explain. But the lacking performance of these previous models
could be discussed with more nuance. A related question is how the models compare in terms of AUC when not leaving out
the fixations attracted by people?
- The abstract states that the ‘human brain’s default task during free viewing is to understand scenes‘. This may be a bit
premature, given the study only tested WEIRD adults. There is a plethora of studies showing individual, cultural and
developmental differences in free-viewing. These differences may mean that not everybody’s gaze is driven by scene
understanding. Alternatively, differences in gaze may reflect differences in scene understanding. The latter seems supported
by recent findings regarding the connection between individual gaze and individual scene descriptions (Kollenda, Reher &
de Haas, 2024 ). Either way, this point seems worth discussing and phrasing with a bit more caution.
Minor:
- The discussion states the prediction of future events as an important function of scene understanding. A recent paper by
Roth et al. (2024 PsychScience) shows that gaze is attracted by perceived potential for change and seems relevant in this
context.
- The example image in Fig 1 does not seem to be part of the stim set uploaded to figshare. Was it not used in the
experiment?
- Typo on page 14: ‘p ! 0.01’
- Fig 4a: The arrangement of the maps is potentially confusing, because the reader is tempted to group them in columns,
while there is no one-to-one relationship between models and experimental conditions. Maybe consider a line between the
upper (predicted) and lower (measured) rows of maps?

=== reviewer_2 ===
Summary: The authors investigate the fundamental goal of human eye movements during free viewing. Prior research has
suggested that fixations are guided by low-level saliency or local meaning. Here a new “theory” is tested: free viewing seeks
to maximize scene understanding by directing gaze toward objects critical to scene interpretation (rather than just salient or
locally meaningful regions). The authors introduce Winograd image pairs, where small visual changes change the scene’s
meaning without changing its saliency or local meaning maps. Eye-tracking experiments across four viewing conditions
(free viewing, scene description, object search, and counting objects) reveal that free-viewing fixations closely resemble
those during scene description (and are significantly different from object search or counting). Furthermore, observers fixate
most frequently on objects that, when removed, alter the scene’s overall interpretation—even more than objects identified as
the most salient or locally meaningful. A forced fixation experiment confirms that fixating on scene-critical objects enhances
comprehension, providing causal evidence that eye movements actively support scene understanding. The study also
compares multiple fixation models (saliency, DeepGaze, meaning maps, and the newly developed Scene Understanding
Maps (SUMs)), showing that SUMs outperform previous models in predicting human fixations.
Overall Evaluation: This paper presents an interesting contribution, but the fixation data are over-interpreted. It is
unsurprising that scene interpretation guides eye movements, and I would hesitate to call this a theory, given that multiple
fixations are required to bring high-resolution information to the brain—especially when relevant details are spatially
distributed. Moreover, in small scenes (as shown in the figures), where no fixation is needed to capture the full visual angle,
the free-viewing framework collapses, reducing the process to covert attention. That said, the use of Winograd image pairs is
a clever approach, effectively disentangling competing explanations and supporting the role of scene interpretation in
fixation behavior.
Major concern: A major limitation of the study in relation to the proposed theory is that it removes fixations on people, even
though humans are often central to scene interpretation. Faces, gaze direction, and hand actions provide crucial contextual
information about events, interactions, and object use, making them integral to understanding a scene’s meaning. By
excluding these fixations, the study risks underestimating the role of social elements in natural vision and may artificially
simplify how scene understanding operates. While this approach isolates object-driven fixations from social biases, it also
creates a paradox: if free-viewing supports scene interpretation, ignoring people—the most semantically rich elements in
many scenes—limits the generalizability of the findings. A more nuanced analysis could compare fixations in “people-rich”
versus “object-rich” scenes or distinguish between fixations on people for social attention versus functional scene
understanding. Additionally, understanding when in a sequence of fixations people are looked at would clarify how the
visual system prioritizes scene information, offering a stronger theory of scene understanding.
Recommendation: As it stands, this paper would be better suited for a specialist journal such as Journal of Vision or Vision
Research rather than a broad-readership publication like Nature Communications. However, if the authors were to revise
their theory of scene interpretation to explicitly incorporate social biases in fixations, the paper would become significantly
more compelling and more aligned with their own fixation data. This would likely require revisiting their analyses and
potentially conducting a control experiment, but I strongly encourage the authors to pursue this approach. Rather than
omitting what may be some of the most insightful findings, embedding social fixations into their theoretical framework would
enhance both the impact and the generalizability of their conclusions.
