The authors integrated spatial, single cell and bulk transcriptomics of carotid plaque, identifying inflammatory smooth muscle cell subtypes and localizing regions of neovascularization and macrophage activity. The authors applied a clever deconvolution algorithm to correct for immune cell bias and estimate true cell type proportions in bulkRNA-Seq data using scRNA-Seq-derived labels. The focus is on VSMCs and macrophages. There are several new and interesting findings:
1. TREM2 macrophages are not intermingled with C1Q macrophages, which sit below the endothelium
2. The authors convincingly discovered that immune cells are overrepresented in scRNA-Seq experiments
3. The authors dicovered that there was no difference between symptomatic and asymptomatic plaques. In many studies, this is the only distinction between plaques provided
Specific comments
1. Previous work has provided systematic pathological classifications (Pasterkamp, Virmanu). Please discuss how your findings relate to these.
2. Note that endarerectomies do not provide access to the adventitia, where many immune cells reside. This may explain why the immune cell content is so low.
3. Recently,TLOs were discovered in human plaque1 using methods similar to yours. Did you see any indications of TLOs?
4. Define CEA (probably the surgery).
5. The samples were macroscopically assessed and dissected into advanced atherosclerotic (plaque) and adjacent healthy/early lesion (control) tissue. It is not clear that the “control” is really healthy.
6. Since some samples had thrombus: what cells were in the thrombus?
7. FC thickness set at 200 μm: This is not easy to measure, because the sections may be at different angles, and cap thickness is not uniform. How reliable is this measure?
8. PI3K has many isoforms. Which ones are DE?
9. CD79A is not an immune regulator, but a B cell marker
10. Page 14: It is not clear which datasets are new (unpublished). Clearly distinguish between new and reanalyzed data.
11. Figure 2H: The immune cells are invisible. Either make an extra panel with a different scale, or use a log scale.
12. Figure 5A: numbers too small (not legible)
13. Figure 6A: show directionality (which genes were up in smokers?)
14. Page 4: “unpaired (n=232, n=65) and paired (n=42) designs, as well as stable (n=97) and unstable (n=126) plaques”. Some may be overlapping. What was the total number of samples?
15. The authors often talk about “carotid plaques”, but much of the resected material is not plaque but media. Maybe call them endarterectomy specimens.
16. SMCs, ECs and fibroblasts show up much better in single nuclei sequencing. Many studies used this approach, mitigating the bias. Please mention this and cite some studies.
17. The authors write that “VSMC-rich media from our CEA specimens (Fig 1A), a structure that has likely not been analysed in previous studies“. Was there a difference in gene expression in the media of adjacent normal vs atherosclerotic artery tissue? Paired analysis should be possible.
18. “Four patients provided paired samples”. Were these bilateral endarterectomies, with one side worse than the other? If so, what was the time elapsed between the two surgeries?
19. Page 6: ”Correlation analysis revealed a strong inverse relationship between NC and lumen” suggests that the sum of the two may be constant and, by inference, the fibrous cap area % must also be constant.
20. The definition of controls is unclear. A sample with 45% intima is not a control. It seems that the authors call samples without NC controls.
21. It is interesting that there was no difference between symptomatic and asymptomatic plaques. This should be emphasized. In many studies, this is the only distinction provided.
22. Some patients showed “two NCs on each side of the lumen”. This is interesting, but not conclusive. They may be connected in another plane.
23. In several scRNA-Seq studies and in at least 2 reviews, about half of the foam cells are SMC-derived and half are macrophages. There are two sets of macrophage foam cells and at least 3 other macrophage sets that are not foamy. The information obtained in the present study should allow these assignments.

=== reviewer_2 ===
Overall Summary:
Pauli et al. present their investigation seeking to integrate multiple transcriptomic methodologies (bulk RNA seq, scRNAseq, and spatial transcriptomics) as a means to molecularly define carotid atherosclerotic disease. Using arterial and atheroma samples collected during CEA, the investigators attempt to elucidate a spatially-resolved molecular architecture underlying plaque development. The authors highlight unique plaque morphologies linked to different cell type compositions, disease heterogeneity (i.e. symptomatology), and clinical demographics (i.e. smoking, etc) with inference towards plaque development and stability. Notably, they uncover spatial associations between HMOX1+ macrophages as they potentially transition to foam cells (TREM2+).
While the manuscript is well written and demonstrates technical rigor, the most important limitation is a lack of methodologic novelty or conceptual impact to our molecular understanding of atherosclerosis. Notably, HMOX1 and TREM2 macrophages are well established in the progression of atherosclerosis (PMID: 39731912 – HMOX1, 38974464 – TREM2) and modulation of macrophage polarity (PMID: 30282830 – HMOX1, 38646596 – TREM2). Furthermore, other spatial transcriptomic investigations of arterial atherosclerosis have recently been published (PMID: 39234691 and 39715784). Considering these limitations, the current manuscript offers incremental advancement.
Other Criticisms include:
1. Association with symptomatology / stability is uncertain. One area of potential significance was the assertion that the current findings molecularly define symptomatic (vs. asymptomatic) carotid artery stenosis. As presented, however, the data do not clearly support these claims. Figure 5 provides an example of this missed opportunity. A clearer presentation of the results would have been based upon symptom status as opposed to various morphologic clusters.
2. Surprising lack of DEG in bulk RNAseq. Figure 2c shows relatively few differences in DEG across stable and unstable plaques. This is in contrast to current literature (39234691), yet no explanation is given.
3. Underpowered study with significant demographic heterogeneity. It is difficult to interpret some of the results due to relatively few patients (N=4 Ctl) and variable clinical demographics.
4. Biased spatial transcriptomic approach based off Panels 1 and 2. Finally, the spatial transcriptomic analysis used a custom (pre-defined) gene set (~500) for cellular and disease status identification. While this approach is helpful in resolving cellular spatial location, it falls short of providing true spatially-resolved, single cell transcriptomic analysis. This undercuts the novelty.

=== reviewer_3 ===
Summary
This manuscript presents a comprehensive spatially resolved transcriptomic analysis of human carotid atherosclerotic plaques. The authors integrate bulk RNA-Seq, single-cell RNA-Seq (scRNA-Seq), and single-cell spatial transcriptomics (Xenium platform) on paired samples from patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy (CEA). Their multimodal approach reveals spatial microenvironments, including distinct VSMC and macrophage subtypes associated with plaque vulnerability, progression, and smoking status. They propose a model of subluminal HMOX1⁺ macrophage transdifferentiation into lipid-handling TREM2⁺ cells. A novel morphological clustering of plaques into “structured” and “chaotic” types is introduced, offering mechanistic insights into spatial immune-VSMC interplay and plaque destabilization.
Major Comments
1. Justification of Technology Choice: The authors employ the Xenium platform for spatial transcriptomics but do not justify its selection over other platforms like 10x Visium HD. A justification regarding resolution, sensitivity, and gene coverage tradeoffs is needed.
2. Immune Cell Overrepresentation Not Corrected: Despite deconvolution, the overrepresentation of immune cells in scRNA-Seq is not adequately addressed in the spatial analysis. This may bias subregion interpretations.
3. Smoking Association Requires Caution: The observed association with smoking is only partially supported by bulk and scRNA-Seq data. Acknowledgment of limited reproducibility is needed.
4. Trajectory Analysis of Macrophages: The proposed HMOX1⁺ to TREM2⁺ trajectory should be validated with orthogonal methods beyond TFvelo and visualized more explicitly.
5. Subregion Definition and Reproducibility: Manual annotation of regions may introduce bias. Providing inter-rater reliability or uncertainty metrics would enhance robustness.
6. Sample Size for Spatial Analysis: The n=12 for spatial transcriptomics limits generalizability. Interpretations of clustering and risk associations should be more cautiously framed.
7. Neighbourhood Cluster Analysis: Statistical support (e.g., permutation tests, spatial proximity significance) for proposed functional zones is missing and should be included.
8. Clinical Utility and Predictive Value: The translational relevance of findings should be discussed. Can DEGs or spatial patterns serve as prognostic markers for plaque rupture?
Minor Comments
1. Terminology Clarification: Terms like 'structured' vs. 'chaotic' could be more quantitatively or mechanistically defined.
2. Figure Readability: Dense color legends in Figures 6–8 make interpretation difficult. Consider enhancing clarity.
3. Figure 2 caption: “-log10 value” => “-log10 p-value”

=== reviewer_1 ===
This manuscript presents one of the first human studies examining the relationship between microplastic (MP) exposure and immune–metabolic disturbances, and it further tests a dietary intervention with composite polyphenols (CP) in a randomized controlled trial (RCT). The integration of metagenomic and metabolomic analyses with clinical phenotyping is ambitious and generates potentially important insights. The study is clearly written, methodologically detailed, and addresses a pressing issue in environmental health.
This study has several key strengths: it is the first population-based trial to test whether polyphenols can help reduce immune effects linked to microplastic exposure; it uses a multi-omics approach that combines microbiome and metabolomic data with clinical measures to give deeper insight; it includes a randomized, placebo-controlled design, which is stronger than the mostly observational studies done before; and it gives clear details on how microplastics were measured, how randomization and blinding were done, and how adherence was monitored,
That said, several aspects of the study design and interpretation limit the strength of the conclusions. In particular, issues around exposure assessment, population representativeness, statistical rigor, and the scope of interpretation should be addressed to ensure the findings are presented with appropriate caution.
Major Concerns
Exposure assessment
MPs were quantified in feces using Py-GC/MS, but fecal levels may not reflect systemic burden; tissue retention could differ in type and concentration. The relatively high concentrations reported compared with previous studies may reflect methodological differences, which complicates cross-study comparisons. The calculation of estimated daily intake (EDI) from fecal data is speculative.
Population representativeness
The study cohort was young (median age 24), largely healthy, and predominantly female. This narrow profile restricts the generalizability of findings to the broader population.Extensive exclusion criteria (smoking, alcohol use, chronic diseases, supplement use) create a homogeneous group but also one that does not fully reflect real-world vulnerability.
Intervention trial
The 28-day trial duration is too short to evaluate sustained effects of polyphenols on MP-related health outcomes. The sample size (~100) is modest, limiting power for subgroup and multi-omics analyses.
Statistical analysis
The handling of multiple testing in large omics datasets is not clearly described. Without appropriate correction, the risk of false positives is high.Some baseline imbalances (e.g., higher IL-6 and triglycerides in the intervention group) complicate interpretation of intervention effects. Many results are reported primarily through p-values. Greater emphasis on effect sizes and clinical relevance would improve interpretation.
Interpretation
Some discussion points overstate causality (e.g., MPs “leading to” neurodegenerative pathways). These should be presented as associations or hypotheses. Proposed mechanistic chains (e.g., Sutterella abundance → lipid metabolism changes → systemic inflammation) remain speculative and should be presented as such. Statements about CP as a “protective strategy” are premature given the short timeframe, modest effect sizes, and absence of clinical endpoints.
Minor Concerns
The description of CP composition is inconsistent across sections (five components vs. inclusion of tannic acid) and should be standardized.
Some figures and tables are overly dense (e.g., volcano plots, KEGG enrichment) and would benefit from simplification, with secondary analyses moved to supplementary material.
Cytokine data reported as quartiles obscure potentially important changes; mean ± SD or effect size plots might better illustrate findings.
The manuscript is generally well written, but certain sections are redundant and could be streamlined for clarity and balance.
In conclsuion, this study provides some of the first human evidence linking microplastic exposure with immune and metabolic disturbances and suggests that composite polyphenols may help mitigate these effects via microbiome and metabolomic pathways. The short intervention period and narrow cohort limit generalizability. The conclusions are supported by the data but should be framed as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Overall, the work is original and timely, though confirmation is needed.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This manuscript addresses an important and timely question: the population-level health impacts of microplastics (MP) exposure and a potential dietary mitigation strategy using a composite polyphenol (CP) formulation. The combination of a pilot population study, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, and an integrated multi-omics approach is innovative and of high potential impact. However, several important methodological clarifications and additional analyses/interpretation are required before the manuscript is acceptable for publication.
1. The manuscript states CP consists of five compounds (quercetin, C3G, gallic acid, rutin, ellagic acid), yet Supplementary Table S1 lists botanical extracts (Goji Berry Extract, Hawthorn Flower Extract, Wild Cherry Berry Extract, Dendrobium officinale Flower Extract, Pomegranate Extract). Please provide a detailed, quantitative breakdown of the CP product:
- mg of each extract per daily dose and the percentage (or mg) of each named polyphenol per gram of extract and per daily dose.
- Information on standardization (e.g., percent total polyphenols, HPLC/LC–MS quantification certificates) and batch-to-batch variability.
- A full list of other abundant bioactive compounds in these extracts (other polyphenols, sugars, fibers, alkaloids, etc.) and their approximate abundances or whether such analyses were performed.
Without this information it is impossible to attribute effects to the named polyphenols specifically, to replicate the study, or to compare dosing to prior literature.
2. Explain why 15 g/day was chosen (e.g., manufacturer recommendation, prior human clinical data, preclinical efficacy/tolerability data, or pilot tolerability studies) and provide supporting references or pilot data. If the dose is based on the manufacturer’s recommended serving, state this explicitly.
3. Selection and detection of targeted microplastics (MPs):
o Explain the criteria used to select the MPs in Table S2 (representativeness, prevalence in environment/human samples, polymer classes, particle size, expected exposure routes).
o Clarify which of the targeted MPs were actually detected in participants’ samples and at what concentrations. Table S6 shows five of eleven, please disclose whether the other six were below detection limits or not analyzed.
o If some targeted MPs were not detected, discuss implications for exposure–effect analyses and whether analyses should focus on the detected subset.
4. Exposure route and source attribution. The manuscript mentions PVC is widely used in construction materials. Provide discussion and (if available) rationale or evidence on likely exposure pathways for the MPs measured (oral/dietary ingestion, inhalation, dermal). State whether the measured MPs in the biological matrix are most plausibly reflecting dietary intake, inhalation, dust ingestion, or mixed routes. Discuss how non-dietary exposure routes could influence gut microbiome-mediated effects (for example, inhaled MPs that are swallowed via mucociliary clearance).
5. The authors report gut microbiome changes (notably Sutterella) associated with MP exposure and CP effects. Explicitly discuss whether microbiome alterations are more likely a cause or a consequence of MP exposure (or of host response to MPs). Clarify limitations of cross-sectional associations and the RCT for causal inference, and propose approaches to test directionality.
6. The manuscript states plasma cholesterol and LDL tended to increase with MP exposure, citing supporting studies. However, some preclinical reports (e.g., Lu L, Wan Z, Luo T, Fu Z, Jin Y. Polystyrene microplastics induce gut microbiota dysbiosis and hepatic lipid metabolism disorder in mice. Sci Total Environ. 2018 Aug 1;631-632:449-458. doi: 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2018.03.051.) show different or opposite lipid effects. Please:
- Acknowledge conflicting evidence explicitly,
- Offer possible reasons for discrepancies (species differences, MP polymer type, particle size, dose, exposure route, diet, duration), and
- Clarify how the present human data fit within this heterogeneous literature.
7. Intervention duration and biological relevance of significant endpoints. A 28-day intervention is short for many cardiometabolic outcomes. The authors already note lack of changes in many clinical indicators. Please discuss whether the significant molecular/microbiome/metabolite changes (e.g., Sutterella and PC (22:5/0:0)) are likely to be transient biomarkers or plausibly predictive of longer-term clinical effects. State explicitly that these molecular changes require replication and longer-term follow-up for clinical interpretation.

=== reviewer_1 ===
This study presents a novel hydrogel material—cell-programmed adaptive contraction (CPAC) hydrogel—that can respond to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) signals secreted by cells, leading to contraction of the embedded microgels within the hydrogel and resulting in local stiffness enhancement, ultimately forming a heterogeneous hydrogel structure. While the CPAC hydrogel demonstrates innovative bio-responsiveness and potential for bone repair, there are several shortcomings and potential gaps in the study. Therefore, we do not recommend the article for publication in Nat. Commun. at this stage.
1.The design of the CPAC hydrogel relies solely on ALP as the key enzymatic marker for regulation. However, it remains unclear whether other enzymes within the phosphatase family could also influence this process, potentially leading to non-specific reactions. Additionally, the dynamics of ALP release during MSC osteogenic differentiation are not well defined.
2.The CPAC hydrogel mimics the mechanical heterogeneity of natural ECM through the contraction of microgels and local stiffness enhancement. However, whether the hydrogel can achieve precise and controllable gradient variations in local stiffness remains a concern. In the complex in vivo biological environment, the hydrogel may be influenced by external factors such as temperature and pH, leading to unpredictable fluctuations in its mechanical properties. This could affect the cells' response to the material, particularly if the local stiffness of the hydrogel becomes uneven, potentially causing misalignment in stem cell differentiation.
3.In this study, the CPAC hydrogel responds to ALP and alters its structure within a short period of time, but its stability in vivo or in vivo or in vivo or in vivo or in long-term experiments has not been sufficiently validated.
4.Although the hydrogel promotes MSC osteogenic differentiation, the effects on cell proliferation and survival have not been adequately explored. The contraction of the microgels may lead to changes in the intercellular space, further affecting cell expansion and proliferation. If the hydrogel does not provide sufficient support or space during differentiation, it may limit the functional repair of the cells.
5.The authors indicate that the expression levels of miR-124, miR-214, and miR-26a are elevated in the CPAC hydrogel group, and this is significantly correlated with a decrease in the expression of EZH2 and its downstream target H3K27me3. However, the lack of validation through anti-miR treatment raises concerns about the reliability of this correlation.
6.In Figure 5g, the immunofluorescence images for the control group are not shown.
7.In Figures 3b, 3c, and 5c, g, a significant proportion of suspected overexposed areas can be observed. This raises concerns about the accuracy of the semi-quantitative analysis based on fluorescence intensity.
8.The regulatory effect of H3K27me3 on osteogenic-related genes has not been validated through relevant experiments.
9.In the in vivo experiments, only data from 8 weeks after hydrogel implantation are provided. This duration does not adequately reflect the effects of local network stiffening in promoting MSC osteogenic differentiation.
10.The size changes of CPAC hydrogel in a 1 U/mL ALP solution have been studied; however, the ALP concentration during in vivo or bone injury healing is unknown, and it remains unclear whether it would be sufficient to trigger the hydrogel's adaptive remodeling. Additionally, the hydrogel's contraction under in vivo conditions has not been characterized.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The authors present a study focused on the development of a hydrogel system that mimics the dynamically evolving and heterogeneous extracellular matrix (ECM) environment during tissue development. Specifically, they engineer a cell-programmed adaptive contraction (CPAC) hydrogel containing ALP-responsive microgels that contract in response to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity. This induces overall hydrogel network contraction and local matrix stiffening, thereby promoting osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). The authors provide and test a hypothesis for the underlying mechanotransduction mechanism including upregulation of microRNA and demonstrate the translational potential of their system in a rat critical-size bone defect model, where they observed enhanced bone formation.
The study presents a dynamic hydrogel platform that responds to cell-released enzymes and modulates stem cell fate through dynamically changing the mechanical signals. The concept is interesting, and the authors have sought to perform both mechanistic investigation and in vivo validation. While the results are promising, additional experiments are required to support their main claims such as ‘‘ALP-induced gel contraction’’, ‘‘local stiffening’’ and ‘‘mechanical heterogeneity’’. Moreover, several aspects of the study require clarification, statistical information or further detail to strengthen its overall scientific rigor, reproducibility and impact.
Major comments:
• Novelty and significance: It would be helpful if the authors can explain more why this work is novel and their findings are significant for a broad impact.
• Study design: While this study probed an interesting concept, their main claims seem to have several gaps, across materials, in vitro- and in vivo models.
o From the materials aspect, the reliability relies on a thorough characterization of the mechanical properties and heterogeneity of their biomaterials.
o The range of mechanical stiffness such as magnitude, anisotropy seems unclear.
o From the cell biology perspective, whether the readouts are solely due to ALP, and cell-secreted ALP, or not, may require more rigorous investigation by setting up controls and perturbation experiments. It is known that cells also secrete other factors that block ALP acitivity.
o From the in vivo aspect, the complexity further increases in terms of proteins and cells in involved. The authors are recommended to add control experiments to demonstrate the enhanced bone formation is not by the gels along, nor other matrix factors, but exactly by their claimed mechanism.
• Abstract clarity: The abstract does not clearly convey how the hydrogel system works. Key elements, such as the main components of the hydrogel as well as the control groups used in the study, are not mentioned but are critical for interpreting the results.
• Introduction:
o The introduction would benefit from a comparison to naturally derived hydrogels such as collagen. How does the contractile behaviour of the presented system compare, and what advantages does it offer over existing ECM-mimetic materials?
o The exact composition of the hydrogel remains unclear in the introduction and Figure 1. Including a schematic that clearly explains the composition and assembly of the hydrogel from microgels and other components for all experimental hydrogel groups would greatly improve clarity. Also pay attention to complete & matching legends for the schematics.
• Figure 2g: It would be helpful to include confocal images of the hydrogels prior to ALP treatment to demonstrate the changes induced by contraction.
• Figure 2h: Please indicate which statistical test was used and annotate significance levels directly on the graph.
• You claim that “CPAC hydrogel can better facilitate stellate spreading”. Please explain where this can be seen or provide more morphological data to support it.
• Figures 3b/c: The CPAC hydrogels appear to have a higher cell density compared to NC controls. Is this a localized effect due to contraction, or does the material promote proliferation? Higher local cell density itself may influence osteogenic differentiation.
Related to this, can you comment on the macroscopic effect of ALP-mediated contraction on the entire hydrogel, does the hydrogel size change?
• Can you specify how the “high-modulus N,N-dimethylacrylamide (DMAA) microgels” compare to the previous control microgels (Phos-HEA) in terms of mechanical properties?
• The claim “NCLS hydrogels showed elevated osteogenic marker expression relative to NC hydrogels” is not evident from the data shown, please justify or explain more.
• Figure 4: Please provide rationale for the selection of mechanotransduction markers (pFAK, pMyosin IIa, Paxillin).
• Figure 4: Why are the microgels not visible in the confocal images like in Figures 3 & 5? The figure caption makes it a bit unclear, if cells were seeded on top of hydrogels rather than embedded.
• Figure 4b: Collagen I appears to be predominantly intracellular. Is there an explanation for this observation?
• The hydrogel is described as responsive to ALP secreted by MSCs, yet the immunofluorescence images show primarily intracellular ALP. Please clarify how this observation aligns with the proposed mechanism of hydrogel contraction, which relies on extracellular ALP activity.
• A 3-day culture period is relatively short for observing osteogenic differentiation. Have longer culture periods been considered?
• Materials and Methods in SI: Several important methodological aspects require clarification:
o How was the microgel shrinkage quantified? Was it done manually, and how many replicates were analysed?
o Please provide more details about your hydrogel preparation from your individual components including precise concentrations and volume ratios. Please also specify the light source, wavelenght and intensity (also for photorheology).
o What were the measurement parameters used for rheological analysis?
o In your nanoindentation measurements, was stiffness assessed in a single 50 µm × 50 µm region or across multiple areas? Are the results shown representative?
o What was the cell seeding density, and what was the source of the hMSCs?
o In the in vivo experiments, was there a contralateral defect used as an internal control in each animal as indicated in Figure 6a?
o Please describe the analysis of micro-CT data in more detail.
o You write that your skull specimens were decalcified for 2 months before fixation, whereas fixation is generally performed before decalcification to preserve tissue, cell and protein integrity. Could you please explain your choice of procedure and whether that could affect the staining results?
o The section “Immunohistochemical staining” describes the use of an anti-ALP antibody, whereas the data in Figure 6 shows OCN. Please correct.
o The section “3D cell culture within hydrogels” seems incomplete, especially regarding the use of the EZH2 inhibitor (starting from line 163).
Minor comments:
• The sequence of figure citations in the text is partially incorrect, for example, Supplementary Figure S11 is cited before S10. Also, the reference to Figure S11 is unclear, is it pertaining to stiffness (text) or ALP concentration (figure)?
• Figure S12: Correct graph labellings “i, ii, iii, iv, v, vi” and their citations in the text.
• The manuscript contains several typos that should be corrected, for example line 68 “promote the of commitment of stem cells”, line 102 “CAPC” instead of “CPAC” or line 272 “this modulus remained larged unchanged”.
• Figure S9: The panel c described in the figure caption does not exist. Additionally, please clarify the meaning of the red and blue vertical lines in the existing panel c. Also the mention of “half of the peak stress relaxation times (τ1/2 = 150 ± 10 s)” doesn’t match the data shown in Figure S9c.
• Figure 2f: Please label the images.

=== reviewer_1 ===
In this study, the authors present a novel diffusion-inhibited complexation strategy that enables low-cost, high-throughput fabrication of protocells and precise, large-scale 3D construction of prototissues. This simple, fully aqueous method yields protocells and prototissues with excellent mechanical strength. The resulting prototissues reach sizes exceeding 10 cm, significantly larger than the millimeter-scale structures reported previously, addressing a long-standing challenge in the field. The permeability and chemical communication of the protocells, as well as the osmotic-pressure-induced deformation and buoyancy-driven motion of the prototissues were thoroughly investigated. This work provides a promising platform for future applications in areas such as soft robotics, biomedical devices and tissue engineering. Therefore, I recommend the publication of the manuscript in Nature Communications after minor revisions.
1. The system used by the authors appears to be quite different from conventional aqueous two-phase systems (ATPS), such as the widely studied PEG-dextran system. In comparison to ATPS, what are the advantages of achieving compartmentalization in pure water? It would also be helpful if the authors could clarify whether spontaneous phase separation occurs upon direct mixing of CNF and PDDA aqueous solutions.
2. While the effects of gas flow rate and extrusion rate on the size of the microcapsules have been investigated. It is recommended to assess the influence of CNF and PDDA concentrations on microcapsule formation and size.
3. The prepared prototissues exhibit excellent mechanical strength in both water and air, which is very impressive. Would the prototissues still maintain their structural stability after complete removal of water from both the internal and external prototissues?
4. The pH values of both CNF and PDDA solutions should be stated in the manuscript, as the pH is a critical role in the strength of electrostatic interactions between CNF and PDDA. In addition, the influence of pH on microcapsule formation is recommended to be explored.
5. Morphological characterization of CNF such as AFM or TEM should be provided.

=== reviewer_2 ===
In this work, Weixiao Feng et al. present a microfluidic method to construct protocells and assemble prototissues with complex 3D architecture. While the methodology is novel and interesting, several aspects of its functioning principles remain unclear and require more thorough investigation before publication. Moreover, beyond the novelty of the production method for protocells and prototissues, the work does not present a significant conceptual advancement in the protocell/prototissue engineering field, as it primarily reproduces results that have already been demonstrated by established leaders in the field such as Bayley, Mann, and Han. Given the limited conceptual progress, issues with the methodology's working principles, and inadequate scholarly presentation, I do not recommend publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications.
Below are specific comments that may help improve the rigor and significance of the work:
Materials Characterization and Methodology
1. Essential details regarding CNF and PDDA are missing, which is fundamental for result reproduction. The authors should report the molecular weight and dispersity of all polymers used, their hydrodynamic radius in the working solvent, and degree of branching. Additionally, why is cellulose negatively charged? Since cellulose and PDDA interact electrostatically, how many charges per polymer chain do they carry?
2. The authors refer to their objects as "microcapsules," but "microspheres" would be more appropriate since they are not hollow structures.
3. The role of Triton-X should be clarified: what concentration was used, and what surface tension is required to achieve microcapsule formation? Can other surfactants be employed, particularly those that are completely biocompatible?
4. The statement "By varying extrusion rate or gas flow rate, the size of microcapsule could be controlled" contradicts Supplementary Figure 3a, which clearly shows that extrusion rate does not influence microcapsule size. This discrepancy should be corrected.
5. The microcapsule structure requires further exploration. Where does PDDA localize? Does it permeate and form a network inside the microsphere, which could explain their resilience and reduced polymer chain mobility?
Permeability Studies
6. The statement "This suggested the poor semi-permeability of membrane, leading to a rapid equilibrium of osmotic pressure across the microcapsules" lacks clarity. It is unclear how membrane permeability can be assessed by placing microcapsules in high-concentration glucose or dextran solutions and observing shrinkage behavior. This requires further explanation.
7. For the permeability experiment using dextran (Supplementary Figure S7), the partition coefficient of FITC-tagged dextran should be provided. Complete characterization of the dextran (molecular weight, dispersity, degree of labeling) is also necessary. Importantly, a molecular weight cut-off for the microspheres should be estimated.
8. There is confusion regarding the statement "It should be noted that if the microcapsules were sufficiently rigid, the shrinkage induced by the hypertonic solution could be suppressed" when earlier the authors mention "no shrinkage of microcapsules was observed within 24 h." This apparent contradiction requires clarification.
Characterization Issues
9. The authors tagged GO with pyrene but did not explain the attachment method or characterize the product. How can they confirm that pyrene is covalently bound rather than physisorbed on GO, which might detach in complex solutions containing diverse polymers and salts? Control experiments are required to validate the conclusions regarding GO localization in microspheres.
10. There is an apparent contradiction regarding GO's effect on permeability. The authors report that GO hinders glucose permeability, with smaller GO amounts leading to faster glucose permeation. However, in earlier experiments (lines 106107), they state that permeability is poor in GO's absence. This needs clarification.
Coacervate Formation and Prototissue Assembly
11. In the discussion from line 213, when using polyethyleneimine, how can the authors confirm coacervate formation rather than simple polymer aggregates formed by electrostatic interactions in a molecularly crowded environment? This claim requires supporting data. Additionally, what is an "egg-shaped coacervate"?
12. The prototissue preparation lacks sufficient detail. The Materials and Methods section only states: "For the preparation of prototissues, 0.3 M electrolyte (e.g., NaCl) was added into the extrusion solution, while other parameters remained unchanged." No explanation of how different shapes are achieved is provided. The term "extrusion droplets" requires definition. Details about the molds (material, fabrication process, filling method, removal procedure) are absent.
13. The nature of microsphere-microsphere adhesion remains unclear. Why does a thicker, more relaxed membrane promote adhesion? While the authors attempt an explanation, this fundamental aspect requires precise understanding supported by experimental data.
Characterization and Applications
14. The authors demonstrate various possibilities that have already been reported in the literature using their new prototissue types but provide insufficient characterization. Detailed mechanical property analysis of protocells and prototissues is necessary to support claims about mechanical properties and bending mechanics of layered prototissues. What forces are exerted during bending?
15. For the buoyant prototissue: what is the intended purpose and biological relevance? What is the buoyancy rate and its dependence on experimental parameters?
Biocompatibility Claims
16. The authors claim biocompatibility in their conclusions without providing supporting data. Triton-X usage could be problematic in this regard. While an in vitro cytotoxicity assay is mentioned in the experimental section, no data are presented in the main text.
Recommendation
The manuscript requires substantial improvements in experimental design, data presentation, and mechanistic understanding before it can meet the publication standards of Nature Communications.

=== reviewer_3 ===
The authors describe the construction of prototissues via adhesive interaction between microgel compartments fabricated from PDDA and CNF. The membrane permeability of the compartments were studied and modulated by inclusion of GO. They also illustrated how osmotic changes can help regulate the morphology of the microgel compartments irreversibly via cross linking of the interior or reversibly via delayed permeability. They further went on to study a two-enzyme cascade within the CNF-GO/PDDA microcapsules and show chemomechanical actuation of the prototissues mediated by osmotic changes and bubble mediated buoyancy.
The comments are as follows:
1) The primary concern is regarding novelty – as a significant part of the paper mostly deals with preparation of the protocells and their osmotic response along with enzyme cascade studies. These are routine studies in protocell field and the authors do well to thoroughly characterize their new protocell model/chasis but these do not add significant novelty to the work.
2) The advantage of a prototissue is that it has compartments which can host a reaction to induce morphological or functional output. In the current design, the authors have used the osmotic response of the protocells and bubble mediated buoyancy to produce actuation. The osmotic pressure mediated actuation due to differential response in the two layer tissue was also illustrated in earlier studies (G. Villar et al. Science 2013, 340, 48-52). The buoyancy-based actuation of prototissues which the authors have shown is quite interesting as it is mediated by reactions within the protocells. However, this reviewer would like to see not just actuation but also recovery and re-actuation over multiple cycles which would then constitute a significant advance in the field.
3) One suggestion would be to use Glucose oxidase mediated consumption of the oxygen bubble to execute multiple cycles of actuation or formulate a different strategy for dissolution of the bubble for recovery of the actuated tissue.
4) The authors have studied the shrinkage of the CNF-GO/PDDA protocells with PEI and PDDA. It is seen that PDDA 100 kDa permeates and cross links but does not form a yolk structure but PEI forms a yolk structure which constitutes a highly cross linked network. Author could conduct FRAP studies to understand the condensation mediated changes in fluidity of the interior and also clarify the why there is difference in morphological outcomes for PEI and PDDA.
5) the facile construction of the prototissue due to sticking interactions at high electrolyte concentrations has the limitation of lacking programmability of the internal structure of the prototissue – in terms of self organization of different protocells to form complex hierarchical structures. This reviewer would like to see the potential of this prototissue design in terms of soft robotics, where these prototissues can manipulate macroscopic objects or these actuatable tissues can be used as artificial muscle to operate a gripper like structure. These experiments would add significant novelty to the manuscript.
6) Another general comment would be that it may be investigated what is the advantage of using a prototissue over an actuatable gel for carrying out these tasks.

The authors present an intriguing study on the modulation of work function exceeding 1 eV in RuO₂/TiO₂ epitaxial
heterostructures, controlled by the thickness of the RuO₂ layer. The observed variation is attributed to interfacial polarization
induced by cation displacements, as revealed through electron ptychography. The manuscript is well-organized and the
experimental findings are of potential interest to researchers in oxide electronics and solid-state physics.
However, I find that the current manuscript remains largely phenomenological. To meet the standards of Nature
Communications, I believe a deeper physical understanding is required. Specifically, I recommend the inclusion of
theoretical modeling or first-principles calculations to substantiate the proposed mechanisms. For instance, how does the
electronic density of states evolve in ultrathin RuO₂/TiO₂ heterostructures? Without such insight, the interpretation of the
experimental data remains speculative. Below, I outline several technical concerns that should be addressed:
1. Oxygen Vacancy Formation at the Interface:
The authors attribute the observed interfacial polarization to cation displacements. However, prior studies (e.g., Phys. Rev. B
86, 140102(R)) suggest that oxygen vacancies can induce similar effects in nominally non-polar oxides. Given the
significant lattice mismatch between RuO₂ and TiO₂, can the authors comment on the possibility of oxygen vacancy
formation at the interface? While post-annealing may suppress bulk vacancies, interfacial vacancies may persist and play a
critical role.
2. Interpretation of Work Function Modulation (Fig. 2b):
• Grounding Configuration: Fig. 2a indicates that the sample is grounded via the TiO₂ substrate, not the RuO₂ film.
Considering the higher work function of RuO₂ relative to the electron affinity of TiO₂, a Schottky barrier is expected at the
interface, especially for thicker RuO₂ films. This could impede electron transfer to ground. Yet, the KPFM data show high
signal-to-noise ratio. The authors should clarify the experimental setup and confirm that the measured signals originate from
RuO₂. Including data for a sample with RuO₂ thickness = 0 nm would be helpful.
• Thickness Dependence: The abrupt increase in work function is attributed to the emergence of polarity in thin RuO₂ films.
However, the subsequent decrease in work function with increasing thickness—falling below the bulk value—is
counterintuitive. If bulk RuO₂ is nonpolar, one would expect the work function to asymptotically approach ~5.1 eV from
above. The authors should provide a physical explanation for this trend.
3. Clarification of Figure 2e:
The schematic for tRuO2>tc suggests the presence of an electric field throughout the film and polarization from the interface
to mid-film, implying surface charge accumulation. The authors should clarify the physical meaning of these illustrations and
distinguish between the cases more explicitly.
4. Carrier Density Trends (Figure 4c):
The observed minimum in 2D carrier density (n2D) as a function of RuO₂ thickness is not explained. Furthermore, the
increase in n2D from 4 nm to 17 nm suggests that the 3D carrier density (n3D=n2D/tRuO) also increases, without signs of
saturation. This implies partial carrier localization even at 17 nm thickness. The authors should discuss the possible origins
of this behavior and its correlation with the work function trend.

Referee report on Nature Communications manuscript NCOMMS-25-58504-T
In this paper, the authors report on the realization of RuO2/TiO2 and TiO2/RuO2/TiO2 structures grown by oxide molecular
beam epitaxy, their characterization, and the study of some electronic properties.
More precisely, advanced STEM analyses allow the polar displacements in TiO2 and at the TiO2/RuO2 interfaces to be
determined. The work function of RuO2 in RuO2/TiO2 structures is studied as a function of the RuO2 thickness using Kelvin
probe microscopy. Finally, transport properties are realized for both RuO2/TiO2 and TiO2/RuO2/TiO2 structures
(conductivity, mobility and Hall effect).
The important finding is that the work function is found to depend on the thickness of the RuO2 layer in a non-monotonic
way. It increases a lot (>1eV) between 2 and 5nm before to decrease abruptly. The maximum work function is found to
correlate with the thickness at which the RuO2 layer relaxes. The STEM analyses show that a polarity is found in TiO2
layers and in the metallic RuO2 layer at the interfaces. This polar region does not extend over more than a few unit cells –
the electric field in this region is thought to modify the work function.
This is a nice paper, interesting and well-written. The results are clearly presented and broadly interesting. I think the paper
can be published in Nature communications if the authors convincingly answer the comments and questions listed below.
Comments and questions:
-A TiO2 buffer layer is used on a TiO2 substrate. Is this necessary because of the unknown state of the substrate “polar”
surface?
-STEM analyses. Can the authors provide the method used to measure the atom displacements in Figure 2c? Also, it seems
that the polarization at the bottom buffer TiO2 layer extends to the bottom edge of the reconstructed image. Does the
polarization also extends to the surface of the capping TiO2 layer? Furthermore, do the authors have information on what
is happening at the TiO2 buffer layer and TiO2 substrate interface?
-The TiO2 layers are polar. I am not sure to understand the origin of this polarity. Is a single TiO2 layer on TiO2 found to be
polar or is this linked to the TiO2/RuO2 interface (although there is no polar discontinuity at the interface).
-The authors talk about metallic RuO2 and metallic polar RuO2 regions (main text and conclusions). At the same time, the
transport analyses reveal the presence of dead layers (precisely the layer region that is polar). Should the phrasing be
modified?
-The KPFM measurements reveal a linear increase of the work function and an anomalous enhancement between 2 and
5nm. What is the physical reason for the linear enhancement with RuO2 thickness?
-In line with this question, the data demonstrate that the RuO2 films relax above 5-6nm. However, there is no marked change
in the work function linear increase with thickness (not taking into account the anomalous enhancement) – and no clear
change on the sheet conductance versus thickness – both seem unaffected by the strain relaxation. Is this understood?
-One is also tempted to conclude from the data that the work function value can simply be tuned by thickness control of the
RuO2 layer.
-A very important point that should be clarified. At 4-5nm thickness, there is an abrupt decrease of the work function. As I
understand, the authors propose that this abrupt decrease is linked to strain relaxation. But what is the reason for the
decrease? What is physically happening? Looking at Fig. 2e, for thick layers, the dipoles are still there – so what is affecting
the work function when strain is released? What is the explanation for the drop in the work function?
-Following on this, do the authors have STEM and polar displacements profiles for “thick films” – something must be different
and this information ideally should allow the work function abrupt change to be understood.
-The authors mention SHG measurements and conclude from a change in SHG intensity as a function of RuO2 thickness
that RuO2 becomes non-polar. I am not sure to understand this sinceTiO2 and the TiO2/RuO2 interface remain polar (Fig.
2e) – why would the SHG signal disappear?
-In the conclusion the authors claimed that the intrinsic conductivity of the RuO2 layers in the heterostructure has
comparable value to bulk RuO2. Can the authors provide an explanation on why can the values of 15875 and 11700 be
comparable with 28400 (lines 218 and 225)? It seems like the values extracted are around half of the bulk value.
-Finally, on Fig. 2c and 2d, the RuO2 film peaks are very difficult to spot – the Figure should be improved.

The manuscript reports a facet-engineering approach using NiS₂ crystal planes ({100} and {111}) to stabilize the β-phase of PVDF, achieving broadband electromagnetic (EM) loss from MHz to THz. The authors combine DFT calculations, structural characterizations (SEM, TEM, XRD, FTIR, AFM-IR, PFM), and EM response analysis to demonstrate that facet modulation enables enhanced polarization and relaxation dynamics, breaking the Kramers–Kronig trade-off. The topic is original, the data are extensive, and the idea of facet-modulated ferroelectricity in polymers is both novel and technologically relevant. However, several methodological, mechanistic, and presentation aspects require significant improvement before acceptance.
1. The manuscript claims that {100} facets of NiS₂ stabilize β-PVDF by lowering its energy below α-PVDF. However, the underlying electronic or interfacial mechanism is insufficiently elaborated.
2. How does charge transfer or dipole alignment differ quantitatively between facets?
3. Can authors provide charge density difference maps or Bader charge analysis to support the interfacial polarization claims?
4. The statement that this mechanism “breaks the Kramers–Kronig constraint” seems physically overstated, since these relations are fundamental. The authors should instead clarify that multi-relaxation mechanisms mitigate the apparent loss–bandwidth trade-off.
5. Is there any specific cause of choosing NiS2 as the filler material?
6. Provide the investigation of a control composite with randomly oriented NiS₂ or another inert filler to confirm that the observed effects are truly facet-specific.
7. The role of NiS₂ conductivity in EM attenuation must be disentangled from ferroelectric polarization effects (conductivity data in Table S1 suggest notable variation).
8. The PFM data (Fig. 3D–G) show phase hysteresis, but there is no macroscopic polarization–electric field (P–E) loop. A P–E measurement or Sawyer–Tower loop is essential to confirm bulk ferroelectricity.
9. The reported coercive voltages (0.41 V and 0.62 V) are relatively low. Clarify whether these values refer to local switching or macroscopic measurement.
10. Table S2 shows strong EM loss compared to other materials, but normalization (per thickness, per filler loading, etc.) is inconsistent.
11. Please include a clear benchmark plot (e.g., attenuation constant vs. frequency) comparing state-of-the-art polymer composites.
12. The claim that the system “overcomes the limitation imposed by Kramers–Kronig relations” is conceptually problematic. These relations are not breakable for causal, linear systems. The authors could instead argue that nonlinear ferroelectric polarization and multi-relaxation processes expand the effective response bandwidth.
13. The reported THz shielding effectiveness (≈30 dB for 0.25 mm) is impressive but could also arise from multiple reflection and scattering effects. Consider adding complex refractive index or impedance spectra to clarify this.
14. The correlation between β-phase fraction and THz attenuation should be statistically supported (e.g., regression of β-phase ratio vs. SET).
15. The SEM/TEM images (Fig. 1B–E) show morphological differences, but facet indexing and atomic models should be more explicitly correlated.
16. A surface energy or coordination number comparison would reinforce the claim that {100} facets are more polarizing.
17. The Introduction could better emphasize how this work differs from previous PVDF–inorganic interface engineering (e.g., doped or hybridized PVDF systems).

The manuscript by B. Cai et al. reports a method for preferential crystallization of the ferroelectric β-phase of PVDF on specific facets of NiS2 nanocrystals. The authors attribute this effect to enhanced S-H interactions at the {100} surface. However, the experimental data do not convincingly support this conclusion, and several key interpretations are either incomplete or unsupported.
1. The XRD diffractograms (Figs. 2A,B and S11) show a dominant β-phase peak in all sample, while the differences in FTIR spectra are minimal and even disappears at 25% NiS2 loading (Figs. 2C,D and S12). These variations fall within the usual batch-to-batch variability of PVDF and cannot be taken as solid evidence of facet-induced β-phase enhancement.
2. A more fundamental issue is that the influence of processing conditions is barely addressed. It is well known that mechanical stretching and elevated temperatures promote α- to β-phase transition in PVDF [https://doi.org/10.1039/C3RA45134H]. The hot-pressing method used by the authors can itself induce β-phase formation, with nanoparticles acting as stress concentrators. A similar effect has already been reported for PVDF-BaTiO3 system [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymertesting.2024.108516]. The authors fail to decouple the contribution of thermal–mechanical processing from any alleged facet-specific effects.
3. The characterization of the PVDF/NiS2 composites physical properties also raises concerns. The PFM data are not convincing. V-shape amplitude loops such of those in Figs. 3E,G are typical of electrostatic artefacts caused by tip-sample interaction, not of genuine piezoresponse [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultramic.2019.112839]. For samples dominated by non-polar α-phase, the authors should have used stiffer AFM probes, controlled surface potential via KPFM, and performed PFM in both contact and non-contact modes to verify that the response is truly piezoelectric rather than electrostatic.
4. The dielectric measurements are also problematic. The authors conclude (lines 253-254) that “…due to the low conductivity of P/N composites (Figure S17, Table S1), the dominant loss mechanism in the 2-18 GHz range is polarization loss…”. This is contradicted by their own data. Table S1 shows a 4-orders-of-magnitude (!) conductivity increase in P/N{100}, when NiS2 loading increases from 15% to 25%. Such a dramatic change should strongly influence conductive losses, yet Fig. 4E shows no effect at all. This discrepancy is ignored, making further discussion of the electromagnetic properties unreliable.
5. The novelty of the “facet engineering” approach proposed by the authors is overstated. Surface-induced polymorphism in both organic and inorganic systems is well established in literature [https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.201503169; https://doi.org/10.1039/C8CS00283E]. β-phase enhancement in PVDF composites with inorganic nanoparticles has already been demonstrated [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymertesting.2024.108516]. The work does not introduce a sufficiently new concept or mechanism.
In summary, the “facet engineering” concept presented here is not novel, and β-phase enhancement in PVDF-nanoparticle composites has already been demonstrated. The experimental evidence is weak, key controls are missing, and several interpretations are questionable or unsupported. Overall, the originality and scientific rigor of the work do not meet the standards of Nature Communications, and the manuscript should not be accepted for publication.

### 1. Significance and Novelty
The work addresses a well-known challenge in polymer science: the thermodynamic instability of the ferroelectric $\beta$-phase in PVDF. The use of facet-engineered inorganic fillers to "lock" the polymer conformation is a conceptually elegant approach. If robust, this provides a scalable pathway for high-performance EM functional materials. The synthesis of NiS2 nanocrystals with controlled facets is well-described. The transition from "facet engineering" to "broadband EM loss" is a significant leap that requires more rigorous bridging.

*   **Phase Quantification:** The manuscript relies heavily on the $\beta$-phase content as a performance metric. The methods section mentions XRD, but does not specify the deconvolution procedure (e.g., the use of the Hernandez-Lopez method or similar) used to quantify the $\beta$-phase fraction. Given the overlap of peaks in PVDF, this is critical for reproducibility.
*   **Sample Preparation:** The hot-pressing conditions (220 °C, 5 MPa) are near the melting point of PVDF. The authors must clarify how they ensure that the NiS2 facet orientation is preserved during the melt-processing stage, as high-temperature processing often leads to recrystallization that may override the initial facet-induced nucleation.

### 4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting
*   **Mechanism:** The discussion of "polarons" in the introduction and conclusion is disconnected from the experimental data. There is no evidence provided (e.g., EPR spectroscopy or conductivity measurements) to support the existence or role of polarons in this composite system. The regression analysis (R²=0.94442, p=0.00738) for the correlation between $\beta$-phase content and THz shielding is a positive step. The authors report on the observation of reentrant superconductivity and a superconductor-to-insulator transition in granular aluminum, a material which acts as a natural Josephson junction (JJ) array.
As the authors correctly say in the introductory section of the manuscript, reentrant superconductivity in JJ arrays has been studied theoretically since a long time but the experimental situation remained elusive. In essence the effect should appear due to an interplay between the Josephson coupling energy E_J and the charging energy E_c, for specific values of the ratio E_J/E_c.
If E_J dominates one obtains a phase coherent state while for a dominating E_c the insulating state is obtained. If E_J/E_c decreases monotonically from values well above 1 to values well below 1, say, as a function of temperature one may observe the superconductor-to-insulator transition (SIT). However, at some moderate temperature quasiparticle screening may reduce E_c and thus increase E_J/E_c, enabling the reappearance of superconductivity. This effect has been observed by the authors. They use granular aluminum, having very small grain sizes of around 2 nm, as the experimental platform and apply an external radio frequency to tune E_J. With this system the SIT has been observed for specific values of the rf power, as summarized in Fig. 1 of the manuscript. The experimental results are accompanied by a detailed theoretical analysis.
The manuscript is well organized, the results are new and convincing. The paper is generally suitable for Nature Communications. The only drawback is that the authors never show current-voltage characteristics (IVCs) of their samples, which would help in understanding the properties of their system. In the past, such IVCs provided clear signature whether a system is Josephson coupled or in the flux-flow regime, if a Coulomb gap is present, if inhomogeneities play a big role, etc. It thus would be great to have comparable curves in the paper.
As I understand the authors primarily record the differential resistance and plot it as the color scale in various 2D plots. However, for example in Fig. S5b they integrate the signal to obtain the actual voltage V. Can the same procedure be used to obtain complete IVCs, i.e. plots of currents I_b vs. V? If so, it would be very helpful to see representative IVCs, say, along the vertical dashed lines in Fig. 1b. This could include a low-temperature IVC, obtained in region SC1, an IVC obtained in the insulating region, around 1.8 K, one in region SC2, and perhaps one or two more in the N regions. These plots could be presented in the Supplementary Information section. With these or a comparable modification I will be happy to recommend the manuscript for publication in Nature Communications.

**Reviewer Report**

**Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**Summary of the Work:**
The authors report the synthesis of six mechanically interlocked supramolecular architectures—three Linear [3]catenanes, two Borromean rings, and one heterometallic Solomon link—using a single rigid pyridyl ligand (L1) and various ruthenium-based building units. The study aims to demonstrate that topological diversity can be controlled by modulating the size, conjugation, and torsional flexibility of the building units. Furthermore, the authors investigate the photothermal conversion properties of these complexes, attributing the observed efficiencies (23%–81%) to synergistic π···π stacking and radical-based effects.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The manuscript addresses a significant challenge in supramolecular chemistry: the rational control of complex topologies from a single ligand precursor. The "two-component construction strategy" is well-motivated, and the successful assembly of a Solomon link using a rigid ligand via silver-mediated conformational modulation is a notable achievement. The attempt to correlate specific topological architectures with photothermal conversion efficiency is timely and adds a functional dimension to structural supramolecular chemistry.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The synthetic strategy is logical, and the use of SC-XRD, NMR, and ESI-TOF-MS provides robust evidence for the identity of the complexes. However, the methodology regarding the photothermal conversion studies requires clarification. The authors claim that the "free radical effect" of the building units contributes to the photothermal efficiency. This is a bold claim that requires more rigorous mechanistic evidence than the provided EPR signal intensity changes.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The structural characterization is generally high-quality. However, the reproducibility of the photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE) measurements is a concern. The authors report a wide range of efficiencies (e.g., 77%–81% for 4(OTf)12). It is unclear if these ranges represent experimental error, concentration dependence, or variations in the laser power density. Furthermore, the stability of these complexes in the presence of the laser (which can induce local heating) needs to be more thoroughly addressed beyond simple TGA data.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
The manuscript is well-written, but several sections lack sufficient detail:
*   **EPR Analysis:** The authors state that the EPR signal intensity increases by 11.66 times for 4(OTf)12 upon light exposure. It is unclear if this is a reversible process or if the light is inducing a permanent chemical change (e.g., ligand degradation or radical generation).
*   **Photothermal Data:** The calculation of PCE (23%–81%) is not sufficiently detailed. The authors should provide the specific equations used and the parameters (e.g., heat capacity of the solvent, laser power, surface area of the container) to allow for independent verification.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
The statistical treatment of the photothermal data is insufficient. The authors report specific efficiency values without providing standard deviations or error bars derived from multiple independent measurements. Given the sensitivity of PCE measurements to environmental factors, at least three independent replicates for each compound are required to support the claims of "remarkable enhancement."

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed:**
*   **Mechanistic Evidence:** The link between "free radical effect" and photothermal efficiency is speculative. The authors must perform control experiments, such as measuring the PCE of the building units alone versus the assembled complexes, and potentially use radical scavengers to determine if the radical species are indeed the primary drivers of the photothermal effect.
*   **Solomon Link Synthesis:** The role of silver ions in the formation of the Solomon link is described as providing "rotational flexibility." This is a significant claim that requires computational support (e.g., DFT calculations) to show the energy landscape of the ligand/building unit interaction with and without Ag(I).
*   **Data Presentation:** Figure 6 and Figure 7 are central to the paper’s claims. The authors must provide the raw data for the temperature-time cooling curves used to calculate the PCE.
*   **Stability:** The TGA data shows the frameworks collapse at temperatures ranging from 191°C to 304°C. While this indicates thermal stability, it does not prove structural integrity under the specific conditions of the photothermal experiments. The authors should provide post-irradiation NMR or XRD data to confirm that the topologies remain intact after the 10-cycle photothermal test.
*   **Clarity on "Free Radical Effect":** The authors attribute the high efficiency of 4(OTf)12 to the "free radical effect of the half-sandwich fragment." Half-sandwich Ru(II) complexes are typically diamagnetic (d6). The authors must clarify the origin of these radicals—are they generated *in situ* by the laser, or are they inherent to the building units? If the latter, the electronic structure of the building units must be explicitly discussed.

=== reviewer_1 ===
In this study, Mialon et al. identify a novel mechanism for the clustering of acetyl choline receptors (AChRs) at neuronal synapses. Using a series of sophisticated manipulations in C. elegans, they convincingly show that extracellular interactions mediated by adhesion molecules of the IgLON family localize the ACR-16 AChR at the synapse. They find that RIG-5, a presynaptic IgLON, and ZIG-8, a postsynaptic IgLON, interact via their N-terminal Ig1 domains to form a trans-synaptic complex. In addition, ZIG-8 interacts in cis with ACR-16 via its Ig2 domain. Using AlphaFold multimer modelling, the authors identify a single amino acid substitution in ACR-16 that is sufficient to perturb its interaction with the ZIG-8 Ig2 domain, resulting in a loss of ACR-16 clustering at synapses. Finally, the authors show that the interaction with the ZIG-8 Ig2 domain is sufficient to mislocalize ACR-16 to GABAergic postsynaptic compartments. Taken together, this study identifies a novel mechanism for localizing AChRs at synapses, which may have implications for mammalian nervous systems. The rationale for the experiments is clearly explained, results are clearly described, elegant assays such as extra- and intracellular split-GFP complementation are used, and the experiments are performed to a high standard. I have only one major comment and several minor ones for improvement of the manuscript.
Major comment
1. The authors test the interaction between ACR-16 or ACR-16(T201R) and ZIG-8 in a co-immunoprecipitation assay in HEK293T cells (Fig. 5B). The blot shown is not entirely convincing and appears to have some smudges on the left side of the RFP blot. The IP of ACR-16 in the condition where it is coexpressed with ZIG-8 (right lane) is weak, resulting in very low levels of coimmunoprecipitated ZIG-8. This blot should be repeated to convincingly show the interaction between ACR-16 and ZIG-8, and absence of the interaction between ACR-16(T201R) and ZIG-8. In addition to showing the pulldown lanes, the authors should also include the input lanes, to show presence of ACR-16 and ZIG-8 across the various conditions.
Minor comments
1. Mutations in rig-5 and zig-8 were identified in a genetic screen. From supplementary table S2 it was not clear to me whether these were the only candidates, or top candidates, or two of multiple candidates, to affect ACR-16 localization. A bit more background on this screen and the identification of rig-5 and zig-8 would be helpful.
2. Fig. 4D (cell type-specific rescues) shows that expression of ZIG-8 in the AVA neurons leads to a strong increase in apparent synaptic puncta density. The reason for this is not entirely clear. From the image in Fig. 4B, there actually appears to be a decrease in ZIG-8 puncta density and an increase in diffuse ZIG-8 signal. Is the increase in puncta density due to the more diffuse distribution of ZIG-8? Are these additional clusters synaptic? Or could this indicate that ZIG-8 can induce additional ACR-16 clusters, partly independent of presynaptic RIG-5? Or could the apparent increase in ACR-16 clusters be due to the presence of RIG-5 in other presynaptic neurons besides the AVE neurons? Please discuss.
3. Related to the comment above: the number of ACR-16 puncta in AVE-to-AVA synapses is ±16 in Fig. 1C and ±29 in Fig. 4D (rescue with presynaptic RIG-5 in AVE and postsynaptic ZIG-8 in AVA neurons). Please comment on these differences.
4. There are many AChRs in C. elegans, but only 2 IgLON orthologs. Do the authors think the interaction with IgLONs might also occur with other AChRs or is this specific for ACR-16? Is the interacting region in ACR-16 (T201) conserved in other AChRs?
5. Any insight on whether RIG-5 and ZIG-8 affect AChR function would further strengthen the manuscript. I understand electrophysiology is not trivial, but possibly other approaches exist? E.g. does AlphaFold multimer modelling show changes in AChR structure in the presence of ZIG-8?

=== reviewer_2 ===
Precise subcellular localization and clustering of NTRs at post-synaptic sites is crucial for proper neuronal function, but how this is achieved, and specifically the roles that extracellular proteins play in this process, is poorly understood. In C.elegans, Ach is the most widely used NT. ACR-16 (the α7-like AChR subunit), was previously shown to cluster in the NMJ by intracellular protein scaffolds, but how it clusters in neuron-neuron synapses remains unknown.
In this study, Mialon and colleagues focus on specific neurons in the worm nerve cord, and find that the IgLON homologs RIG-5 and ZIG-8 localize to pre- and postsynapes, respectively, and trans-neuronally interact (via Ig1) to control the localization of one another. Moreover, ZIG-8 directly binds and recruits ACR-16 via its Ig2 domain. Thus, they uncover a novel mechanism controlling the synaptic localization of an AChR via extracellular interactions with IgSF synaptic molecules.
This is a very elegant study, well-constructed and addressing the majority of the critical aspects required for the authors to establish their hypothesis. It is carefully designed and highly convincing, and its potential implications on other neuronal systems and higher organisms – given the conserved nature of all molecules involved – is of a broad interest to the molecular neuroscience community. I actually think that if the authors would have written the paper in a bit more broader manner, and perhaps focusing on synaptic targeting rather than NTR localization, this study could be published in the top journals. That said - in its current state and with minor textual changes and improvements of figure presentation - this is a top paper for Nature Comm.
1) Annotation of the figures in many places is lacking and they are sometimes confusing or difficult to interpret (in some cases even after reading the entire legend). The system is not straightforward and involves many types of neurons that is difficult for the non-worm expert to follow. There are some schemes throughout which try to clarify, but they are not clear enough (e.g., 1D doesn't show AVE, 1F is tiny and hard to understand - zoom in would help). Better annotation of the images themselves would also be helpful (e.g. S Fig. 5, and other places - two types of arrows indicate two different neurons - but the legend doesn't say which type points to what).
2) The intro is, in my opinion, a bit tedious. Too many facts and gene names. It's a stylish preference - so completely up to the authors - but one could make the paper lighter and more interesting to the general reader.
3) Tissue specific manipulation - again worm specific, but I could not find specifics on how the authors control the tissue-specificity of the AID experiments (Fig. 1B) – how is the auxin administered/introduced to the animal?
4) The screen - no hard data or information is provided about the genetic screen in which zig8 and rig5 were identified.

We appreciate the authors’ efforts to address the methodological concerns raised about this paper. Most were addressed with useful caveats and acknowledged limitations in the text. The absence of spillover is not biologically plausible, in general, but only possible in specific circumstances. The question is what this study sheds insight regarding what are those circumstances and whether current AMR monitoring strategies are sufficient, compared to better or more comprehensive approaches to monitoring. The difficulty in assessing whether the study is sufficiently powered, the geographical clustering, the lack of data on actual ties between communities (mobility of people), and the lack of information about potential confounders like the use of antibiotics in local livestock raising (which unfortunately in West Africa is prevalent among both small farmers and intensive farming operations —https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/agr.21770) make determining what those insights are challenging. Taking into account the study’s limitations, it might be useful to rethink whether one should be calling for continuing just more of the same AMR monitoring strategies or improved vigilance (“Our findings support current AMR monitoring strategies in sentinel villages, as we found no evidence of geographic spillover, which could cause these surveillance strategies to underestimate AMR selection during the initial years of MDA implementation...”). In this current study, Wang et al studies the differential pH between the dense and dilute phases of complex coacervates across the condensate interface. They first show (confirm) previously reported results that such a difference in pH exists between nucleoplasm and nucleolus in live cells. Then they use a simple model system, complex coacervates formed by R10+D10, and study the differential pH across the interface and how that changes by the addition of salt and H+, and OH- ions. Although the results are interesting, by no means, these coacervates formed by polyelectrolyte mixtures close to the cellular structures. Very interestingly, from their cellular experiments, they observed that inhibition of rRNA production by CX5461 disrupts the pH difference between the nucleolus and nucleoplasm, hinting at the role of active processes in creating such a proton gradient. Such processes are absent in R10+D10 coacervates. Finally, the authors employ a few common enzymes, such as Gox and urease, that can produce H+ or OH- ions as byproducts in these coacervate droplets. They also attempted PCR reaction and IVTT in these droplets.
The reported studies are highly qualitative in nature. There are at least a few recent reports(Ausserwöger et al. 2024; King et al. 2024; Dai et al. 2024) that established that the concentration of H+ ions and other types of ions across the condensate interface can be unequal, leading to an apparent difference in pH between the dense and dilute phases. However, it is important to note that there is no “gradient” per se, since that would mean that the system is out of equilibrium. The concentrations of the ions and/or protons are different across the condensate interface, similar to the concentration of macromolecules that make up the condensate. This is also supported by the data showing CX5461 disrupts the pH difference between the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.
The model system (R10+D10) is interesting, but the characterization of such systems by the addition of salt and pH change is not new. It is conceivable that as the system moves closer to the single phase regime by the addition of salt, the differences in the H+ or OH- concentrations decrease between the dense and dilute phase since the density of the macromolecules that make up the dense phase decreases as well. It will be good to establish quantitative phase diagrams and how they relate to the differences in the pH between the dense and dilute phases.
The addition of enzymes to these condensates is also interesting, but similar studies have been done at a much greater depth(Jambon-Puillet et al. 2024; Testa et al. 2021).
Finally, it will be great if the authors can focus on understanding the enzyme kinetics in condensates and how they are impacted via differences in the intra-condensate pH. Such active systems may show emergent properties due to phase separation-driven changes in the bulk pH, but to decipher that, more rigorous analysis is needed.
Minor comments: the MD simulations and the use of microfluidics to generate coacervates are not really needed for this study, are they? Some claims are not supported by the data, such as “bioreactors,” “protocells,” etc.; such terms should not be used loosely. Finally, schematics like Fig. 1 are not helpful to occupy one figure in an article; rather, they may be better reserved for SI. Describing how the enzyme reaction rates were measured at the section where the results were described would be useful for the readers.

The enzymatic reactions of GOx and Urease release products that influence the pH and therefore the substrate concentration serves as a handle to regulate enzyme kinetics.
