From the title, we expected a paper with a more significant fraction of computational design. This is quite limited here, with the use of replica exchange MD to sample conformers, of Rosetta FastDesign to build a library and the use of LigandMPNN (for some unclear purpose). The main strength of the paper lies in the choice of its targets (nitazenes) which appear to raise significant health issues in the US (at least), the use of PYR1 as a multi-purpose platform for sensor design, a nice mixture of protein engineering (combinatorial libraries, FACS, Yeast display, Y2H, sequencing) and simple computational protein design in the pocket of PYR1 (with a small number of mutable residues) and eventually, an extensive work that ends up in functional sensors, tested also in complex media (urine).
The novelty in terms of protocol remains however more moderate. Some of the authors have already published at least one paper that is closely related to this work:
[A] Beltrán, J., Steiner, P.J., Bedewitz, M. et al. Rapid biosensor development using plant hormone receptors as reprogrammable scaffolds. Nat Biotechnol 40, 1855–1861 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-022-01364-5
Reference [A] modifies PYR1 to develop sensors for a range of small molecules, including structurally diverse natural and synthetic cannabinoids and several organophosphates. On the computational side, it uses Rosetta to predict the stability of PYR1 variants inside a small combinatorial library. The pipeline presented in this paper is very close in substance to the protocol used in reference [A], the main difference being in the use of replica exchange MD to select most frequent conformers of the ligand. The use of Rosetta is quite similar, using FastDesign instead of a simple stability assessment. In itself, the use of replica exchange to sample conformers fairly is not a surprise [B] and the use of FastDesign in a very small pocket is far less computationally challenging that most computational protein design projects.
[B] Okumura, H., Gallicchio, E. and Levy, R.M., 2010. Conformational populations of ligand‐sized molecules by replica exchange molecular dynamics and temperature reweighting. Journal of computational chemistry, 31(7), pp.1357-1367.
Overall, the paper reaches a very nice objective, developing two sensors with different detection properties for nitazenes that are tested in a complex matrix (urine), but the importance and novelty in terms of computational protein design remains limited. This contrasts with the title, that brings computational design forward.
If the questions detailed in the comments below are answered, my main remaining concern with the paper would be the relative lack of methodological (molecular, experimental or computational) novelty given reference [A] which uses PYR1 as a basis for biosensor development (including cannabinoids), replica exchange for conformer sampling (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2848294/) and computational design with Rosetta FastDesign.
Local comments and Questions
The role of LigandMPNN in the protocol is extremely unclear and a bit confusing. It seems to serve no purpose (it’s not used to design the library) and its only use seems to be motivated by an a posteriori check that the (already experimentally checked as beneficial) mutation A159H is effectively present in a small fraction of LigandMPNN’s output. But the value of this information remains limited. Its main interest would be to compare it with other sequence design tools: does LigandMPNN performs, better, e.g, than Carbonara in this respect (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50571-y), or simply than Rosetta FastDesign? If the use of LigandMPNN does not contribute at all to the used pipeline, it’s probably better to remove it to avoid confusion. If this is not removed, please give the sampling temperature.
The legend of Fig1. says « This process is iterated over conformer and alignment perturbations and filtered to identify sets of sequences. A library is encoded using position-specific and local residue preferences ». What filtering is performed ? How are the params files built ? Did you use QM/Gaussian to determine partial charges ? It’s unclear how the output of Rosetta FastDesign (a set of sequences) was transformed into the ultramer specifications for NitaZeneLib1 (Table S4). How many sequences were sampled by FastDesign? How/why are they filtered ? What percentage of the set of FastDesign sequences is covered by the theoretical ultramer coverage of the 3 libraries (ABC) of Table S5? Was a computational tool used to build the librairies and cassettes definitions? (such as DeCoDe for example: https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/36/11/3357/5807608). The precision of the description contrasts here with the extremely detailed description of the SVD usage for conformer docking (which uses a significant amount of space for folklore knowledge. This space could be use to detail how the library is designed instead).
« We use supervised learning »: why not immediately say « We use regularized linear regressions » ? How were the regularization penalties fixed ?
« Yielded no sensors when nearly the same panel was used » : why « nearly » ? What changed ?
Deep sequencing: what type of sequencing technology was used, how long are the reads ? Are they short reads assembled by Quintara or long (eg. ONT/PacBio) reads ?
Looking into Flash, I understand paired short reads but it’s better if it’s said.
In Fig. 1, it would be nice to have the water molecule represented as a dipole (a full H2O) to better visualize the H-bonds.
« Backbone and side-chains by fast-grd reach » => fast-grid
Fig. S10: not very useful given that LigandMPNN has apparently not been used to design libraries.
A quick explanation of tables S2 (same for S6) would be welcome. In table S2 for example, with V83VW in the library, how do we get a « M » for N-desethyl etonitazene1?
Table S3: why mandiprodamid and Win55;212-2 here. I don’t think I have seen these mentioned anywhere in the paper.
Menitazine -> menitazene ?
Latin (de novo) could be italicized.
Code trial: the code executes properly, although one is stopped at some point when the « Ligands.csv » file needs to be filled. Ligands.csv files for the considered system/conformers here would be required for better reproducibility.

=== reviewer_3 ===
Leonard et al. present a computational protocol for redesigning the plant abscisic acid receptor PYR1 to bind diverse nitazenes, an emerging class of synthetic opioids, while preserving its dynamic transduction mechanism. The authors demonstrate that the optimized sensor variant exhibits low nanomolar detection limits in vitro for nitazene and menitazene. Additionally, deep mutational scanning identified sensor variants capable of detecting a range of clinically relevant nitazenes, including their common metabolic byproduct, with limited cross-specificity against unrelated opioids. The authors propose that applying protein design methodologies to versatile receptors such as PYR1 could facilitate the development of generalized biosensors applicable to numerous contexts both in vitro and in vivo.
Overall, the manuscript is clearly written and presents potentially valuable advancements in sensor engineering, making it a candidate for publication in Nature Communications. However, several major and minor issues need to be addressed prior to publication:
Major Issues:
1. Figures 4C and S16: The authors demonstrate sensor performance in various biological matrices using ratiometric assay data for PYR1 (Fig. S15) and PYR1nitav2 (Fig. 4B) in buffer and urine. However, the sensors PANnita.1 (Fig. 4C) and PANnita (Fig. S16) have been validated only in buffer. It is critical to validate these sensors in urine to fully demonstrate their utility. Additionally, the manuscript does not specify the source of urine used, which should be clearly stated.
2. Throughout the manuscript, the sensor performance is assessed primarily based on affinity (e.g., EC50) and specificity. However, other critical performance parameters should be investigated, including solubility, kinetics, and thermostability. Given the clinical relevance proposed for these sensors, the authors should experimentally determine the solubility of the PYR1 variants, measure the kinetics of ligand-induced protein dimerization between the PYR1 variant and HAB1, and evaluate the thermostability of the variants at relevant temperatures. The reviewer is concerned that extensive mutations within the ligand-binding pocket may negatively affect these parameters.
3. Figure 3D: The authors hypothesize the roles of specific mutations in ligand binding by the PYR1 variants. Additionally, earlier in the manuscript (page 3), the authors discuss the significance of a water molecule in the PYR1 biosensor. Would it be feasible to include modeling that incorporates the ligand and the critical water molecule to explain the impact of these mutations on sensor performance? Such modeling would greatly strengthen the mechanistic insights presented.
Minor Issues:
1. Figures 3G, S14, S16: The statistical tests employed should be explicitly described in the figure captions.
2. Reference 51: This study is now published in Science, volume 388, eadr7094 (2025). The authors should update this citation accordingly.

This paper demonstrated that: condensates formed by minimalistic histidine-containing peptides can catalyze ester hydrolysis via two pathways: a Zn²⁺-dependent mechanism activating bound water and a metal-free mechanism driven by LBHB. The concept is of highly interested and the discovery is exciting. However, the authors want to address the following technical considerations before this can be published.
1. This work suffers from a fundamental flaw, namely the overlooking of the effect of pH on hydrolysis reactions. It is well known that pH affects hydrolysis reactions. Recently, more and more studies have shown that phase separation can create a distinct pH within condensates (see, doi.org/10.1101/2024.05.23.595321). The mechanism underlying this distinct pH environment is the partitioning of ions (including protons) during LLPS. In this study, the authors tested (1) condensates made of different peptides and (2) condensates formed in the presence of Zn²⁺ or other ions , both conditions that can create distinct intra-condensate pH. (1) condensates made of different peptides possess the same (or at least similar) pH;
(2) condensates formed at different Zn²⁺ concentrations possess the same (or at least similar) pH.

(3) study how distinct pH can modulate the reactions.

Rhodamine B is a charged molecule, so its partitioning and diffusion can be affected by electrostatic interactions with the charged peptides. Because the hydrolysis substrates used in this article are non-charged, the authors should replace rhodamine B with a neutral fluorescent molecule.

The manuscript by authors Y. Jiang et al., presents a study of interlayer excitonic states in a moiré heterostructure of transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) semiconductors. Using power-dependent photoluminescence (PL) measurements, the authors report presence of moire-trapped interlayer biexcitons (IXX) in WS2/WSe2 heterostructure, 30 meV above the interlayer exciton (IX). In addition, using polarization-resolved PL measurements, it is shown that the circular polarization of both IX and IXX states evolves as a function of the incident power. Interestingly, both states exhibit significant negative polarization (>25%) at high powers, which is in contradiction to what has been reported so far in these systems. The authors explain the presence of interlayer biexcitons based on the Bose-Hubbard model for moiré-trapped states. Further, they attribute the negative circular polarization to the fine structure of the biexciton. A temperature-dependent PL study is performed to confirm the validity of this model. The manuscript is well written and organized. The experimental results and arguments of the authors are convincing. I think this manuscript will add to the ongoing discussions of moiré physics in two-dimensional systems. The paper deserves to be published in Nature Communications, once the authors reply to a few minor points raised as follows: 1) The samples have been fabricated using mechanical exfoliation. In general, such samples show residual doping at low temperatures. This could affect the formation of multi-particle states like biexcitons. Could the authors include a PL of both the individual layers (WS2 and WSe2) as well as the heterostructure near the energy of their intrinsic intralayer excitons? This would help estimate the doping level of the monolayers based on the intensity of the trions. Also, the quality of the samples (dielectric environment inhomogeneity) can be assessed better by probing the broadening of these states. 2) In Fig. 1d, a power-dependent PL of IX and IXX states is presented. At 4K, the data is restricted to 1 microW incident power. Why is this the case? Also, as it is observed later in the manuscript that these states show significant negative circular polarization, I believe it would be important to mention the polarization conditions in this measurement. 3) Also on a related note, in Fig. 3b, it is shown that the IXX emission gets broader at higher excitation power due to excitation of different states in the fine structure of the biexciton. In general, for the intralayer excitons in monolayer TMDs, a temperature-dependent red shift in emission energy is observed at higher temperature (M. M. Ugeda et al, Nature Mater 13, 1091-1095, 2014). Why is such a shift not observed for the interlayer states?

The solvation structure of magnesium polysulfides is considered to dominate the conversion chemistry and regulate the performances of Mg−S batteries. In this work, the discharging behaviors, kinetic characteristics and electrochemical deposition models were detailed analyzed in this work by introducing a series of solvents with different coordination ability. Cells with a G2 based electrolyte demonstrate the considerable improvements in cyclic stability and specific capacity. However, the novelty and the insight of this work are still lacking. I cannot support this work to be published in Nat. Comm. My comments are as follow: 1. The crucial role of the polysulfides solvation structure in determining the charging/discharging behaviors and cell performance has been reported by some works, e.g. Adv. Mater. 2022, 34, 2205284; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64 e202424547; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2023, 62, e202309968. Particularly, the selected solvents in this work have been identified to function in tailoring the electrochemical deposition morphologies and models (Adv. Energy Mater. 2019, 9, 1802207). So, what is the key difference between this work and the previously reported works? 2. It is accepted that the coordination ability from G1 to G2 gradually increase. In this case, the abilities of the solvents in shielding the interaction between Mg2+ and PS should be orderly enhanced. However, this work did not detailly discuss why the G2 based electrolyte delivered the extraordinary cell performance from the perspective of solvation structure. Besides, what is identification of the "high shielding ability" of solvents mentioned in this work and how does it dominate the solvation structures of MgPS and determine the cell performance?

**Summary of the Work:**
The manuscript investigates the role of ether-based solvent solvation structures in modulating the Mg²⁺–polysulfide (MgPS) interaction in magnesium–sulfur (Mg–S) batteries. The authors propose a "shielding ability" parameter ($I_{s/p}$), defined by the ratio of Mg–solvent to Mg–PS bond orders, to predict the efficacy of solvents (DME, G2, G3, G4) in facilitating sulfur conversion kinetics. The study concludes that G2-based electrolytes provide an optimal solvation environment, promoting 3D nucleation of MgS and improved electrochemical performance.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study addresses a critical bottleneck in Mg–S battery chemistry: the sluggish kinetics caused by strong Mg²⁺–polysulfide coordination. The concept of using solvent-directed solvation modulation to tune the Mg–PS binding energy is scientifically sound and relevant to the field of multivalent battery electrolytes. However, the novelty is somewhat tempered by the fact that ether-based solvents are well-studied in Mg-battery literature, and the "shielding" effect is a known phenomenon in coordination chemistry. The manuscript would benefit from a more explicit comparison of how this specific $I_{s/p}$ metric provides predictive power over existing descriptors (e.g., Gutmann donor number).

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
*   **Electrolyte Preparation:** The authors use Mg(TFSI)₂ with iodine additives. It is well-documented that iodine can act as a redox mediator or cathode activator in Mg–S systems. The manuscript does not sufficiently decouple the effect of the solvent (G2) from the potential catalytic effect of the iodine additive.
*   **PITT Analysis:** The use of Potentiostatic Intermittent Titration Technique (PITT) to distinguish between 3D nucleation modes is appropriate. However, the claim that G3 and G4 show "no current signals" in PITT is concerning. If the cells are functional, there must be a current response; the lack of signal suggests either an experimental failure or that the kinetics are so sluggish they fall outside the measurement window. This requires clarification.
*   **Three-electrode setup:** The use of a three-electrode cell is commendable for isolating electrode contributions, but the reference electrode stability in Mg(TFSI)₂/ether systems is notoriously difficult. The authors should provide evidence of the reference electrode potential stability over the duration of the test.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
*   **Sulfur Loading:** The sulfur loading (0.6–1.0 mg cm⁻²) is relatively low for a study claiming practical relevance. The authors should discuss the impact of higher mass loadings on the proposed 3D nucleation mechanism, as pore clogging becomes significantly more severe at higher loadings.
*   **Cycle Life:** The coin cell cycling is limited to 120 cycles, and the pouch cell data is limited to 18 cycles. Given the rapid capacity fading mentioned in the introduction, 18 cycles is insufficient to demonstrate "extended cycle life" or to validate the stability of the proposed solvation mechanism.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
*   The manuscript is generally well-written, but the definition of $I_{s/p}$ needs more rigorous mathematical justification. Is this ratio derived from DFT calculations? If so, the computational details (functional, basis set, solvent model) are missing from the Methods section.
*   The transition from "solvation modulation" to "3D nucleation" is logical, but the link between the two is largely correlative. More direct evidence (e.g., operando spectroscopy) would strengthen the claim that the solvation structure *directly* dictates the nucleation morphology.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   The manuscript lacks error bars on electrochemical performance plots (e.g., Fig 6c, 6d). Given the sensitivity of Mg–S batteries to assembly conditions, reporting mean values from at least 3–5 cells is essential to demonstrate reproducibility.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Computational Details:** Provide the full computational methodology for the Mayer bond order calculations.
*   **Iodine Role:** Perform control experiments (G2 electrolyte without iodine) to determine if the observed performance is due to the solvent or the additive.

*   **Energy Density:** The specific energy values (22–31 Wh kg⁻¹) are quite low. The authors should clarify if these are based on the total cell mass or just the active material, and compare these values against state-of-the-art Mg–S systems.

=== reviewer_1 ===
The authors demonstrate the use of a Gradient-weighted Class Activation Map (Grad-CAM) to investigate how a machine learning algorithm decodes anomalous diffusion. First they demonstrate that Grad-CAM captures the relevant features of a trajectory by testing the performance changes when erasing the parts of a trajectory with the highest Grad-CAM scores. Additionally they propose and test a targeted augmentation procedure utilising Grad-CAM, for which trajectories with high Grad-CAM scores are preferred for augmentation. Building on depictions of two-dimensional projections of the activation vectors in intermediate layers of their convolutional neural network, they also construct features that are likely to be used at each step in the machine's classification process. They verify their feature selection by analysing the correlations between feature-magnitude and Grad-CAM scores, as well as by measuring the change in misclassification when a particular feature is distorted.
Overall the authors present a very well presented work, with a detailed and interesting analysis. This work will certainly widen the scope of the field of advanced data analysis of anomalous stochastic analysis. Due to the wide applicability and importance of their results in various fields I strongly support publication of this work in Nature Communications, after minor changes.
(1) Could you clarify whether the training set for part II/III included noise, and if yes, which type and level of noise? In the text I only find that the set in part IV is noiseless.
(2) While I can easily understand what different Grad-cam scores within a trajectory mean, I have difficulty visualising what differences in Grad-cam between trajectories entail (as used in part IIIc). Maybe there is a way to clarify this?
(3) For reference, could you include the overall accuracy of ResAnDi for part IV, since the testing/training set features constant trajectory length (and is noiseless), I assume it would be higher than the 90\% mentioned before?
(4) Could you clarify whether part V uses the data set from part IV or the previous one?
(5) Could you clarify what is meant by the bar notation in Eqs. (4), (6), (7).
(7) The authors should also mention feature-based analyses, e.g., as developed in these papers: J. Phys. A 55, 244005 (2022); Entropy 22, 1436 (2020).
(8) Could the authors accommodate a change-point analysis in their approach? This is of increasing relevance in data analysis, see, e.g., the discussion in J. Phys. Photon. 6, 045025 (2024); Biophys. J. 122, 4360 (2023); Phys. Rev. Res. 6 013054 (2024).

=== reviewer_3 ===
Bae et al. use a standard convolutional neural network (ResNet) architecture to classify single-particle trajectories undergoing anomalous diffusion and use Grad-CAM to identify the trajectory segments most relevant for the model decision. They further investigate correlations between Grad-CAM scores and statistical features, with the goal of extracting interpretable insights.
While the application of explainable AI in this context is timely and relevant, the manuscript raises substantial concerns regarding novelty, the robustness of the proposed evaluation strategies, and the interpretation of results.
In my opinion, key claims, such as those related to the informativeness of Grad-CAM scores and the inferred links to physical mechanisms, are insufficiently supported or rely on questionable assumptions. Overall, the contribution to the field remains limited. For these reasons, I cannot recommend the publication in its current form.
Comments:
1) Convolutional Neural Networks, such as ResNet, have demonstrated good performance in classification tasks like the one discussed in the manuscript. However, their application to time series or sequential data is not necessarily optimal. Time series exhibit correlations that are better captured by architectures such as Recurrent Neural Networks or attention-based models. In RNNs, gradients can similarly be backpropagated from the output to hidden states, allowing a weighted combination of activations to highlight important time steps (see, e.g., 10.48550/arXiv.1706.07206). Therefore, a discussion of alternative architectures and a rationale for selecting a CNN over RNNs or other sequential models is warranted. This is a critical point, especially in the context of interpretability, as the relevance and granularity of the Grad-CAM results may also depend on the network architecture used.
2) On page 1, the authors claim: “More recently, deep learning was also applied to analyze anomalous diffusion.” This statement lacks proper references. I suggest citing the pioneering works for this field, such as Ref. 28, Ref. 33, 10.1103/PhysRevE.100.032410, and 10.1088/1367-2630/ab6065
3) The set of references [27–33] used to support the statement about the improved performance of deep learning methods seems arbitrarily selected. It is unclear why other top-performing approaches in the AnDi challenge, which also outperformed classical methods, are not cited. The authors should justify the criteria for inclusion.
4) The authors reference works on explainable AI broadly, but in the specific context of time-series and trajectories, they might consider including /10.1038/s42256-022-00595-0, where attention heads are used to quantify the relevance of time-points for trajectory classification.
5) I have doubts concerning the validity of Grad-CAM evaluation in Section III.B. The experiment of removing high Grad-CAM scoring segments is inherently self-referential and tautological, since the segments determined as most important by the model are naturally expected to affect classification when removed. A more meaningful control could involve randomly shuffling trajectory segments of varying lengths (e.g., from segments as short as 2 points) and observing the classification accuracy.
6) I’m also puzzled by the data augmentation via rotation of Section II.C. Since trajectory rotation preserves all intrinsic statistical properties except for the absolute direction, they effectively replicates trajectories without introducing true variability, thus artificially enriching and biasing the dataset.
7) On page 4, the authors state: “These suggest that certain parts of the particle trajectories contain more information about the underlying diffusion mechanism than others, and that the Grad-CAM score can be used as an indicator of those crucial parts.” Why do different parts of the trajectories encode more information about anomalous diffusion? This point is extremely relevant. One can intuitively understand it for inhomogeneous models, but it is surprising for models like FBM.
8) Section IV starts by stating: “Now that the relevance of Grad-CAM to the classification of anomalous diffusion mechanisms has been demonstrated, …” Based on the previous comments, I find this claim an overstatement. Even if proved by proper tests, it could at most be claimed that Grad-CAM can qualitatively account for the relative importance of different parts of the trajectory for the trained task. But this is what Grad-CAM has been built for in the case of images, so it would only show that this holds for a different type of data.
9) In the same section, they use a different model trained on noiseless data without sufficient justification. The phrase “for the ease of statistical analysis” is vague and should be clarified.
10) The interpretation of the results presented in Fig. 6 is highly speculative. The data presented does not provide direct evidence of what information is encoded by each block. Trajectory generation based on the features extracted at each block, e.g., as done for images in style transfer or deepdreams might help to better elucidate what information each layer captures from the trajectory.
11) The correlation properties of FBM and LW are well established in the literature. The other measures introduced can be inferred based on knowledge of the theoretical models. The logic for selecting these features seems loosely tied to the evidence presented on the basis of ResNet.
12) The authors define a non-Gaussianity parameter that is formally similar to the kurtosis, and conceptually related to trajectory-level ergodicity breaking parameters (e.g., as proposed in 10.1103/PhysRevE.93.052146). It would be useful to clarify the connection or distinction between these metrics.
13) The measure referred to as “consistency” by the authors resembles what is more commonly called “persistence” in the study of stochastic trajectories. Also in this case, it would be useful to clarify the connection or distinction between these metrics.
14) The rationale for introducing the "singularity" measure, as well as its physical interpretation, is not presented and needs a more detailed discussion.
15) Crucially, it remains unclear what role Grad-CAM played, if any, in motivating the selection of these statistical descriptors. The plots in Fig. 6 represent features from the ResNet model and have no apparent connection to the Grad-CAM scores discussed elsewhere in the paper. Without a direct link between the interpretability method (Grad-CAM) and the statistical features analyzed, the subsequent correlation analysis feels disjointed and adds little beyond reiterating known properties.
16) The histogram in Fig. 3 does not start from 0, which is misleading and exaggerates visual differences. This is not considered good practice in data visualization.
17) The accompanying code is poorly documented. Dependencies are not listed, and the notebooks mainly show final outputs without clear instructions on reproducing results or applying the method to other datasets. This limits reproducibility and broader adoption.
18) Reference 47 is incomplete; I believe it should be: 10.5281/zenodo.4775311
19) References 18 and 56 appear to be duplicates.

=== reviewer_4 ===
This article builds on the datasets of the dataset created by the AnDi challenge to explore some novel ideas on how to extract information from anomalous diffusion from trajectories of particles.
In particular it constructs a ResNet classifier and uses the GradCam algorithm to determine the parts of the trajectories that most contribute to the classification of the trajectories into super-, sub- and diffusive (as well as the various kinds of anomalous diffusion models).
About the approach, I think it's very interesting and sufficiently novel from the machine learnign point of view.
The work is well described, with enough details to permit reproduction of the results (even though I haven't tried to reproduce them myself as part of this referee process).
There are some important poins that I'd like to see addressed before this article is published:
It'd be good to add some figure to show what are the portions of the trajectories (in 2D plots) that most contribution to the classification in each case. This would help in gaining some intuition about how this approach works.
What happens when trajectories with switching points are provided to the network? This is actually an very interesting topic in itself and should be addressed in the body of the article.
I have also an additional question: Why the accuracy in figures 3 and 4 doesn't seem to reach the level of 90+% stated in page 2?
About the code: I checked the GitHub repository, which looks good and well organized, but I haven't tested it myself.

In “Seasonal Enhancement of the Viral Shunt Catalyzes a Subsurface Oxygen Maximum in the Sargasso Sea,” Gilbert et al
used transcripts, polonies for cyanophage abundance, and ipolonies for picocyanobacterial infection on a cruise in the
Sargasso Sea in October 2019. They combine this data with a re-analysis of BATS oxygen and viral-like particle timeseries
data. The purpose of the paper is to link Subsurface Oxygen Maxima (SOM) to Prochlorococcus productivity and viral lysis.
They found increased numbers of Prochlorococcus cells, cyanophage viruses, infected Prochlorococcus cells and
cyanophage transcriptional activity at the SOM. In the literature, viral lysis is often linked to biogeochemistry in a vague
hand-wavy way, so any paper that can link the two in a concrete fashion is very cool. I was happy with the bioinformatic
analyses and the polonies are always interesting and useful. This paper is very interesting, but it could be pushed a bit
farther to be a better paper. Particularly, the authors should incorporate existing primary productivity and bacterial
productivity measurements from BATS to see if that data upholds their hypothesis. Also, rather than simply dismissing the
physics aspects, it would be good if the physics was included in a small way (see below). And please make sure that the
DOE/JGI sequencing is submitted to NCBI and acknowledged appropriately.
One thing that I found confusing about this paper was that it starts sounding like it is known that the Sargasso Sea and BATS
have SOMs, but then the first thing the authors do is prove that BATS has SOMs. Chen and McKinley (2019) analyzed 26
years of BATS data plus floats. It would good to know what this current paper did that was different. I think they just had to do
the work over again because the authors are non-overlapping.

biology side. However, the real ocean isn’t physics or biology, it is physics and biology. Chen and McKinley (2019) say that

By integrating historical BATS data with high-resolution Lagrangian cruise data (metatranscriptomics, metaviromics, and iPolony-based infection assays), the authors provide a compelling, multi-faceted argument for a biological contribution to SOM formation. **1. Significance and Novelty:**
The study addresses a long-standing controversy regarding the physical versus biological origins of SOMs. By moving beyond descriptive oceanography to mechanistic molecular ecology, the authors provide a novel link between viral infection dynamics and oxygen supersaturation. This work is highly relevant to the *Nature Communications* readership, as it bridges microbial ecology and global biogeochemical modeling.

**2. Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The Lagrangian sampling design is well-suited for capturing the temporal dynamics of a specific water mass. The use of iPolony to quantify *Prochlorococcus* infection is a sophisticated and appropriate choice for this study. The integration of metatranscriptomics with physical CTD data is sound. However, the reliance on a single 6-day cruise in October 2019 to represent a "recurrent" seasonal feature is a limitation. While the authors attempt to mitigate this by reanalyzing 30 years of BATS data, the causal link between the viral shunt and oxygen production remains correlative.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The data processing steps (e.g., Nadaray-Watson kernel smoothing, ‘rain’ rhythmicity detection) are clearly described. The inclusion of Supplementary Data files and the use of established bioinformatics pipelines (e.g., vOTU identification) suggest high reproducibility. The authors have been transparent about the limitations of their inference, particularly regarding the focus on a single study site.

**4. Clarity and Reporting:**
The manuscript is generally well-written. However, the Results section contains some repetitive phrasing (e.g., the description of T7-like cyanophage abundance in the final paragraph of the Results). The figures are informative, but the connection between the "dusk *Prochlorococcus* *amt* expression" and the "enhanced beam attenuation" needs to be more explicitly linked in the text to support the claim of metabolic coupling.

**6. Specific Weaknesses to Address:**
*   **Physical vs. Biological Contribution:** The authors define the SOM depth using a density criterion (0.125 kg/m³). It is well-established that physical subduction can trap oxygenated water. === reviewer_1 ===
The manuscript titled “Unlocking limited electric double-layer capacity via electrochemically-driven continuous partial desolvations in carbon nanopores” authored by Fan et el. aims to investigate the solvation environment of inserted Na+ into YP50F activated carbon. However, there are some major concerns on data collection and interpretation, as described below:
• My major concern is on the EQCM data interpretation, which is a very important part of discussion in the manuscript. The authors did not explain how the mass was calculated. It seems the authors applied Sauerbrey equation to convert the frequency change to mass change. However, the frequency change measured by EQCM can be contributed by mass change, viscoelastic property changes (the density, viscosity, and elasticity of the film electrode material) or sample roughness change [Ref: Acc. Chem. Res. 2018, 51, 69−79; J Polym Sci. 2021;1–18; Chem. Rev. 1992, 92, 1355]. The Sauerbrey Equation is only valid when the film remains stiff, uniform, flat, and no dissipation during cycling. With the way the authors prepared the electrolyte (dripcasting tens or hundreds µm size of YP50F particles on the quartz), the electrode roughness is already high. In addition, the electrolyte is more viscous than aqueous electrolyte, which further increased the dissipation of the resonance of the quartz. This will cause an extremely broadened frequency peak, which might lead to inaccurate reading of the resonance peak. Furthermore, during cycling, there is SEI formation and potential morphological electrode changes caused by the ion insertion. Both phenomena can also contribute to frequency change. Therefore, the authors will need to provide dissipation information (or Q factor, internal resistance, etc) during cycling to justify the mass change and solvation number discussion. Without dissipation information, the EQCM results are highly questionable. This obviously impact the validity of the discussion on solvation number.
• Another major point is that the way the authors described their observation is confusing and misleading. The term “electrical double layer (EDL)” described ion forming on at the electrode/electrolyte interface. The EDL naturally form on any immersed surface, whether the electrode is charged or at open circuit potential. When the YP50F is immersed in the electrolyte, all the accessible pores will be filled with ions already. Higher overpotential even reaching SEI formation, will drive more ions and/or solvents into the pore and also decompose the electrolyte to form SEI, but there is always EDL layer on the surface. The term the authors should use is “double layer capacitive behavior”. The authors described the charging process it as “When cycled towards lower potential, the EDL will disappear”. In fact, the EDL layer is always present, just the redox related current kicked in and becomes the main capacity contribution.
• In the experimental section for the BET measurement, there is no details given regarding the drying process of the sample. If the post-cycle sample is conducted without thorough drying, the pores will be packed with adsorbed liquid, which will also give an extremely low SA.
Based on the above-mentioned reasons, this work is not qualified to be published in Nature Communications.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The authors present a novel and systematic study aimed at enhancing the energy storage capacity of a commercial porous carbon electrode (YP50F) by extending the operating voltage window (Δφ) to 2.95 V. The ion desolvation and SEI plays a critical role in enabling stable and reversible Na⁺ ion adsorption/desorption in this high-voltage regime. The work thoroughly investigates the interplay between electrolyte composition and SEI formation on Na⁺ storage mechanisms. A high specific capacity of 141 mAh g⁻¹ was achieved, surpassing previously reported values in both organic and ionic liquid electrolytes. Unlike intercalation-based mechanisms, the charge storage here is governed by electric double-layer (EDL)-type Na⁺ ion adsorption, which is favorable for high-power applications. This is well-supported by the pouch cell demonstration provided in the manuscript. The authors also conducted comprehensive characterizations of the SEI composition and its role in the charge storage process. Notably, partial desolvation of Na⁺ facilitated by the SEI is proposed as a key factor driving performance improvement, which aligns well with recent studies in the field. The manuscript is well-organized and presents significant findings. I recommend its publication in Nature Communications after minor revisions.
Specific Comments:
1. Sodium adsorption mechanism
a) In Fig1b, I agree that the CV get distorted below 1V because of the irreversible charge storage process. However, I disagree with the full desolvation mechanism (of Na ions) as proposed in Fig1c. Generally speaking, a full desolvation typically leads to higher capacity, since the ion get closer to the electrode, as the authors also noted in this manuscript. Also, the stronger interaction between ions/host materials also enhances charge transfer, which also increase the capacity (Nature Communications, 2025, 16(1): 3813). However, in the present data, the difference of sodium insertion capacity below 1V is relatively small (0.5 A/g Fig1b vs 0.4 A/g, Fig1c. A rough estimation based on complete Na⁺ occupation in the pores of YP50F (0.7 cm³/g pore volume, Na atomic radius ≈ 0.19 nm) yields a theoretical capacity of ~1154 mAh/g, suggesting that Na ions are far away from full desolvation. The authors are encouraged to elaborate more on the mechanism in the EC:DMC electrolyte.
b) The butterfly-shaped CV deviates from the classical rectangular profile of pure EDL behavior, indicating potential-dependent ion–electrode interactions. This behavior is often influenced by specific ion effect (specific ion-electrode interactions, REF28). Using different cations rather than Na+ may be beyond the scope of this work, but a brief discussion of how Na⁺-YP50F specific interactions contribute to the CV shape would enrich the interpretation. The effects of surface functionalities, graphitization degree, and average pore size (confinement) would be interesting for future works.
2. Question about EQCM measurements
a) There appears to be a large irreversible current at low potentials (Supplementary Figure 16), likely due to electrolyte decomposition. This complicates the use of EQCM for accurate Na⁺ desolvation analysis, as side reactions being emphasized on the gold-coated quartz surface at slower scan rates. Thus, molecular weight calculations based on irreversible charge may not reliably reflect the solvation state.
b) The integrated charge values from CV curves at 5 mV/s (Fig. 2b) are noticeably lower than those shown in Fig. 2c. For better clarity and reproducibility, it is strongly recommended that the authors ensure both figures reflect data from the same sample and experimental conditions.
c) In Fig2c, similar to my previous comments, the same applies here that the molecular weight calculation based on slope in region iii (0.25-0.05 V) is a bit challenging. There is also irreversible current (side reaction) at the negative scan (Na adsorption), alternatively, the reverse scan (positive scan) may provide more reliable insights into the solvation state, considering that the EDL adsorption/desorption process are highly reversible in coin cells (Figure 1d, 1e).
3. Minor corrections:
a) Page 3, Line 49: Remove “with” for grammatical clarity.
b) Page 3, Line 52: Standardize the citation format for “ref 2”.
c) Page 6, Line 118: Replace “box-like CV” with “butterfly-shaped CV” or “symmetric CV” will be more accurate.
d) Page 9, Line 206: Avoid the term “EDL reaction,” which may be confused with faradic reactions.

In this work, the authors study the sodium storage mechanism in a supercapacitor with an ether-based electrolyte under increased potential window by EQCM and NMR.
The NMR section effectively demonstrates, consistent with previous studies, that Na⁺ ions located inside and outside the pores can be clearly distinguished. The in situ experiments reveal reversible sodium insertion into the pores without the Knight shift typically associated with the formation of Na⁰ clusters or “pore filling” seen in hard carbon. Additionally, broader in-pore signals are observed, indicating stronger interactions between Na⁺ ions and the pores, as well as a decrease in the distance between the Na⁺ ions and the carbon surface. These changes correlate well with the partial desodiation results obtained from EQCM measurements, showing good alignment between the two techniques.
Minor points to consider include correcting the spelling of “shifts” in the caption of Figure S21 and potentially adjusting the colour scheme in Figure S22, as some voltage ranges (0.05–3.0 V and 2.5–3.0 V) are represented by similar colours, which may reduce clarity.
Overall, I am satisfied with this section and have no major concerns.

=== reviewer_5 ===
Electrochemical capacitors are characterised by their high-power density but are limited by their gravimetric capacitance and capacity. Typically, they operate in a narrow potential window before the formation of an SEI. In this manuscript, the authors present a carbon nanosphere-based supercapacitor with a diethylene-glycol-dimethyl-ether (DGDE) electrolyte, which can operate under a large potential difference of -2.95 V between the TOC and discharged state. This leads to a high specific capacitance of 172 F/g and capacity of 508 C/g.
The authors introduce Na+-based DGDE as an electrolyte which forms an SEI layer that allows the migration of solvated Na+ ions into nanospheres, in contrast to the SEI formed by ethylene carbonate that strips the solvation shell during Na ion migration. The authors claim that expanding the potential range can electrochemically drive a partial desolvation, reducing the distance between the carbonaceous surface and the sodium ions, and therefore increasing the capacitance. SEM and TEM combined with CV measurements showed a thick SEI on the carbon particles when using an EC/DMC-based electrolyte, which was accompanied by a significant decrease in the specific surface area. In contrast to this, the same YP50F electrode material showed a box-like CV during an expanding potential range when using the DGDE electrolyte.
EQCM was used to analyse the flow into nanopores. Using EC/DMC-based electrolytes, this resulted in mass changes per electron that the authors assign to a PF6- anion adsorption mechanism in the potential window between 3-4 V, and an adsorption of desolvated Na+ ions in the potential window 3-0.05 V vs. Na/Na+. In addition, the mass change differs significantly between the cycles. In contrast to this, the DGDE electrolyte showed more reversible mass changes and regions of different mass changes per transferred electron. The authors attribute these different mass changes to ion exchange, counter-ion adsorption, and the flux of partially desolvated Na+ Ions into the nanopores. The authors claim to support this idea with in situ NMR measurements and the broadening of the in-pore peak with increasing potential. The capacity and capacitance were further verified in pouch cells using NVP as a counter electrode that does not require an additional pre-sodiation process.
General comments and questions:
1) Is there supporting evidence for the assumptions of the different stages of ion flux at the potential ranges when using DGDE as an electrolyte? As the mass changes only approximately match the masses of the assigned ions, the uncertainty seems to be very high. Could the authors comment on the discrepancies between the observed mass changes and those that they are proposing? The authors state several times that the observed mass changes are “close to” the mass changes they are proposing, but they can differ by over 25%.
2) The correct term in l. 162 should be “ring current effects” instead of “ring effects”
3) Is there evidence for the assumption that the 23Na NMR signal at -10.5 ppm belongs to the electrolyte in the porous electrode? Were spectra recorded at variable temperature to rule out the possibility of it being an exchange peak between the free electrolyte and the in-pore electrolyte?
4) The signal-to-noise ratio of the 23Na NMR signal assigned to the fraction of Na in nanopores is very weak. Mixing of this signal with random noise might lead to high uncertainties in the peak position, and all information about the peak shape is lost. Is there a possibility to conduct measurements with more scans to verify the peak position, and to analyse if the peak shoulder is real or an artefact from random noise?
5) The description of Supp. Figure 21 includes the phrase “reversible shits” instead of “reversible shifts”
6) The fits of the NMR spectra in Supp. Fig. 23 do not always match the experimental spectra. Especially the ones recorded at higher potentials might be fitted better with broader in-pore peaks, which would contradict the author’s hypothesis.
7) Were any ex situ experiments done under MAS conditions? This would improve the resolution and allow for more definitive peak assignment.
8) Could the authors comment on the use of 23Na for the in situ experiments? Better resolution would be afforded by 19F NMR. 19F NMR would also provide insight into whether the mechanism proposed in Figure S.18 is valid.
9) Please check Figure S.13. The captions for part c) and f) are the same and the schematics show that the SEIs formed in both solvents sieve the solvents, which contradicts what the authors say.
10) Could the authors comment on the supposed broadening of the “in-pore” during discharge? What is the source of the broadening? Why does the peak width remain constant from 0.25 V?
11) All other characterization techniques were performed on cells using DGDE and on cells using EC:DMC, except for NMR. Have the authors performed in situ NMR experiments on cells using EC:DMC electrolyte? If not, these measurements should be done to confirm the interpretation of the 23Na NMR spectra of the DGDE system.
In conclusion, the manuscript presents an interesting finding of an electrolyte that forms a supercapacitor-compatible SEI and therefore works well at low potentials. Nevertheless, the supporting evidence for the assumptions about the mechanisms is not very strong. If the authors could provide more supporting information in the form of the additional experiments listed above, then it will be suitable for publication in Nature Communications.

The article describes high-harmonic generation in nonlinear crystals in terms of quantum walks. Specifically, it analyzes the
spin and orbital angular momentum (SAM and OAM) spectrum of each harmonic and shows that, as the harmonic order
increases, the corresponding state in the SAM–OAM space exhibits features characteristic of quantum walks when the step
number is identified with the harmonic order. Experimental results are presented for output states containing up to four
harmonic orders.
The system is introduced as a platform for realizing quantum walks in a non-cascaded configuration, since all step numbers
are implemented within a single crystal rather than through a sequence of separate devices.
The general idea is interesting; however, in my opinion it does not meet the impact criteria required for publication in Nature
Communications. To justify publication, the authors should provide stronger evidence that their approach constitutes a
genuine alternative to standard cascaded platforms for optical information processing. Currently, this does not appear to be
the case: the system does not seem scalable, it cannot be applied to single-photon states, and it lacks programmability. I will
elaborate on these points in the detailed remarks below.
Major remarks
- In a quantum walk, the state at step j is obtained from the state at step j–1 through the action of a single-step unitary
operator. In the present work, I see how the state at a given harmonic order is linked to the input state via n-photon
absorption and selection rules. However, is this truly equivalent to a quantum walk? Is there a well-defined analogue of the
single-step operator here, linking two states at consecutive time-steps?
- How programmable is this platform? In standard quantum-walk implementations, tuning the optical parameters of
successive layers allows one to realize arbitrary walks. How could different types of quantum walks be accessed in the
present scheme?
- What is represented on the horizontal axis of Figs. 3(C–E)? If s denotes the SAM index, it should only take two values. My
understanding is that the walk occurs on a one-dimensional lattice spanned by the OAM modes.
- How scalable is this approach? What is the main factor limiting the harmonic order? How could higher orders be
accessed?
- The spectra shown in Fig. 4 are only theoretical. An experimental measurement of these spectra would considerably
strengthen the work, especially if the analysis is extended to different input states.
- Why are both a quarter-wave plate and a q-plate required to prepare an input state different from a single Gaussian beam
with l=0?
- What is the role of the crystal symmetries? Would different symmetries lead to different walks?
For the reasons outlined above, I cannot recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications. In my view,
its main contribution lies in the interpretation of the high-harmonic generation spectrum within the framework of a quantum
walk. After appropriate revisions, the work could be better published in a more specialized technical journal.

=== reviewer_1 ===
The authors Zhang et al. study error correction circuits (repetition codes and surface code) on two superconducting quantum processors, insert Pauli errors at various rates, decode the logical observables, and apply noise mitigation techniques to improve estimates of logical observables.
Combining error decoding of logically encoded qubits with error mitigation techniques has a good chance to build a bridge between noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) circuits and fully error-corrected circuits.
The work therefore addresses a timely topic.
The experiments seem to have been carried out on state-of-the-art superconducting quantum processing units featuring high-fidelity gates and readout.
The paper is well written and likely resonate with a broader readership.
Generally, I therefore recommend publication in Nat. Comm. assuming that the authors seriously address the following comments and concerns in their revised manuscript:
1) The first experimental demonstration studies a circuit which prepares three copies of the same state |theta> = R(theta)|0>, maps pairwise parity onto two ancillas, applies artificial errors, and maps parity again to detect possible errors. While it is instructive to explain the concept on a simple example, I find the particular choice more confusing then helpful, because the essence is hidden in an unnecessary complication.
Since all instances are rejected in which an error E_2 gets detected, the entire circuit does nothing but checking if a bit flip has occurred on Q0 or not. This could be detected in a much more straightforward way by using only a second qubit Q1, perform the two CNOT gates and measure mu1. All actions involving qubits Q2, Q3, Q4 are therefore completely irrelevant. As such the example and its discussion could be greatly simplified making the main point clearer.
2) In all the numerical simulation in which observables are simulated vs. noise parameter r (e.g. dashed lines in Fig. 3e), the curves seems to exhibit a slight oscillatory behavior – at least less smooth than one may naively expect when varying a noise parameter continuously. Can the authors clarify?
3) The third paragraph on pg. 5starts provides a general discussion and resource and performance estimates when scaling to larger systems. Why is this not part of the general discussion but placed between the repetition code and surface code results?
4) In Fig. 3d the scatter plots appear for the first time and the authors state that extrapolation is done “for all possible choices of r1, … , rK”. This needs to be explained in the main text more clearly what this exactly means.
5) The discussion about the surface code results falls short. Streamlining the first example as pointed out above in 1) will free up space for extending the discussion on the surface code.

=== reviewer_2 ===
Summary
The manuscript reports an experimental study that integrates quantum error correction (QEC) with a practically used error mitigation strategy, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), on superconducting processors. The authors implement ZNE at the physical qubit level by deliberately amplifying noise and then extrapolating expectation values to the zero-noise limit using polynomial fitting. They test this approach on repetition and surface codes up to distance seven, showing improved extraction of expectation values and demonstrating that ZNE remains effective in both multi-round error-correction circuits and surface-code experiments. The authors argue that this hybrid strategy can enhance the performance of early fault-tolerant quantum computers and could be extended to more complex logical operations.
Review
The manuscript is technically strong and makes a novel contribution, as error mitigation has so far been demonstrated mainly on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) circuits rather than on logical qubits. The hardware performance (coherence times, CZ fidelities, readout fidelities) is state-of-the-art, enabling meaningful improvements from logical encoding and feedback-based error correction. The results clearly show reduced logical error bias compared to both unmitigated and purely error-corrected cases. Experimental data are consistent with numerical simulations, supporting the validity of the noise modeling.
The paper is generally well written, though somewhat dense in places. Clarifying certain definitions and presenting figures with mild modifications would significantly improve accessibility and reader comprehension.
1. Page 2, left column: It was unclear what the authors meant by ‘K non-constant terms’.
2. Fig.1: I appreciate this thoughtful presentation trying to convey the main message of the paper. However, it took me quite some time to understand that the blue coin represented a noise-free qubit. It would be helpful to mention that explicitly in the caption.
3. Fig.2a: The figure is slightly misleading as the measurements were performed simultaneously and the conditional X gate was applied in software. I would suggest to aligning all the measurement symbols vertically and modify it to reflect the NOT operation being applied afterwards.
4. Fig.2 caption: It was unclear why r=1 and 3 only were used. Please elaborate.
5. Page 3, left column: While the author mentioned about known schemes for increasing ‘r’, they didn’t mention which scheme was actually used in their experiments.
6. Page 3, left column: It would be nice to mention the mapping of the measurement outcome to the qubit state, i.e. \mu = -1 indicates the qubit is in the excited state.
7. Fig.3b: Are the syndrome qubits reset to |0> after each measurement? If yes, the figure should be modified accordingly.
8. Fig.3c: It would be nice to mention M=1 in the figure.
9. Page 5, left column: The sentence ‘.. can reduce the logical error by a factor of about 0.025..’ reads a bit strange. While I understand the intention of the authors, it may be better to use the reciprocal of 0.025.
Recommendation:
The manuscript introduces a novel concept supported by clear experimental demonstrations with potential near-term relevance for quantum computing hardware. I recommend acceptance after the authors address the points raised above.

=== reviewer_3 ===
This manuscript demonstrates a series of experiments whereby the zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) technique is applied to error-corrected qubits on superconducting quantum processors. To bypass the challenges that arise when applying ZNE to logical errors, the authors apply the technique to physical errors in the logical system; they derive the fitting function analytically, design the experimental protocol, and present thorough analyses. They show reductions of logical errors using the repetition code and surface code across multiple code distances and numbers of parity check repetitions, and specify the sampling overhead for each case. Experimental details, including the protocol and implementation tricks, were discussed in the supplementary material, which would be useful for others to perform similar experiments.
The paper is well-written, with good motivations in the introduction, detailed justifications of their experiments, and an in-depth analysis of the resources and performance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental demonstration of a quantum error mitigation (QEM) technique being applied to an error-corrected system, successfully reducing logical errors. The results of this work may inspire similar approaches in the future, including those that aim for early demonstrations of practical quantum computation -- this work may provide useful guidelines. Therefore, we would like to recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications, given that the following comments are appropriately addressed:
1. The authors mention in the Discussion that this is the first time that a QEM technique has been applied to an error-corrected system. If this is the case, we suggest stating this in the introduction, and highlighting that the cited IBM ZNE experiment was performed on a few hundred uncorrected qubits.
2. In the introduction, we recommend explicitly comparing your technique to Wahl et al., who considered ZNE on logical qubits via distance-scaling. Would this prior work be more efficient in terms of the sampling overhead?
3. FIG. 1 can be made clearer by explaining in the caption the difference between the paired lines and shadows, as well as by using the same colour for the pair.
4. In the Results section, to improve clarity, we recommend including an overview of the experiments that were run in between the device descriptions and the experiments (or elsewhere), listing the 1) parity check experiment with and without error correction, 2) repetition code experiment, and 3) surface code experiment. Optionally, structuring into titled subsections would allow the readers to more easily navigate through the paper.
5. Since you inject noise using random Pauli gates, you could also apply probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) instead. Could you comment on the choice of using ZNE? More generally, how much of this work is applicable to other QEM techniques?
6. In the supplementary material S5, you mention that error bars are too small to visualize in the main text. This should be stated in the corresponding figure captions in the main text, or else readers would not be sure how reliable the data are.
7. How did authors choose the unit error probabilities? Are they the minimum achievable error rates on the devices?
8. Please explain what the term “operational stage” means, and mention at this point that the experiments in the main text do not consider errors in stabiliser measurements, but the supplementary materials do.
9. In FIG. 2, could authors comment on why the extrapolation is performed using only two data points, even though many other data points were taken?
10. Authors state that “our protocol can reduce the logical error by a factor of about 0.025”, but “reduced by a factor of” means dividing by the number. We think the correct phrasing should be along the lines of “reduced by a factor of 40”.
11. In FIG. 3, it is not immediately clear that subfigures c and e correspond to the unmitigated case. Moreover, could you explain why the x axes of subfigures c and e have different scales? Is it because subfigure e deals with a “fixed total error rate in all rounds”? It is a bit difficult to compare subfigures in FIG. 3.
12. “In surface codes, quantum computing are driven by the parity-check measurements” should replace “are” with “is”.
13. In the caption of FIG. 2b, could authors mention that this is experimental data? Moreover, in the caption of FIG. 4b, it can be made clearer which results are error-corrected and which are not.
14. Regarding FIG. 3, it is noted that “the performance of ZNE can be further improved by accounting for parity-check measurement errors in the noise amplification”. This is noted towards the end of the following paragraph, but we think it is already worth mentioning here that you observe that the improvement does not diminish with the increase of code distance, as opposed to what FIG. 3d suggests.

In this manuscript, Bok et al. present a microfluidic-based in vitro model of the human spinal cord, termed the microfluidic spinal cord-like structure (μSCLS), to investigate dorsoventral (DV) patterning driven by opposing gradients of morphogens. Building on their previously established human neural tube-like structure platform, the authors apply an antiparallel gradient of BMP4 (dorsalizing) and SAG (ventralizing) to induce DV patterning in μSCLS. Notably, they report the emergence and ventral migration of neural crest cells (NCCs) from the dorsal region in response to a chemoattractant cue, mimicking in vivo behavior. Furthermore, they perform single-cell transcriptomic analysis to demonstrate the presence of all 13 neuroepithelial (NE) subtypes along the DV axis of spinal cord, suggesting that the μSCLS model recapitulates key aspects of human embryonic spinal cord development. An additional and intriguing finding is the dorsalizing effect of retinoic acid (RA) in their system with the potential crosstalk with BMP signaling pathway, which appears to contradict prior in vitro findings but aligns with certain in vivo studies, as discussed in the manuscript. Overall, this study provides a valuable contribution to the field of spinal cord organoid models, with a clear focus on DV patterning. However, to enhance the novelty, rigor, and impact of the study, several critical points should be addressed:

Major Comment:
A central claim of the manuscript is that the μSCLS faithfully recapitulates the full DV axis of the human spinal cord, including all 13 NE subtypes. While this is supported by single-cell transcriptomic data, spatial validation of these subtypes remains limited. Although the immunofluorescence results demonstrate spatial patterning, only a subset of markers is presented, and not all 13 NE subtypes along the DV axis are spatially confirmed. As a result, the manuscript’s core claim remains insufficiently substantiated at the spatial level.
Given that the μSCLS model exhibits a broader DV width compared to the previously reported human neural tube-like system, it provides a valuable opportunity to demonstrate more refined and extended DV patterning. Capitalizing on this advantage through enhanced spatial validation would further highlight the strength and novelty of the model.
To underscore the distinctiveness and impact of the current system, it would be essential to include spatial resolution of cell types across the DV axis using spatial mapping methods/techniques such as spatial transcriptomics, multiplexed or iterative immunofluorescence. The key hallmark of DV patterning in the spinal cord is the precise spatial organization of progenitor domains in response to opposing morphogen gradients. A more detailed spatial analysis would substantially strengthen the manuscript and clearly differentiate it from prior work.

Minor Comments:
1. In Figure 1h, the authors present regional immunofluorescence images (boxes I–III) showing SOX10, LMX1A, and FOXA2 expression. To aid interpretation and provide context, it would be beneficial to include an overview image of the entire tissue adjacent to these panels, similar to the layout used in Figure 1g. This would help readers appreciate the spatial relationships between regions and better assess the DV organization of the markers shown.
2. On page 9, the authors note the presence of mesodermal cells, attributed to early WNT activation during neural induction and transient induction of a neuromesodermal progenitor (NMP) state. It would be informative to clarify the spatial distribution of these mesodermal populations although they are very small number of cells within the μSCLS. Specifically, do they localize preferentially to the dorsal or ventral regions, or are they interspersed throughout the tissue?
3. The manuscript hints that the observed NCCs are of trunk identity but does not directly state the regional identity of the NCCs in AP axis. It would be helpful to specify the regional/axial identity of the NCCs; for example, if they express HOX genes consistent with a trunk-level identity. Inclusion of this information, either through transcriptomic data or immunostaining, would provide a clearer understanding of the axial identity of the NCCs and further validate the model’s relevance to trunk-level spinal cord development.

This study establishes a human neural tube–like model using a microfluidic system to investigate dorsal-ventral (D–V) patterning under retinoic acid (RA) regulation and to examine neural crest cell (NCC) migration. While the work is technically sound and the system well executed, the manuscript would benefit from clarification on its novelty and deeper mechanistic insights to clearly distinguish it from the authors’ prior publications. The findings on RA–BMP crosstalk and NCC migration are intriguing but need further elaboration. Below are major and specific points for improvement.

Major Concerns：
The methodology and some key findings (D–V patterning) closely resemble the authors’ previous publications. The manuscript should explicitly highlight: What new biological insights are provided here (mechanistic understanding of RA–BMP interactions, detailed NCC migration dynamics). Whether the microfluidic system itself is novel, or if this work represents new applications.
The authors identify BMP downstream genes with RA binding sites, but it remains unclear:Which of these genes are functionally relevant for D–V patterning?Are these genes direct targets of both RA and BMP, or is their regulation indirect?
For the Neural Crest Cell Migration:Do NCCs migrate along the μSCL microfluidic scaffolds, or do they delaminate fully into the Matrigel/gelatin?Are there any fate changes in NCCs during or after migration?

Specific Concerns to Address:
1.The abstract mentions “human-specific features,” but these are not clearly defined or highlighted in the results.
2.More markers for the 11 neural progenitor subtypes should be included via staining to strengthen cell identity claims.
3.Dextran diffusion is used to mimic morphogen gradients, but it may not fully replicate endogenous conditions—this limitation should be discussed.
4.RA is known to regulate anterior–posterior (A–P) identity. How do the authors exclude A–P patterning effects in their D–V model?
5.The “dorsal intermediate” region is defined solely by Pax3/Pax6 overlap. Additional markers would help refine and validate this domain.
6.NMPs are typically caudal/posterior, yet the model claims thoracic identity. Did the authors observe any T/SOX2 double-positive cells in the model?
7.The absence of V3 interneurons might reflect either low abundance or a true lack of specification. A specific V3 marker should be used to determine whether these progenitors are simply rare or genuinely missing.
8.The manuscript does not address whether NCCs undergo fate transitions during migration. Clarifying this would strengthen the interpretation of NCC behavior.

Bok et al. presents a microfluidics-based, human PSC-derived model recapitulating Dorsal-Ventral (DV) patterning of the spinal cord and neural crest cells (NCCs) migration. They then used the platform to study the role of Retinoic Acid (RA) in DV patterning and found a synergistic crosstalk between RA and BMP signaling. They further analyzed cellular dynamics of NCCs and demonstrated a role of CXCL12 in regulating migration.
In my view, this system represents the epitome of recent efforts in harnessing the power of stem cells to illuminate development. Not only can this system recapitulate essential features of DV patterning and NCC migration, but also it allows deep mechanistic investigations (live imaging, controllable parameters, etc.). Although many in vitro systems capturing spinal cord development have been published, including a recent one (Luo et al. 2025 Cell Stem Cell) that also focused on DV patterning, the system here offers controllable and quantitative powers that could be very useful for future mechanistic studies. I have a few comments regarding rigor:
1. Although the authors showed a phenotypic interaction between RA and BMP and demonstrated that RA treatment increases SMAD1/5 phosphorylation, the proposed molecular mechanism regarding RAR binding to regulatory elements of BMP pathway-associated genes is highly speculative. I suggest the authors tone down the language used in the abstract “… clarifies the dual role of RA…”.
2. Does the RA-BMP crosstalk need input from Shh signaling at all? The authors showed that RA produced a dorsalizing effect under BMP-SAG opposing gradients but had no effect on patterning when BMP gradient was withdrawn. Would RA still dorsalize patterning if SAG gradient is removed? This experiment could further probe RA’s effects on DV patterning.
3. Could the authors speculate why their system acquires a thoracic identity? Only HOXC9 and HOXC10 were investigated, could the single cell data further support the thoracic identity?
4. In the SOX10 lineage tracing experiment, the ZsGreen signals emerged after delamination. Could this delay be an artifact of the lineage tracing system? For example, following SOX10 expression, it takes time to express Cre and then fluorescence expression. So the ZsGreen signal might not reflect the onset of SOX10 expression.

The study addresses a critical gap in developmental biology: the lack of human-relevant, controllable models for spinal cord patterning and NCC lineage bifurcation. The novelty lies in the integration of microfluidic gradient control with hPSC-derived neural tissues to achieve full DV patterning (11 progenitor domains plus RP and FP). The identification of a GDF3-mediated crosstalk between RA and BMP signaling is a significant mechanistic contribution that clarifies long-standing ambiguities regarding the role of RA in SC development. The experimental design is robust. The manuscript is clearly written and the figures are well-annotated. The reporting of the microfluidic setup and the lineage-tracing strategy is sufficiently detailed to allow for replication. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more detailed discussion of the "human-specific transcriptional signatures" mentioned in the abstract; while the model is claimed to be human-relevant, a direct comparison (e.g., via differential expression analysis) between the µSCLS transcriptome and existing human fetal SC datasets would strengthen this claim.

Overall Evaluation
This manuscript introduces the novel concept of "dielectrocapillarity," demonstrating how electric field gradients (EFGs) can
regulate phase behavior, capillary condensation, and adsorption of confined fluids. By integrating classical density
functional theory (cDFT) with deep learning, the authors develop a multiscale framework that offers new strategies for
applications in nanoporous energy storage, gas separation, and neuromorphic devices. The study addresses a critical gap
in understanding electrostrictive effects in fluids, with innovative methodology and clear logical progression. While the
theoretical framework and simulations provide robust support for key conclusions, the work could be strengthened by deeper
experimental validation, comparative analysis with competing techniques, and expanded discussion of its limitations. The
research holds significant promise for both fundamental science and applied technology, though further refinements are
recommended to enhance its broader impact.
Detailed Comments
Limited Experimental Validation: The study relies predominantly on theoretical simulations and model derivations without
direct experimental data (e.g., observations of dielectrocapillary effects in actual nanofluidic devices). The authors should
supplement the manuscript with comparisons to existing experimental techniques (e.g., atomic force microscopy,
dielectrophoresis experiments) or provide proof-of-concept experimental results to reinforce the credibility of the findings.
Incomplete Comparison with Traditional Electric Field Methods: While the manuscript distinguishes between uniform electric
fields and EFGs, it lacks a systematic comparison of dielectrocapillarity with conventional techniques like electrowetting or
dielectrophoresis in terms of control precision, energy consumption, and applicability. A clear articulation of the method’s
unique advantages and limitations is necessary.
Generalizability to Multicomponent Fluids: The current focus on single-component polar fluids limits relevance to real-world
