The paper by J. Yao et. al. describes a series of nonlinear focusing measurements involving the illumination of nonlocal metalenses with femtosecond laser pulses. The nonlocal resonance in the metalens leads to an amplification of 2nd and 3rd harmonic generation as well as a reduction on illumination power required to induce thermo-optic nonlinear limiting. Moreover, the authors reveal that weak structural symmetry breaking caused by the elevated index of the substrate produces directional nearfield build up within the nonlocal resonance, causing the efficiencies of the various nonlinear focusing phenomena to vary dramatically depending on which side is illuminated. The underlying platform has been introduced by the authors before; all be it without directional nonlinearity. That said, the use of nonlocal metasurfaces to directionally boost wavefront shaped nonlinear optical effects is timely. While the resonant enhancement is modest and many of the mechanisms discussed, including geometric phase based nonlocal meta focusing and asymmetry from magneto-electric coupling, are not new, I do not believe asymmetric nonlinear focusing has been boosted by a nonlocal resonance before. Further improvements to the platform to bring the nonlinear efficiency gains over other platforms from small to large, would be exciting to see. I do, therefore, recommend the manuscript for publication after minor corrections have been made.
Detailed comments are provided below.
1. On line 70, the statement “Moreover, asymmetric wavefront shaping based on optical nonlinearity remains unexplored” is not true. Explorations may be few and may have limitations, but they do exist. The authors should refine this statement.
2. On lines 72-73, “These challenges highlight opportunities for new design strategies to effectively balance these trade-offs.” is a very clumsy sentence. It is not clear which challenges and trade-offs will be addressed.

5. The final section is labeled “Nonreciprocal wavefront shaping in the linear regime”, but the measurements performed do not compare reciprocal illumination. The reciprocal of plane wave illumination from one side is collimation from the other side.

This manuscript demonstrates asymmetric nonlinear wavefront shaping using silicon metasurfaces that combine local Mie-type and nonlocal quasi-bound state in the continuum (q-BIC) resonances. They further show nonreciprocal focusing, forming a custom power diode, which is particularly enticing. The key is a vertical asymmetry of the near field when pumping from the substrate or superstrate, an effect enhanced by the high Q-factor of the q-BIC resonance (similar to Ref 31, but here with local phase control).
The work presents interesting physics and novel design principles, extending the authors’ previous results on similarly-looking devices from linear to nonlinear experiments. It is well explained, and the results are compelling. We find it likely to make a significant impact in the field, and find it appropriate for the journal. However, several issues must be addressed before accepting it to the journal.

Could the authors perhaps comment on the metasurface's long-term stability and optical damage threshold under these high-power conditions? Furthermore, it would be insightful to hear their perspective on how the device might perform in lower-power regimes, which are more common in practical applications. === reviewer_3 ===
Yao et al. present in their manuscript an asymmetric wave propagation while simultaneously controlling the spatial wavefront at the example of a meta-lens. Such asymmetry in propagation was already demonstrated earlier by metasurfaces for frequency conversion. Here, the only novelty seems to be the additional spatial wavefront control for second- and third-harmonic generation. Overall, the manuscript is well written and the explanation of the underlying concepts is convincingly discussed. However, I feel the topic is more suitable for a specialized optics journal like Light:Science&Applications rather than Nature Communications. One reason for that is the poor performance (contrast) of asymmetry for the fundamental wavelength.
For a revised version of the manuscript, I would recommend to address a few points:
• The title seems somehow misleading to me. I am not sure if “asymmetric” is the best word to choose here because it can give the idea the wavefronts are laterally asymmetrically shaped which is a standard process. Although the authors explain their definition of asymmetry in the text later, I personally feel there are better ways of expressing the propagation properties of the light for the two directions.
• What do the authors mean with magneto-electric coupling within the IRUs? An explanation would be helpful.
• If the authors use the passive nonlinearity of the system, then why is there a saturation effect observable at these relative low powers? For polarization induced nonlinear processes these effects are normally not be able to observe so easily. Did the authors check that the resonance is not shifting spectrally with the higher powers due to Kerr or thermal effects? Such an effect has nothing to do with saturation. I feel the authors need to be here more precise in their wording.
• I also do not agree with the term “nonreciprocal focusing in the linear regime.” In the linear optical regime (without losses or gain) the system is always reciprocal. Linear optical regime also means that there are no dependencies of the properties on the light intensity. I understand that the authors are unexperienced in the field of nonlinear optics but what they mean is that they observe a nonlinear effect at the fundamental wavelength. That has nothing do to with linear optics. I recommend to rephrase these statements.
• How are the phase values in Fig. 2d calculated? For a single unit or a period pattern where all elements are oriented in the same way? What is the error in phase if the elements like in the metalens are all differently oriented?
• The assumed nonlinear third-order permittivity of silicon to model the refractive index change seems extremely high. Typical values in the NIR range are 10E-18 to 10E-19 m2/V2. This is three to four orders of magnitude smaller than the value the authors used in their simulations.

=== reviewer_1 ===
This research group recently published a lot of important findings about tree bud dormancy using genetic approaches. Especially, they reported that ABA has central role for bud dormancy establishment and proposed the dense TEM signal in plasmodesmata (they called plasmodesmata sphincter, Tylewicz et al., 2018, Science) is found only in normal WT but not in abi1-1 mutant, suggesting it is critical morphological marker of dormancy establishment. They also reported that low-temperature-induced dormancy release (later stage) is mediated by LIM1, FT1 and GA pathways (Pandey et al., 2024, EMBO J.). These published studies are consistent with important pioneer findings published by van der Schoot group [Rinne et al. (2001), Rinne et al. (2011)], which have facilitated recent bud dormancy study. This study demonstrated that warm spikes during dormancy release period suppress bud break through the thermal responsiveness of plasmodesmata. Moreover, GA pathways are also involved in this response. Quantification of callose levels in plasmodesmata using callose-specific antibody and genetic approach using transgenic plants provided solid evidence to support some parts of their thoughts. My first concern is the appropriateness of the use of the word “robust bud dormancy release” in the title. As previously reported, dormancy sphincter removal should be the right word of “dormancy release”, to my understanding. Therefore, the process from plasmodesmata closure to opening may represent “later stage of dormancy release” or “the stage towards bud break”. The topic in this study is not about dormancy sphincter removal but PD opening, which corresponds to “late dormancy release towards bud break”. Therefore, I suggest the use of “bud break” rather than “dormancy release” for the title. Fig5 (a) model does not represent “dormancy release” but “bud break transition”. My second concern is the link between bet hedging (heterogeneity in bud break) and plasmodesmata. Although the authors proposed there is close link between them in the abstract and Fig. 4, the authors did not investigate callose level in buds under variable cold (2h-W). They also did not investigate callose level in abi1-1 mutant at all. Under this circumstance, the relationship between plasmodesmata and bud break heterogeneity or bet-hedging has not been well-validated in this study. Fig4 title is not appropriate. ABA controls PD sphincter (Tylewicz et al., 2018) but ABA also important for callose level in PD? Is this validated? There are other comments 1. While FT1 and GA20OX show similar expression patterns under the 11WSD, Cold, and Variable Cold treatments, this observation alone may not be sufficient to clarify how FT1 regulates PD opening independently of the LIM1 and SVP pathways. Additional mechanistic evidence would help substantiate the proposed model. 2. In Fig. 3. Including ft1 knockout comparisons under both Cold and Variable Cold conditions would substantially strengthen the conclusions. This would clarify whether FT1 is essential for temperature-induced dormancy release and whether its reduced expression under Variable Cold is a primary cause of dormancy failure. Without this analysis, the proposed role of FT1 remains speculative. 3. The authors present an interesting and valuable set of phenotypic data for abi1-1, (ft1, should be included) and the abi1/ft1 double mutant under various environmental treatments. However, the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. To better understand the genetic interactions and clarify whether ABI1 and FT1 act in the same or parallel pathways, it would be helpful to analyze the expression levels of key genes such as SVL, LIM1, FT1, and GA20ox in these mutant backgrounds. Specifically, comparing gene expressions across 11WSD, constant cold, and variable cold conditions could provide more direct evidence of the regulatory roles and relationships among these genes. This would significantly strengthen the mechanistic interpretation of the observed phenotypes under variable cold. Fig. 1b, Fig. S7- Could the authors clarify why the WT plant in Fig. 1b (11WSD) appears to retain its leaves, while the WT plant shown in Fig. S7 (10WSD) seems to have entered dormancy and shed its leaves? This apparent inconsistency raises some confusion—was there a mistake in photo selection or labeling? Or is there another explanation?

=== reviewer_2 ===
Pandey et al. address how poplar buds are released from dormancy by environmental signals, thus adding to an existing body of work on this highly important physiological response of plants and the end of the winter season. The authors describe and investigate a previously insufficiently characterised mechanism, whereby poplar plants suppress bud break in response to fluctuating outside temperature. Understanding plant responses to such "real life" scenarios and variable environments is highly relevant, not only for our fundamental understanding of plant development, but also to explore and possibly predict plant responses to changing current and future climate scenarios. The authors investigate the expression and functional role of key regulators of bud break in poplar, including transcription factors, hormones, and mobile factors that are known as floral inducers, such as FT1. The manuscript reports on a key role for FT1 in triggering dormancy release, mediated by opening of plasmodesmata by reducing callose levels, and how short warm periods that interrupt cold phases can basically erase the effect of extended cold, resulting in suppression of bud break. The authors propose that FT1 is a key factor in this response, and that the underlying mechanism supports bet hedging, i.e. a differential response of buds to the same environmental input in order to increase reproductive success. The experiments are well presented and described. I very much enjoyed the high quality of the analysis of callose deposition at PDs, based on antibody detection using fluorescence labelling for entire meristems, and detailed surveys via electron microscopy with gold labelled antibodies! Overall, a well written manuscript which addresses dormancy and the role of plasmodesmata in bud break from a new angle, which was a pleasure to read. Nevertheless, there are a few points that the authors should consider and address to further strengthen the manuscript, which I have detailed below. 1) A key point the authors make in the manuscript is that FT1 expression is sufficient and can subsitute for cold in inducing PD opening and dormancy release. This statement is based, among other experiments, on an inducible FT1 transgenic line, which can overcome environmental regulation and induce bud break and PD opening (judged by reduction in callose). However, the authors have analysed changes in callose accumulation at PDs several weeks after FT1 induction, so FT1 might be a rather indirect regulator of PD callose. This problem (correlation, causality) could be resolved by assaying PD callose levels shortly after FT1 induction, and before bud break. In that context, I would like to quote a sentence from the manuscript, which highlights this more: "Altogether, these results indicate that warm spikes act via FT1 to suppress downregulation of callose which then prevents dormancy release". It would be equally possible to argue that warm spikes act via FT1 (and possible LIM1) to prevent dormancy release, which would normally result on PD opening and callose reduction. 2) To determine whether defects in callose deposition/degradation could affect bud dormancy break the authors used the abi1 mutant, which was previously reported to break dormancy even in cold condition, because plasmodesmata are always open in this mutant background. They showed here that the mutant displayed dormancy break also in the variable cold condition, i.e. with warm spikes interrupting the cold period.; also, they are insensitive to the warm spikes, that inhibit dormancy break in wt condition. Determining the level of callose at PDs in the three conditions (11WSD, constant cold and variable cold) in the abi1 background is important to evaluate whether a decrease in callose accumulation at the plasmodesmata is necessary and sufficient to trigger break dormancy. 3) One feature to assess bud dormancy is the presence of lipid droplets. As a matter of fact, the authors nicely observed lipid droplets in the 11WSD treatment. The information whether also buds from variable cold condition showed lipid droplets is missing (lipid droplets of what??) 4) A reported pathway to trigger dormancy release relies upon the simultaneous downregulation and upregulation of SVL and LIM1, respectively. The authors therefore assayed expression of SVL and LIM1 in entire buds by qRT-PCR in the three different conditions. They point out that under both continuous cold and warm spiked conditions, SVL is still repressed, and LIM1 is still induced. FigS4 shows, in my opinion, a strong difference in the response of LIM1 under the two key conditions. Is that statistically different? Do all cells in a bud behave in the same manner, i.e., could there be regional differences in expression levels? A possible interpretation of the data, which differs from the authors point of view, could be that LIM1 is not sufficiently induced in the warm-spiked situation, and therefore dormancy is not broken. 5) FT1 has been previously reported to be a cold induced promoter of dormancy release. *   **Quantification of PD:** The manuscript mentions PD regulation but lacks high-resolution imaging data (e.g., TEM or aniline blue staining quantification) in the main figures to support the claim that callose levels are the primary driver of the observed phenotypes.

*   **"Warm Spike" Definition:** The authors define warm spikes as 4h at 20°C in some experiments and 2h in others. The rationale for these specific durations is not sufficiently justified. *   **FT1 and GA Pathway:** The authors claim *FT1* regulates *GA20-oxidase*. The manuscript presents a high-impact mechanism for temperature sensing in trees. The authors define new quantum supercritical regime, where -- as they show – small variations of the symmetry-breaking field induce large variations in temperature. The authors experimentally demonstrate a microwave source capable of generating GHz microwave pulses with a peak power of 1 MW, at a 100 Hz repetition rate. Their system is tunable (across 1 GHz) and displays time jitter below 20 ps. The modus operandi, in a nut shell, is that a high-peak-power, modulated, tunable and pulsed laser illuminates a semiconductor wide bandgap material and generates a microwave via a photoconductive mechanism. They also propose a model that provides a relatively satisfying agreement with experiments.
Many applications in microwave engineering are in need of such powerful sources. From that perspective, this work certainly has merit. However, I think that the paper is not very clear, and I fail to see the broad impact needed to be published in a journal like Nature Communications.
Additionally, I would like the authors to consider the points below:
- I can see and appreciate the efforts from the authors to provide as much information as needed, but as a result, the paper ends up being extremely dense and quite poorly written. An obvious illustration of this shortcoming is the very first sentence of Section 2, which is “The relationship among the material resistance ( RSiC ), substrate thickness ( d ), electrode area ( S0 ), and photo-generated carrier concentration ( n t( )) is expressed in Equation (1), while the relationship between the output voltage (Uout ) and the bias voltage (Ubias ) is described in Equation (2).” How is the reader even expected to understand what these parameters are about, just immediately after reading the general introduction?
- Along the same line, the paper lacks a clear figure for the full microwave generator (NdYAG laser system at input, GHz microwave at output). One has to go through a large number of auxiliary figures and text to self-build a coherent, synthetic idea of the architecture of the proposed generator. The reader is referred to Fig S10 (the 10th figure of the supplementary material) for a general architecture, and even that figure looks quite incomplete to me.
- As a minor point, the authors present their system as a “An optoelectronic microwave source with high power and frequency tunability”. This can be misleading as from this title alone, one can think that their system outputs a continuous wave signal. The title should reflect the fact that the source is pulsed.
- Authors claim that their systems output pure microwaves but offer no proof of such purity (purity is different from the stability of the pulse train). From the time traces, I would guess that the microwaves are not very pure.
- The authors indicate that the time jitter for the pulses is less than 20 ps. The authors have to indicate clearly the bandwidth over which this time jitter is integrated.

**Summary of the Work:**
The manuscript presents an optoelectronic microwave source (OEMS) utilizing 4H-SiC photoconductive semiconductor devices (PCSDs) to achieve megawatt-level peak power with frequency tunability across the P–L band. The authors demonstrate a vertical device architecture with transparent electrodes and a single-reflection optical coupling scheme, achieving 55 MW power-handling capacity and 1.36 MW peak output power at 1 GHz. The study further explores array synthesis, reporting high spatial synthesis efficiency (98.6%) and low timing jitter (11 ps).

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The work addresses a critical bottleneck in high-power microwave (HPM) technology: the trade-off between frequency agility and peak power. The use of 4H-SiC in a vertical photoconductive configuration is well-motivated, and the reported performance metrics (1 MW peak power, P–L band tunability) represent a significant advancement over traditional solid-state power amplifiers (SSPAs) and vacuum electronic devices (VEDs) for specific integrated applications. The novelty lies in the successful integration of high-voltage SiC PCSDs into a coherent array, which is a non-trivial engineering achievement.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The experimental design is generally robust. The use of a vertical electrode configuration to mitigate surface flashover is appropriate for the power levels described. However, there are concerns regarding the characterization of the "tunability." The manuscript claims "continuously tunable pulsed microwave emission," yet the results focus heavily on 1 GHz operation. The methodology for achieving continuous tuning across the 0.25–1.3 GHz range is not sufficiently detailed in the main text. Is the tuning achieved via pulse shaping, load modulation, or external filtering? This must be clarified.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility of the Results:**
The results are internally consistent and supported by the provided supplementary data. The array synthesis efficiency of 98.6% is impressive, though the sample size for these measurements (50 pulses) is relatively small for a high-power system where stochastic breakdown events are common. The authors should comment on the long-term reliability and the impact of cumulative pulse degradation on the SiC substrate, as photoconductive switches are prone to filamentation and surface damage over time.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
The manuscript is well-written, but the reliance on "Supplementary Notes" for critical performance data (e.g., saturation thresholds, power capacity calculations, and frequency-dependent power degradation) makes the main text difficult to evaluate in isolation.
*   **Specific Request:** The authors must provide a clearer explanation of the "coaxial tapered structure" mentioned in the Results. How does this structure maintain impedance matching across the 0–3 GHz bandwidth?
*   **Figure 5b:** The peak power decrease with frequency is mentioned but not physically explained. Is this due to the RC time constant of the PCSD, the antenna bandwidth, or the laser pulse duration?

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
The statistical treatment of timing jitter (1×10⁴ data points) is excellent. However, the amplitude stability measurements (50 pulses) are insufficient to characterize the reliability of a high-power system. Given the potential for dielectric fatigue in SiC, the authors should provide a discussion on the variance of the breakdown voltage over a larger number of pulses (e.g., 10³–10⁴).

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed:**
*   **Frequency Tuning Mechanism:** The authors claim "continuous tunability." Please provide a plot or description of the waveform generation process that allows for frequency agility. Is the frequency determined by the laser pulse repetition rate, the circuit resonance, or an external modulation?
*   **Harmonic Content:** The authors identify series load division as the source of second-harmonic content. Given the high power levels, please provide a more rigorous analysis of the nonlinearities introduced by the AZO/SiC interface.
*   **Thermal Management:** At 100 Hz repetition rate and megawatt peak power, thermal accumulation in the SiC substrate is a significant concern. The manuscript lacks a discussion on the thermal design or the duty cycle limitations of the device.
*   **Comparison with State-of-the-Art:** While Supplementary Note 19 is mentioned, the main text should include a summary table comparing this OEMS to existing HEMT-based and VED-based systems, specifically highlighting the "power-bandwidth product," which is the standard metric for HPM sources.
*   **Clarification of "Linear Regime":** The authors state they operate in the linear regime but acknowledge potential nonlinearities at higher bias. Please define the specific "linear" range for the bias voltage and optical energy more explicitly in the main text.

**Conclusion:**
The manuscript is a strong candidate for publication in *Nature Communications* provided the authors address the mechanism of frequency tuning and provide a more comprehensive discussion on the long-term reliability and thermal constraints of the SiC PCSD.

these findings would be to provide a series of BR-AFM images at different tip-sample distances to corroborate the

The application of BR-AFM to resolve H-bond directionality and the use of tip-induced manipulation to switch proton-ordering states are highly innovative. The work successfully bridges the gap between static imaging and dynamic quantum behavior, providing a compelling case for the role of NQEs in stabilizing specific proton-ordered states in cyclic molecular assemblies. The findings are of significant interest to the fields of surface chemistry, quantum biology, and molecular electronics.

The experimental design is robust. The use of a CO-terminated qPlus sensor at 4.8 K is the gold standard for bond-resolved imaging. The manuscript is generally well-written and logically structured. The figures are of high quality and effectively communicate complex concepts such as the four-state interconversion cycle. The statistical treatment of the spectroscopic data (line-FS) is appropriate. The use of the Sader-Jarvis method for force conversion is standard. The problem of predicting second-life battery health without historical data is of high industrial and environmental significance. While the authors use SHAP and ablation studies to justify the architecture, the link between the "expert weights" and specific electrochemical degradation mechanisms (e.g., SEI growth, lithium plating, active material loss) remains largely correlative rather than explicitly physical.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The methodology is generally sound, particularly the use of diverse datasets (UL and TPSL) and the inclusion of ablation studies to isolate the contributions of the AMDP and FORNN modules. The "history-free" approach is a major strength. However, there are concerns regarding the input data:
*   **Data Sampling:** The authors claim compatibility with "random state of charge (SOC) regions." It is unclear how the model handles the high variance in signal-to-noise ratios when sampling at different SOCs. Does the model require a specific minimum voltage window?
*   **Expert Definition:** The authors state that experts are "learned from battery capacity-voltage and relaxation data." It is not clear if these experts are initialized with physical constraints or if they are purely data-driven clusters. If the latter, the claim of "interpretable" physical mechanism-awareness is overstated.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility:**
The results are impressive, with a reported MAPE of 0.95%. The inclusion of uncertainty analysis and performance across different SOH intervals (80%–50%) adds credibility. However, reproducibility is hindered by the lack of detail regarding the "pruned 5MB training data." The manuscript is well-structured, but the technical description of the FORNN is sparse. The authors mention "use-dependent" recurrent networks, but the mechanism by which future load conditions are encoded into the hidden state of the RNN is not sufficiently detailed in the main text. The transition from the AMDP latent space to the FORNN input needs a more formal mathematical definition.

The statistical analysis is generally robust, with standard deviations provided for most metrics. However, the comparison with Informer and PatchTST (Fig. 5d) shows a significant performance gap. *   **Physical Interpretability:** The authors must provide a more explicit mapping between the 5 experts and known electrochemical degradation phenomena. If the experts are purely latent, the term "interpretable" should be qualified as "feature-importance-based" rather than "mechanism-aware."

*   **Data Leakage:** Clarify if the "randomly sampled SOC regions" were strictly held out during the training of the AMDP module to prevent data leakage.

**Conclusion:**
The paper presents a compelling framework for second-life battery management. With a more rigorous justification of the "physical" nature of the experts and a clearer explanation of the input data requirements, this work will be a valuable contribution to the field.

This manuscript investigates the role of collective water dynamics in stabilizing ferroelectric-like behavior in graphene nanoribbon (Gr NR) field-effect transistors. The authors propose that water molecules bridging graphene layers form clusters via intermolecular Coulomb interactions, which are essential for temperature-stable remnant polarization.

### 1. Significance and Novelty
The study addresses a timely and important topic: the influence of ambient species on the electronic properties of low-dimensional materials. The observation that a minimum bi-layer thickness is required for temperature-stable ferroelectricity is a compelling finding that bridges the gap between molecular-level adsorption and device-level performance. The work is highly relevant to the fields of nanoelectronics and neuromorphic computing. However, the novelty is somewhat tempered by the authors' own admission that this work builds directly upon previous studies (Refs 10, 11). The primary contribution is the mechanistic elucidation of the "water neck" bridging effect, which is a significant conceptual advancement.

### 2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design
The experimental design is generally robust, utilizing a combination of nanofabrication (hot-wall epitaxy, RIE), electrical transport measurements, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The use of deterministic dry transfer methods is appropriate for high-quality heterostructures. 

However, there are concerns regarding the control of the "water environment." The authors state that devices were exposed to ambient air (22–26% humidity) and then measured under vacuum. The reproducibility of the water content at the edges is a critical variable. While the authors claim no significant difference between freshly etched devices and those stored for days, this is surprising given the dynamic nature of water adsorption/desorption. A more rigorous quantification of the water coverage (e.g., via spectroscopic methods or controlled humidity chambers) would strengthen the claims.

### 3. Quality and Reproducibility of the Results
The electrical characterization is extensive, covering a wide temperature range (4.2–425 K). The data presented in Fig. 4 regarding the remanence of the field is convincing. However, the MD simulations rely on a 4 ns timescale, which the authors acknowledge is insufficient for full relaxation at low temperatures. This discrepancy between the experimental timescales (minutes/hours) and simulation timescales (nanoseconds) makes the quantitative comparison of remnant field values speculative. The authors should clarify if the "collective dynamics" observed in MD are truly representative of the experimental steady-state or if they are observing transient phenomena.

### 4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting
The manuscript is well-written and the logic flows clearly from the experimental observation of hysteresis to the MD-based mechanistic explanation. The inclusion of Supplementary Information is helpful, particularly the details on the atomistic model. However, the description of the "water neck" formation could be more explicitly linked to the specific interlayer spacing of the bi-layer graphene. Does the interlayer distance change upon water adsorption? This would be a key structural signature of the proposed mechanism.

### 5. Statistical Rigor
The statistical treatment of the decay constants ($\tau$) is provided, which is commendable. However, the sample size ($N$) for the devices tested is not explicitly stated. Given the sensitivity of Gr NR devices to edge defects and contamination, it is vital to know how many devices were fabricated and if the reported hysteresis behavior is consistent across the entire batch or if it represents a "best-case" device.

### 6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed
*   **Humidity Control:** The reliance on ambient exposure is a potential source of uncontrolled variability. The authors should provide evidence that the water content is consistent or discuss how variations in humidity affect the hysteresis window.
*   **MD vs. Experiment Timescales:** The authors must provide a more rigorous justification for why the 4 ns MD simulations are predictive of the 600+ second experimental decay. A discussion on the activation energy barriers for water migration would be more convincing than the current qualitative comparison.
*   **Edge Chemistry:** The RIE process is described as "oxygenating the nanoribbon edges." The authors should provide characterization (e.g., XPS or Raman D-peak analysis) to confirm the chemical state of the edges, as the ferroelectric effect is highly sensitive to the specific functional groups present.
*   **Device Statistics:** Please include the number of devices tested and the variance in the hysteresis window width across different samples to demonstrate the robustness of the effect.
*   **Interlayer Spacing:** If the mechanism relies on "bridging," the authors should discuss whether the interlayer distance in the bi-layer Gr NR is expanded compared to pristine bi-layer graphene, as this would be a direct consequence of the proposed water-neck model.

The authors present an extension of optimal transport theory to open quantum systems with long-range hopping and interactions. They highlight the importance of decoherence-free subspaces for transport over long distances. The results are derived analytically and framed within a general open-system formalism, aiming to extend known bounds on transport velocities to dissipative settings.
While technically competent, the manuscript suffers from a lack of conceptual advances or striking results, making it unsuitable for a high-impact venue
Major issues
- In the case of driven-dissipative systems, the authors mention the existence of decoherence-free subspaces but fail to relate them to the relatively longer distances over which transport can occur. In particular, it remains unexplained why, despite the existence of decoherence-free subspaces comprised of extensive states, transport in general remains limited to finite distances.
- The authors emphasize that they treat quantum systems; however, the results equally apply to bosons and fermions, and the described transport appears to be entirely classical. Hence, the question arises to what extent these results are useful in any quantum applications. One could speculate that, due to the exponential loss of coherence in the presence of loss, the quantum mechanical description provided here offers no additional information compared to the equivalent classical statements derived from rate equations. Along these lines, it would be desirable, if possible applications were highlighted in the manuscript.
- The discussion section concludes with a long, unstructured list of platforms and techniques that realize individual parts of the model under consideration. Instead, the authors should focus on those candidates that can (potentially) realize all parts of the model, including the required preparation and measurements. In the current form, the reader is left to wonder whether such an experiment is at all feasible. The paper does not convincingly bridge theory and experiment.
Minor issues
- In the first sentence of the abstract, '... provides a more general [...] perspective on particle transport.', it is not mentioned what perspective the present work is to be compared with.
- The introduction should specify to which systems their treatment applies. In particular, it is incorrect to claim that all quantum many-body systems inevitably lose particles. It appears the authors exclusively refer to AMO systems, where this is typically the case, but disregard solid-state materials and platforms.
- In Eq. (1), the index notation in h_Z is not accurately defined.
The paper is well written and accessible to a broad audience of physicists; it provides a useful generalization of optimal transport theory to open systems. However, in light of the major issues raised above, the manuscript does not meet the necessary criteria to warrant publication in a high-impact journal. In particular, the relevance of these results in light of the inevitable loss of coherence is insufficiently justified. In fact, it could be argued that similar results are obtained from the related classical rate equations. This lack of broader impact weakens its suitability for a multidisciplinary journal like Nature Communications. Furthermore, the manuscript offers limited conceptual progress, deriving only intuitively anticipated results.

=== reviewer_1 ===
Dear Editor,
The authors present a challenging absorption spectroscopy investigation of the optical band-gap of diamond anvils as a function of pressure, up to 520 GPa and in the IR-UV spectral range. It is shown a pronounced loss of transparency upon increasing pressure with an inferred metallization (band-gap closure) at about 560 GPa. Very importantly, this behaviour is shown to be dominated by the fact that a micron-size slab of the anvil at the sample interface is tetragonally distorted, and it is so for different anvil geometries: beveled and toroidal. The authors also refine the Raman edge pressure scale and show that it too is universal, i.e. independent of the anvil geometry. The study is of crucial importance for the spectroscopic investigation of metallization of materials in the multi-Mbar regime and, particularly, for hydrogen. To my opinion the study is compelling, timing, and robust and I recommend its publication on Nature Communications after some minor issues are resolved.
1. On page 4 and figure 2, the authors discuss Raman phonon measurements of diamond under hydrostatic compression. The figure shows pressure shift of the diamond phonon frequency. Could the authors also provide some spectra for these measurements and specify the compression medium?
2. At page 7: “In our case,…the sample pressure at 523 ± 13 GPa (Fig. 2),…”. I do not see data at this pressure in figure 2.
3. In figure 1, there is a data gap between approximately 160 GPa and 280 GPa. What is the reason? Please comment on the article.
4. In figure 1, panel B, I see absorbance peaks at wavelengths below 250 nm, for the lowest pressures. Similar peaks at high photon energies also appear in Extended Data, figures 1 and 2. I presume these peaks are artifacts related to absorption saturation rather than true maxima. Isn’t that the case?
5. In the caption of figure 2, could the authors specify also “ 0” in the P-   relationship for the diamond Raman edge?
6. There are some inconsistencies between the absorbance A reported in figure 1 and square root of A seen in figure 3. For instance, the maximum value of sqrtA at 146 GPa is equal to about 1.9 (fig. 3, panel A), which leads to a maximum in A of 3.6, whereas all absorbance values are cut well below 3.0 in figure 1, panel B.
7. In figure 3, it would be good to specify which data are measured using beveled or toroidal diamonds, either in the caption or through labels.
8. In figure 4, panel A, I presume “m” for m-H and so on means metallic. Please, specify.
9. In the methods, I think it would be helpful to show a schematic cross-sectional figure of toroidal diamonds, for the benefit of the reader.
10. Equation 1 for the normal stress. I think a minus sign should be applied to the right-hand side to be consistent with Extended Data figure 4, panel A.
11. In the caption of Extended Data Fig. 6: “Coupled Raman spectroscopy…”, the second “(B)” should be a “(C)”.

=== reviewer_2 ===
This paper reports on the diamond band gap closure under non-hydrostatic stresses up to pressures of 520 GPa that has implications for researchers performing spectroscopic measurements at high pressures including claims of metallic hydrogen that have appeared periodically in the literature. The paper reports on absorption studies on a variety of diamond geometrical configurations under high pressures including beveled anvils as well as recently developed toroidal diamonds. The studies reported are exhaustive and have some technical relevance. However, scientific impact of this study is debatable as it has been known since the 1990s that diamonds do change colors under non-hydrostatic stresses and appear dark red in reflection around 300-400 GPa through a metallic gasket indicating bandgap approaching infrared frequencies (Ref.19-20).
There are several additional comments regarding this submission that need attention.
(1) Fig. 1 A needs a scale to indicate dimensions of the sample assembly, and it is not clear what the dark region near the middle of the cell in the neon medium. Is that a pressure marker, toroidal culet outline, or some other sample that needs to be clarified. Also, the orange/dark region at 307 GPa appears to at the edge of the sample hole. It should be pointed out that the biaxial state of stress with a fixed delta = 0.6 assumed throughout this paper is true only near the center of diamond anvil and that could complicate the interpretation of the absorption spectra presented in this work.
(2) It appears that “diamond edge pressure calibration” in Figure 2 A has been carried out to 420 GPa. This is likely due to the absorption by diamond of the 600 nm laser used for Raman excitation. Any claims of pressures higher than 420 should be substantiated with x-ray diffraction included of the appropriate pressure standards.
(3) The experimental data in Figure 4 suggests band gap closure to near 600 GPa. In the introduction, it is stated that diamond anvils have reached pressures of 1000 GPa (Ref.7). These two statements are in contradiction as it is highly unlikely that metallic diamond would be able to support largely shear stresses as is known for its covalently bonded state. Therefore, claims of 1000 GPa are questionable and have not been reproduced by other researchers in the field. The manuscript describes the results of broadband absorption measurements over a wide range of electromagnetic radiation (from ultraviolet to infrared wavelengths) in diamond anvils at pressures exceeding 500 GPa, which reveal a pronounced loss of transparency with pressure. At pressures up to ~200 GPa, beveled anvils were employed, and above that — toroidal ones. The authors claim that they have documented the closing of the band gap in diamond under uniaxial stress, quantified the effect, and expect metallization of the anvils above ~560 GPa. The experiments appear carefully performed, the reproducibility of the results is well demonstrated, and the text is clearly written.
However, there are several major problems with accepting the authors’ results and conclusions. The most important points are outlined below.
1. Effect of compressed medium (Ne):
In all experiments, neon was used as the pressure-transmitting medium. While both theoretical and experimental works (including those considered here) suggest that diamond under stress changes its structural, vibrational, and electronic properties, an appropriate discussion of similar effects in neon is missing. One cannot a priori be sure that the enormous uniaxial stresses in the TPa pressure range do not affect the absorption of Ne. If comparable experiments using He or Ar, for example, resulted in the same absorption effects as those observed with Ne, the influence of the compressed medium could be excluded.
2. Anvil deformation and optical effects:
Even at moderate pressures, diamond anvil tips are known to deform (“cupping”), forming a concave lens. Above ~300 GPa, such shape changes become severe: light may refract, reflect, and scatter within the tip and surrounding diamond. These effects are not considered by the authors at all, and therefore it is unclear whether the observed loss of transparency is caused by changes in the electronic structure of the stressed anvil or by its mechanical deformation. In fact, there is a clear indication that the authors’ interpretation is not correct, or at least not complete. In Figure 1a changes in anvil transparency are visible not only at the point of maximum pressure (in the middle), but also over a much larger area at moderate pressures. It is well known that in toroidal anvils, pressure typically drops by a factor of 2–3 away from the central region, and at pressures of 2–2.5 Mbar rhenium behaves as a normal metal, reflecting light strongly. Where Re had to be observed, we do not see it. Thus, what is shown in Fig. 1a is not related to changes in electronic properties of diamond.
3. Incorrect assumption of tetragonal distortion:
The assumption that anvil distortion is simply tetragonal is not correct even at moderate pressures, and certainly invalid at multi-megabar pressures. Even if one assumes purely elastic deformation and stress along the [100] direction, additional stresses from the gasket acting on the bevel and pavilion reduce the symmetry below tetragonal. In the toroidal case, the situation is even more complex. At sufficiently high pressures —above several hundred GPa certainly — the anvil undergoes plastic deformation, so purely elastic considerations no longer apply. If certain observations of anvil behavior (for example, Fig. 2c) can be described under the assumption of tetragonal stress, this means either (i) the stress/pressure is not sufficiently high (in Fig. 2c it is ~76 GPa, that is incomparable with ~500 GPa of interest here), (ii) the methodology is not sensitive to the symmetry and type of distortion, or (iii) the agreement between observation and model is coincidental.
4. Figure 1a and presentation issues:
As the manuscript is, in my opinion, not ready for publication and must be substantially revised before further consideration, a detailed analysis of technical deficiencies would be premature. However, I would like to comment on Figure 1a, which is crucial for the entire presentation. It is not clear what is shown in this figure. What are the darker areas within the transparent toroidal part? Why is one circular and another irregular in shape? Where is the scale for these photos? How are the photographs related to the spectra shown in the same figure?
To summarize:
The amount of work performed by the authors and the complexity of the experiments are impressive. The implications for attempts to “see” hydrogen metallization using beveled, toroidal, and probably double-stage anvils are obvious — and the prospects, unfortunately, appear grim. This outcome is important for the high-pressure and, to some extent, solid-state physics communities, and should be published in a specialized physics journal. Metallization of diamond due to deformation requires real experimental investigation, probably accompanied by careful theoretical analysis.

abruptness at the heterojunction or heterointerface (i.e., how many monolayers the transition from one material to another

indeed corresponds to a single atomic layer, the question arises as to how piezoelectric charge can be uniformly distributed

General Assessment
The authors present a comprehensive investigation into how strain-induced polarization in piezoelectric semiconductors can
be exploited as an interface engineering mechanism to modulate the interface width and the junction capacitance under AC
operation in Schottky-diodes structures. The study combines finite element simulations and experimental measurements on
single and dual GaN-based Schottky diodes to explore how controlled compressive strain affects the built-in potential,
interface width, and capacitance, reporting strain sensitivities exceeding those of commercial capacitive pressure sensors.
Furthermore, the authors illustrate the potential of these mechanisms in practical applications by demonstrating
implementations in communication circuits such as frequency modulators and filtering systems.
The manuscript provides a substantial amount of material supporting the main claims, including
physical descriptions, finite element simulations, and a broad set of experimental results. The
mechanisms are interpreted with an appropriate level of detail, and the inclusion of practical
applications and comparative analyses strengthens the overall study. Nevertheless, several aspects of
the work would benefit from clarification and refinement to further improve its rigor and readability
before it can be considered for publication.
General Revisions
It should be noted that capacitance variation in piezoelectric and piezotronic devices under mechanical stress has been
reported previously; for instance, in bulk ceramics (Cho et al., JJAP, 1995 10.1143/JJAP.34.1591) and in ZnO-based
Schottky structures (Zhang et al., Sensors 2021, 21(6), 2253; https://doi.org/10.3390/s21062253).In this respect, the present
manuscript goes beyond those studies and offers a conceptual and practical advance.
Nevertheless, in light of the existing literature, the authors are encouraged to cite and briefly discuss these and others prior

The oxidation of gallium to its oxyhydroxide is described, with release of hydrogen. Ultrasonication and 70 C were required before a photothermal reaction using a halogen lamp. The efficiency is low and requires at least an hour, depending on wavelength. Generating hydrogen in sunlight can detonate in air. The reaction relies on 5N gallium and the oxyhydroxide product is not a commodity compound. It must all be reduced back to gallium metal, more than negating the energy benefit of the hydrogen release. It would be very difficult and expensive to cost effectively scale up to even 1 kg of H2. I do not recommend publication in Nature Communications. Some additional comments ordered by line number/appearance are included below.
Line 63: The authors say that alloys containing aluminum produce aluminum oxide compound that require high energy input to reduce to produce primary aluminum.
Yet, this is an important technology to the world’s economy and is the source of gallium needed for their reaction, produced as a minor byproduct.
Line 64: According to the cited reference 14, sonication produces nanorods of gallium that are more efficient in producing GaO(OH) than are photothermal generated Ga nanospheres. For their current work, the authors produce polydisperse Ga nanospheres by sonication and the nanospheres are inefficient, producing much heat. The authors report a 12.9% maximum efficiency for their hydrogen production but don’t show how this was calculated and whether they included the energy input needed before and during the reaction.
Line 74: Authors claim that Ga is environmentally friendly as it is primarily recovered as a byproduct of existing mining operation.
They cite Ref. 44, which describes various methods used in recovering Ga from the mining waste called “Bayer liquor”, also known as “red mud”, one of the world’s most polluting industrial wastes.
Line 92: Authors report that the reaction of Ga with water remains highly efficient even in saline environment, such as seawater.
Only aqueous NaCl was tested. Seawater should be tested since it contains other metallic impurities such as iron and vanadium that could make recovery of pure Ga difficult (see Ref. 44).
How much of the 0.2 g of 99.999% Ga is recovered in their process? Given the 5N expense, the recovery would have to be near 100% to back up their “circular” claim.
What’s the yield of hydrogen when no light is used for the entire reaction rather than cycling on/off? In Figure 3, the % hydrogen released would be much more informative than mL of hydrogen, which depends on the masses used. Also in Figure 3, specify the mW/m^2. The amount of light is said to be “6 suns of concentrated sunlight”. Was the light concentrated/focused? The flux needs to be compared to the standard AM 1.5G. It would be helpful to include the oxygen EDX map in Figure 4c.
How continuous is their hydrogen generation? One gets the impression it’s a labor intensive, expensive and inefficient batch process. The supplementary video is clearly sped up and the factor is not given. How much gallium would be needed for continuous supply to a 100W fuel cell, e.g. for an hour?
Line 227: They claim that they could reduce GaO(OH) electrochemically using a carbon paper (CP) cathode at a very small scale but do not comment about greenhouse gases (GHGs) produced during this electrolysis process. They do not give the percentage of recovered Ga from the very acidic Ga electrolyte containing aqueous sulfuric acid. It therefore cannot be labeled as a green chemistry process.

**Reviewer Report**

**Reviewer Recommendation:** Major Revision

**Summary of the work:**
The authors present a circular hydrogen production pathway utilizing the photothermal oxidation of liquid gallium (Ga) droplets in water, followed by the electrochemical reduction of the resulting gallium oxyhydroxide (GaOOH) back to metallic Ga. The study highlights the role of light in both thermal activation and potential photo-electrochemical enhancement of the oxidation process. The authors demonstrate hydrogen production from both freshwater and seawater and provide a proof-of-concept for the regeneration of the metal.

**1. Significance and Novelty:**
The proposed method is conceptually interesting, particularly the use of liquid metal droplets to facilitate a circular hydrogen production cycle. The ability to utilize seawater is a notable practical advantage. However, the novelty is somewhat tempered by the existing literature on liquid metal-water reactions (e.g., Al-Ga systems). The primary contribution lies in the "circular" aspect via electrochemical regeneration. The significance of this work would be greatly enhanced by a more rigorous comparison of the energy efficiency of this cycle versus conventional water electrolysis, which is currently lacking in the manuscript.

**2. Soundness of Methodology and Experimental Design:**
The experimental design is generally logical, but there are significant concerns regarding the control experiments:
*   **Photothermal vs. Photochemical:** The authors claim a "photochemical" contribution to the reaction. However, the distinction between pure photothermal heating and photo-induced charge carrier generation is not clearly decoupled. The temperature measurements provided (e.g., 79.5 °C) are high enough that the reaction kinetics are likely dominated by thermal effects. The authors must provide a control experiment where the system is heated to the same temperature in the dark to definitively isolate the "photochemical" contribution.
*   **Seawater Stability:** The manuscript mentions seawater experiments but does not adequately address the potential for chloride-induced corrosion of the Ga droplets or the formation of secondary precipitates (e.g., Mg/Ca salts) that could passivate the surface and inhibit long-term hydrogen production.

**3. Quality and Reproducibility of the Results:**
*   The hydrogen yield measurements (98.4% and 99.4%) are impressive, but the reproducibility across different batches of Ga droplets needs more robust statistical treatment.
*   The "95% recovery yield" is stated as a conservative estimate, but the mass balance is not fully closed. The authors should provide a detailed mass balance accounting for all Ga species (metallic, ionic, and oxyhydroxide) throughout the cycle to confirm the "circular" claim.

**4. Clarity and Completeness of Reporting:**
*   The manuscript is generally well-written, but the "Techno-economic analysis" mentioned in the text is relegated to the Supplementary Information. Given that Ga is a high-cost material, the economic viability is a central claim of the paper and should be summarized in the main text, including a comparison of the cost of Ga loss/regeneration versus the value of the H2 produced.
*   The description of the electrochemical reduction process (Section: "Electrochemical reduction of gallium oxyhydroxide") is truncated in the provided text. The full manuscript must ensure that the specific energy consumption (kWh/kg H2) for the regeneration step is clearly reported.

**5. Statistical Rigor:**
*   The authors mention n=3 replicates for gas collection, which is acceptable. However, the error bars are omitted for "visual clarity." In a scientific publication, error bars or shaded regions representing standard deviation are mandatory for all quantitative plots (e.g., Fig 2d, 2e, 4b).

**6. Specific Weaknesses to be Addressed:**
*   **Decoupling Thermal and Light Effects:** Perform a dark control experiment at the exact temperature reached under illumination to quantify the true photochemical enhancement.
*   **Mass Balance:** Provide a comprehensive mass balance table for the Ga cycle. The current "95% recovery" is insufficient to prove the long-term viability of a circular process.
*   **Surface Characterization:** The authors claim the Ga surface is "activated" by light. Please provide XPS or Auger electron spectroscopy data comparing the surface oxide thickness/composition *in situ* under light vs. dark conditions to support the mechanism of oxide layer disruption.
*   **Electrochemical Efficiency:** The energy cost of the electrochemical reduction of GaOOH is the "Achilles' heel" of this process. The authors must explicitly state the Faradaic efficiency and the energy input required for the regeneration step and compare this to the energy content of the H2 produced.
*   **Seawater Impurities:** Provide ICP-OES analysis of the H2 gas and the electrolyte after seawater experiments to ensure no volatile impurities or toxic by-products are generated.

The manuscript shows promise, but the claims regarding the "photochemical" mechanism and the economic/energetic viability of the circular process require more rigorous experimental validation and quantitative analysis before it can be considered for publication in *Nature Communications*.

=== reviewer_1 ===
The ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway is typically involved in the degradation of misfolded or misfolding-prone proteins in the ER through the cytosolic proteasome system. HRD1, an ER-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase, plays a central role in ERAD by directly binding and ubiquitinating substrates for retrotranslocation and proteasomal degradation. In this study, Zhao et al. have identified TLR3 as a new substrate of HRD1. Specifically, HRD1 binds to and facilitates the ubiquitination of TLR3 at K813 on the ER, thereby promoting the trafficking of TLR3 via the Golgi to the endolysosome for cleavage and activation through the ESCRT machinery, demonstrating a role of HRD1 in TLR3 sorting and trafficking rather than degradation in conventional ERAD. Consistently, the authors observed that TLR3 downstream signaling e.g. the expression of inflammatory genes and the production of inflammatory cytokines was compromised upon TLR3 stimulation when HRD is deficient or inhibited. In addition, the TLR3K813R knockin mice phenocopy the Hrd1-/- mice regarding TLR3 activation. This study reveals a novel role of HRD1 in the trafficking and maturation of the innate immune sensor TLR3 and a new mechanism for TLR3 activation, which advances our understanding of innate immune regulation. Overall, the manuscript is well-written and the data presented are of high quality.
Major concerns:
1. The authors show that the K813R mutation in TLR3 significantly impairs its cleavage and signaling using TLR3-stably expressed HEK293T cells and BMDMs from TLR3 K813R knock-in mice. To further confirm the physiological relevance of K813 ubiquitination, it is recommended to examine phenotypic differences between TLR3 WT and K813R KI mice after poly(I:C) challenges, such as circulating cytokines levels and tissue inflammation.
2. The study shows that TLR3 binds to HRD1 but not to SEL1L. However, knockdown of SEL1L results in increased inflammatory gene expression without affecting HRD1 protein levels, which is unexpected. It would be beneficial to assess whether SEL1L influences TLR3 protein stability in SEL1L-deficient macrophages to better understand this effect.
3. The discussion briefly mentions the potential implications of HRD1-mediated regulation of TLR3 and STING in cancer therapy. Since this study does not explore HRD1 or TLR3 functions in the context of cancer, it would be more appropriate to omit or reframe this section to maintain focus on the current study's findings.
Minor comments:
1. In Fig 6d, the Y-axis label is missing, making it difficult to interpret the correlation method and the data presented.
2. Because TLR7/9 require similar sorting and cleavage for activation as TLR3, it would be better if the authors test (or at least discuss) whether HRD1 regulates the activation of TLR7/9.
3. The manuscript contains several grammatical errors that need to be corrected to improve clarity.

=== reviewer_2 ===
The manuscript by Zhao L et al., titled ‘The HRD1 quality control pathway is essential for TLR3-mediated innate immunity by regulating its trafficking,’ explores the regulatory mechanisms of TLR3 trafficking. Using co-immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry (CoIP-MS), the authors unexpectedly identified the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase HMG-CoA reductase degradation protein 1 (HRD1), a key factor in ER-associated degradation (ERAD), as an interactor with TLR3, influencing its signaling. Mechanistically, the authors propose that HRD1 mediates TLR3 ubiquitination at lysine 813, and facilitates its trafficking from the Golgi to endolysosomes via the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) machinery, ultimately regulating TLR3-mediated immune responses. Importantly, they assert that HRD1’s role in TLR3 trafficking is independent of its conventional ERAD function. Although the manuscript introduces a novel function for HRD1 in TLR3 ubiquitination and trafficking, the presented data are insufficient to fully substantiate the authors’ claims, as detailed below:
Major comments:
1. In this manuscript, the majority of the data, except for Fig. 7h-i, were generated using HEK293T or RAW264.7 cell lines. To validate their conclusions, the authors should validate their findings in more physiologically relevant systems, such as primary macrophages or mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). This includes confirming TLR3 signaling, cytokine expression, as well as TLR3 ubiquitination and cleavage in these primary cell types.
2. In this study, the authors focused exclusively on the influence of HRD1 on TLR3. To provide a broader understanding of HRD1’s role in the innate immune response, the authors should also assess whether HRD1 is involved in regulating other TLRs, particularly endosomal TLRs such as TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9, which share similarities in trafficking and signaling pathways with TLR3.
3. HRD1 is primarily responsible for the recognition and removal of misfolded and aberrant proteins in the ER through ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. How does HRD1 mediate both K48- and K63-linked ubiquitination on TLR3 to promote its trafficking to endolysosomes rather than catalyzing K27-linked ubiquitination, which typically leads to ERAD-dependent degradation? The authors should clarify the mechanism by which HRD1 distinguishes between its protein substrates, directing them either toward endolysosomal trafficking or ERAD-mediated degradation.
4. It is well known that TLR3 undergoes proteolytic processing in acidic endosomes (PMID: 22865861). If HRD1-mediated TLR3 ubiquitination is critical for its trafficking from the Golgi to endolysosomes, one would expect a significant reduction in the cleaved, mature form of TLR3 in HRD1-deficient cells. However, in Figures 6k and 6m, the cleaved TLR3 form shows only a marginal decrease in HRD1-deficient cells. Additionally, if TLR3 cleavage is impaired in HRD1-deficient cells, one would expect an accumulation of the full-length TLR3. Contrary to this, both the full-length and cleaved forms of TLR3 are decreased in HRD1 knockout cells, suggesting that HRD1's primary role might not be in trafficking but rather in TLR3 degradation after activation.
5. The authors state that HRD1 directly ubiquitinates TLR3; however, they do not provide any supporting evidence for this claim. To strengthen their argument, the authors should perform in vitro ubiquitination assays.
6. Poly(I:C) is a synthetic ligand for TLR3, and while the authors claim that HRD1 is involved in TLR3-mediated antiviral function, Figure 2f only indirectly assesses type I interferon levels by monitoring the anti-HSV-1 effect. To provide more direct evidence, the authors should evaluate HRD1’s role in TLR3 signaling, immune responses, and anti-viral immunity after actual viral challenge, such as with encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV), to further substantiate HRD1’s involvement in antiviral defense both in vitro and in vivo.
7. The authors claim that TLR3 signaling induces HRD1 expression via ERK1/2-EST1 activity. However, the data presented only demonstrate that ERK1/2 stimulates HRD1 and EST1 expression, without directly showing the essential role of EST1 in TLR3-triggered HRD1 expression. The authors need to specifically investigate and demonstrate the involvement of EST1 in the TLR3-mediated induction of HRD1 to support their claim.
8. In Fig. 4a-c, the authors assessed whether HRD1 regulates TLR3 protein levels at steady state. However, since poly(I:C) induces the interaction between HRD1 and TLR3, the authors should also evaluate TLR3 protein levels in wild-type and HRD1-deficient cells at different time points following poly(I:C) stimulation. This time-course analysis would provide important insights into whether HRD1 regulates TLR3 protein folding and stability during inflammation.
9. In Fig. 4a-f, the authors conclude that the compromised TLR3 signaling in Hrd1-deficient cells is not due to the inhibition of ERAD activity or the induction of ER stress. However, the authors do not provide direct comparisons of TLR3 signaling between wild-type and Hrd1-deficient cells under conditions of ERAD inhibition or ER stress induction. Without this comparison, it is unclear how the authors arrived at this conclusion. The authors should perform these experiments to substantiate their claim.
10. In Fig. 4g, the authors should include a treatment group with only poly(I:C) to allow for a direct comparison of the effects of IRE1alpha on HRD1-mediated TLR3 signaling.
11. A previous study reported that only cleaved endosomal TLRs are located in endosomes/phagosomes after activation (PMID: 18820679). In Fig. 6n and 7e, the authors should show the protein levels of both full-length and cleaved TLR3 in all cellular fractions, including the endosomal fraction, to fully support their conclusion about the trafficking and localization of TLR3.
12. In Fig. S6d, the TLR3 K746R mutant, rather than the K813R mutant, showed a more pronounced reduction in ubiquitination by HRD1. The authors should perform a detailed quantification analysis of the ubiquitination levels for all mutants. Additionally, the authors should validate whether HRD1 also ubiquitinates TLR3 at K746 and consider generating a double mutant (TLR3 K746R/K813R) if necessary to fully assess HRD1's role in TLR3 ubiquitination.
13. Since previous studies have demonstrated that TRIM3 ubiquitinates TLR3 at the same lysine residue (K813) to regulate its trafficking to endolysosomes and subsequent immune responses (PMID: 32878999), the data presented in Fig. 7 are not novel and do not adequately support the claim that HRD1 modulates TLR3 trafficking and inflammatory response through ubiquitination at the K813 residue. The authors should investigate whether the depletion of HRD1 in TLR3K813R knock-in cells results in any further reduction of TLR3-mediated signaling and cytokine production.
Minor comments:
1. The authors utilized LS-102 to inhibit HRD1 ligase activity in this manuscript. However, does LS-102 specifically target HRD1? It may be beneficial for the authors to generate an enzymatically inactive form of HRD1 (C291A) as previously described (PMID: 19864457) and evaluate its impact on TLR3 trafficking and signaling.
2. In Fig. S2e, poly(I:C)-induced NF-κB promoter activity was only marginally reduced in HRD1-deficient cells compared to WT cells, which contrasts with the authors' claim of significant reduction. Additionally, since TLR3-driven type I IFN production plays a critical role in antiviral immune responses, the authors should also perform an interferon promoter-driven luciferase reporter assay in HRD1-deficient cells to more comprehensively assess the impact of HRD1 on TLR3 signaling.

This is an interesting and comprehensive study showing through several sound approaches that ubiquitination of TLR3 by HRD1 regulates TLR3 trafficking and function and that this is unexpectedly not through the ERAD pathway. The following concerns should be addressed.

In the manuscript entitled "The HRD1 Quality Control Pathway is Essential for TLR3-Mediated Innate Immunity by Regulating Its Trafficking," the authors propose a hypothesis to explain the mechanisms enabling the intracellular transport and cleavage of TLR3 to regulate the innate immune response. Central to this hypothesis is HRD1, a protein residing in the endoplasmic reticulum and a member of the ERAD machinery that ubiquitinates and targets proteins for proteasomal degradation. The authors claim that in the case of TLR3, HRD1 labels TLR3 for activation rather than degradation, despite functioning as an E3 ubiquitin ligase in the context of ERAD. While the hypothesis is intriguing, the authors fail to demonstrate that the ubiquitin activation of TLR3 is attributable to HRD1:
1. The authors assert that the impairment "is caused by a marked reduction in TLR3 trafficking from the Golgi to endolysosomes and its subsequent proteolytic cleavage." However, the experiments showing a) intracellular localization by immunofluorescence, b) isolation of the ER, Golgi, and endosomes, and c) glycosylation of TLR3 are unconvincing. First, the co-localization studies do not demonstrate an increase in endosomal trafficking; the Mander’s coefficient shows only weak significance. The isolation of organelles appears to lack resolution, and TLR3 is not found diminished in endosomes. The EndoH and PNGase experiments did not reveal marked differences in TLR3 in the absence of HRD1. None of these experiments were performed with at least three biological replicates, and the blots were not quantified or shown with error bars.

The next claim, "Importantly, HRD1's role in TLR3 trafficking is decoupled from its canonical ERAD activity and the ER stress sensor inositol-requiring enzyme 1 alpha (IRE1α)," is not demonstrated. **1. Decoupling HRD1-mediated ubiquitination from ERAD:**

The authors suggest HRD1 acts in the ER to "prime" TLR3 for ESCRT recognition. However, the ESCRT machinery is primarily associated with endosomal membranes. This is a high-quality study that significantly advances our understanding of TLR3 regulation. In the work of Li et al, the authors proposed an image reconstruction method using the point cloud-based representation for
3D photoacoustic imaging. This idea was translated from the Gaussian splatting technique in the field of computer vision

the paper is interesting, clearly presented and is novel in methodology and has shown some

important challenges in large-scale 3D PA reconstruction. However, I think this works need further improvements to warrant
publishing in Nature Communications. Particularly, the authors should compare their proposed method with current state-of-
the-art algorithms, the model-based iterative reconstruction methods, instead of only with the UBP algorithms. After all,
model-based iterative reconstruction methods have been studied and developed for 3D PA imaging in the last ten years,
and some of them were proposed to address the same problem just like this work, while the addressed problem size may be
a bit smaller. I recommend the following works [1-3] for the authors' reference.

1, Details on how the PA signals of the hand vessel were simulated must be provided. I guess the PA signals were obtained
with the proposed differentiable rapid radiator model. While the basis of this model (Eq. 1) has been widely used for UBP-
based PA image reconstruction, it does not simulate real wave propagation, as well as the spatial and electrical response
function of the receiver. The authors should at least acknowledge this limitation. Using k-wave to simulate the signals is a
better choice, the authors are encouraged to demonstrate the capability of the rapid radiator model in modeling real PA
signals. The title 'real PA signal' of Supplementary Fig. 1a is misleading. It gives readers the impression that the PA signal is

This manuscript reports effects of C1q on human neural stem cells (hNSCs) mediated by the receptor BAI1. The authors describe effects of C1q on hNSC proliferation and other aspects of the cells’ physiology. In parallel studies, the authors provide insight into the signaling pathways that are engaged when C1q binds BAI1, specifically i) regulation of mdm2 to control p53 and ii) endocytosis of C1q to modulate p32. These findings are novel, although the connections between the signaling pathways elucidated and the effects of C1q on hNSC proliferation are more hypothetical than directly shown. Specific comments are as follows:
1. The central physiological effect reported by the authors is a striking effect of C1q on hNSC proliferation (Fig. 1a). The authors also provide evidence that this effect is mediated by C1q engagement of BAI1 (Fig. 6). Separately, the authors provide evidence that C1q can regulate p53 levels in hNSCs (Fig. 3) and additionally regulate p32 and aerobic glycolysis after gaining entry into hNSCs via BAI1 (Fig. 4-5). However, it is not clear from the data presented whether these mechanisms actually account for the striking effect of C1q on hNSC proliferation shown in Figure 1. To put it another way: Figs. 1 & 6 show that C1q regulates hNSC proliferation in a BAI1-dependent manner, and the data from Fig. 3-5 provide insight into various signaling pathways that are activated when C1q engages BAI1 in hNSCs. What’s not shown, though, is whether these signaling pathways are directly responsible for the effect of C1q on hNSC proliferation. Given that BAI1 is known to couple to other signaling pathways (Rac, Rho, etc) that are capable of affecting proliferation, the authors need to support their proposed model by more definitively demonstrating that the mechanisms they describe (regulation of p53 and p32) are in fact responsible for directly mediating the ability of C1q to regulate hNSC proliferation.
2. In creating the BAI1 KO cell line, the authors show the proper DNA fragment sizes (Extended Data, Figure 2). However, in the Western blot data shown in Fig. 3b, there are still BAI1-positive bands in the BAI1 KO lanes, which means that BAI1 may not actually be deleted at the protein level. The authors should address this point. If the authors believe these bands in the KO lanes to be non-specific, they should state what evidence leads them to this conclusion. This is an important issue to resolve, given that many of the authors’ conclusions depend on BAI1 being fully deleted from the KO cell line.
3. For the experiments with the BAI1 neutralizing antibody (nAb) shown in Fig. 6, it is unclear which BAI1 antibody was used by the authors for these experiments. Also, how was this antibody characterized? How do the authors know that it is truly a neutralizing antibody? Obviously, it is possible for antibodies to bind to a receptor but not neutralize ligand binding, and thus it is important for the authors to provide more information about the characterization of this antibody. The authors provide a citation for a previous characterization of the C1q nAb that was used in these studies, but no comparable citation is provided for the BAI1 nAb.

=== reviewer_2 ===
Review of the manuscript entitled “C1q drives neural stem cell quiescence by regulating cell cycle and metabolism through BAI1”.
In this manuscript, the authors describe a role for the complement-derived pattern recognition molecule C1q in neural stem cell (NSC) quiescence. The team had previously identified several new receptors for C1q, including brain angiogenesis inhibitor (BAI1). Here, they follow up this functional interaction and demonstrate C1q binding to BAI1 on NSCs induces, at minimum, two events: firstly, BAI1-mediated sequestering of MDM2 which, in turn, increases p53 phosphorylation and blocks cell cycle progression an secondly, BAI1-depenent internalization of C1q which enables interaction of C1q with the mitochondrial C1q receptor p32. The latter than induces a shift from OXPHOS to aerobic glycolysis which also supports quiescence. As a general model, the authors argue that age- or inflammation/trauma induced increases in local C1q production may sustain NSC quiescence and inhibit activation when desired (during tissue repair, etc.).
The team makes its case using a set of elegant and detailed in vitro experiments and argues that this pathway is important in vivo by showing that the engraftment of BAI-KO human NSC into the brains of mice exposed to an acute CNS injury model (which is associated with local increases in C1q) rescues the decline in hNSC proliferation when compared to WT hNSC.
Overall, the study is interesting and timely and its strength lays in the fact that it further explored a new C1q-receptor interaction. Given the emerging central role for C1q across human disease and specifically in CNS pathology settings, C1q is becoming a valuable therapeutic target. The large majority in the field, however, focusses on the ‘canonical’ C1q-repetior interactions (gC1qR and cC1qR). C1q biology is highly complex, and it is therefore paramount to better understand its biology for successful future targeted interventions. This leads to the second strength of the work: the authors argue that the effects of C1q in each tissue will depend on the C1q receptor ‘availability’ which then also dictates the specific outcome of C1q activity. This aligns well with the emerging realization that local complement impact is highly cell and context specific.
There are several areas where the work can (and needs to be improved):
1. A major issue is that the authors have not satisfactorily dissected the effects on proliferation, self-renewal, cell death and survival. Particularly Extended data Figure 3B and C is difficult to reconcile as the control phenotype seems to be driven by a single cell that divides extensively.
